They had a good salad bar last week. Anyway, you were saying about dinner— shouldn’t we consider being creative instead of pizza again?      Not today, I suppose. I want to try a sauce I bought from the new place. It said  fourteen-year-old wine  was used— I mean it, not joking.      Should that be baked into the sauce or will it cause a funny reaction when we open a glass of it alongside? I think I once used a blender instead of a tablespoon and ruined a perfectly good stew.      Then we can always add some  equine welfare  thoughts to the dish if the taste isn't right— maybe something about not treading on the metaphorical hooves.      Something like that. Just don’t expect me to follow the recipe notes entirely. I’ll likely manage the main bits and leave some of the rest to chance.      You always do. As long as it doesn’t end up like that time we made  burgers over a bed of ice , I suppose it can’t hurt.

Right, I’m just trying to decide what to wear for the bar later. I’ve got that new pouty pink dress, but I’m not sure if it’s too much for a midweek night out. Thoughts?      Look, love, if you're wearing the pink one, it’s bound to be  too much  for you, but I reckon it’ll be perfect for everyone else. You’ve only got to think about the side of yourself you want to see reflected back. Plus, who needs to match a Wednesday when you’ve got heels on?      Honestly, I don’t even know how you even  walk  in heels, Lucy. I tried them once, and I managed to trip over a light switch. Still have a knot the size of a bottle cap on my shins.      I think heels are overrated. It’s 2024! Why do we feel we have to step into some sort of Game of Thrones duel over who can suffer the most in shoes, right? I’m sticking with boots. Comfort is key, imo.      Yeah, listen to Karen. I’m with her. I’ve still got grief from last week when I tried to wear those Jimmy Choos for work do and then walked into a relative. My ankle still won’t bend the same, and now I dream about walking up stairs into puddles of apple juice.      Oh, I already foresee Liam at the bar, dressed in his usual ‘big boy in a suit’ vibe trying to spot a girl in a flashy dress. You  have  to out him with the pink one and be like, “Ay, Liam, come and save my heels” about five times.      Hah, typical Liam. Poor guy thinks a clipboard and a crisp white shirt make him look like Mr. Spock. Still, he’s not bad company. Just don’t let him guestimate your pint volume again. The last time he said a pint was a third was one of the scariest evenings I’ve had since I accidently OD’d on chilli sauce.      Ugh, why do lads think they’re so funny when they mess with you on units of measure? It’s like the number one classic go-to of the man-vodka generation.      Speaking of pints, I’m not even going to mention how bad the draft at your bar was last time. I nearly made it to the kiosk before it hit me.

So do you remember how we used to do those personality quizzes back when we were in our teens? The kind that told you if you were an extrovert, or if you had a fiery temper, or a “sparkling sun sign” or whatever the latest fad was?      Yeah, I remember the one with the ice cream flavours representing your   soul   type. Classic. You were strawberry with a nutmeg twist. “Warm, kind, but always protecting yourself with a crunchy shell.” Dramatic as ever.      Oh come on, it was accurate. Still is. I saw one the other day online,  this  one talked about whether you were a hippo or a deer or a sloth when it came to   spiritual journeys  . I did it, and I came out as a deer—cautious, but determined. You did it too, didn’t you?      Yeah, I happened to be a   hippo  . I didn’t read the explanation, though. If I had to have a spiritual journey, I’d like to go with a big, waterproof, sturdy animal—hippos don’t struggle in the rain.      That’s only because they live in the water! You wouldn’t last a day in the rain here at the weekend. Remember how the roof leaked and you barely moved from the sofa?      All I know is that I’d rather be a hippo than a flamingo, which is what you said your friend came up with. “Delicate, a bit dramatic, oddly loud at night.”        She   said  you  would come out as a flamingo, but you refused to do it. I think she was trying to start something.      Maybe I  was  a flamingo that she didn’t know about. Who knows? Maybe we’re all just reborn animals every few decades. I say if I had to pick a period to visit, I would pick the Medievals—knights, feasts, scheming nobles. We could run our own   imaginary party   out of a castle with lunches delivered by pigeons and guards with fake beards.      You’re not interested in the 1920s? I think life would be perfect there. Art deco, jazz, champagne in the bath, and no one asking you to pay the electricity bill due to a mysterious system called “war reparations.”      Well, you’d need a   soul mate   to survive either era, wouldn’t you? Only I’m not sure you’d find the right kind of person to accompany you into the 1920s, romantic as it seems.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, running a business—it's like trying to herd cats half the time. I've had four staff calls today already. I can't cover all the sales calls and admin work at the same time.      It must be so tough managing it all. I'm just at a civil service job with very set hours and if someone's off sick, they're off with a note and I don’t worry so much. I envy that, actually.      Oh, and you think  that  sounds easy? If it wasn’t for the big office budget and the fact I’ve got a proper system in HR, I'd be out of my mind. On top of that, our receptionist called in with a gout flare-up this morning! I had to move the interview for the cleaner and I’m still waiting for the temporary sub she recommended.      I envy you both actually. I’m thinking of handing some of the admin over, maybe setting up an online booking system to cut down the calls. But I'm not sure how to explain it to some of the older clients—some of them still think the internet is a dangerous place with spiders and things.      Oh, I reckon you'd have to give them the old “it's safe – I swear!” line. I helped my gran set up video calls once. She still calls it “the webchat thing” and keeps accidentally hanging up on me.      Honestly, this is why businesses in Peterborough need more young people like you chipping in. We do talk about it at the council—encouraging young and old to work together. It’s such a shame there’s still a stigma with older people and technology. I remember the last seminar we had on “Digital Inclusivity” and not one of the attendees knew what a PDF was.      That just hits so close to home. My sister’s in her 70s and still sends me documents as scanned photos. I asked her once why she didn't just email the actual PDFs and she said, “Because that’s what they did in the war with proper paper.”      Now, while we’re on the topic of things that are old-fashioned—did you hear about the new graveyard on the edge of town? They’re planning to install air conditioning in the chapel.

So did you lot hear about what’s going down at the student union building this Sunday? They’re having like... some big house party or something. I’m not sure if it’s an actual event or just a “collective vibe” or whatever they call it nowadays.      Yeah, yeah I saw the Facebook post last night. It says 'Bring your own alcohol and try to be nice to each other'. A classic, innit? Sounds like a recipe for chaos.      Honestly, if it’s like the last one, someone tried to light the microwave with a gas canister... like, literally, don’t ask. But I’m in. What’s the point of university if you don’t at least try to get banned from an event within the first term?      D’you think Ewan and Aisling are going? I was about to text them.      I just happened to see Ewan in Tesco this morning. He looked like he hadn’t slept in weeks. Also, he was buying like... twelve packets of mince pies, and it was midweek.      What did he say to you?      Told me not to eat any sugar because then I’d “feel like a –  and then he fairly mumbled and I barely heard the rest  – ‘crazy dance donkey’ or something. Silly innit?      Hahah, classic Ewan. That guy should be paid to read books aloud. He’s oddly captivating when he’s flapping about.      Anyways, more importantly,  has anyone actually done their tax return about our shared housing yet?  I’m the only one who filed mine. I’m not doing it for any of you. Not doing it.      I did. My grandma helped me. She still thinks tax is evil and called HMRC 'a modern-day dragon'. I was told not to give them my money because 'they will hoard it in a cave while you die'.      That’s brilliant. Please record a video of your nan next time and send it over. I’m delivering a presentation this week on presentation skills and I can go full  evidence-based grandma nonsense  for ten minutes.      I’m not even going to mention how bad my nan is at all of this. She asked me  why  I had to pay tax and when I said it was basically because the government wants to feed the military, she replied, “Well, at least they’re not using the money on  secondhand shoes .”

Rather skip the starter an’ go straigh’ in with the calamari, then, if it’s that good.      It is good, love. But you’ll want a starter first, otherwise you won’t leave room for the main—  Liam   gets enough for two when he’s eating now, I don’t want you all   starvin’   on top o’ it.      Ayup! Proper big, Mum. Headaches if she don’t eat.      Very funny, Liam.      Tch, I’m fine. Honestly. I just—Managed to get a 2:1 in my Environmental Sciences degree this time.      No! Blimey, about time, ain’t it? D’you get the certificate in the post?      Yeah, it came last week, but I’ve been waitin’ for a good occasion to open it, you know?      A very good occasion. One I would expect you to treat with a decent meal—  not   a chip butty in the garage.      And welcome to Istria, by the way—it’s the least we can do, compliments of Liam’s mother’s persistence.      Oh, it was  his  idea too, wasn’t it?      Naa, no way. I might be a teenager, but I know not to meddle in   that   war.      Funny thing—  you’d   have been in the exact same place, Paul, if you had to come up with a career in about five days like I did.      Oh I had a plan, no thanks to my   over-ambitious   father. Architecture, medicine, law—none of them, ‘course. I ended up here.      And now you sort profits and losses for suits in nice jackets.      You must sort out   a lot   of people's lives being a consultant and all. Do people ever thank you properly?      Some do. Most are too busy trying not to cry on the train home.      So, Liam, how’s your GCSE prep going?      Alright, I reckon. Proper boring, though. We all have to sit it together in this poky room, and Ms. Taylor never   shuts up   about how we’re going to be poorer if we don’t get an A .      That’s exactly how I was taught.      You? Right, you did O-levels when the whole UK used to collapse into snow and before social media, so obviously your experience is very much   not   the same as hers.      Cheeky. But true.      Liam, you ever think about your future?      D’you mean like, university? Maybe. I dunno. Mums says I’m ‘stuck in a fog’, but no one’s ever asked me if I just fancy a   bike ride   over thinking about debt.

Rather skipper, you've got some rather swarthy cheeks from the sun in Cornwall, ‘aven’t you?      Oh, Tom, don’t start with the swarthy business! It is a sun tan, not a crime. We’ve been walking, cycling, eating — proper holidaying, mind you, and we even got to see that little lighthouse by St Agnes.      That’s the one I always wanted to see, Marjorie. Imagine standing in a place where the light used to guide ships for over a hundred years. It must’ve felt a bit like stepping into the past, even if it’s just a holiday.      Still, I managed to get the turkey on the spit without burning it to a cinder this time. I made properYorkshire pudding while you were gone. If you don’t like it, I’ll just eat it all myself. I still haven’t forgiven that curry incident in 2009.      Oh, Tom, don’t drag that up again. That was my  one  time trying something new, and it was a very good curry!      Still smells faintly like the Orient on you today, though. I can tell.      Speak for yourself. I remember the time you brought back a gift from Bognor Regis and claimed it was a rare Bronze Age relic.      For what it’s worth, I might’ve been mistaken. But at least I put an effort in. I won’t just sit at home playing cards with the telly on like the old crowd at the village hall.      That’s true, Tom. You’ve put about as much effort into this weekend as a man in his late 70s can — what with your hip and all that.      Aye, well, I do stretch, ‘cos I’m not made of clockwork. I did manage to get to the cycle race in Norfolk last weekend too, just watched it, no strain, but bless my legs!      Now that’s what I call getting out! I’ve been spending more time with the YHA volunteers since retiring. Even set up a couple of trips for kids in the Midlands to enjoy the countryside. You’d be surprised how many of them haven’t seen a real line of daffodils.      Oh, what a lovely thing you do! We’ve made it a habit to travel a bit every year — last year it was Yorkshire in a day, and we saw that ‘Harry Potter’ valley or whatever they call it up there.

Right, thanks a lot for dinner, Sophie. That stew is proper good—definitely better than any takeaway I got in Doncaster last week.      Erm, thanks, Liv. Knew we were gonna have you and Harry here, so I picked a recipe that wouldn’t burn in half an hour.      Honestly, Harry, you underestimate Sophie all the time. This is probably A-grade stuff. I’ve had this exact recipe on a few training courses. It’s got that little kick of cinnamon in it, right? That’s class.      Oh, like, whatever. Still, I made it. I don’t need a medal, just a bit of peace and quiet while I eat.      Well, peace and quiet ain’t the main event round here, Harry. If you remember, we had an argument in about the cat’s diet last breakfast, and then debate over whether jam should ever go on eggs.      Honestly, Harry, even if you say the wrong thing, I reckon we’d argue about it. My Aunty Doris says I’ve got the short attention span of a goldfish. She only realises when I’m interrupting her watching  Strictly Come Dancing .      Ha – Mate, I got a mate, Dean, he just moved in up near the industrial estate. It’s got to be the worst council place I’ve seen in Cambridge. Makes the toilets in the supermarkets at work look like four-star restaurants.      Rude, Harry. You work in a decent environment now. Or at least you say you do. I’ve had your colleague, Neil, at a few of the university conferences I’ve organised. He wears the same green overalls most days.      Don’t know why I’m complaining. At least I’m not sat in a ‘cosy’ little office all day like you two.      You know, I was thinking about relationships the other day. How you just sort of expect your partner to know what you like. My ex, Mark—God knows where he is now—used to swear he knew I preferred oysters to mussels, but one day I find a bag of mussels go bad in my fridge. I rated our communication about a two outta ten.      Honestly, Sophie, that’s wild. I’m with you. My ex, James, asked me to marry him after two months. I said no. Big mistake. But I did talk him into a holiday in Egypt anyway—big mistake number two.

: You’re back! So how was Barcelona? You post like five Instagram stories in the time it takes me to make tea.     : Blimey, I know! It was a mad weekend—non-stop. I finally went to that beach club I told you about, the one with the infinity pool.  So  worth it.     : Classic. You always go all out. What about your mate Alice? Did she survive the whole trip?     : She did! She was like a tourist on amphetamines, but fun. We went to these little tapas places off the main streets—no queues, no hassle, and the paella was  insane .     : Ooh, jealous. I just stayed in and watched  Sex Education  for the third time. Pretty much my idea of adventure now.     : You really need to step outside more! You know I’ve been meaning to ask… is everything okay with you and Liam? You two have been MIA from each other a lot lately.     : Honestly… I don’t know. We’re both working so much. He got that freelance design gig in… well, basically everywhere. We’re arguing less, but it just feels like we’re drifting, y’know?     : Yeah, I do. I’ve been there after Silas and I split up last year. It’s tough when the day-to-day starts to feel like a grind. But hey, at least your love language is definitely  quality time , judging by how moody you get if he’s even 10 minutes late.     : Harsh! I prefer to think of it as  value time . Not just any old time—he should be giving me value. Rolling my eyes.     : My point  exactly ! Anyway, enough doom and gloom. Since I’m back, what’s the plan? I assume I can have some of your leftover月饼 [mooncake]? We barely ate proper food over there.     : Please, I haven’t touched those. I took them out last week for  mood purposes . They’re practically fossils.     : Ugh, don’t worry—I mean it as a line of inquiry. Also, do you want to plan a trip soon? Maybe Paris? I’m all for visiting somewhere that feels a little less “Instagram’d to death.”     : Paris? Sure. But only if we avoid the Cliché Tourist Trap. Sights like the Eiffel Tower are  fine , but I want hidden little wine bars, croissants at 8 a.m., and the kind of flan that melts in your mouth.     : Boom—said my last French babe crush. So next weekend?

Rather lovely to sit out here on a Sunday morning, isn't it? The sea breeze and that string of minarets beyond the hills—like dining in a postcard!      You’re not wrong. Though honestly, I half expected the sea to be a bit more… turquoise. Got a bit of a  Casablanca  moment in me, I reckon.      I think North Cyprus has this way of slowly convincing you it’s warmer and easier than you expect. Especially when you’re served filtered coffee this good.      You’re getting the full British Cyprus package! Sitting in a seaside restaurant, drinking the only decent drink around, and trying not to think about the price list back home. Fun life’s a funny old thing, isn’t it?      Oh, definitely. I spend most of my time now convincing Year 7 that British history is more than just tea, cricket, and the Queen. Today’s lesson was  The Vikings, They’re Not All Bad!       Bold move, challenging the stereotypes. I used to be in advertising, quite a while ago. Told people for a living that shoes they didn’t need would solve all their problems.      Ha – that’s a new twist on curriculum planning! At least you weren’t lying about the Vikings. What happened to you next? Silly question—I can already see you as an entrepreneur, huh?      You weren’t wrong. After advertising, I noticed a gap in the market— wait for it —cloud-based admin tools for small businesses. Now I make a living telling people how to save about five minutes a week by not using Excel the right way.      Five minutes that are then spent blaming the software. You sound like my stepdad. Running a Burgers and Brews place in Bournemouth since 2008. He’s convinced his Wi-Fi is cursed during the lunch rush.      Sounds like the perfect hybrid—entrepreneurial dreams of global domination, topped with lunches of fries and whining about the Wi-Fi. Was it always set in stone for you to head back into the classroom?      Not if you mean  always  at preordained line in the sand that I was always dragging box across until something stopped. No, I was in retail for years—selling uniforms and kettles in poxy cheap shops, mostly. But as life tends to do, I changed course over a glass of Ceylon tea and a documentary on Sir Ken Robinson.      Sir Ken always had a way of making me sound like a cattle rustler by comparison.

Rather annoying my new housemate eh?      Aye, her or ‘im? Which one’s the trouble?      It’s both, honest. First one’s always leavin’ ‘is muddy boots inna hall and the second one — well, ‘e’s alright but eeny weeny bit of a drama queen if ya ask me.      Yeah? What kind o’ drama? Slap ‘er too much or summun?      Nah, it’s just… everything’s a bleedin’ issue. Had an argument with ‘im last week cos ‘e put a baked potato inna microwave. I said, “Bit strange don’tcha think?” an’ ‘e goes, “Why? It’s got cheese on it!” As if that makes it okay!     [Laughter] Blimey, that’s bonkers! Why doesn’t ‘e just use the oven then?      That’s what I said! But no, ‘e’s dead set on the microwave. I swear, if I give ‘im a baked potato again I’m just gonna chuck it inna bin.      And the other one, then — the one with the muddy boots. Does ‘e do much else?      Well, fairly alright, I think. Just don’t know ‘is own strength or somethin’. Throws ‘is tea mugs inna sink an’ shatters ‘em. Like, someone said to me, “I’ve not seen a mug since the war.” [Laughs] Some o’ the china things gone now too.      Aye, that’s a bugger. I about lost me ‘ead once when I binned a proper good cups-and-saucers cos I couldn’t be bothered to be careful with ‘em.      You’re not binin’ for mugs like me, though — I’m about to bin the lot me. No one round ‘ere ‘as a clue how to treat china.      We could always tell ‘em. You know, politely suggest they read the 'use a caddy' memo.      Oh for  gods  sake, like that’ll work. Then go talk bin on ‘em about muddy boots again.      Yeah, I’m seein’ this goin’ bad. You might ‘ave to chuck ‘em both out in the end.      Well, I can’t even bellyache properly to the landlady or ‘er mate cos the lot o them are like… what’s the word...  vibrant .      That's one word, yeah.      She’s alright, I guess she’s just got ‘air that goes, like, straight up. I don’t know, she looks like a bender. All that pink on ‘er face.      Aye, e'en if she is, that face says, “Don’t mess wi’ me.”      Exactly!

Rather a lot today, wasn't it? That supermarket in town’s grown like tops—the tills take forever to get to.      It did, I know. I've been over ten years since I first retired and started doin’ the weekly shop by myself, yet every time it’s a trek! Mind you, I got the bread rolls and that little cherry cheese you like—still in the plastic bag by the door.      Oh, top of the world. It was a bit of a journey today, though. I got stranded at the stop when the bus broke down. Had to fetch the three young ones from school. They were awful nice, though the oldest, Olivia, kept asking me if I remembered her dad's old dog, who I left at home this morning! I said, "Olivia, I haven't forgotten him—remember he’s asleep under the lilac bush!" Made her snort, no doubt about that!      Aye, they’s charmers, aren’t they? I do miss the old bunch sometimes. I reckon I’d like to give it a go again—just part-time, maybe occasional. But with your health as it is, and the house, it feels like there's something watching us.      Speak for yourself. I remember the days we used to clean out the garage, and the ghost of my great-aunt supposedly walks by every time there’s thunder! You know what I blame? That old house we live in. Our place here in Costessey—proper ancient. I swear, the floorboards creak at night with whispers. Not that I mind, mind you. Adds a bit of spice to the quietness, eh?      I know what you mean. Sometimes when the wind's blowing through the garden door, you could almost think it’s telling you something. Doesn’t sound unkind, but it’s just...  there —like it's part of the walls now. The children at the school used to tell tales about ‘haunted houses,’ and I thought them just little ones getting silly with the stories. Now I’m not sure. I mean, this house has stories of its own, probably.      Defo. I remember my dad talking about the man who built it goin’ daft in his old age—always shoutin’ at the trees in the orchard. Never could find out if it was true or one of them tales. But then again, it feels like this place’s been around long enough to know a few secrets, wouldn’t you say?

Rather annoying this newfit in the kitchen floor. Thoughtful of 'em to chuck it in when we couldn’t be here.      It’s only floorboards, love. A bit of noise is par for the course with builders about. Be grateful it's sorted now.      Aye, I’ll say. Me 'n 'Reg were stuck on the landline most a' day. Lost touch with me daughter in Leeds. Old fingers 'udn't work them new touch 'phones.      You're never going to get the hang of those devices, Ma. Take it from me, I still can't get me telly to work without help.      Just 'cos you're lazy, Da. It’s just a button to press, not magic. But I suppose I’ll be the one futzing with it again later.      Let's not get started on tech wars, I've got a GCSE paper to mark later and my head’s already spinning.      Aye, you mark it, and I'll make the tea—proper one, not that posh leaf stuff you've taken to.      Speaking of, how's work been, then, Dottie? Still piling those essays in with the same delight as ever?      More or less. All these kids think they're Shakespeare if they write one sentence with a hyphen. There’s a joke someone made in one essay—about Pythagoras arguing with the bus timetable—made me laugh out loud.      Was it being marked out of ten?      Out of about five. Subtract two for the "Pythagoras the Bus Driver" bit. Overall a four-point-seven! Going easy on ‘em!      Maybe they’re the future, ‘cos I swear you lot were no better at grammar when you were young.      You got that right. I still call a ‘rectangle’ a ‘square stick’ to this day.      He knows the proper names now, thank you! Since he took the GCSE, you remember, Reg.      Oh yeah go on then, make it about you. I’m still waiting for "rectangle" in the dictionary, not just in the box of Lego.      So, have you made it to the new allotment yet, Gran?      Aye, planted the tulips ‘n' the beans. They're growing like mad. You’ll get a job there at the library, Reg, if you don’t watch it.      Me? Why me?      Cos you named every single seedling "Harry" again.      Now now, enough. You promised me you'd help me with sorting the shed this Saturday, love.

So did you lot see the latest health supplement post on TikTok? I swear it's just a glorified protein shake and some chill tablets.      Nah, I've been into that type of thing before. Not sure I trust the guys in those videos half the time. Most of ’em just want clicks.      Honestly, I reckon it depends on your needs. If you're into fitness like I am, having that kind of support can be helpful. I started taking some magnesium last term—it helps me sleep better after the gym. Didn’t even want to touch it at first, though.      I’ve been into technology more than supplements, to be honest. Just got a new smartwatch. You know, the one that’s supposed to track your stress levels and everything. D’you think it’s worth it?      They’ve got to be useful if you're scientifically-minded. I mean, I’ve got one too and it’s cracked for tracking my runs, but the sleep tracking is so patchy. I wake up and it says I slept ten hours—personally I’m not convinced I left the bed.      It’s funny how much we’ve got on our wrists these days. I remember when all we needed was a watch to tell the time, and a phone in our pocket for everything else.      Times did change fast after uni. I remember my nan still using a flip phone, and now even she’s got a tablet for FaceTiming me. Makes me a bit sad, but it's good she’s still connected with the family.      That’s true. Technology can be good for family stuff, even if it does take the personal touch out of some things. I had my nan over for Sunday roast not long ago. She still barely knows how to use a kettle, but she’s trying, so that’s something.      Roast dinners are always a win. I used to have ‘em all the time when I was little. You ever try making one while you’re living away from home?      Please, I once tried to braise a leg of lamb and burnt it beyond salvation. Then had to FaceTime my mam to explain.      Haha, I feel that. I once tried to make Shepherd’s pie and completely forgot the carrots until the minute I had to mash the spuds.      You lot are joking. I made a proper pie last week and it tasted just like Gran’s.

Right, I’m just going to write the shopping list now. We need eggs, bread, milk, and... got to pick some apples for the crumble later. I can’t remember if we have flour or not, Lucy? Do we?      I think there’s a bag in the cupboard, but if you could pick more while you're out, just to be safe.      Can we get some crisps? I want the salty ones, not the weird veggie ones.      Crisps? Isn’t that the third time this week? But fine, one bag. But only if you promise to do your homework before dinner.      Yeah, yeah.      On that note, I left the kettle boiling and there was some wasp buzzing around. I ended up squishing it. I know it's harsh, but there’s something about them when they hover near your head.      Oh dear, was it stung anyone?      No, but I still got bitten by something earlier—arm went all red and itchy. I put some antiseptic on, but it’s still throbbing a little.      Sounds like a wasp or something else. Have you got any hydrocortisone cream at home?      There’s some in the first-aid box in the hallway. I’ll have a dab when I get back.      I got bitten by a big one last week. My finger was like a balloon for a day. I put toothpaste on it and it helped a bit.      Toothpaste? That’s a bit of a myth, isn’t it? I’ve heard people swear by it, but I think most of it is just distraction.      I’d go for baking soda mixed with water to form a paste. That’s the natural stuff that actually helps reduce inflammation.      Sounds like it's time for a biology lesson again, Lucy.      I’m just being practical! Those bites can’t be taken lightly if you ignore the symptoms.      Okay, okay, let’s change the topic before it turns into a first-aid seminar. Jack, did you get your football homework done?      Yeah, just about. It was brutal. We had to write an essay on what your team means to you. I wrote about how we won the match last week against St. Giles.      Oh right, we saw that game over the weekend. That was a proper comeback. You lads really nailed it in the second half.      That's the spirit, love. Listen, while we're on the topic, I’ve got an early shift tomorrow before the weekend, so we’ll need to go shopping early as well.

Okay, I just got locked out of my Instagram again. Like, literally WHY. Is it ‘password penguin123’ or ‘passwordpenguin123’? I've been over this a thousand times.      Look, it’s because you wouldn't just  listen . You always say the hackers can't guess it with the '123' at the end… but clearly the algorithm is A) smarter than us and B) just hates you.      Ugh, it’s not me! My aunt said she doesn't chase when she watches the new vegan YouTubers but I guess even they can't help with a broken password.      Yeah, like that Mykie Beans bloke? I watched him last week, tried to do his protein pancakes for P.E. But I used the wrong kind of protein powder—my mum was  so  confused. Ended up with something that looked like brown gym socks.      Blooming hell. I tried that fidget spinner latté hack from the Good Girl Cooks bloke. My teacher Mr. Ellis had to throw it away because I put two spoons of cinnamon in by accident and the whole class kept laughing. He was like, “Miss Green, is this a science experiment or is it Halloween already?      At least you had the  courage  to try. I don’t even know what the difference is between the protein pancakes and normal pancakes. Like, is it just a ‘big boy’ version of flapjacks? Or are they just for people who do  a lot  of pull-ups?      Anyway, forget the pancakes! Look, are we doing the science about mitosis on Thursday? Because I’m not touchin’ that one. I tried revising last night and now I’m dreaming about chromosomes splitting and dancing. Like, I woke up screaming and my  cat  was hiding under my desk.      I’m dreading the whole lesson. My brother James said he used to knit little models for his biology class. We could do that as like… a joke. Make chromosomes out of wool and glue a little “mitosis happening” sign?      That’s amazing. We could make the nucleus out of goop or something. My P.E. teacher, Miss Lambert, made us line up in order of muscle mass before the fitness test last week. I swear to God, I was directly behind James Dean from Year 9 and he had biceps like, like… like  Christian Bale  on a protein smoothie.      Imagine! It wasn’t fair either—I was near the end and they were taking about six minutes off my time just to see if I had “improved technique.”

Rather annoying this, am I? I’ve been stuck with this cold ages now. Felt like it was clearing up and then it just flared up again. Blows!      Aw, that’s not fair. You’ve had a busy month at work, though—Deerfield site and all that. That can mess with your immune system. Still, better you than me.      Yeah, but I’m so fed up. The whole house smells like steam and Echinacea to me! You’d think I lived in a naturopathy store. Still, I’ve had the vaccination this year.      Oh good! I haven’t got round to it yet. My GP keeps saying I’ve got an appointment left from last December. Probably forgotten to reschedule. D’you know, I think the world is just waiting for everyone to drop dead and forget to wear a face mask in public?      Honestly, don’t get me started. I was watching some documentary the other night about how the NHS is still under so much strain over post-pandemic patients. I mean, I’m not in hospital, thank God, but you read the headlines and it still gives me shivers.      Be fair, I’ve seen some of those stats too—it’s nuts, innit? Anyway, back to you. You reckon it’s just a winter cold or have you tested for anything else? Liam at work had a case of food poisoning someone at the same conference—thought it was a virus at first, then it turned out he’d had something dodgy at a buffet.      Ugh, don’t mention food! I nearly did the business off steak pie the other day. Probably the chilli I had with it. My friend Jane swears it’s all to do with the digestive issues after sending bodies back to the jungle, like overcoding the processing somehow.      That’s some theory. You know, I was reading about scientists trying to improve body language recognition for cameras on TVs. We’re already getting motion sensors that know if you’re frowning or not. Imagine a TV that whines at you if you don’t smile for ten minutes after a Pixar ad.      Oh God, that’s if you don’t deactivate the emotional features—still, it’s interesting that they even consider it. I mean, it’s one thing with technology in NHS operations, but seriously, why do we need to track every expression now?

Rather annoying isn't it, the traffic outside. I couldn't get out this morning, it was completely gridlocked near the shopping centre.      I know, I've been stuck in there twice this week. Not only that, the butcher’s shop queue was ridiculous. Ten minutes for mince and two carrots!      Well, I reckon it's all that self-service trolleys. A lot of people just walk around too slowly, picking items up and then leaving them in the aisle.      And don’t get me started on the kids these days not knowing how to shop without a screen! Not like back in my day when the only entertainment was reading the music magazines like  Beat Instrumental  or  Melody Maker .      We had the odd copy lying around the house I think. I remember sneaking a glance now and then.      I actually tried to post about it on Facebook last night. People went mad about it! Said I should start a group called 'Eras of Magazines’. It might actually get somewhere, you know.      I think that’s a very good idea. I’ve seen quite a few people nostalgic for those old paperbacks. But perhaps it's time we got back to the game?      Agreed, because I'm trying to get the word 'zeugma' down next and I want to win this one!      Now, what's a zeugma again?      It's when a word is used in connection with two other terms in different ways. For example, "He opened the door and his heart." Kind of about dual meaning.      Oh yes, very literary. I remember using that in my classes all the time to explain dramatic writing.      Well, I found it on the Scrabble dictionary and boy do I intend to use it.      Let's just make sure it works with the letters you've got. I don't know if you've got a 'z' lying around.      I do! Let me just check.      Then so do I! I'll claim it go ahead of you!      Just don't expect me to not call out that it's a bit of a stretch to use what your actual heart was doing at the time.      That was a cheap jibe by the way, from your third move.      Only because you mentioned your headache last night. I thought it was a fitting touch of irony.      And to think earlier this week you were stuck in a queue and then want to talk about irony, you old devil.

Rather a lot of people here today, isn't it? I do miss the days when it was just a few of us and some quiet chats about the old press types. Not that I've got anything against a little buzz, mind you.      Ah yes, well things do change, don’t they? I remember when I used to trawl the halls of big exhibitions in Germany—Frankfurt most often—showing off the latest printing systems I'd helped create. Noisy but rewarding. It gave me a sense of purpose.      Oh, I daresay you left your mark on the industry. I had my art gallery and antique shop back in Taunton, and printing was always an interest of mine. I used to collect old printing blocks and presses—rather like you, I imagine, but without the science of it.      Haha, now that’s an understatement. I spent years perfecting the alignment of ink, pressure and speed. It was all about the details! Germany, though—ah, the clientele there. One time, I was demonstrating a printer and this chap—German, of course—checked the alignment with a ruler and a magnifying glass like I was setting up a war machine. It was rather fun, in a way.      Ha! I can picture it. I, on the other hand, was more interested in the aesthetic of printing—woodcuttings and letterpress. I’d sell prints alongside the antiquities, and some people just couldn’t get enough of the old school charm. Children of the digital world oddly nostalgic for the tactile.      That’s interesting. I suppose in a way, I was building the bridges between past and present. I always admired those who kept the traditional touch alive. We were on opposite sides of the coin, but you know—I’d pop into your gallery if it were near one of my exhibitions. The two worlds made for rather a nice balance.      I’d remember you. I had a few regulars from the printing world—people you knew, I expect. We’d talk about the state of the industry over a nice pot of tea. Rather a different pace from your time in Germany, I would imagine.      Oh, it was. No vast gothic exhibition halls, no rows of engineers and salesmen shouting features at each other in separate languages. Just a quiet corner with a cup of Earl Grey and some fine prints. It reminded me I wasn’t entirely obsessed with speed after all.

Dad, I just wanted to say, our journey’s taking ages. I thought it would be quicker from Manchester to Cornwall.      It's not that far, love, but you gotta take little dips in between. We wouldn’t want to kill ourself on motorways all day, eh? Besides, we got a few stops to make along the way.      Yeah, I guess. A lot of this area's got weird spellings, like Wigan and Rochdale. Why's it not just called “Weggon” or “Roshdal” or somethin’?      Well, that's the thing, innit? English is like that. A mix of old Norman French, Germanic stuff, and just plain messed up from years of foreigners chuckin’ their language in. Think of words like "knight"—you say it one way, it's written another. Same with “pneumonia,” “island,” and “subtle.”      Man, why do we even have to learn all that? English is already so annoying with all the rules that don’t even make sense.      Fair point. But it’s brilliant how it changes over time too. Like “awful” used to mean something amazing, not something bad. And “nice” used to mean ignorant. Doesn’t make sense to you now, but it was what it was back then!      Haha, yeah. But also, I’m trying to decide if I want to study English at uni or something more practical like business or economics.      Both make sense in their way, love. I mean, university is a big ask, but English can take you places—journalism, copywriting, even teaching. But if you’re more numbers-minded, business could be good too. My sister’s got a mate who runs her own marketing firm and did economics. Bit more money on the side, if you know what I mean.      Speaking of which, while you’re thinking about that, what do you reckon to trying the lunches at a couple of service stations? I’ve seen a few that do proper home-cooked meals, like roast dinners and fish and chips. They’re usually a bit more friendly there than at the big chain places.      Honestly, I’d rather something with quinoa or lentils. I’m trying to be a bit healthier and eat less meat.      Oh, quinoa? Sounds like a potion from a fantasy film. But I respect it. My cousin tried goin’ vegan for a month, ended up with weird dreams of suffering cows. You gotta do you, luv.

Rather skip the newfit meat eh?      Aye, it's always a muck when you don’t cook it properly. I’m more after a bit o’ chicken anyway. Beans and rice is a solid side to that.      You wouldn't say that if you had een tasted the chicken I brought last week. Not 'cos I reckon it was any good… just most a' it was still frozen. Fair dos, this lot isn’t much easier to handle.      Well, we ain't doing the frozen chicken again. I want something hot and proper. I saw a shop near the train station that sells fresh tikka masala the other day. Could do with trying that.      Tikka masala? I like that. Probably better than the chicken sandwiches Oliver brought up last time. If he turned up at all, mind, cos he was working until 6, wasn’t he?      Yeah, he’s been needing the hours. His dad's working on the spare room so he’s got to help out, like. I swear, if I had a dad who was up for that sort a' thing, I might’ve tried to be a bit more responsible.      You'd've been out of the house so fast, Steve, they'd've put a notice in the window for you to come back. You were the worst about that whole thing when you were a kid. ‘Balances the room’ you used to say.      Saying what I meant! I wasn’t just playing up. I was out there helping the law weigh things up and down and being fair. Can’t fault me for that, Laura.      Steve was a legend back then, talking bollocks and chucking things off roofs. My sister Jackie once caught him trying to fix the kitchen tap with a wrench and his bare hands. That ‘cos he was playing construction man for the day.      Aye, it was a mess. The whole tap came off and water was gushing everywhere. My nan had to rush down and sort it out. She ended up quoting the entire Bible at the poor guy.      That's your gran, Laura. She quotes like it's her job. I bet if I tried to use a sander again, she'd find a line in the Good Book to go with it.      Pass the salt will you Steve? I can't see it and I reckon we're going to need it for what we've got to do next.

So do you live close here? Or do you come in from far?      Oh, I’m actually from Hitchin, so I come down from Hertfordshire most days. It's a bit of a trek, honestly, but I’ve got a motor now, so it’s not too bad. Yourself?      Born and bred in B’ham, luv. Haven’t left it too often apart from uni. I got a BTEC and degree in hospitality, but it’s just me slingin’ pints at the pub when I get the chance. You’re a language teacher, right?      Yep, I teach French and Spanish at a secondary school in the city. I did my degree in French and postgrad in education. I’m actually between contracts at the moment, which is why I’m here today—taking a break between terms. How do you like the bar scene then?      It’s alright. Keeps you busy, especially on nights, and the punters can be hilarious. I like it, though. I do a bit of reading on the side—some philosophy, short stories, a bit of poetry. Do you read much?      I do, actually. I was just reading “The Shadow of the Wind” last week. I love literature, it really helps with language skills. You ever think about doing something more permanent than the bar? Like, maybe stepping into education or something?      Nah, not really. I like my shift work. Besides, I can’t face being stuck in a classroom for ten hours a day. But look at you—passed exams, got a PG, all that. Did you always know you wanted to teach?      Not really. I switched from wanting to be an architect to languages in the end. My parents moved to France for a while when I was young, and that sparked my interest. So, what about relationships, then? Any prospects holding any pints at the moment?      Ha! We’re not at that level. Though I’ve had a bit of a 'thing' with someone from the club I do the bar work at. She’s a fitness instructor by the way, so I end up getting free sessions most days if you know what I mean.      Sounds like you're living the dream bloke. A bit of sport and a bit of charm. I seriously envy that. You ever think about going for your full driver’s license, by the way?      I’ve passed my theory!

Rather skip the newfit and go through the short cut, do you?      Oh, no, I’ll take the longer way today, actually. I need to stop off at the florist for a few things. I’ve promised Mrs. Haydock a fresh arrangement for her conservatory again on Friday.      You and your flowers, Bill. I tell you what, I reckon that woman could buy her own greenhouse if she wasn’t always begging you for free ones.      Nonsense, Reg. She doesn’t chase me, I promise you. I just fetch the same arrangement each week, and she can’t seem to live without it, bless her.      Just keep an eye on yourself though. I read this article the other day about something called Münchhausen Syndrome. Apparently, some people make themselves sick just for attention. Rather worrying if you’re looking after old dear’s gardens and all.      I pity the poor sods, really. If you want attention that bad, I reckon you’d do nearly anything for it, wouldn’t you?      Aye, as long as you don’t do something stupid like leave a donation tin on the shelf for extra coin and then get got by it. My old Mate Harry did that once—set up fake collection boxes for charity, but the council found him out after someone noticed he was the one collecting the most ‘donations’. Sent him to jail for six months.      Oh dear! That does sound rather bad. I do wonder what made him do it. After all, real collecting comes through the Postcode Lottery for us in St Mary’s Church, about helping the young mums in the town.      Not much sense in doing good if you are doing it to get noticed, if you ask me.      True. I rather like that. All the banners around here for the Gambia appeal. I donated a few pounds myself last time I dropped in. I mean, it's a good cause, even if it's a long way off.      It is, dear. I took the kids there when they were little—lovely country. I told the mums in the room I run it if you ever fancy a real adventure, pack your dentures, but that’s just me being a joker.      You could have been a tour guide with that glib tongue of yours, Rita.      Ha! I’d have got overcharged at the food places, that's for sure.

Okay, so, I just downloaded this new mobile app called "Plates." It's supposed to let you plan meals and link it to your local grocery store so you can order your ingredients.      Oh yeah, we've got one like that—  Larder Locker  , I think it's called. It doesn't seem to work very well for me, honestly. I tried it once, and I ended up with three tubs of hummus and no bread.      Haha, same! My last grocery order got delivered when I was in the middle of dinner. I opened the door to this giant box full of frozen lasagnes, and the guy just smiled and said "Hope you like My turkey!"      Yeah, no—what if I’m watching horror films while I’m waiting for the delivery? I screamed at the most inopportune moments last time.      I know! I was watching  Hereditary  the other night and looked up to see my ordering history pop up on my phone. It suggested I buy "votive candles"—like, are we casting a spell next?      Did you ever get scared off  Hereditary ? I stopped watching it during the audio taper scene. That got way too intense for my liking.      Honestly, I don’t know why people like horror films. All that screaming and shadows. You know what I like? When the plot isn't just relying on jump scares. Oh, my friend Jake went to a haunted house with his brother last weekend. Turns out the guy running it was a real creepy dude and they got locked in a room for over an hour!      That does not surprise me. Jake wears the kind of jeans that smell like a house fire and fails at iPhone photography.      So, while we’re on the topic of over-the-top experiences, what’s your dream holiday? Mine would just be me on a tropical beach where surfers are surfing and there’s no Wi-Fi.      Me too, but I’d also love to go to Japan with lunches delivered right to the hotel—ramen, tempura, sushis, the whole shootin’ match.      I think I’m more of a road-trip kind of person. Nothing like being in the car with the boxset bloopers playlist your friends made you. I have one called "The Essence of Adventure" it includes every cheap theme park soundtrack ever made.      Oh, please—your playlist is just them songs you heard in the cinema pre-show.

Rather annoying this, having to wait for the mechanic again. I swear the one in Fakenham takes forever to get the seats sorted out on the van.      Aye, mechanics seem to be in short supply these days. Me and Mavis were saying the other day how it’s not just cars that’s falling apart—it’s everything. Me boiler’s leaking again and I’ve been relying on a hot water bottle since Sunday.      Oh, don’t tell me! I know someone in Potterspury who had to sleep in a caravan because the heating broke down over Christmas. Not to mention, George,  you  still haven’t got the Citroen sorted? That thing’s older than me!      I know! I’m not the only one with a dodgy car in the area, though. It seems like half the old crowd have been breakfasting in Bucks or Bury St. Edmunds for weeks just to stay with their kids so they don’t have to drive those battered old tin cans.      I do tell you—personally, I’d take the train if it wasn’t for the cost. And the hobbling up and down the stairs at Norwich station with my walking stick. Be a struggle.      Well, I’m not surprised, it is  winter  after all. Roads are like black ice one minute and slush the next. Last week, I nearly ended up in the ditch just trying to get to my daughter’s for Sunday lunch.      That’s what you get for driving a ten-year-old estate. But seriously, Margot, I heard you’ve been helping out with about five different people’s cars this season just to get them home. You’re part of a  national service , you are.      I’ll have you know I’m charging now. Just a couple of quid to cut down the strain.      Oh, I’ll have none of that. I’m still getting your expert help for free as long as I can. Even if it does take me four hours to get from Diss to Thetford.      Then again, George, the alternative is staying in the room on your own if you don’t get a ride home.      You don’t say! I can see it already—me with a sandwich and the telly for company on a Saturday night after everyone else has gone home.      Just don’t fall asleep over the controller.

Rather annoying this new traffic system on the M6, isn't it?      Oh, I don’t know—new system or not, it’s still murder this time of day. At least we've got tea and biscuits to keep us going.      I’ve always found motorways calming, honestly. Just one long, open stretch of road. Almost like being on a cruise with wheels.      If you say so, love. I just keep thinking about the roadworks and how many times I'll.Fatalfanstay outside when we get to Manchester. You'd think the council would build bigger roads if we've got all these houses and people moving around these days.      Touching on that—you mentioned last week you were looking to move to Manchester, yes, Vivian? Easier access to the airport?      Mm. My breakfast club—yes, I've been thinking about it for a while. The old flat’s getting a bit cramped, even if I am the only one living there full-time. I mean, it's not like I need a bigger place for people to visit me anymore. Still, I’d like to be near the city center, in something a little roomier.      And what about the commute? Don't you find it stressful, all the traffic and noise? I’m no fan of cities myself.      She already knows what it's like, Ronan. They've got cousins in Manchester—she's been over there a few times. I remember the last time you were all at their mum's house for Christmas and you got lost trying to find your way back to the hotel in about five square miles of a street!      Very funny. And I suppose you found the hotel without getting lost then?      Maybe.      Ah, classic Manchester. Everything looks the same, and the cabs never stop bloody moving!      It's not just the traffic. It's the healthcare. My doctor said I’d benefit from a change of scenery and scenery with less damp. Some fresh air would do wonders.      That's true. I go there a fair bit for work and I always notice how clean the air is compared to Birkenhead. It's a bit blooming expensive, what your budget looks like for all that though?      That’s where you come in, Annie. It's your turn to talk me through spreadsheets and make sense of all the websites listing 100 square feet of floor space and asking for a mortgage I can’t afford!

Mum, I just wanted to say sorry again about the post I put online saying someone had nicked your bike... I was so upset I didn’t really think about it properly!      Aw, it’s okay, honestly! I appreciated you speaking up at first, like, it was good that someone saw something. But yeah, the language was a   bit   strong. Teenagers on social media saw it and started listing off every person in the village who has a black bike.      Oh no! Did people take it the wrong way?      A little. I like to keep things friendly in the village. But regardless, someone did see it and came forward. It’s been returned, by the way! Someone who found it near the shop just dropped it off at the café, and Toni brought it round in the morning.      What?! Seriously?! Wait, does it still have that bell that’s wonky? The one that sounds like a cat getting electrocuted?      Yes, that one! I haven’t got round to fixing it properly—there are more important things than a rude-sounding bell, love.      It’s not rude, it’s  character . Anyway, so no one actually stole it then? Just someone took it by accident?      Seems like it. The person who found it said they saw it leaning up against the wall outside the post office, just someone who must have borrowed it without asking. Probably just a rush to work or something.      Still sucks, though. It being gone for two days. I was cycling every day because of sport, and I couldn’t even use mine.      I know. I’ve been trying not to worry about it too much, but it is a bit strange how much we rely on bikes for everything now. I mean, you go to college, I go to work, the shops, the library—it all takes place   on a bike   for most people in Hastings these days.      Yeah, especially with how the lunches cost a fortune in the student café. I grab a sandwich and ride straight home after college.      Exactly. So really I just wanted to thank you for using social media for something useful once in a while, even if it was a bit dramatic.      So I’m not in trouble then?      Not if you promise not to post anything to Facebook next time unless it’s something positive, like food photos.      Deal. I could post a picture of the cat-sounding bell.

Right, so the next train we're trying to get is from Cardiff to Swansea. Someone’s already claimed first class, and I’m not sure if we should compete for second or take a scenic route. What do you think, Rhys?      Ah! C’mon now, I’ve already een plotatin’ a route from Newport to Aberystwyth if someone claims Swansea as well. It’s a long one, but if we block that route off, it’ll stick it to whoever was gonna go that way. We can chuck in a few tunnels or stations for speed, but the board says not too many—if we go over, we’ve gotta pay fuel, innit?      Yeah, but that’s turkey on Christmas Day, you know! Ten quid to play the safety card on the last stretch. If Aunty Sharon claims that stretch, we’ve died.      Bucksy agreement this happened. When I was in Singapore, the railways ran five trains an hour, you didn’t have to think—just clamber aboard and hope the tickets weren’t out of order. But here, eh… I mean, we even had one timetable once that said the train was early today, but it didn’t exist tomorrow.      That’s nothin’. My nan used to catch the 7:02 to Hay-on-Wye every Saturday. She reckoned that train was the only one that’d understand her! One day it didn’t run. She just wandered into the waiting room with two sacks of potatoes, a chaffin oddly sour look on her face, and said, “Well, I thought it was obvious.”      Oh! You know what about the food counters? I’ve brought biccies, tea, and— shall I open the provision bag now? There’s scones, cheese, and for the bravest of you lads—spicy sausages? Any offers? ‘Cause I know someone who tried to bluff their way through a “cumin” rush and ended up sprite-pale at the dinner table.      Aye, I took the kids to that road trip near Pembroke once and thought I’d impress ’em goin’ on aboot Thai food. Big mistake. One lad made a line in the sand that read, “Dad tastes bad,” and the other just sat there with his mouth open like a kipper.      You should’ve seen Uncle Bryn tryin’ to be posh last Sunday. He said “marmalade” like it was a Channel Five presenter and then tried to make rhyming couplets for our nephews.

Rather skip the starter and just go for the main, don't you?      Oh, come on, James—let’s be proper. We’ve got time, and besides, this isn’t just a game. It’s a bit of a cultural journey. First things first, starter or not?      Fine, fine, but I reckon people just want to get to the main event. A lot of games now, they rush straight to the kill or the big payoff. Like, someone once played Monopoly and was like, “I just wanna auction everything off and see who goes bankrupt.” Where’s the fun in that?      You mean, where’s the leisure in that? My uncle, bless him, he plays Cribbage like it’s a sacred ritual. Sets the board on the kitchen table, uses the same little brass cards he bought in the 80s, doesn’t touch a drink till the final peg goes in. The ritual’s the point.      Exactly. I think the English have a strange relationship with leisure—especially over the last few decades. On one hand, we rush through everything, like we’re all still trying to finish our tea by half past five. On the other, we trot out these games like they’re church.      And let’s not forget the drink culture that often goes with it. Now don’t get me wrong, I’m all for a decent G and T while we assess our strategic options, but sometimes people just get too absorbed in trying to be the perfect host. I had a housemate in London—every game night, he’d make gin-based cocktails with names like  “The Staggering Sorcerer” . Once I even woke up on the wrong side of the bed with no recollection of what card I had.      Doesn’t sound unappealing, to be honest, but for me, it’s less about the drinks and more about the pacing. Like board games. If you play too quickly, it’s like eating a whole cake in one bite. If you take too long, people get fidgety and start trying to catch up elsewhere on their phones. There’s this sweet spot in the middle where everything comes together.      That’s the bit I usually aim for. It’s about managing expectations, really. If you go into a game thinking it’s a bloke-off or a proper challenge, you might as well bring in the betting chips and champagne flute.

Rather skip the new house for now. You know what a nightmare that has been.      What's the problem this time—electrical, plumbing, or just something left out by mistake?      I'll have you know, it's been  mildly  eventful, if you can call builders drilling somewhere they shouldn't 'eventful.' Almost had them drilling into a pipe that Aneurin swore was in this exact spot, but wasn't. Imagine what would've happened if they had!      Didn’t your builders get the plans wrong last time? Or was that a different property altogether?      Oh, don’t remind me. Last time the turkey came out undercooked because the oven got disconnected in the back! Rather you lot talkin’ aboot weekend plans again? I’ve been hearin’ bits ‘n’ bobs o’ winter campin’ now for weeks. I’ve asked what it involves, but I’ve got a foggiest idea. What is it? Well, I’ll tell ye this: one night I was campin' by Loch.Percent, and I woke up to see the northern lights over the valley. It een’t like        Aye, sounds like a bit of fun. Right, who’s ready for a story tonight? Or maybe we could try one of your characters on the typewriter app again?      I want to write a story about unicorns and typewriters fighting dragons. Only if your dragons help you stick to 10  exactly . Also, if you promise with your right hand on the laptop like the Brownie Promise. That way you remember it.      Can I make up a Brownie Promise for unicorns? I promise to fight mean typewriters and not let them eat clouds. And I promise to stay up ALL NIGHT if they need me to.      That’s a wonderful promise, love. Now, anyone ready to write this on the typewriter app or shall we use Excel’s “cloud destruction” table?      I think we need a "cloud" font so the table looks like real clouds.      Oh, alright, then we’re moving into typography territory.

So did I! The ending was wild — I needed a minute. I was watching it with my cousin and she got so worked up she spilled her tea on her Blundells Ale cover. Rather annoying isn't it? The amount of work they give us. I was up late last night transcribing yet another interview and it just never seems to stop.      I feel you, darling. That’s too bad. I was going to suggest a group walk this afternoon if you’re feeling up to it. It's the only way to get out of the house for a bit, honestly. It's supposed to be modern and eco-friendly. But of course, the old part of the town, where we all live, just keeps rising in price. It’s a bit mad really.      It’s the same everywhere. One minute you’re walking past terraced houses, the next they're gone and it's some development with pre-fab kitchens. I tried to tell the agent that today, but he didn’t have time for any of it. Rather annoying really, am I right?      Yeah, I mean, it’s not like it’s the end of the world, is it? But I can understand how it would drive you a little mad.      Look, I’ve got a job sorting through a bunch of old transcripts—mind-numbing, honestly. It’s like I haven’t left the office all week.      What’s the project called again? You were managing one of those open-air language café things, weren’t you?      Aye, and you were at the musical in Shaftesbury Avenue—was it  Les Mis ?      Oh right, yes. I played Enjolras—had them fitting a crown on the wrong side of my head for a month. Totally worth it.      You were mad good, luv. I mean, the kind of mad good that makes you think, “Here’s a lad with some major stars ahead of him.”

Rather annoying isn’t it? I mean I think they’re trying to make people think it’s real but it’s got the most unrealistic ending.      I know what you mean. Time to time. Though some of the older lads I teach, they’re obsessed with roles in blockbusters. “I want to act in a Bond film,” they say, “or be in the new Marvel film.”

Rather annoying this, having to pull over every so often for fuel.
