Enexpected lass passed away, you know.      Aye, was quite tragic. We don’t talk about it much anymore, but I hope he’s holding up. He’s doing alright now, probably with some support or the other.      Support?  Sighs  I had t’do the same when my go was really on the edge. It's not talked about enough, lad. You sure? It’s not a weakness.      I know, Nanny. I just sometimes get overwhelmed with school and all that.      Aye, that’s to be expected. But if you ever feel down, talk to them! It’s better than keepin all that to yourself.      Right lass, it always helps to talk. And we’re here for that lad, no doubt about it.      Aye, speaking of support—this colander, last one had a tea-cake go, didn’t it?

Right, lads, here we go — new laptop, brand spanking fresh outta the box. Fingers crossed it don’t crash within five minutes like me last one. This time I've gone for proper specs, ain’t no £200 dicky thing as before.      Got eeny weeny passive cooling fan? Or one o' them big boys that's as loud as a jet engine? A lot o' students buy one too powerful but then wonder why it makes tea noises.      Nah, nah, it's the mid-power, but with a proper SSD drive... like, decent enough for art editing and not blowing me head off the first night I try to edit something like Photoshop My turkey dinner.      Can it run Tenet or ain't I getting DMC'd by my mates in the garden? Half my phone photos now are just me saying: "Boys, I gone and downloaded a film with a helicopter in it!"      Nah, you'll be fine. Just don't download over 50MB of content without a plan—personally I still use the 1995 internet as it is. Ten seconds for a YouTube thumbnail to load: treasured memory.      Tell me about it. My nan still uses dial-up, but least she's got a stable connection. One time her broadband cut out and she sent me a letter on the internet ‘cos email didn’t work, and the ISP was someone called BT.      That's classic. Me I had a Windows 98 rig at uni. Boot up time of forever, but at least no updates to download every second. Kinda about to miss Steve Ballmer's ghost haunting the task bar.      Ronseal! Going retro with Windows 10 and it still does updates when I ain't looking, like that time I left for a walk and came back to a tiled screen. Like a screensaver meets a landmine.      I dunno, I still stick to my trusty Chrome. Runs everything off Websites陉 Except Steam, but that's on another laptop—my “gaming” machine, which is a Raspberry Pi with a bit o' magic.      If you want to talk about real computing, though, you gotta go back to MacBooks. Me box might be Windows-based, but all my art goes final on a Mac. There's this weird European thing I'm doing with Procreate and Wacom... it’s a bit like poetry with pressure-sensitive tools.      Pressure-sensitive... my only pressure sensitive is if I touch the ring of my lager, it always falls over.

Rather skip the new barista café up the road, don't you think? I mean, they’re all over the place now, same old shtick with the overpriced flat whites and over-hyped “artisan” everything.      Yeah, I agree. But this bistro is different, isn't it? I mean, they actually   seem   like they’ve put real thought into the menu. I liked the beetroot and feta salad, and the queso was   actually   reasonable for a place like this.      Oh, don't get me wrong — I like the vibe of it, honestly. A bit more community-driven than the usual tourist traps. It's like they're trying to establish roots here, you know? I just feel like more places need to do that, especially after the pandemic.      It's funny you mention the pandemic. I was talking to a friend earlier this week about how a lot of people lost their sense of identity during that time, you know? With no routines, no commutes, no shared spaces — it’s like, who are we supposed to be if we don’t have all that?      That’s such a good point… I reckon it's why so many people are falling back into old habits – addiction, overspending, emotional eating – because it's easier to fall back into something familiar rather than figure out   who you want to be  .      Absolutely. I mean, someone recently told me they stopped meditating because they felt like they just couldn't cope with the silence anymore. Like, it   forced   them to be with themselves too much. I get it, honestly.      That makes me think of the   dreams  , though. Not the nighttime kind, but the   life   kind. I've met so many younger people who are just so confident, so   aware   of what they want — and others, not so much. Like, the pressure to have it all figured out by 25 is ridiculous. You're 24 and you're   supposed   to know what you want from life?      Right? Some people still want to be  comfortable , not necessarily  excited . Don't go chasing a dream just because you think it’s what you're meant to do. I think people confuse  passion  with  performance .      So true. I mean, I used to be one of those people who believed that if you truly gave your heart to something — like, yoga or fitness or whatever — it would magically transform your life. I did all that for years and it was good, kind of, but it's always been more about   self-image  .

So did you get the tickets for the Dorset Steam Fair yet, Gran? I saw it’s on next weekend, and I thought we could all go together as a family!      Tickets? Oh yes, I did! I rang the box office on Thursday, and the gentleman was very helpful. Right nice sort, he was. Kept apologising for the prices, mind — said they’ve gone up a tenner this year!      Ten pounds? That’s quite a hike, innit! I remember when I used to pop along for the day with the lads from the care home, and it cost you barely a fiver! Still, the fair’s always lovely. I miss the tea bar — still got the outdoor seats, though? The one near the fun fair?      Oh yes, love, the little grassy patch by the steam engines. They put out breakfasts and teas all day — proper cups with saucers — and the cakes, the scones, you remember them? Rich and thick with clotted cream! The man at the ticket office did mention they’ve got a ramp up near that area, so it’s all good for you, Joan, since you can’t manage the steps.      That’s very good of them – very good indeed. I’ve not been for a while, but the last time I went, I thought to myself, “This fair was built for people like me! All the toilets and the restrooms, not full of steps and suspicious carpeting!” Thank the good Lord for that!      I was just telling you earlier, actually, I’ve been thinking about buying a place in Bournemouth long-term. I’m finally saving up! But the landlords here — they keep saying property prices are bouncing back and not to worry. Honestly, I think they just want a bigger deposit out of me!      Oh, well you shouldn’t listen to that lot — they'll tell you anything for a bloody quid. I remember when I used to rent near Christchurch all those years back, and that was nothing like what it is now.      Ah yes, and the rent back then would buy a house now with a bit left over for the cat food! I remember your old man had this cat called Tiddles, didn’t he, Frank? Always had a habit of sitting in the middle of the hallway and waiting for the milk.      Oh heavens, yes! And after I gave him belly rubs, he used to start putting his paws on the furniture and knocking everything over.

Rather chilly this evening, isn't it? That north wind cuts straight through you. Mind if I put on a warming?      I’m more than happy, Eileen. I’d say a little heat wouldn’t go amiss. Look at George—  gestures to the teenager under a blanket on the sofa  ,  not even a full inch out of his phone .      I’m just transcription facts, alright? Got that assignment due Monday, Miss Ward. Miss, what d'you think of this whole “Z-day” thing on the news?      You mean the frozen forecasts for next week? Sounds like a snowpocalypse. I told my class if we get that much snow, I’ll be posting exams on TikTok.      I’m not laughing, Darcy, I’m sad. A world where kids spend their evenings scrolling about snow and forget how to breakfast, no doubt. I remember mastering ice cricket after a good fall at Kendal.      Ken, give it a rest—those were simpler times. The world’s moved on, and whether we like it or not, I’m seeing snow flurries from this flicker of warmth, let alone the bloody forecast.      Oh, then put your “new world” –?      –right, because nothing’s more modern than the weather. NowSpeaking of moving, what did you think of the vicar’s sermon at church on Sunday? He mentioned something about “plans beyond us” and “developing in chaos.”      That’s floring, is it not? What’s next, tea ceremonies under the church pews?      I found it quite profound, all things considered. You can’t take this job or thar house for granted. Going are life are like weather—unpredictable, but not without meaning.      Poetic stuff, Ma’am. Although, personally, I’m more worked up about tomorrow’s event at the pottery studio. I tried making a cup once and ended up with a jagged side and a hole in the base. He called it 'modern abstract expressionism'.      Hmm. You think you'd get a nice tuppence for that nonsense in gothic shops on the coast if you tried.      I just started penning a short piece about the lives of bakers in the Lake District. It's all puffing, rising, crumbling—like roles in life. And yes, I even got photos from a third-gen bakery in Harrogate over Twitter.      Really? Now that’s something I could read at a staff meeting. “The Rise and Fall of the Flour Economy”—replace Dickens, we’re done.

So do you lot remember when we had our last tooth check-ups? I know Ashaad’s mum said he’s got to go to the dentist after school today.      Yeah, he said he was scared because the dentist gave him a bit of a telling off for not flossing.      That  is  important, you know. Flossing at least once a week is a must. A lot of kids don’t do it and end up with unpleasant surprises.      I do! My teacher was saying the other day that people who don’t floss often get grumpy teeth, whatever that even means.      That’s probably someone’s attempt at making it sound fun! I remember my left molar used to be really sensitive – I had to go in for a root canal. Pretty unpleasant. You take it for granted until something goes wrong.      I hated going to the dentist when I was little. I used to cry when they told me to open wide. Also, the drilling sound is  weird .      Yeah, it used to scare me too, until one time the dental nurse sat me on her knee while we watched Tangled on the ceiling. That was a lightbulb moment. Humour – it’s a healer!      Did you have to get the numb stuff in your cheeks?      Oh yes. And then you can’t taste your food for ages. My first chicken curry post-numb was a disaster.      I think Ashaad said something happened at his hearing test too. Something about not hearing a certain sound.      He said about half the class didn’t hear the bleep in the highest octave. The lady said it might be because some of them listen to music too loud on their earphones.      That  is  the most common reason for young hearing issues. Parents – we have to be the ones to set the limits, I’m afraid.      I sort of remember being at hearing tests when I was in primary school. Yellow headphones with weird bleeps and whistles.      That sounds familiar. You had to raise your hand the moment you heard the sound. I remember your brother couldn’t raise his hand at all.      Because it was behind the box! He was arguing the whole time with the technician.      I think those were the best parts of the hearing tests.      Alright, but while we’re on the subject of school—how’s everyone feeling about moving up into secondary?

So did I! The turkey was amazing.      It was, wasn't it? I got the recipe from my aunt. She said your mum used to make something like it.      Yeah, my nan would make a spiced one with chestnuts. Do you remember?      Oh my God, yes! We always used to fight over the chestnut bits. A total mess.      Still is, but worth it.      So, what's the plan this week? I want to start prepping some of my shift plans for next month, but also need to go to the vet with Indie. He's been coughing up hairballs like it's going out of fashion.      Ugh, yes, I feel that. I think he's just getting older, but it’s still gross to watch. I've been trying to tidy this place up, though — in between editing my social media copy.      Managing the chaos?      You know it. My flat looks like a DIY shop exploded. I’m never going to make it to the open house viewing for that flat near Canterbury.      Wait, seriously? You told me last week you were going to rent out your spare room and move somewhere cheaper.      I was! But now I’m thinking maybe I’ll just wait until June when that developer finishes those new apartments near the station. Prices are supposed to drop.      You’re definitely waiting out the market, then. It's wild up and down here.      Oh, it most certainly is. I’m just hoping the goldfish doesn’t die while I’m stressing over mortgages and whatnot. Speaking of which, are you and Josh still housing his sister up for the winter?      Yes, unfortunately. She passed her exams, so now it's a month of celebrating and probably being quite noisy.      You poor thing. We had to do that with my cousin as well. Her band rehearsals were louder than the whole construction site next door.      I swear, this entire generation thinks the ceiling is made of bubble wrap. But life goes on.      True. I just miss living alone. Although it was lovely last week when my parents came over. We all watched that old tape from your conference in Bristol in '09.      Oh right, the one where I overcooked the beans and forgot my notes.      I remember that! We were so young then. You were all romantic and kissed me on the cheek after the mixer.      You said I tasted like baked beans.

Rather do a half bottle of burgundy rather than a full one. I know it's supposed to breathe first... but I rather fancy one glass each now and more later. Not sure what the wine is, though. I don’t remember the label. Look like a continental one. Just like the place was burgundy on the label.      Yes, I think it is. Look like they don’t clean the bottles before they put them in the box. I’ve had quite a few of these, interesting as it is. Put wine in the wine cellar when you're in, but the rest of the meat... frozen.      A bit much, isn’t it, only wine in the wine cellar? My turkey, Christmas turkey, I still remember left it in the wine cellars to mature for two or three days, and I think it turned out very well.      The last breakfast, no doubt about that. Well, here’s to the wine at least, you know, and we can follow the rest of the story in the morning over full breakfast. I mean, do tell, tell me, what are we up to in Prague next week?      We were going to book a room at the municipal building, and it turns out it got booked out. So – cheek it: got tickets for the Municipal Gallery because they were on the website. You know the deal: if you go through their website, they give you press passes at the door, and then you just walk in full house. Perfect.      That's oddly clever. You can’t just walk into a museum in London these days with a press pass – no matter your age, or how many decades about you.      Interesting touch the municipal library as well. It’s absolutely full and not part of that arrangement. I mean, it is a classic building in its own right, but for the price you’d pay for anything here, it's exceptional.      Let's talk about it again in the morning, you know. After a full breakfast. As good as we can manage in this part of the world with lunches delivered a couple of days ago. Now, the recent planning application for the solar panels around town – how did the proposal go?      Oh, it was approved – just barely. I think the planners were trying to be accommodating. That bloke on the council said something like, “We have to future-proof the conservation area,” and it was amazing how many local people had objections anyway.

So do you think an online learning platform for case studies in moving images could really take off here in Australia? I mean, the education sector is pretty conservative, isn’t it?      It's probably got its challenges, but I also think there’s a gap for something like that. Teachers in secondary and tertiary education are  constantly  on the hunt for engaging, digital-ready content—especially around film and media. A lot of them would love more visual and social learning resources, but they just don’t know where to start sourcing quality material.      Right—and if we could make it not only educational but shareable on social networks too, that could be a big win. I’ve been thinking about how platforms like MySpace and YouTube have reshaped communication and social interaction, especially for younger audiences. Why not harness that for education?      Exactly. Film case studies could help educators address communication skills, cultural awareness, even ethical thinking. Like, using a doco or a narrative film, and then breaking it down into modules: group activities, discussion prompts, videos, and shared reflections via forums or even social networking groups?      I like that. What about using Facebook or LinkedIn groups for community building? Imagine a teacher sharing a mini-case study with students and then getting them to post their interpretations—maybe even collaborating with other classes across the country.      Yeah, and not just for students. Educators could use the platform to share best practices, collaborate on curriculum design, even co-teach using shared case study content. That way, the platform isn’t just a repository of lessons—it’s a hub for continued professional growth.      That’s solid. So, how would we structure the content? Maybe partner with film festivals or local filmmakers who can contribute case studies from their real projects? We could also integrate that data with learning analytics—so teachers can track student progress and engagement.      Oh, that’s a good idea. Parents would love to see where their kids are at. And think about the development angle—the way you’ve run your tech startups in the past, you could probably scale this up with minimal overhead. Just a website, some cloud storage, and a few smart plugs into social media APIs.      Absolutely. From an entrepreneur's point of view, it’s cost-effective and has real scalability potential. We just need to make sure the technical team can support user growth—and design the platform to be intuitive.

I can't believe we've never done this before. Just a proper seaside day. Honestly, it's ridiculous. We teach about the coast, the tides, even superstitions surrounding the sea, and we've only owned a house 15 minutes from the beach for three years. Right? I feel like we're both very 'academic theory' people and not as much 'physical experience' people. That's a bit harsh, isn't it? I was in Cornwall as a kid. My dad was obsessed with collecting seaglass when he was younger. Oh, I had no idea. He never mentioned it, but the glint in that old box in the hallway at home, I get it now. Seaglass is like bottle money, isn't it? It is in some places. But he probably just liked the idea of something raw and ancient, washed up. Yeah... I used to live in Norfolk, and I remember walking along the coast path near Hunstanton. The North Sea was so different from here—you can feel it being aggressive. I know what you mean. The Channel here is calmer, like more predictable. It's watching it during a storm that would have been terrifying. Mate, I got knocked off my feet by a wave once on the Hunstanton slipway. All that salt in the phone. You don't say. Lost irreplaceable photos, I'm guessing? Precisely. Rovers game, a failed relationship, my uncle at 60—gone in a split second under a wall of seawater. I mean, I know the coast can be romantic—but the sea is chaotic. Not just a backdrop for your holiday photos. Exactly. People talk about the sea in romantic terms, like ‘endless horizons’ and ‘ocean of emotions’. But the sea could swallow a thousand metaphors any afternoon. That's what makes it so powerful. We study it, as if we can control or predict it, but the reality is—it just keeps doing its thing. Reminds me of something my old head of department told me early in my job. He said life was like the sea. Didn't he? Goes with the flow. "No, he said," you don't have to control it to live in it. Just don't get so close to the rocks." True to his heart, he drowned two years later walking the Cumbrian coast. That's... That's a heavy quote. But kind of beautiful, in an absurd way.

So do you lot reckon this whole "clean girl aesthetic" is just another one of those cycles that kills like... actual style?      Honestly, I think it’s more about minimalism than a fashion statement at this point. Like, the key is being low-maintenance but still putting effort in. I saw an influencer last week who just wore neutral tones and had this ultra-organised gym bag—it felt so...  calm .      Yeah, but don’t get me started on it. I taught a primary class the other day and one of the kids said he couldn’t draw a fashion trend because it had to be made "without messy stuff". What even is that?      My nan would’ve called that being "proper tidy", but this is more than just picking laces out of your shoes and curling your eyelashes. It feels like it’s selling something very specific—especially with all those white T-shirts and linen jumpsuits.      And the oversized everything hides, you know, bulges—and I mean not just size, but like biceps or abs if someone had them. It’s almost antifit, even.      It’s funny because only a few years ago we were all buying extra-strong skinny jeans from Marks & Spencer. Now it's like: “No, no, no, just  blend in  into a cloud-like tomboy look.”      I blame Kim Kardashian for that. Like she flipped the world on its head and now everyone’s trying not to stand out. But then we end up with everyone dressing the same and it's just as bad as being told what to wear in school.      I do like the practicality side of it, though. No more high heels for me. I’ve switched to Danish loafers and I can barely hear myself walk. Less sound, more productivity. My boss  loves  it.      On the flip side, though, don’t you think it’s all a bit... boring? I’m not waiting till I’m a grown-up to stop being flamboyant. Even in the classroom with lunches and lego, the kids have such strong opinions about what's "cool". I try not to kill it with their imagination by goading them on.      That’s one of the reasons I started liking sustainable fashion again. Going back to basics—like high street brands that make you feel like you’ve made a special choice, even if it’s just a £20 T-shirt.

Mum, I just got my college results in. I got into that photography course in Brighton!      Oh, really? That’s brilliant, love! I knew you’d get in — you’re so talented. Do they do lots of film work as well as digital?      Yeah, there’s a module on both. I really want to learn how to develop my own prints. I’ve only done stuff on my phone so far.      Well, you know you can use the darkroom at the community centre when you're home, don’t you? I remember you fiddling about with it last summer.      Yeah, thanks. I miss that place.      So, what’s the course start date then? I know you’ve been panicking about the move.      October 2nd. I’ve got my room in dorms sorted, but I’m kinda scared.      Scared? You?! Come on, you’re the one who would climb that cliff in Bexhill if someone dared you.      Well, it’s different. It’s not like hanging with friends in the park… it’s proper living by yourself.      Yeah, but it’s also a chance, you know? You'll grow up a bit, learn to make your own decisions. You’ll still come back to see us, won’t you?      Oh yes. I’m not getting rid of you that easily. I’ll definitely visit on the weekends.      Good. Anyway, speaking of growing up, did you finish reading  The Song of Achilles  yet?      Oh, I loved it. I’ve already started the sequel. I’m trying to read more this year. English teacher said to do 20 books before the new term.      That’s ambitious, but I know you’ll cope. Do you prefer fiction or non-fiction?      Definitely fiction. I like escaping into other lives. Non-fiction feels like… work.      I get that. Even I remember when I used to read like that. Before the dayjob took over my life.      What was your college like, Mum? I’ve never really asked.      It was ages ago — 1988. I studied secretarial science. Not so exciting by today’s standards, I know.      But you’ve had a proper job ever since. I think that’s pretty cool.      Right back at you. You're going to make me sound ancient now, aren’t you?      Yeah, but I love you just as much.      You cheeky. Oh, by the way, have you seen that new comedy on YouTube?

Rather annoying lot, them builders. I'm sat in me own house and I can 'ear ‘em like I got the seats at Wembley. It's not even football season yet, but they're shouting like it's half-time at a derby.      Oh, Andrew, I’ve heard eeny weeny about the builders. It was the baby birds that woke me up all last week—they sounded like they were hollering for their mummy and daddy every ten minutes. I swear one of them fell out the window and landed in me teacup.      You're telling me! I only came round to sort out the application form for that new job in Solihull, but I haven’t even got to the form yet. Ten minutes I’ve been here and already shouted at a cockerel, turned down a piece of shabby fence, and got into an argument about 3D printing!      Aye, what’s that 3D printing malarkey? I told the man, why would you want to print a wall when a bit of brick and a pint of cement would do the job ten times as quick and proper?      Oh dear, did he not mention it’s for a little boy who needed a new toy – a duck with a fairly long bill and webbed feet? Very clever, the lad printed it in black and white and all! Should’ve been brighter, Mark said, but the boy’s proud of what he got.      That’s just a taster for the sort of thing they’re chuckin at me these days. I want to teach again, but all the head teachers are looking for now is about problem children and “multi-educational strategies.” I’m just a man who can count to 30 and know that not all kids behave the same way after a lardy dinner.      Pooh, education’s gone to pieces. When I was at me secondary school it was a matter of discipline and a clean blackboard. Not some fancy-pants “arranged seating” and words that mean nothing. And don’t get me started on houses and “hollow walls.” Some of them young builders think they know something about craftsmanship!      Oh go on then, don’t be like that. They did at least finish the line in the garden that had all the mud from last winter. And what your builders didn’t finish at the back, the 3D printer’s going to help you with, dear.

Rather than going out and doing something fun weekend, I have to drive all the way to Glasgow to pick up... Well, my daughter she’s coming to live here permanently now! Finally, someone decent in this house. I don’t know quite what to expect, truth be told.      Oh eeny dear! That’s fantastic news, isn’t it? Someone young and lively in the place? I mean obviously I love you to pieces, but this house has felt like a museum for far too long! When is she arriving?      Next month. Apparently, she’s had a hard time getting everything sorted out with her visa and all that. I keep thinking to myself, "Why do they make this so complicated?" Just bring the child! She’s left London, you know – finally made the right decision, if you ask me.      Living in London was far too distracting for a girl her age. I’m glad to hear she’s making a change. What sort of job has she got lined up, then?      Good question, and that’s the one thing she hasn’t told me yet. She says I don’t need to worry about it and she’ll tell me "when the time is right". Sounds like fun, doesn’t it? She got herself a room at the back of the house all furnished, and I barely had a say in it. I didn’t even know there was a wardrobe that high up! She’s got a very strange sense of space.      That’s also suspicious. Is she just a bit of a clutterbug or are we in for the full modern interior design?      Can’t say I like it, but it looks clean, and I’m not about to argue with the touch-up she did on the walls. Honestly, you know me – I’m not fussy. I just want a bit of peace to do my reading and for someone to keep the guest bathroom clean. I did not expect to have to clean the loo for any teenager, I can tell you that!      Eeny, you didn’t have to clean the loo for me either, but I keep the whole place running fairly well, thank you. You just remember, you’re not alone in this place anymore. She’s your daughter, your life, your chaos now.      Ugh, I’m not worried about the chaos, I’m worried what your lot will make of her.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, just listened to it on the radio last weekend. Never mind whether it was pro or anti, it was all such a tangle of figures and promises. Not sure I'll ever understand half of it fully.      Got eeny idea when I try to read about it either. But if it all goes through, what's aye gonna do? My flat just over the border in Berwick. Not sure how that’d go down if it suddenly wasn't in the UK anymore.      Well, I reckon you'd get a duplicate passport, even if it made no sense. Still, the real debate seems to be among politicians like actors at a festival. You’ve met enough to know how they like their dramatic bits.      Aye, I think the world listens up when you're making a speech and forgets when breakfast's due. But I've been thinking more about work in all this. I had an interview last week, you remember?      Oh yes, at that new uni over in Canterbury, right? How’d it go?      Fair enough. The panel were all real deadly serious, like they were marking my thesis again. But it was a good shot. They seemed impressed – at least one of them laughed at least, so that’s a start. One of the staff there was mentioning they want someone with a bit more “political awareness” these days. Dunno what that means exactly.      Sounds like they just want someone who can discuss it at dinner with students without looking lost.      Exactly what I thought – but I suppose it’s better to be in on the act than absent. Although I’m not certain the job is mine yet. Still waiting on an email.      Aye, it always does take ages. I remember applying for my first lectureship back in Manchester. Took three months to hear back and I feared they’d forgotten my name was on the list.      Not waiting long enough for me. As good as being stuck on a constant Moodle update.      Gracious, I’ve had enough of those in my day. But something else caught my ear – you mentioned your daughter goin' on that trip to the countryside soon?      Yeah, she’s off to stay with her gran in Gloucestershire. She says it’s supposed to be good for her to get away from the screen and the usual clutter.

Rather annoying isn't it when you're trying to build a mousetrap game for the kids and it comes with bits and pieces from China or something and you're not even sure how it fits together.      Not quite as simple as the kind of things you used to get in the past when eeny every single bit had to do with the mousetrap and it all had to be in a line with the cheese and stuff.      So what are you trying to do, dump someone in a box at the end?      Well no, well we're not getting that far yet, are we.      What I found when I was in America like well My turkey came here for Thanksgiving you know and left again on the Ten o'clock shuttle from the airport, I mean he was gone in the morning and came back with Black Friday dress clothes and stuff. So do you think I should go for the used car or just keep the bus for a bit longer?      Honestly, it really depends on what you’re going for. Nana, could you take a look at this maths paper for me? It's our GCSE prep and I got stuck on some of the algebra questions.      Course I’ll have a peek, lad. I still remember the old system—numbers, squaws, and logarithms, not 'alf as nice as dottering about graphs and whatnot.      Alright, Tom, pass it 'ere.  Right , let me see. What’s troubling you?      It’s question five, the one about linear simultaneous equations. I tried subbing one into the other, but I keep gettin’ the same x-value an’ it ain’t matchin’ the book’s answer.      Hmmm… right, so if you’ve got 2x + 3y = 12 and x - y = 3, the trick is to rearrange the second one first. Like, x = y + 3. Then you substitute  that  into the first equation. Let’s try workin’ it out together.      Oh, right! So like, 2 times plus 3y equals 12?      That’s the ticket! Now, expand that out. Let’s see.      Rovers were doing a right good job in the first half last Saturday, weren’t they, Tom? I thought  they  looked better than most people about half-time. Tom, come back t’the maths— nearly  got it! If you do 2 times , that’s 2y + 6, right? Then 2y + 6 + 3y = 12.      So that’s 5y + 6 = 12. Then subtract six, 5y = 6. Wait, so y is one point two?      That's it! Then plug that backs into the second equation for x and you’ll be right as rain. Bit messy with decimals, but better than quadratics later on, eh?      Blimey, Tom, you’ll be a doctor or an engineer next once you finish all that—end up payin’  us  to live with you!      Now, don’t be going above y’rself, child! You be a maths examiner and no more!

Right, who’s ready for dinner, love? I’ve just got the macaroni cheese in the oven... got to let it bubble for ten minutes.      I’m  super  hungry, Mummy! We had Pirates topic at school today! Rather skip to the part when they actually shackled him, do you?      Oh, come on, James—let’s not make more of it! You were having a perfectly reasonable disagreement over maritime law. Not to mention a bit of a temper at the time.      Right, temper? I’ll say. I was   telling   him not to sail that damn thing with that motor from Jeddah before the coastline changed again, but did he listen? No, he just said, “I'm not moving the boot  y chase  , Stan.” That's what came out of his mouth.      Stan, listen—      "Booty chase My dear!" I said,   booty chase   is not a brand of motorboat, you Oliver. But he was already halfway out the marina with an empty bottle of port and a first-aid kit full of antiseptic wipes.      And I'm the one who hides the bottle?!      Good grief, I thought I was over the worst of it being in Saudi Arabia—until I started seeing the land of ungodly early grief. You’d think as an EFL teacher, I’d have learned something in all those years. But no—he showed me how to say "unknown, and/or death," in Indonesian.      All that time in the east trying to win battles with language, and your greatest failure was never learning what someone means when they ask,   “Do you like a rush of blood to the head?”        Or the real one being:   “Do you speak your colleague’s passport?”   I about blocked his number after he asked that. But touch the soul, Jane—how did it feel, being hauled into that frosty cold office and told, unironically, that the kingdom found your   coding techniques   troubling?      Coding?! He taught them the finer points of surfacing meaning through the   eleventh affirmative  ! You must have told one too many good queens and yellow lemons.      No, no, that was the   eleventh glass  , Ronald.      But the best part was when the Coast Guard came for him, and he had   dental magazines   floating off the boat like confetti. He tried to present one to the young officer as a gift. It said,  “The Essence of Smile Crafting in Persistent Cases of Malodor” —and this lad looked at it like it was a bribe.      That’s when my jaw dropped like a   cigarette in a tea cup  —he handed it to the kid like it was a gift to the Red Cross.

Rather skip the hotel bar and go to the truffle place. I've had enough euros squintin' at menus and white wine sheers. If I looked like a goon, I wouldn’t be looking like this in the first place.      So how're the bills? Gas and elec?      I had to turn the heating off on the coldest day of the year. Colder them this.      I'm paying for the microwave meal and the George Forman, but that's it.      You and the George Forman. Still swear you won’t eat anything else.      It's efficient. The lot of us. You, me, Nana, Aunt Carol – it's the great equaliser of cooked food.      I miss your mother’s proper Yorkshire pudding and gravy.

Rather skip the new coins and go for the old ones, do you?      Oh, I don’t know—new coins are shiny, and I like a bit of a sparkler! Got me a full £20 spread the other day—  Lidl   ran it for a day and then it vanished like sunshine after a bad twitch moment. Still reckon it was worthwhile—saved me a trip to the A & P.      Trouble is, you don’t   get   sparklers if you’ve nothing to buy. Not when you chase the coins but the sweets. Had to fetch chips three times last week, just because I fancied a bait and switch supply of sugar.      Just keep the coins somewhere safe though. I dropped mine and boy, they flew like bolts from a pastry pusher I used to work with. Living with cash was far harder—used to vanish when you weren’t looking and you’d be stuck with drive-thru horror stories, you ever looked for a fiver in your spare sock and got the sock stained with sauce and fish?      That’s a familiar one I can relate with. Got one from last week—outhouse, old-school design—used to be municipal, but now it’s all services. You ever notice how the buses are held back by roads, and sometimes it just builds up until you’re late and the apple pie has already gone through the first batch?      And toilets—well, what someone said in one of the   ANON   articles? It just goes oddly sour when you’re floring the floor yourself. Or trying to.      I don’t   get   it—I flise the place every day.      Oh, but let’s not be too gloomy—you know that new   Reading   building up near the cemetery? It’s all copper, like someone thought the whole construction was a bit like a brass sundial and just dished the whole strip into something shiny. I mean, it looked like you just waiting for someone to stick a bell on it and ring it as though it were a clock with lunches delivered right on time with your steak and chips extra.      Then again, if you started watching the   plane crash   on your own, you risk getting cut off at the kerb line in the morning, between the siren box and the main road. Road rage is a funny thing—it only takes one to hurt and then the rest of the hours just fall apart with bellyache and a third glass of tea that went over the cooling line faster than the catering suggestion at ANON’s suppliers.

Okay, I swear the art teacher’s just out to get us. I had her in Year 7 and she got annoyed because I put glitter in my clay sculpture and I got a C.      Oh my god, that’s the same one as us. Oh no, did he get your essay about  Macbeth  or did you fake a dent in the paper again to skip it?      Pass. He’s like  “I can see you’re avoiding the deeper themes of ambition and power, Miss,”  as if I’ve been hiding in the loo doing crime. I’m just not a Shakespeare fan.

So do you think nuns are like the Matrix, grans? I mean, like, they’re like... in the real world or something?      Oh, love, I dunno much about the Matrix. Not really my sort of film. But nuns are like volunteering to be like that. It’s kinda the same idea but flipped.      I live with Grans, so I pick and I pick! The little boy—Speaker_3—tugs at his plate, smacking a spoon against his bowl. Speaker_2 lets out a soft, distracted laugh as she hides a roll in the pocket of her cardigan to give to the toddler later.      Yeah, but listen—what I mean is, like, both the Matrix and nuns are about... controlling your reality. The Matrix shows how people can be trapped in a simulation, and nuns—?      Right, right, but don’t go mixing the two up too much. Nuns are all about faith and helping others, not machines! Though, I suppose some people out there think scientology is also suspicious. Like a real cult or something.      Ugh, is it a cult?      Not sure, but your dad spoke to a friend who did some training years ago and said it was the most weird thing he’d ever done. All about aliens and thulians and stuff. Supposedly it helped him lose weight but that’s just a bonus for the price you pay!      Parents were total hippies, so it makes sense. But, I mean, I dunno, is RELIGION just all about control? Like, if you believe in something, you’re just letting it control you?      Hmm. That's a big question for a teenager, innit? From what I go by, I think it's more about  comfort  than control. Like me and your grans, we always go to Mass on Sundays when we can. It’s like having something steady in the world. Especially with a toddler around— chuckles —you need a bit more structure in life, I think.      But like… what if you go all your life not believing anything, and then you die and there's nothing?

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode about the Queen and the internet scandal was wild.      Ugh, I’m so behind on it. Oh, your teacher was one of those  "he was a victim of his times!"  people. As if that absolves everything. Also, moving topic: do you think I’m too young to do ballet? My friend’s starting a beginner’s class, and it’s either that or I end up watching  Bridgerton  all night again.      Why do you ask like you’re thirty? Time isn’t what your legs think you are—it’s what you make them bend to.      Ugh, that was profound. Do you talk like that on consulting job reports too or do you hold it in?

Right, I just wanted to say, this whole Istria thing is bonkers. We’ve only been like... three hours and I’m already half-soaked from sweating in the back seat. I mean, do we have to do the whole “we’re trying to live off this travel budget” thing all the time or are we allowed to treat ourselves to a festival or something?      There’s a festival in Pula in two weeks. Klapa music. You could say it’s the folk version of a European Sons of Anarchy-type vibe—meets sea shanty.      Klapa and Sons of Anarchy? You really are setting the bar for weird comparisons today.      And don’t even get me started on the wines.

So do you lot remember when we were all at Fran’s house last summer and her nan walked in when we were playing "Truth or Dare"?      Oh my god, yes! That was mad. One of us dared another person to film their partner giving them a hand job while someone else recorded on their phone. And then we were all just like   "Don’t panic, don't panic!"        Yeah! That was too much. Everyone was cracking up, except   Fran’s nan  , obviously! She walked in like halfway and just said, “You don’t say things like that in my house,” and then left.      What shocked me was how Fran stayed calm like that. I would’ve screamed first!      I know, right? I was the one filming, and I literally dropped the phone. It fell in the pizza box and rolled into Domino breakfast, no joke. I had to film with a bit in my hand panicking.      Oh, I remembah the video actually. One bloke was doing it, and another had to shout out rules: “No talking, no moving, no fingers. And only ten seconds max, or the next person takes it.”      Was that Tony from sixth form?      Yeah, that was him. He timed it with his phone and everything. It was like a whole method or something. And we were all shushing him because he kept going on about  "analectal efficiency"  or whatever.      [laughing] He’d been reading   "How to Please a Woman in 10 Steps"   or something like that.      I think he picked the book up from his mum’s vibes. Honestly, you could tell he was practicing.      And after we finished, we all just stared at the video and were like, “Is that…” [mimics whispering] “…allowed to be funny?”      Then we tried to rewatch it later but the video had gotten corrupted. Some bloke had taken it onto their phone and tried to “enhance the quality” and it just exploded into green pixels.      Still, we named the video  “Tony’s 10 Second Anal Dream”  and played it in the common room at college. People were either laughing or horrified.      Honestly, I think Fran let us stay at her house that night just so she could see it again to prove it wasn’t a dream.      Aye, I’m not lying—keeping that one in the diary. Totally classic.      You know, I think we made our own version of the video last week.

Rather skip the queue for the canteen today, me. That chicken and rice last time ‘ad bits in it, an’ I wasn’t keen on that. I prefer a good ol’ toastie, y’know? Cheese, ham, the lot. I reported it, but you know what happens—nobody replies.      You lot are missing the point of the library. Don’t get it wrong—this is goin’ on your tab if you ask me again. But yeah, brung in, innit.      You know what your problem is, Lew? You take work seriously, but you don’t take yourself. Rest up, feed yourself like a person, and we’ll see if you can still shuffle up on that keyboard later.      Arr, so you think I’m tired, do y’? Well, it’s probably ‘cos y’knew when I last had a proper meal.      You better start taking this seriously, Lew.

So do you lot ever actually get through anything with all this Twitter business?      You mean apart from the fact it's driving half the faculty spare?      Yeah, exactly! One minute we’re putting up resources, the next we're explaining to them how to search for a book on the cat code  not  the one they posted about saying “meow” all day.      Oh, I saw that one. Someone even started a petition to introduce a “meow filter” so the search doesn’t chase it up the pixie dust. Ten-year-olds on Facebook who are seven on LinkedIn, and I think the world is run by an Edmodo echo chamber.      Edmodo? I thought that drowned with a lack of engagement at GCSE. Why is it still floating?      I dunno, maybe it’s like Watergate or Brexit, it just carries on. Though I have to say, the least we’ve got to grief over.      Honestly, watching the number of students confuse Instagram stories with reference guides is like watching a Baptism of Fire. I almost had to take one girl to the reference section and say “this is not TikTok, Silly.”      Oh that girl, she posted in Stories someone said in one of the books “if you don’t know your poison, you definitely don’t know your Rousseau.”      And she replying: “Well he’s a bit romantic but I about blocked his account after he talked about the state of nature like it was an Airbnb.”      I mean, it is a bit like that to some of them. Burgers and bad grammar, no ability to cite a source that wasn’t copied off a student blog.      At least SlideShare is fairly dormant these days. We had to clear up after that one bloke whose entire profile was just lunches and a couple of thesis snippets.      The guy once posted a LinkedIn update saying, “Just hit 500 references on Word—let me know if anyone wants one formatted in APA.”      And we were all like—oh thank God your actual thesis is finished at least.      You think we’d go digital with all this social networking, but to me it’s like the ‘80s when we used to post missing posters for the photocopiers.      Yeah, and now the social network's always copyin’ our ideas faster than the photocopier.

Rather annoying isn't it? I mean, I understand the need for the recording, but it's not like it's the first time we've had to do a consultation on a major project like this.      True, but this one is different—  L  . We're dealing with end-of-life care now, and that tends to bring out   stronger reactions   from the public than most.      Absolutely. We need to make sure the   Business Case   clearly sets out the rationale. We've got to tie the location into the current configuration of local health services. You know, like how the hospices already work with GPs and community nurses.      Yeah, that's a good point. I was just thinking last night—  what if   the public misunderstood the role of the hospice as being a   nursing home   for the elderly? We need to clarify, in the consultation, that this is for active management in end-of-life care, not just a place to   wait out   the final days.      Right—  and   we need to stress the benefits:   improving quality of life  , reducing unnecessary hospital admissions, and relieving pressure on the local health budget. That last part will go down well with the council—they're always looking for cost-effective measures, and with these health budgets being as tight as a   clenched fist  , anything that eases the load will be   welcomed  .      Yes, and we also need to think about   the building itself  . I don't want it to look like a   clinical   facility. More like a home—something welcoming,   calming  , not clinical about it. I was talking to   the architect   the other day—she suggested a   cottage-like   aesthetic, with soft curves and a garden area.      That could work. A lot of hospice clients do better when they feel   calm  , when the environment is peaceful. And as for the   estate agents  , I think waiting till the final site is confirmed is   prudent  .      Definitely. I think we also need to   engage   with the local hospice already in the area. They've got a wealth of go-to information on best practice, and they're   key stakeholders   in this. If we can show them we're not here to compete, but to supplement, we’ll smooth the path for future collaboration.      Agreed—there's   geography   to consider as well. Tunbridge Wells is in the middle of a natural   healthcare hub  , so positioning the project at the crossroads of where the   local services   converge is a   strategic boost  .

Rather skip horror films tbh. They do mental damage. Like proper sticks it in your head for weeks. I got scared out me mind by  The Shining  once, honest. Gave my nan a whike, she was like "I’m not scared of ghosts, but that’s just  weird ".      Well, you heard her—she’s not scared of ghosts, just strange dolls and over-enthusiastic actors pretending like they’re not sleepwalkers.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, all these emails in the evening promising you free trials and ‘limited offers’ when you've barely had time to wind down yet. Just want to know I've got a bed, a decent kitchen to make my tea in, and the heating works. Still, I suppose it's better than staying in a hotel. Used to have to write letters once to arrange a room for a night or two. We had to trust that the post came through. Websites speed everything up, but speed can be a bit of a double-edged sword.      Definitely. Though I think the best part is not wasting time on the phone if you don’t want to.

I usually just order whatever the page recommends. Last time I asked, the takeaway guy said it was "spiced like a My Chemical Romance concert" and I still ended up with a lump of sadness.      Ro, and I think he meant that literally.      Anyway, enough breakfast, um—dinner curry musings. Shane, in your lads, you ever feel like you’re on the windpipe of the world? You’re doing all that to avoid an awkward silence, though. Websites say awkward silence is a sign of bad conversation, but in our house, it’s like a sacred ritual.      That's because go-to topics are usually podcasts about suffocation or why Marvel doesn't make posters like in the old days.      Oh, what your lads, Shane, have you seen the new Suicide Squad? They tried to make those jokes earnest. It’s like hearing your dad laugh at a bad pun over Zoom.      I’m not entirely sure what that means, but I think it’s kind of like my English teacher always explaining words that no one uses anymore. She once said, “arbitrage” was on Google 0.02 times.

So do you reckon we’ll get through the cloud cover once we get onto the M65? The peregrines were flying really low near the reservoir earlier. If you’re on a nudist beach and someone takes a photo without permission, is it a privacy violation or a freedom of expression thing? I had a colleague spend a weekend at a nudist resort doing research for a case.      Ew. I don’t even like sports fields that are muddy. I mean, muddy car parks are worse—why do supermarkets  have  to flood their parking lots after it rains?      Speaking of supermarkets, have you all  seen  the prices for decent avocados lately? We paid seven quid for one last week. It’s like trying to budget on a salary from the 1970s.      Welcome to living in the real world away from the university halls. But if you ask me, real food comes from the allotment, not the supermarket. Although I did manage to get some fresh eggs from Mike’s latest neighbor.      Uncle Gary, did you watch Bear Grylls last night? He slept on a mountain and drank something out of a cowpat. Is that even legal? I reckoned I could’ve done better.

So do you guys actually miss eating meat? I mean, I used to eat it all the time when I worked in the pub, but now I find it so weird I can't even look at a steak without thinking about how it used to be a cow somewhere.      Honestly, I don’t miss it that much, but I do miss the taste. I think it's more about the texture than the actual flavor. I still crave that chewy, meaty bite. Oh, and cheese—I still eat that because dairy wasn't as bad ethically for me.      I get that. I went full vegan a couple months back, so no meat, no dairy, no eggs. Honestly, the hardest part was turkey on Christmas. I just watched my nan’s face when I said I wasn’t eating the main event anymore. Made me feel like the little rebel in the family again.      I still take vitamin B12 tablets. My blood work last time said my levels were low, and I panicked, to be honest. I mean, why would my body be like “oh no, you’ve stopped eating animals, now you have to supplement”?      I think it's more like we’ve been farming domestic animals for so long that our biology sort of evolved alongside meat consumption. But it's also fairly recent, like, in evolutionary terms. It’s not like we need it for survival now.      Right, and then there's the whole animal cruelty aspect. I watched this documentary last week—it was about factory farming. It just felt oddly similar to some of the histories of human oppression. So much control and suffering crowded into tiny spaces. I don't know how anyone can look at that and not walk away different.      Oh, have you seen this new synthetic meat stuff? They call it shmeat, right? Like, cultured in a lab. It’s supposed to look like beef or chicken but without the animal. I think it could be the future if people stop being grossed out by it.      I did see an episode of  Curb Your Enthusiasm  where Larry tries lab-grown meat and gets super annoyed because he can’t tell the difference. But the idea freaks him out so much he can’t finish it. It's funny, but I wonder how soon it'll become the norm.      Honestly, I’m more interested in the environmental angle.

Right, I just clicked "buy" on that phone, so I’m hurrobin’ it in. Think I’m sorted for a bit.      Erm, you’d best wait and make sure you don’t regret it in like five minutes after watchin’ YouTube reviews for six hours een your face.      Which one is it this time? The one that looks a bit like Ane’s but just costs ten grand and has a weird camera?      Oh, bollocks! How d’you lot know?      You show us everything, remember? Still, if you can afford it, more power to ya. Still stuck on theitunes apps My turkey still cost me fifty quid though last week, you know. I ain’t workin’, so every purchase is sad.      I’m about to wait for Christmas for breakfast, innit. I’ve been savin’ for this phone and the new Call of Duty. That’s, like, both. Though if ya lot are playin’, I’ll still shout it on the telly.      You know what? I’m stuck on Netflix already. Watched that BBC drama again. Like, someone said "pavilion" thirteen times.      Oh aye— The Crown ?? Don’t get started on that lot. Can’t even make a ballet without Prime Minister speeches and about five candles.      I still haven’t finished Half-Life 3 yet. Wait—okay sorry that was a joke. Still no, innit?      Oh yeah, you’re still playin’ that rubbish. Betcha can’t even log in on any console, can ya?      Arse. We all know it’s not out yet.      So, have you two told your mums if you're comin' round for Christmas?      Yeah, goin’ on the 23rd. Think mine wants me to open the front door for her between 8-9 bloomin’ minutes.      That sounds familiar. Me mum and auntie are doin’ “The Great Whitehaven Pie Swap” like it’s some hidden competition over whether the pastry is fluffy or not.      I swear, if they don’t stop with the “traditional” thing, half the town'll be on the same dish when we all meet up.      Should we get them something… unique? Like, you know, not another mug with a photo of someone who looks like us slightly aged?      I e-bayed “end of the world” candles last year.

So did you go back to Lincoln for the summer or just do everything online this time?      Oh yeah, I actually went back for a few weeks! It was nice to see my family after being in Cambridge all year. Did you go home as well?      Not really—just holidays in France with the grandparents. I’ve been working on this project all summer, remote but with field transcription from different regions. Got to listen to a ton of French kids talking about holidays, which is oddly relatable considering we were doing the same when we were little, don’t you think?      Oh, honestly, I still remember learning French at primary school and thinking holidays were  such  an important topic. "Je suis allée en Espagne" and all that. It obsessed me, going on holidays and eating crepes the entire time. But actually, my job hasn’t taken me out of the UK at all this summer. Just a bunch of replying to emails, setting up files, and scheduling meetings for the team—and honestly, I’m ready for a holiday myself!      I hear that! I mean, don’t get me wrong, working on the language project is interesting, but it’s been nonstop. I’m seriously thinking of just grabbing a train to somewhere like Cornwall or Brighton just to not be surrounded by laptops for a few days. You know how it is when you’re in academic work—your brain never switches off!      Oh someone  definitely  get the sea air. I tried to go to the Lake District once with my sister, and it was glorious and peaceful and… cold as hell. But I did get away from my emails, so points for that. I think you just need to schedule a holiday where you literally can’t be reached—that failsafe iPhone airplane mode trick!      Maybe I’ll do that, but for now I’ve got guest speaker sessions to attend for the faculty and more transcription to edit. Speaking of, have you ever thought about visiting another country for work or study? My colleague just came back from a project in Edinburgh doing Scottish regional dialects with kids, and she said it was amazing how different the intonations are from London where I’m used to!      Yeah I think I would like to go to Edinburgh at some point—if not for language work, then just for the city vibe.

Rather annoying I just wanted to say.      What's up then?      Just me and Anna went to see the careers advisor at sixthform today      Right? Thanks love I dunno what I'd do without your expert input      Nonsense, but if you do want to keep on writing your personal statement, I can read it when you're ready for a second opinion.      Mm I might well take you up on that And in other news today in the morning I had a really good box massage      Reckon I have to get me one of those then      I think you should, your legs are knackered from standing over in the shop all day      I reckons I'm getting a bit stiff in them old bones of mine      Aye very much.      So, how was it before?      Actually very much, I was expecting some kind of bumbling mechanic to just tug on my shoulders and do a bit of tough love, but it was just a very calm, super chilled environment, and the bloke was really kind

Rather skip the newspaper today. You know, too much talk about that Calais business. Makes a chap feel right out of sorts.      I know what you mean, Richard. It's heartbreaking, honestly. You see those poor families camped out in the cold with nothing. It’s on all the news, and I try not to bring it up at school, but the children have heard a lot. A lot too much for their age.      Don't get me started, dear. Today one of the kids asked me why they don’t just get a house in England. I had to sit down with them and explain—what a heavy thing for children to understand.      It’s a right mess, that’s for sure. I remember when I was young, the world felt a bit smaller, and I think people were more willing to take in strangers. Now? Everyone’s fearful. Not sure why that is.      Maybe it’s the news, the way they show it, or the politics. Either way, people like them don’t stand a chance.      I’ve been thinking about it a lot lately. I’ve made a few calls to the local church, they’re organizing a little donation drive. Clothes, blankets, maybe even non-perishable food. I know it doesn’t fix everything, but it’s something.      Bless you, Angelina. That’s the sort of thing you bring to the table—well, both that and chicken casserole. Just trying to keep a sense of normalcy around the house with all this hullabaloo.      The casseroles are  chef’s kiss . You two have about the best Midweek Lunch setup I’ve ever had the pleasure of sitting at.      Stop it, that was just barely warmed up! But thank you, Sarah. It’s a bit of distraction, isn’t it? A nice pile of food, and at least for a while, you stop thinking about all the horrors.      Aye, nothing like good food and decent company to clear the cobwebs. Now, about the future plans—Sarah, do you remember the weekend class you mentioned? Art something?      That’s right! The pottery one. I was supposed to sign up for it, and I just haven’t got around to it. But with all the school planning and your holiday coming up in Cornwall, Richard, it feels a bit like one more thing to tick off the never-ending list.      Why not do it this weekend, then?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You've got that leak in the upstairs bathroom again, haven't you?      Oh aye, it's sod all, that one. The tiles are doing it again. Chased three different contractors and none of 'em can figure it out. Got eeny weeny drops of water comin' down just where the loo cistern used to be.      That's infuriating. I had something similar last year when I rewired the whole place. Found the cause eventually—it was the chase through the wall. The guy who'd fitted the prior bathroom hadn't sealed it properly. Cost me a fortune to fix, but at least it's sorted now.      Aye, well, you'd be the one who’d do the job properly, wouldn’t you? Me? I'm lucky if I can fix a leakin’ tap, let alone figure out where a continuous drip is coming in.      You know, you might not have to do the whole thing over, mind. I mean, do tell, have you considered taking out just the tiles in that one section and checking the pipes behind them? It's cheaper, maybe.      Eh, I was thinkin’ that. My partner says it's bale not, and I suppose she’s right. We were planning somethin’ bigger anyway—had our eye on the kitchen. You ever heard of the firm up the road, someone said they're good? Gary's Kitchens or sommet like that.      Ah, Gary's? I worked with him through a university contract once. Good chap, good work. I had them do mine after I moved back here from Cairo. It's quite an adventure reconstructing what you've not seen for years.      Aye, I bet. My sister ‘ad hers re-faced and it was like going back in time. She shows me photos all the time. Mine's all automated now. Lights, heating, even if the taps are on or off—it's very modern. Just depends if you're the person to manage it all when it goes pear-shaped.      Aye, sounds a bit out my league! I think I’m happy with a kettle on the hob for now. Speaking of, I was just over at Gwen and Derek’s the other week.

So did you lot find the chicken?      Aye, it's in the oven. It got a bit cold out there after the curry run. I can't believe you found a proper Indian place in Cork. Not bad for a town like this.      Aye, it's all about knowing where to look. It was either that or we eat dusty supermarket chicken again. Though I reckon that curry might've been just the thing this little one needed.      Mmmf!      Told you... he’s licking his lips already. He’s like a junior demon at a garlic festival!      My son still tries to eat metal. I left a spoon on the table, and the next thing I know, he's chewing on it. I swear he's either super strong or eventually going to end up with no teeth.      Haha, he’s not the first. I remember we had this kid at school who was obsessed with eating paper. He thought he was one of those super-powered bookworms. Eventually he got it out of his head. Probably still has grief from the dentists, though.      Super powers, aye. Tell him he's one – saves the hassle with the experts, and he might just stop trying to bend the spoon. NowSpeaking of that, what do you think of the idea of night deposit boxes? Like, those banks in the old days with the ones you dropped money into from your cart. Pretty cool, no?      I mean, it’s way more groovy than scanning a card through a machine and watching it eat your balance. I’m just not sure what a man in the street would do with one. I suppose you could write a bank note that says ‘Fire me if you want to be rich', pop it in there for posterity and call it done.      I’m trying to figure it out for something else entirely. Recently, I tried to plan a little birthday thing for a friend, and I had to arrange everything from scratch. No cake, no plan, and definitely no budget. Now I'm going back and forward trying to get a nice birthday card that's not cringey. It's harder than I thought.      You’re just not trying hard enough. Go with the boxset vibe – lay out your cards with a themed message. I made it all about how impressive it is that she's survived her thirties, and to date, it’s going down a storm.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do we?      We’d be taking our chances with them bobbies today, Doris! Not today, we’d best stick to the front. Not worth explaining why the school fete frightened us off. Deirdre’s een bit vocal at the mention of the bobbies, but I reckon it’s best to agree with her. She’s only had a cup of tay this morning, and I don’t fancy being the one who causes a scene.      Funny you should mention, Jerry. The school fete... my Estelle said it's  horrible . All the children and the noise and such. Course, they had the turkey leg stall, but you couldn’t hear yourself think. Tenpence a look, as Darcy would say. I think he turned down a piece of cake for a look at the better half.      Dad’s still obsessed with the turkey leg stall, isn’t he! I told you to leave it. You got the free ones, didn’t you? I do not want a book on it.      Aha! See, she’s only ten, and still remembers that. Me watching the stall for two hours and then getting told “you’re too old for fairy bread, sir!”      Sounds like a fair enough response. It was a kids’ stall, for goodness’ sake. You don’t see fifty-year-olds trying to claim someone else’s liminal phase.      Besides, we had a  far  better time at the bonfire and pumpkin patch. The kids were all dressed up, and it wasn’t all bunting and birthday hats. I think you picked the right one, Jerry.      Wait! Did you take us to a bonfire and pumpkin patch  without  me?! My science homework for next week is on places. All about seasons and sundials and stupid stuff. You could’ve told me you were touring the autumnal worlds!      We did talk about you and that sprite of yours, Monica. She’d’ve wanted a new dress and probably the full works – face paint, fake fangs, the lot. But you told us to leave gothic details on your own if you don’t mind. Said it made her feel “too spook-tofy,” in her words.      She  did  say that! I mean, ghouls and ghosts are fun, but I’m not dressing up like a serial killer for a school photo. Only Mums do that.      I remember helping you with that Halloween drama last year.

Rather annoying this traffic, isn't it? I mean, do we really have to get stuck behind a bus that’s moving at half-speed? We’re already running late for the fair, and we’d have a better chance of finding £20 in the gutter than a parking spot.      Traffic’s always like this on the weekend. It was the same when I was still driving all over London for a living. A lot worse, if I’m being honest. Still, easier said than done now, pulling someone over and telling them to move faster. You get old, you get civil.      Not to mention the hassle once we get there. I heard someone the other day only got a parking permit after waiting six months, and that was for an elderly bungalow in the countryside! I’m not saying you two should live in one just yet, but imagine trying to get anywhere near a decent place to park if you need a space for your van.      Oh don’t remind me about disabled parking — I saw this lady near the bus stop the other day, sat in a regular seat with her badge clearly visible, and a老爷 takes the space instead. Like it’s their birthright or something.      It’s a shame, really. I remember when people got more respect. Back in my day, if you needed a parking spot because you had a bad back or something, people would just give it up without thinking twice. Now it’s like you need to chase them down the street with someone on the phone to prove you’re not a fraud.      And let’s not ignore the housing crisis. I work in a home, and most of the people there come from council housing. I’ve seen seniors living in tiny two-up, two-downs that don’t have any facilities for wheelchairs or mobility aids. Not to mention the time it takes to get moved into sheltered housing.      It’s crazy how much better it was for them compared to where the system is now. I mean, the government’s always talking about supporting the elderly, but all they really do is hand them a leaflet and expect them to navigate a maze of forms and waitlists.      You think I’m getting off lightly by retiring and not having to deal with that? I remember life was more or less about work and home, and you accepted the rations you got.

So do you really think an allotment is a good idea? I mean, I haven’t even mowed my own lawn in months!      Oh, come on, you’ll be fine! It’s not about perfection, it’s about getting your hands dirty and enjoying the process. I’ve always wanted to try it, and with the community one down by the park, it's easy access.      Yeah, but I’m more of a "how do you eat an elephant"—one bite at a time—kind of person. I don’t know where to start. Do I even have space for everything?      Well, no pressure to do it all at once. You can start small—maybe a couple of rows for veg like potatoes and carrots, and then add tomatoes or herbs later.      I love the idea of growing my own tomatoes, but do you ever have problems with bugs or whatever?      Oh definitely—slugs are the worst! But there are natural ways to deal with them—beer traps, copper tape, that kind of thing. Plus, a bit of neem oil if you want to keep your leaves healthy.      That sounds fancy. Neem oil—what even is that?      It's a natural pesticide. I got it from the local gardening centre. You can use it on a lot of plants without messing things up for beneficial insects like bees. Oh, and I’ve been told companion planting is useful. Like, planting marigolds with tomatoes to deter pests.      That’s interesting. So is it a community thing then? Like, do we all share tools and stuff, or do we have to bring our own?      Oh, we share tools—there’s a shed where everyone leaves their spades and trowels and things. There's also fertiliser and compost, so you don’t have to buy your own. And if you’ve got more than you need, you swap. I’ve already got a few people saying I can have leftover courgettes or apples from their trees!      That’s brilliant. I keep meaning to grow my own veggies, but it always feels like such a learning curve.      Yeah, go at your own pace. I’ve been there. Just turn up, dig a bit, water occasionally, and before you know it, you’ll be your own self-sufficient veg magician.      You make it sound amazing. I think I’ll go this week to check it out. Maybe I can bribe the neighbours to join us too.

So did you go up to Cambridge this weekend to see anyone?      Yeah, I saw my cousin and some old mates from sixth form. Blimey, it was a laugh!      Aw that’s so nice. You lot must’ve had a proper night in. I saw the timeline on Facebook and it looked wild!      It was! We went to that little pub by the Cam, had too much cider, and then wandered around checking out some of the colleges. We took the photographer from the family when we were younger, but now he's just on my mobile, taking blurry photos!      That's classic Cambridge, innit? You like that vibe, don’t you? All those big buildings and rich vibes.      D’you know what I think is the best bit? It's just being there and seeing how far I've come from where I started in Donny. I used to live over on the estate by the motorway, didn’t have a clue what the uni world would be like—now I'm here, larking about in a place I never thought I'd land!      For real! I’m just finishing up my A Levels, and it’s all a bit “what next?” – but it's nice thinking I could still end up slap bang in the middle of that history and donuts and all them quills.      You could, yeah! Honestly, just work at it and get the grades. That place has a bit of a snobby vibe on the surface, but once you crack in, you get a proper sense of belonging.      Sounds good. I’ve always been a bit nervous about the talking part though, like, I'm not posher and I worry I won’t fit in.      Nah, don’t think like that. I’ve got mates from all over the country with all sorts of accents and ways of talking – it was all fine. We still ended up shouting about the price of a pint. The work is hard, no doubting that, but you don’t have to be a genius—if you chuck in enough study hours and team up with blokes who know what they're doing, you can get through.      That’d help. I really want to do art and design, but I feel like every other place is more practical and them big unis are all about science and money stuff.

Rather skip the new films, eh, love? I mean, what they call films these days — it's all got too much noise and no story, if you ask me!      I mean, it   can   be a bit much, sometimes! I had to mute the first episode because my flatmate said I was scaring the cat with the volume!      That's right, that Basil Fawlty was treacherous. All that shouting about tourists — and I remember him as a nice bloke at the pottery once! I tried his lemon meringue once. We lost two good queens over that pie.      Wait,  two ? Gran!      Oh don't start — it was a disaster, all I can go on is my memories, if you don’t mind! But anyway, I do suggest you let Mia try  Are You Being Served?  Proper cheerful lot of ladies.
