Aye, it's lookin’ more like a donkey’s tail!

Rather skip the pub tonight, eh? You know what a nightmare that place gets on a Friday.      Aye, I was thinking more of staying in. I've been over that bar scene for a while now. Just seems like I end up queueing for things more than actually getting to drink them.      Not to mention the price! You could get better lager in a supermarket these days. Much better, in my opinion.      It's not just the money—there's the noise, the smoke, the way people get aggressive with the bar staff... Not to mention the amount of bloody celebrities I see every week.      Oh yeah, that Myra name-dropping bloke who always goes on about his "racing connections"—do you ever get sick of that?      Honestly, it’s a bit much. I get it—people love their stories—but everyone thinks they’re in a TV drama, you know?      I say the only drama I'm interested in is what I can do here,  [points to the kitchen] . I mean, did you try that broccoli last week? It was deadly. Like someone had deep-fried it in lemon and rhythm and then put it in the oven at –5 degrees.     [ laughs ] No, the broccoli wasn’t quite up to scratch. I think it was cooked by one of Liam’s mates who’d clearly never seen a pan before. But to be fair, his fish was alright—at least he didn’t overcook it.      You mean the piece of rubber he called haddock? Yeah, that would’ve made about five edible molecules. Still, you can’t blame the lad, I s’pose.      Nah, you can’t really. The lad was decent enough to do the cooking. Just put the lad in charge of expressing opinions on politics. That’s when it all goes wrong.     [ laughs ] Aye, I’ll give you that one. So what’ll we have tonight then? Something Indian? I’ve a new recipe from my nan—uses red lentils and a bit of something I can’t pronounce.      Sounds brilliant. If I could just stop myself burning the microwave—still not sure if it’s broken or just ignoring me.      Don’t worry, I’ve made it 300 times in Cambridge kitchens. It’s solid. You might find your dad on the telly tonight over the lentils, mind.      You mean that one chap from Channel Five?      Yeah, the one who said you should cut the cauliflower into clouds to keep it flaky.

Right, so the next one is on "blue cards" — anyone wants to go first? I know  I  don’t fancy being first after the last one. I said "beach" over and over and everyone was like “No! No! No!” and it was  desert . I still don’t understand that one.      'Cause you’re supposed to not say "beach" if the word is "desert", so that’s a top one. If you watched me, I just sat there and said nothing and then the others gave up. But, come on, you could have said like, "Sunburn" or "heatwave," couldn't you?      Yeah, well what’s a 30-year-old teacher got against a game of  Articulate ? Darcy, pick one.      Blimey, aren’t you giving yourself enough credit, Jenn? You said "beach" after I said "sand." I said "sand," that's, like, near a beach, but not actually the word. I was defending it.      Oh, let’s not start with your histories. We still haven’t got over "village people" in 2015. I said, "Community," which is totally fair?      No, no, no. "Village people" is an actual thing, you know? Silly Nige. Silly silly Nige. Anyway, let's just someone just pick one. Let’s not lose the spirit of the game.      Alright, alright, I’ll have a go. Any word at random – here we go. Okay… it’s in the category: Entertainment. I’ll show it to the others first to keep it fair. Nancy, you’re not allowed to be the first! I’m taking it seriously, for once.      Oh no. Enexpected. All right.      Well, if it's a game, you can expect nothing.      Argh, come on, we’re not that far into the night for grand statements.      Right! Okay, the word is…  bookstore . You got this, Darcy?      Yeah, man, I got this. Think slowly. Let me… line it up. I wanna do this properly, bloke.      Shaw. It’s not complicated.      I'm going for effect, Nancy. You gave me a chance to talk like a proper presenter.      Just say the description. I can feel the build-up and I'm getting nervous.      Okay, okay, place where you can buy printed material and, um… it’s also got literature.      That… actually works. Not bad, Darcy.      Yeah, on a dark night.      Would you like to just say “place where you buy books”?      Well… yes, but look at you, taking the easy route.

Right, I’m just dealing out the cards. This is going to be a disaster—the state of my piling last weekend was dire enough.      Aye, and I’m not sorry to say I won  both  of our games. Ten out of ten for eeny-meeny-miny-mo for the best card player!      You’re just lucky, Steve. If I had a card game face like you, I’d be winning too. Look at me—lost three games in a row already.      You’re just not concentrating properly, Rhys. Last time I played with someone like you, they left their deck in the toaster the next morning.      Oh, come on! I’m not the only one with bad memory. I once dropped the entire game in the washing-up water. Cats went mental for a week—still think I’m a witch.      I pity the poor sod that told you to do the laundry first.      Alright, alright, let’s get back to this. So the rules again—no splitting your hand in half, and only one reshuffle.      And if any of you cheat like you did last time, Steve?      That was a  mistake . Someone had black cards, and I couldn’t be sure.      Oh please. You just wanted to pretend you had a suspicious aura. You’d have given Madame Blavatsky a run for her money.      Madame who?      Never mind. Focus on winning this round, okay?      Actually, this reminds me—there was this time at my old place, we played a card game called “Muck.” The table collapsed halfway through. Nobody died, but my son Eddie passed out laughing.      Oh, I was at Eddie’s birthday once. That was the time your cake started raining jelly.      That  was  good. Kids were shouting  “it’s raining!”  and ran about like mad things.      Imagine goosing someone on your own birthday and surviving it.      I’d do that to you any day, Rhys.      So, have you made the special rules yet? We can’t go hours with just us and cards. We need more stakes—like, whoever loses has to do the dishes for a week.      You mean  no  dishes for a week. That’s the real deal.      Or whoever loses has to wear Eddie’s clown shoes for dinner tomorrow.      Och, now  that  would be a sight. Steve, you on your own with that!      I’m in. Anyone else?      Aye, if he’s doing it, I’m doing it too.

Okay, so I've just watched this new series called  "Shadow Units."  Have any of you seen it yet? It's like a mix of  The Crown  and  Mr. Robot  — super intense and totally gripping.      No, I haven't. Is it on ITV again? That one drama channel gives me the most sore brain by the end of the night — like trying to do A-level AQA maths but worse.      Oh yeah,  Shadow Units  is that one where the girl works for the government or something? I saw the trailer and was like, "Do I even want to make  this  emotional," you know? I'm still recovering from  Midnight Rain .      Oh my gosh, I haven't watched anything good in weeks, honestly, because I’ve been swamped with work. It's like being a trainee accountant during breakfast, bedtime, and weekends. My mum says I'm in "work mode forever," and I’m like, "Yeah, I am."      It's so true, like, I had to choose between watching the last episode of  Shadow Units  or finishing my human geography coursework, and I did the coursework… but now I’m haunted by it.      Honestly, I stopped watching TV series last year, because I was trying to get into Royal Navy basic training. You don’t have time for  Shadow Units . You're either training for three hours a day or someone’s in your face about your posture.      I can’t even imagine that. Also, I just spent three hours looking at tax codes this week —  that  is its own form of torture.      I know! But you lot are lucky. I just work 10 hours a week doing care support. Doesn’t sound like much, but I do 12 patients every day. My feet are dead at 5 p.m. — no time for TV or coursework.      That’s how I am too, honestly. I’m part-time at Aldi as well as trying to study for my BTEC. It’s like being in the simulation class at school but for  real . My brain can’t handle any more gothic poetry on top of this.      Speaking of education, anyone got uni offers yet? I’ve got an offer from KCL for anthropology. I can’t believe I’m 18 and moving to London.      That’s proper impressive, seriously. Uni is overrated, but I’m glad it's working for you. I’ve signed up for Royal Navy initial training — kind of like my version of a gap year, but more dangerous and less spicy.

Rather annoying isn't it, this traffic. I used to walk into the shops in Cambridge, but now it's got so big, I can't be bothered more than I have to.      Yeah, it's hectic. I try to bike in as much as I can—it’s faster if you take the right routes, and it’s good for the planet. Plus, I’m in better shape than I used to be before I worked in the shop every day.      I’d cycle, but it’s just me and the bike. Not worth the hassle when I don't even go out that often. I mean, even if I wanted to go to the cinema or out for a bite to eat, like that Myra, I’d probably just get in the car and be done with it.      Cars, cars, cars—everyone’s driving nowadays. I was about to try to walk back when I moved here, but this happened. I looked for a shopping bag to hold my shopping—and I still dropped one of the tomatoes.      You know, there are loads of cycle paths if you plan your route. I got a bike off my old uni, and it’s brilliant. I tried walking one day, but got way too hot and – no disrespect – got fairly sweaty, and I had to go to work after. You can't impress customers if you smell like you've been dragged through a hedge backwards!      Well, someone got full marks for effort. I’d rather just stay home and have a cup of tea with you lot, than have to get on my bike and look like a fool trying to negotiate those roundabouts.      I know what you mean. One day last week, I had to stop a motorbike and ask where Crown Court was. I’d only been out a few weeks, and the driver, well he gave me directions, but he looked at me like I was from another planet.      That's Cambridge for you. It's buzzing, especially with students. We get lost all the time. Though being from out of town probably helps people not notice.      Some people, no doubt lost and looking for a nice quiet snack—which the city provides in goody bags on pond life if you ask me.      Still, I’m trying to be independent—no bloomin’ taxi fare today, no way.

Rather lovely to be here at Cambridge Law Faculty for Alumni Day. I’m one of the Language Research Coordinators from the Centre for Language Studies. I’m more of a phonetics nut, especially where regional dialects meet international languages. You wouldn’t have studied Spanish as a second language, would you?      Actually, I did a degree in Spanish and Mandarin at SOAS in London. Now I work in administration for a language research project at King's College. The overlap with legal terminology was quite surprising, especially with China and private sector translations. They treat contract law in a very bilateral way compared to the UK.      Interesting. I’ve been a law lecturer at the University of Manchester for decades and made a career of visiting Spain for research trips. Particularly the Basque Country. Fascinating to hear how their autonomous legal system overlaps and sometimes contradicts the national framework. It reminded me a lot of Wales, honestly. When I was your age, I’d visit Wales for rugby matches at the Arms Park and marvel at how local governance was evolving side-by-side with the rest of the UK.      Oh yes! Rugby is a good example of regional identity influencing international sport as well. Did you know that Wales and the Basque region both have strong codes of local rhythm in their speech patterns? It's amazing – even though Basque is a language isolate, it still has a huge cultural influence on sport and law.      That’s what I found in China as well. Despite the dominance of Mandarin, local dialects like Cantonese still thrive, especially in legal and community spheres. I remember being in court in Guangzhou and noticing how some of the older judges still used colloquial phrases when explaining verdicts in public. It’s like a linguistic bridge between the official register and the common man.      That reminds me of London. I once met a solicitor in Chancery Lane who, despite his formal credentials, quoted Monty Python at me during a tax case. He said the client had a “flair for the dramatic” and that it reminded him of a “certain French existentialist and a middle-aged Argentinian with a fondness for cricket.” Strange cocktail of influences, if you ask me.      Haha, that's the beauty of language in law—it’s not just rules and restrictions. It’s full of human expression. I’m actually leading a team looking into how inflected languages, especially from Eastern Europe and Arabic-speaking regions, influence courtroom argumentation styles.

So did you see the video of Aunty Fran with that ice bucket? She looked absolutely freezing!      Oh yes, I saw it on Facebook! Poor thing, she wore that long-sleeved dress with the shawl, and then—  plop  —ice water. She’s brave if nothing else.      I reckon it was all in good fun, but you should’ve seen Uncle Rupert’s face when she challenged him. He said he’d rather donate ten pounds and let the kids do it.      Apparently, the kids  did  do it. I mean, even Mary got wet and shouted, “I’ve raised fifty like that!”      Ha! She’s a firecracker, isn’t she? D’you know, I think Aunty Fran mentioned she might actually consider adoption eventually. She’s always talking about her sister’s stepkids.      Oh, you think so? That sounds serious. She’s had so much on with her arthritis and that—moving house and everything. But she loved taking care of the cousins that short time.      It’s wild how much has changed in two years. I mean, I remember when all we talked about was school and cheeky dares. Now, I’m barely getting through my CELTA, and you’re telling me Fran’s thinking about adopting?      Time flies, doesn’t it? Last week at the vet, I saw my first university friend, Lucy, with  two  kids—looked like she hadn’t slept in months.      No way! You went to uni with Lucy? I always thought she went traveling round the world or something.      Maybe she did! Anyway, I bet she’d take it as a compliment if she heard you mention her.      Honestly, I miss those daft nights at uni. You know, when we got all philosophical about life and tried to stuff ten people into a small flat.      Right, but also when we were  all  on the same digestive diet and took the kettle as far away from the loo as we could!      That one time we had that antipasti picnic at the park, and it rained, and we all had to sit under the one awning like a family. It was mad.      Remember when John tripped over the bench and gave himself a right black eye?      We laughed so hard. I swear the neighbours thought we were having a crisis.      Speaking of, my half-brother is coming over this weekend to help me sort out the adoption papers—I’m starting as a consultant next month, and I need to start filling in forms

Rather annoying this new coffee machine. It’s so delicate, do you need a manual for it or does it just read your mind now?      Oh I know, I've been over this with it for days. Not only do you have to fiddle with the buttons like you're trying to solve a calculator problem, but the damn thing doesn’t heat up properly if you use it too much in a morning.      Fair dos. Why not just go back to the old one? It’s not like we’re trying to win the World Barista Championship in a small village.      Right, but it was broken. Someone apparently tried to retrofit it with a decaffeination module or something like that. Honestly, I’m not even sure what the point is. Ten pounds, gone.      I used to think modern appliances were worth it, back in my teaching days. Now I just see a bunch of things that break when you blink.      And the worst part is, you can’t even fix the damn thing. It’s all sealed up like it’s a nuclear reactor. You can’t replace the filter or the valve without a PhD in engineering and a warrant.      Honestly, it’s the circle of life in domestic appliances these days. Buy one – it’s new, fairly simple, and actually does the job. By the time it dies, you're somehow already halfway through the next upgrade cycle.      And let’s not even talk about the cost of storage and removal when we move in a year. That’s another unnecessary €200 each way for a box and some bloke who’s clearly using a calculator he bought when Prime Minister Johnson was about five.      I know! And what’s this “fragile” sticker doing on the side of that box you barely opened last week? You’d think it was the Hope Diamond in there. Maybe it’s haunted. I passed a moth the other day at 6 a.m. flapping desperately as it tried to find a way out of the kitchen. Trauma.      You think of it like it knows the coffee machine is the one that killed it.      Still, I’m more concerned by how everything’s slowing down in govt. I mean, if you ask me, real progress is made when you actually, you know, do stuff.      Speak your truth. Look at all the noise made by the Labour conference and the promises made.

Rather skip ahead a bit here. So I sat at the Seven Stars Pub with her, and it was like... What was I supposed to say after that?      You didn’t have to say anything, love. You were just there to listen—get her to talk about it.      I know, I know—and I   did   listen. I wanted to make sure she felt supported. But when she just said,  “I’m fine,”  and started fidgeting with her coffee cup... It was like the awkward silence that only a mum and daughter can create.      Still, it’s a good start, isn’t it? That she opened up at all? My turkey was definitely undercooked last year though. I’m not sure if I’m admitting to that or if it was just sad in a good way.      Mm. Well, I made a mental note to ask everyone for a recipe in advance this year, you know, in case I’m stuck looking up  How to Carve Christmas Turkey for Dummies  again.      Oh, you’ll make short work of it. You might even end up teaching your own kids to carve properly… although I suspect it’ll take a little more than “just a bit of practice.”      Let’s just say if I ever open a cooking class called  Mastering the Perfect Silly Goose Carving Technique , you’ll be the first guest.      Sounds grand. And speaking of… have you thought more about doing a teaching certificate in something festive?      Like what?  Yuletide Language Studies for ESL?  I did just finish up an online course on “How to Teach Values Through Festive Traditions.” It was pretty niche.      Doesn’t sound uncool, though. I bet kids  love  that kind of stuff. All the sparkle, the explanation of why we leave the biscuits out for Father Christmas, all the talking about Santa as you know him.      Mm… Though I’m not sure if trying to teach multicultural holiday traditions counts as “values” if the kids just end up asking,  “But are these Santa man’s real or goody bag fake?”       Oh, kids are just inquisitive that way. And it’s all part of it. Pass it on, learn it, maybe even make up a new tradition one year.      You know, I’ve been thinking about that. Maybe this year we could do something a little… different. Like go all out with paper decorations for our tree, instead of the usual bulbs and baubles.

Rather skip the starter an’ go straigh’ in with the Richmond sausages, if yer askin’ me. Never had nothin’ like ‘em since they changed their name away from Waterfields. I swear they used to do ‘em better when it was a proper bakers.      I know wot yeh mean, but I tried them last week an’… they were a bit dry, innit? Not like the good old days.      Nah, I think it’s just me. I’ve got a cold or summat, or maybe it’s the central heating in this pub—it dries out everything. I reckon it’s the same reason I can’t sleep in now that Myra lives with me. She snorres like a chainsaw! I’m constantly countin’ sheep, but then I hear a sheep screamed down the phone in the background an’ it just makes breakfast worse.      Ohhh, I used to live with me nan and she’d snore, too, but she was a proper grumpy old bird. If I said nothin’ about it, she’d start up about how if I couldn’t sleep with her, I could be stuffed with a handkerchief and be done with it. Still, she always got her sarcastic come-back?      Nah, I live on my own now. Me and uni flatmates used to have fights all the time ’cause some ‘un’d bring mexican food in an’ claim someone else did it. Honestly, I’d rather live with a pack o’wolves an’ a snoring nan.      Anyroad, Margot messaged me yesterday, said she’s in about five relationships at once an’ still can’t touch the ground with a man. I said what you doin’ talkin’ to ‘im again if he’s up for five? She just laugh ‘n’ says "he’s got a nice backside". Baffled me to the core.      Oh, I dunno, maybe he’s a nice’un. She did say he lends her books from his nan’s collection. An’ I think he works at the garage? Wasn’t that where you met?      I met ‘im goin’ on aboot if you wash yer car properly at home wi’ a microfibre cloth it don’t go ‘n’ ruin the finish. I was like mate, I’ve made it to 24 and never seen a microfibre cloth in me life. But I had to say, “Oh, so’s that a guy thing then,” an’ he buys it.      That’s.related to yeh, innit, Karen?

So did you go anywhere at all this weekend, Dad? I’ve been trying to get out but it was either raining or my laptop had some sort of meltdown. Absolute nightmare!      Aw, I’m sorry to hear that lass. No, I didn't really do much much. Got eeny weeny bit of farming done, you know, just the usual springtime stuff. Bit of a clean up, checking the fences, that sort of thing. Sat down with a few records and some cups of tea. Not much more to it.      Well, I envy you the lack of stress. My weekends these days are so unpredictable. One minute I’m planning to paint the house and the next My turkey is doorstep delivered at seven in the morning. It’s ridiculous!      Aye, and I hear you. These days it's everyone for themselves, really. I remember when you couldn’t order anything online and everyone still bought their food at the local shop. Everyone looked you in the eye and said good morning. Real community.      I know, you get nostalgic, I get it. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like the convenience, but ... it’s odd not watching the farmer's market rhythm of life from the window. Though at the same time, I can't be bothered to walk to the shop these days unless it's on my way to the pub.      Ha! Still your type, huh? Well, someone’s gotta bring us the beer! Listen, though, I’ve been meaning to ask – what you up to this Saturday? Cos I was thinking of heading up to the canal for a bit of bird watching and a picnic. Not far from where the bridge is.      Honestly? I’ve nothing much else planned. I was just going to get up, watch some superhero nonsense and do laundry, so that works for me. Do you fancy me coming along? Might make it more fun. I can bring something sweet, I know how you always forget them.      That’d be grand. You being there’d be grand. And I’ll keep the chips from falling in the path of the ducks, you remember that time they nearly chased me into the canal?      How could I forget! You looked like a man who just ticked “mad old man with a box of digestive biscuits” off your to-do list. It was iconic.

So did you go back to work yet?      Not really, no. The first few weeks were a whirlwind with the baby, so I just took a few months off. I’m thinking about going back part-time eventually.      That’s totally understandable. I remember when I had my kids, I felt like I was constantly sleep-deprived and dazed. It’s miraculous that I even remembered to make a cup of tea half the time.      Haha, yes! It was like my brain short-circuited into baby mode. You don’t even realize how much you juggle when you're a teacher until you're at home with a screaming newborn and no one’s answering the bell!      I know! I had to switch to home-schooling for a while after the pandemic and then teaching online in the mornings. It was a nightmare when the kids would run past me while I was marking assignments in pyjamas, demanding cereal milk!      Oh God, that’s relatable. It’s funny how we both got into teaching, isn’t it? I mean, we were both in it for the human interaction initially, not the early starts and essay correcting.      For sure. I studied Spanish and French at uni, so I got into languages because I thought it would be fun and inspiring. It is, honestly, when you see the students actually picking it up! Though the homework they turn in feels someone just cast an invisibility spell over the French past tenses. Gone.      Ah, I teach science and maths and it’s surprising how logical most students are in those subjects, but when I ask them to conjugate verbs or read a paragraph, their confidence plummets. I’ve always found that fascinating.      Yeah, I think it's because the rules in languages are often baked into culture and idiom. It’s not just about grammar—they have to learn to think differently sometimes. Speaking of, I tried learning some Croatian recently because I’m going on holiday with my family. You think of learning languages when you want to impress a new friend with your "dobar dan," but it turns out, learning a Slavic language in the context of a go-to-place-to-chill-and-forget-all-the-grammar is not very effective.      Haha, that’s exactly what your holiday-speak system is for! The bits to get you through the ice-cream bar and the taxi ride.

Rather a lot of activity in the garden today, eh, George? That pair of sparrows ‘ave been dartin’ in and out of the feeder like they’re in a race.      Aye, I noticed them too. Look like they’ve got a bit of a nest goin’ on in the hawthorn tree by the fence. Small things, eh? Build their own homes and all that.      Such a miracle, really. You’d think with all the noise of the world and the trees bein’ trimmed back so much, they’d still manage. Nature reminds you not to take it for granted.      That’s what I call resilience. Course, they probably wouldn’t still be here if it weren’t for the feeders and the bits of cake I toss out now and again. I reckon the world’s goin’ mental, but a sparrow still finds breakfast, no matter what.      Speaking of which, what’s for tea then, Ruby? Smells like you’ve outdone yourself again. Not too sickly, I hope.      Oh, just one of my old recipes—Victoria sponge with a few extra sultanas. A bit of treacle for the birds and a bit for the old man. Though I must say, I’ve been careful with the sugar these days. Doctor says I’ve got somethin’ to do with the blood.      Diabetes? Aye, they’re gettin’ at us one by one. I had my glucose test last month. Nothing to worry about—yet. But better safe than sorry, as the politicians ‘say.      Aye, and I’ve noticed the old folk round the village—Bella, Fred, Charlie—they’re all a bit more cautious now. Drinkin’ more water, walkin’ a bit more, that lot. Makes you stop and think, doesn’t it?      It certainly does. You start to see time stretch out in front of you like a long road waiting to be walked—or not, if you’re clumsy. Still, I’d rather have the lunches and a little cake with my old friends than be anywhere else.      You're not wrong there. I reckon goin’ on about life improvements is all well and good, but I’d just as soon sit in the garden with a boxset and a biscuit.      Aye, and let’s not forget we had a tea with puppets last week, Ruby. Do you think we could get over this hump again and do another one at Christmas? I reckoned that one with the talking sausage was a riot.

I can't believe the number of people who come to Northern Cyprus for the summer and think it's a secret. It's not a well-kept one now, more of a known fact by word of mouth, isn't it? No, I know what you mean, Martha. It was very different back in the '70s when I was posted here on holiday. Now it's full of expats with dogs, teenagers, and families trying to avoid the UK summer. Oh, and of course, there's that chap in the corner feeding his cat from what looks like a leftover cod. That’s poor Horace. I mean, I don't blame him. I had a friend back in Dorset who once turkey-bathed in the sea. Funniest thing I've ever seen, to be honest. Now I think I remember that. Wasn't he about 80 then and breakfast still in him? Yes, and in his rolled-up socks, no less! That's the thing about age. People do the most erratic things when they're past their prime. I’ve noticed that I can hear a lot better now with these hearing aids. For instance, I can clearly hear that couple behind us. The man says, “How many languages do you actually know?” and she answers, “Only enough to order food and count to ten in Turkish.” It's heartening how people have adapted. I suppose we all have. Our daughter Georgia speaks in four languages and still can’t read a menu without me. I had a school friend who had a fatal illness a few years ago and still she remembered to wish me happy birthday in German every year. I think people who face death often have a clarity the rest of us miss. That's true. Going back to spiritual matters—have you looked into shamanism or dowsing, like that friend of yours, Samuel? He told me about this experience he had with a local healer who told him he was meant to live by the sea. Oh yes. Samuel had a bit of a breakdown after his divorce, and the 'shaman' told him to "lose the mania and follow water." He did come back changed. Now he writes poetry in goa trance on the coast of Spain. Well, I like the idea of destiny. It gives a pattern to the randomness. It's all part of the bigger question of how we meet people and where those meetings lead us.

Mum, I swear the house is haunted. That light in the kitchen keeps flickering, and it does it when no one’s even near it. I’m starting to think it’s something supernatural      Nonsense, Georgia! That sound like the same light that wouldn't work two years ago when I tried to cook a nice chicken casserole and   it shorted out on me   completely. I reckon that wiring is ancient.      Well, if it’s not   haunted  , it must be dying.   It makes the   most awful buzzing noise before it goes. You'd think the house is trying to talk to me.      Aye, we've all had that problem before, lassie. The eccentricities of old houses. My Gran had the same thing in her kitchen, and I   mean the   light would go off for about a minute sometimes if she boiled the kettle and turned the oven on.      That’s exactly the issue! You can't even boil a kettle and have the toaster on, or it'll trip the whole thing. You know, I’ve been thinking about getting that fixed. What with all the electrical grief   and the old plumbing situation  , this house is becoming a proper death trap.      Yeah – Mate, have you actually considered getting a new house? You know, something with a decent flat kitchen and not   a labyrinth under the floorboards  ?      There’s character in that though, love. Saying   that  , though, a new kitchen wouldn't sour the lemon out of things, is it   too much to want a proper granite worktop?        I did offer to help with a renovation fund, but   you said something about “not spending a fortune on bricks and plaster”  .   I think you meant it as a joke but I was just trying to be useful.        Oh, that wasn’t me trying to dissuade you, sweetheart. If   we start extending the kitchen into the garden   again, you’d be   proud of the view  .      A garden! Persevere the snow in October you remember, luv. Picked up the spade and go straight on my knees. I   looked like a proper gravedigger   in the morning trying to save the tulips blooming on the edge.      God, seriously, why live in a house that   chats back to you   in the form of mysterious creaks and overcooked dinners when we can just modernise it? You know my boss is always talking about how   good property investments can be once they’re properly kissed up  .

So did y'fit watch the Jeremy Kyle show last week? That one with her 'ex' pretending to be some other bloke on Facebook?      Yeah, I did! That Catfishing lark. So cringe. Look at her being all emotional, like she actually thought he was een real friend or something!      I know, right? I wanted to say, “Just check the facts, luv.” Proper daft, honestly. And he used a   filter   or something to change his voice, like he were playing a daft game or summat. You'd think the signs were enough!      I swear, the worst part was when her "boyfriend" turned up on the show, too. Oi, no one needs more drama on daytime TV.      I think he turned up just to make everyone watch while he cried buckets. Like, if you're that 'umbled, why not message her in advance and sort it out like a grown-up? No, no—it's gotta be the big  Jeremy Kyle  cliffhanger.      I mean, I get it though, innit. We all play games with social media. Like, there was this lad on my course who kept liking my photos just to get me to talk to him. Typical Liverpool chap, chekin' the box!      Oh don’t start comparing your love life to mine! I got one bloke who made a fake profile in Doncaster just to send me a suspicious wink. Wink? Really?      Some people just need to grow up. I swear, being online is turning us all into drama queens and queens of bad judgement about half the time. I mean, I know   my   old man had to delete a picture of him at the pub because I egged him and it went viral on Facebook.      Oh yeah, you looked like a right disgrace! But fair play, at least it’s funny. I was stuck on a night out once where some mate tried to persuأد me to dance to “never gonna give you up.” Even mentioned it in the 'gram with the “hilarious” location tag. Classy.      Ugh! I get so fed up with all the lies online, sometimes. If everyone was just a bit braver in the real world, they could go out and say "oi, your face is on the internet," like I did to that lad who posted my photo with those stupid cat ears filters.      Same here, I told this guy’s sister to tell him to stop using my pic as a profile pic for League of Legends.

So did you go to Paris last summer?      Yes, it was beautiful. We had a small exhibition at a gallery near Montmartre. I got to meet some very interesting artists there.      No way! Did you speak to them in French or was it mostly English?      A bit of both. Some people spoke wonderful English, especially the younger ones. A lot of them would switch to English if I mentioned I lived in England. But I know just enough French to manage.      Me too, but I'm more of a... language crash student. I mostly listen to podcasts. I've got the audio for  Les Mis  anditunes on MyMac, but I’ve never watched it.      You should, it's a classic. Paris is full of history and stories—like your Classics degree, really.      Yeah, I mean, I did Classics in university. People usually expect Greek and Rome, but you'd be surprised how much Roman stuff survived over in France. I mean, Paris was Lutetia back in the day.      Oh, you know your stuff. I remember visiting the site of the old Roman baths. Absolutely fascinating.      Oh Mate, you got to see the Roman stuff in Belgium too, right? When you were in Italy?      Oh darling, Italy and Vienna are two different places! I was just saying Berlin in May for a show. That was lovely. It rained oddly little.      I want to go to Italy. Anywhere but Rome. I heard it’s packed and most people about die from heat. I prefer somewhere like the Dolomites or... bees. Wait, what's your take on bees? I know you've painted landscapes.      My, you've gone from Paris to bees.      I have, haven't I? I was just saying I watched this doc yesterday about how bee colonies are getting hit by these strange diseases and mysterious things. They say it’s because of the pesticides and all the big farming operations.      Oh yes, I read about it. I started noticing the decline in the countryside I usually paint in. Not as many wildflowers, fewer butterflies and bees, fewer buzzing around. It’s a shame.      It really is. I mean, if bees disappear...      Then we’re all in trouble, right?      Precisely. I was thinking about that the other day when I got so stuck trying to fix my laptop. I want to write my thesis on ancient agricultural practices and how they worked with nature, not against it.

So do you think we should pull over and check the Sat Nav or just keep going? I think it told Dad we turned left, but we went right.      Don't you start with that again, Elise. I’ve driven from London to Dorset enough times in my day. Got a good sense of the road. Sat Navs are good for what, panic attacks and unnecessary left turns?      Honestly, Arthur, I don’t care if you used to drive trucks pulling horse floats. We’ve been stuck behind the same lorry for the last twenty minutes. And it’s raining like someone’s trying to drown the A35.      Yeah, Dad, like that one curve a couple of miles back—you nearly left the road. Ten more seconds and we’d have been on some farmer's beetroot plantation.      You’ve got to admit, when you're old, your reflexes are still alright for the road. People’s eyesight is better than they think. Some of the young drivers these days, they don’t even look up from their phones—proper dangerous.      Oh come on, it’s not like I do that. I did pass my driving test, you know.      And I remember the first time you got behind the wheel and tried to parallel park on the first go. Nearly took out the whole line of parked Audis.      That was a one-time thing. Who knew people in London actually park!      That’s because I never drove you through London. I drove you through Harlow and through Kent—nice quiet roads. No, save the big city challenge for later.      Speaking of challenges, I had to take a day off work yesterday because of that dodgy back. Jan, the manager, says I need to take a proper break. Maybe you should tell her I passed my A-levels and have a degree. Who do you think got through university without ever missing a lecture? Me.      Ugh, I know what you mean. Even trying to do my thesis on English language variation in Dorset is stressing me out. I swear the dialect shifts by every village. From Bournemouth gothic to Weymouth plonker territory.      I don’t see what's so difficult. You say "mate" and they accept you. It's only fluency if you know when to say "innit."      Oh right, because you’ve clearly been doing academic studies on language yourself.      Fair point.

Rather a damp day, isn't it?      That it is, Henry. Feels like the whole house is damp through the skinnies. I swear, the old Victorian steam systems are doing us no favours.      Aye, aye. Me old een don’t like a fog more than a sore 'ead. Ay, I were tellin’ Fred on the day centre about it. He said that this weather brings out the old 'ostilities in some folks.      I hope you weren’t chase after his opinions with a spoonful of custard, as you did last week when he were goin’ on about supply chains.      Aye, bless Fred! He were left with a look like a cod on toast, yes, sir! Always thought I'd be the eldest of the pack in the world, and yet here we are, no wiser 'an a cat with a blocked drain.      You lot, you were puffin’ so hard the day I dropped off that new terracotta statue you got for the garden. I thought I’d be next to a heart attack myself carryin’ that thing up the garden path.      Oh, that thing cost more than most of my grandchildren’s first bicycles. I told me daughter it was a wise investment. She weren’t havin’ none of it. Silly cow! She said terracotta might crack, and I said what’s the point in being retired if you can’t live a little?      Well, judging by the look of the thing and being through a frost and all, your grandmother would be proud. I about blocked the gate walkin’ up with the thing the other day.      Another damp day is that frost gone! I tell you, if we went out to the garden, we’d be wet through within minutes. All that mucking about with the greenhouse me grandsons would do – probably removed all the heat-good bits from it.      Not to worry, Henry. You've got me to keep you company 'ere. I were told by the doctor last week, no grand exercise, no risk of shootin’ my man into the sky goin’ on pond life improvements. So I’m settled at home, watching line in, no surprises.      You're what your mother was, Viv. Always planning ahead! Me? I like spontaneity. Last week, I had a new hearing aid fitted on a Friday, and over the weekend, I was at the theatre. Now that’s my kind of spontaneity!

Rather do I aye, this weather’s mental, innit? I was out in the garden earlier and it went from sun to rain in five minutes.      Yeah, it’s a proper British summer classic. Charming. Look, I’ve planted some cosmos near the back fence. Got a packet of seeds from Mum last week. Not sure if I’m doing it right though. You ever do much gardening?      Not much, to be honest. I’ve got a window pot with a basil plant and it’s practically seen me through three lockdowns. But I reckon you’re doing fine. You’ve got that  green finger  thing, innit?      Aye, if only! The basil left mine last week. Probably felt the vibe I was giving. But anyway, I was thinking the other night—remember when Tom used to try to busk outside the pub with that guitar? Mate’s still doing jazz in his basemen’s flat five years later.      God, he’s still doing it? I mean, it’s nice—personally I listen to the occasional Spotify while baking cookies, as if I were supplying the warmth and everything.      Be serious. You’re a research manager at the uni, right? So you’ve got to listen to some weird instrumental stuff for focus.      Aye, I’ve got this ambient lo-fi playlist that’s basically just someone counting in Japanese for ten hours. That stuff works a treat, honestly.      Also, have you seen the message from Laura? She’s trying to get a meet-up going for the weekend about five friends. Says she’s brought “a touch of Mexican sun” with her. Wonder what that means. Going to be smoothie shots or something, if she’s anything to go by.      Definitely not. Laura passed out after one kebab at 6pm. She told us she was  capturing the moment  or some mad Arty-Farty crack. Probably bringing handmade yellow chilli things or something.      Aye, the fiesta of our lives, set to a medley of mariachi and the odd acoustic set. Look, I’ll see if I can cook up something passable—maybe some nachos or that green bean salad you hate but say you love.      That sounds  perfect  . As long as it doesn’t involve your famous beetroot latte.      C’mon! It’s a  functional food fusion . Beetroot is for energy.      And alcohol, clearly. Listen, we haven’t seen most of the others in ages.

So did I tell you about the meeting I had with the council last week?      No, what was it about?      They asked me to help draft a policy on how we support unemployed graduates in the area. You’d think people wouldn’t be out of work after uni, right? But yeah, even with degrees, people just can’t get a foot in the door.      I know. My sister got top marks in her English degree and still couldn’t find a teaching job. She ended up working at a pub. It’s rough.      It really is. And when I talk to people, the thing that comes up again and again is that the fees still hang over them like a dark cloud. Even when they’re working, the repayments are a nightmare.      Yeah. It’s like they’ve got to pay back this loan before they’ve even started mastering their career. I remember when I was doing my PhD, I thought, “Right, I’ll get a job, pay off the damn loan, and move on.” But it’s harder than it looks.      Definitely. Did I tell you, by the way, that I went to  Les Mis  last week?      Mate, of course you did, and I know you were trying to get me to go with you.      I was! And I don’t even know, maybe I just needed someone to full-on rage with me to “Do You Hear the People Sing?” because I was out there yelling the words like a madwoman.      That’s your thing, isn’t it? I mean, I remember us all at uni, trying to pass exams and you going off about  Cats  or whatever that was.       Cats  was just a warm-up. I’ve always got time for musicals. They speak to the soul.      Well, the soul’s tired, I’ll grant you that. We both know how hard it can be to get out of bed in the morning, right?      Ugh, yes. I swear I run on three hours of sleep and a strong cup of tea. But it’s getting better now. I mean, I’m active in the mornings, I go to the box gym up the road.      That’s great! You’re looking good, mind you.      It’s just a bit of strength work and some proper walking. I’m surprised how much better I feel since I’ve been doing it.

Nana Dunlop, look at this book I found in the cupboard—it’s got a dragon on the front! What do you think? Could we read it to Ethan? He asked for a bedtime story last night and I couldn’t think of anything.      Oh, aye, that’s eeny weeny  The Adventures of Crog the Dragon , if it isn’t! I read it a hundred times to your grandfa—your grandpa’s son, Tim, y’know. It’s got a clarty plot, but the pictures were always me favourite. Did your mam read it to you?       Oh, no, love , the only dragons I read to Alice about were the My Little Pony ones. Honestly, who even owns a dragon book anymore? I didn’t know what a draco-lexicon was until she screamed about it at the library last week.      Mam, that’s just because you didn’t grow up with dragons, you’re not wrong though, some of the My Little Pony dragons look like over-baked jelly—wrinkly and scaly!       Oh, well said , to be fair, I did once colour a book in properly… it was the one with the dot-to-dot cows. Excellent cow at the end.       Ah, now there’s a proper family tradition!  My side did dinasours and fairies, while your mam’s lot did cows, and your grandpa’s side did trains. Strictly compartmentalised stories, none of them mixing. Funny thing—everyone had their niche.      So Nana, does  Crog the Dragon  have a happy ending? I’m not trying to read the whole book now, I just need to know what happens—he fails at fire-breathing or something?      Aye, he does. Starts off being all brash and proud, thinking he can fly and breathe fire by the age of three. Then, he tries to fly off a mountain, crashes into a sheep field, loses all his flame… ends up doing a job in retail with his friend a Grumpy Griddle the Gremlin. Not the grandest ending, but it’s honest.       Oh my goodness , if that’s not a description of your dad at six in the back of the car refusing to speak for an hour after the Disney trip went wrong. I said it was too much. He said it was culture.      It was both, mam. He tried to fly over the Matterhorn and failed.       You were five and complained about the height of it!

So did you go and sort out that weekend job yet, or are we still just fantasising about it like it’s the next James Bond movie?      Not yet, I’ve been putting it off for a full £20 and the promise of being stared at by elderly customers who make judgements on your grooming habits.      Which   obviously   depends on your leg hair choices. You’ve gone full jungle this year, have you?      I’ve   noticed   you haven’t exactly been grinding the razors for months either. Just want to keep it real.      Oh yeah,  I’m  a natural look now, full hippie convert. You want that My Chemical look, go right ahead. I got no problem with it. I’m just saying.      I   thought   your eyebrows had gone feral at uni. Lecturers were asking if you’d gone commando in the eyebrow department.      And what is wrong with my eyebrows?! You lot have never looked at a  natural  eyebrow in your life.      I’m not knocking your eyebrows, don’t get rude. I’m saying when you start letting everything go—legs, arms, even armpit terrain—it becomes a bit of a personality – very survivalist, very “I’m living off the land and judgment”.      Mate, you try and find a razor when you’re poor and busy with exams, huh? Like, someone said  "smooth is free" —unless you count the time and effort.      Fair point, I   have   been overwhelmed with college essays too – but I drew the line at hairy forearms about five weeks ago. Just not doing it.      You’re just a posh Cambridge person with her legs smooth like butter and her armpits as clean as that student union.      And you’re a scruffy Doncaster rebel with more dandruff than you do any self-care strategy.      I am not scruffy! I’m  natural . I’m being  political . It’s a body confidence thing.      Yeah, well, when you’re delivering newspapers around this tannoy-echoing suburb go ahead and let your legs be wild. If someone judges you, just say you’re in mourning for the razors you’ve lost.      Exactly! So I’m gonna keep it 100%, hairy and proud. Unless, obviously… I go on a date next week. Then I might be in the loo with a razor at midnight—again.      Only when the love is   real  .      Only when the love is   real and slightly dirty  .

So did I! The alphabet game’s a classic, innit. I was just trying to think of a drink called "Z". Maybe Zoom Zoom? I heard of that at a gym bar once. It's like vodka with… £20 and a cherry.      Ha, yeah, I saw that at a uni event last year. 'Zoom Zoom' it was called—three shots, a lime wedge, and a side of shame. Proper show-offy. But yeah, what was it pulling you to do a PhD in the States?      Oh, well, I thought I'd spread my wings. Lakelands is a nice enough place to write code and sip coffee for six hours a day, but I fancied something a bit leftfield. Plus, there was this guy who served keg beer and used boxing metaphors for every sandwich— “Your BLT’s got a body shot, mate.”  I just happened to volunteer after that in his café.      You, ordering body shots and eating tuna? That’s full culture clash—vibrating like,  person-to-person —British Research Manager in America land. Want to order a few of those "vibrating" body shots later?      Nah, I’ve had enough already. I’m on a soft drink tonight, because tomorrow’s a long day. I’ve got this black box model thing to present. If I’m already drunk, I might just say “this is what someone said in an exam” and they’d read it like it counts for something. Funny thing—job interviews, is it me or do people talk like their brain is a black box too?      Oh, absolutely. I’ve had a couple of supervisors who had this “trust the process” vibe—that failsafe “we don’t trust the applicants, but the process ensures we’re not biased, so trust the process” kind of thing. As if human bias can just be programmed out. I remember this one professor saying scientists are colour-blind, as if restricting your vision makes your brain stop noticing. Like, that’s literally how racism works.      Ugggh. I took the M54 route once, where a teammate made a joke about the EPL goonie map being accurate if you colour everyone yellow or red for "not white." Imagine hearing that between technical team huddles— “We can all agree on the algorithm, right?”  Wrong. We’re humans first, colleagues second.      Yeah, it’s like that ‘neutral’ pronoun debate at work. One guy once said,  “We should all be colour-blind.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, Doreen? I've been trying to get those old windows replaced for ages and the council just keeps sending the same run-around. I mean, sure, they say they support conservation, but when it comes to the actual funding—  poof  —they're nowhere to be found.      It's ridiculous really. I had the same issue last year with a 17th-century manor in Buckinghamshire. I drew up the most thorough business case, pulling in local tourism stats and even projected long-term energy savings from new glass, but the bloke at the grant office just looked at me like I was speaking Latin and said, “We focus only on structures with clear historical relevance.”      Typical. Funniest thing is, most of the "historically relevant" buildings they pick are already in a state of decay because nobody actually  lives  there. Whereas I, I'm actually working this place. Keeping a home in rep at the same time as trying to run a business—don’t get me started!      I know, it’s the worst of both worlds. You’ve got the full weight of heritage rules to contend with and the real-world pressures of property maintenance. I sometimes wonder if it'd be easier to just convert one of the side buildings?      That’s what I tried once, back in the late '90s when I bought the place. I hired some young developer—had big ideas, big dreams, and someone who definitely knew how to sell a vision. unfortunately, the old building didn’t match the new ideas. Also, he didn’t seem to understand that “16th century” doesn’t mean "19th century with period props"—a bad move if the council come sniffing.      Ha! That sounds very familiar. I had a client once, a retired schoolteacher, who wanted a ‘heritage wet room’ with underfloor heating and a glass tiled shower. The planning office threw a fit. They insisted it had to look like something you’d find in a damp Victorian dormer. Ended up using hand-painted tiles and brass fittings with a copper drain.      Some people would kill for a copper drain these days.      Oh, go on then, come see if you'd be interested. I've got a line on a supplier that can match any period, and the costs are genuinely competitive if you get in early. I might be past conservation conference season, but I'm still holding talks at some of the smaller architectural societies next month.

Rather annoying isn’t it? I mean I sat in that meeting for ages trying to get it through to them that we don’t need to change the demographics unless the client specifies it. I've been over this a thousand times with my team. Honestly, the way they collect data is so scattergun it’s not even funny. I swear, I’ll take one look at the query and 90% of the time I already know what they’re gonna say before they even open their mouths. Oh but don’t get me started on that. What’s that you’re making for tea? Looks nice, smells like bergamot or something like that.      A bit much, isn’t it, yeah? You know I like that My turkey university grants me absolution for being left alone in this roomr, but I still catch myself stealing glances and thinking "I could be solving this if I was at uni!" especially if it doesn’t rain again. I've been thinking about a bit in my thesis about social media and discourse markers — how, like, people say so much more in one sentence now than they used to do ten years ago. You’d say, “What are you doing?” and now it’s “So, like, what are you up to at the moment?” You'd think it was from the same person. Ha – but yeah, with your job, you must see all these patterns in data too.      Oh definitely. I use NLP to detect language sentiment in our social media feeds. Our biggest challenge at the moment is also dealing with linguistic differences between regions. Like, we had a campaign out in the north and it performed 40% better than in the south-east — which is strange because the content was about the same. Turns out the phrasing the copywriters used had a very midlands-centric tone, and not enough northernisms to plug in. It's weird how subtle shifts in phrasing can change whole responses. I’ve been thinking about doing more regional segmentation based on dialects, actually. I’d love to know what it sounds like in Sunderland — you from up there, yeah?      Yeah, born and bred! Except I've been to a couple spots over the last few years — Sardinia for a couple of months with a course I joined up to study gothic dialects — it was wild.

Right, so today I spoke to Miss Jenkins at the school. They’re saying her lunch money’s been running low again, Claire. And I’m not sure how many times we need to send extra over this term.      Do we not een-a use the  biscuit  one?      No, that only works when they’re  supposed  to eat lunch, not when you're sneaking snacks to the dinner ladies. Did she still say she won’t eat the school dinners, even if we made sure she had enough money?      Oh yes! She said the pea mash looks like sludge and the chicken smells like bin-liner and I think the head teacher’s got an evil twin who’s running the canteen, no doubt about it!      I hear the lunch lady hides carrots in the sauce now. Should I tell her?      Noooo!      But Mummy, today we had this… this   GIRL – she said she was coming to the school show – dressed as a GIRAFFE, and she had cards for selling bananas. And then  POOF  – she turned into a flamingo and did a  waltz , and also she winked at me like this – — and had a sparkle in her nose!      That’s gross!      I get it. The circus idea for the sports day does sound like fun. But we need to focus on more important things. Did you both put the forms for the tennis tournament into your lunchboxes?      I did! But Billy James said he brought a stone and tried to smash the chairperson’s teeth with it as he walked past. Also, he said he’d draw on his face with glue pens if he had the chance.      Right. Enough of that. That leaves us goin’ on the back of your parents’ responses – and yes, I do mean  your  parents. And don’t forget the chips.      But Grandmother makes  sausage rolls  and they’re  better  than the ones in the canteen ’cause they taste like ‘appy hippopotams.      Mummy, can we go to Granny's for our lunch  instead  of school dinners?      Not every day you little bee. But I’ll speak to her later. I just might give her a heads-up before you two pitch a tent in the back garden with the goat.      We’re not  elephants , Mummy!      But we  are  going to be the stars of the show! Like the one with the hats and the clowns and the lady who  walked on her hands in the middle of the lake .

Rather skip the new Disney one. Saw a clip and couldn't get into it. Felt like it was... I don’t know, maybe too much like the others? Not sure what annoyed me more, the music or the pacing.      Honestly, I agree. Went with a few colleagues on Friday and we  all  felt it was blokeish and overhyped. Though they did a decent job with the visuals. Not that that helps if the story is flat.      Oh, now you're just saying that because you never had the right education. I remember watching the original on the telly as a kid—those were much better films.      You sound like Mycroft from  Sherlock . The telly’s version doesn’t count, Dad. That was decades ago, and very different in style.      Fair point. Though it’s funny, isn’t it? The whole debate here in Cambridge last week about how we even teach history these days, right? Some group arguing that we should stop glorifying politicians and focus more on the people, the underdogs, the—what I mean—everyone else.      And what, let the kids go on about revolutions and how it’s all been about the struggle? I’m not denying that. But you can't ignore the role that leaders have played. Churchill, Gandhi—what would we do without them?      Dad, I might be wrong, but from what someone at the debate said—someone from the university—it's not just about  who  led, but about the context. Like, how real people lived through their leadership. That  is  history, not just a list of dates and famous men.      Oh come now. You’re just trying to make me sound like the old-man who only knows kings and queens. I did have a proper education for the time.      And you were  into  it as a student?      I was, I’ll grant you that. We had to write essays and memorise facts. No exams like today with 'soft marks' and whining about being hard done by. You just  learned .      Yeah, go on then, Dad. Name me a major turning point in pre-20th-century history that  didn’t  involve a monarch or a powerful figure.      The Black Death? That was more about God smiting the heathen, as they said back then. But that was over a lot of Europe at once.      Fair enough. But going back to the national curriculum debate, both of you—what do you think about the move to include more vocational training at university?

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed me thick socks and that wooly ‘at when I went out to fetch the paper.      I know, I've been humming about turning on the central ‘eating all week. That blast of winds from the east is giving it a proper old een to the place.      It’ll blow over, I’m sure. You don’t want to be burning too much fuel before the frost bites, if you know what I mean. I’ve got to keep an eye on the heat at the depot – runnin’ a business, you learn to tighten the purse strings when it comes to utility bills.      Still, I’ve been thinking about that old turkey on the mantelpiece. Terry left it in storage when he was renovatin’ the Dinning Room last year. If he don’t need it, I’d say we try to put it to good use.      Aha! The turkey ornamental, you mean?      That’s the one. It’s over fifty years old—vintage thing, if you know what I mean. Got some decent value, even if it’s still got a few dents from the war years. Speaking of, I was remembering something about when Granddad was in the RAF – tales of fox-hunting and air raids, all mixed in his old head. You lot ever hear those?      Oh, I ‘eard a few. Like the one where he ‘ad to hide in a barn with a French farmer and they shared a bottle of ‘idden wine while the bombs dropped. Rather romantic if you ask me!      Romantic or not, it was a proper war effort. That generation went through a lot. Still, I’m glad most of it is history and not repeatin’ itself like some say’s it is now with the mess in the Middle East. Got me thinking about the ones in detention centres here, cut off and all. Seems a right slap in the face, if you ask me.      I don't know, mate. Sometimes I feel as though we’re always trying to catch our breath and whaddaya know—something else is takin' us by the collar.      Yeah, goin’ on about life improvements and all that, but at the end of the day, we’re still stuck with the ‘untry on edge and your basic copper’s more likely to take you for a chat than give a pat on the head.

Right, so today is Chinese New Year weekend, and I thought we could talk about it and maybe think of a couple of fun things to do. I’m thinking lanterns, maybe something with red envelopes, and perhaps doing a small act of kindness as the tradition kind of says. What do you two think?      I don’t think I want to do acts of kindness. It’s not very fun. I only like giving money to the old man who sits on the bench near school.      What’s wrong with doing kind things? Didn’t Mummy teach us that being nice feels good?      Well, yeah, but we can’t go giving money to people in the street. It’s not allowed, Mummy said.      We don’t have to give money, love. Acts of kindness don’t always involve cash, you know. How about we do something like baking something nice for someone? Maybe a lactose-free cake or some cookies for Mrs. Baker, our neighbor? She told me the other day she can’t have dairy anymore.      Yeah, that would be nice! But what about the Draughts and Chess pieces we’ve still got in the hallway? We can use them as pretend money. That way we can give some “money” to Mrs. Baker and still act like we’re doing something fun.      That’s Silly. Why not just give real money? What’s the difference? They’re just coins and bits of paper.      Because we’re not supposed to use other people’s things without asking, and the coins are real money – not toys. The game pieces make it a game.      I want red hair like the Year of the Dragon stuff on TV. Maybe you could dye your hair red, Mummy, and we can all look like something from the parade.      Hun, Mummy’s hair isn’t going red. But I was thinking maybe we can get some temporary color for your hair, or maybe stick on some paper dragon ears. That’s safer.      I want to die my hair black! It’s cool like spies and ninjas.      Yeah, go for it! But it might make our heads smell like chemicals, and I don’t like that.      Time to plan what your actual kindness will be. Maybe you can make a small card and leave it on the neighbor’s door step with the cake? Or we can talk about adopting a charity this year, like giving them a bag of clothes or toys?

Mummy, did you know that Alice in Wonderland is supposed to be a real place in Oxford?      No, love, is it? I thought it was just a fantasy story by Lewis Carroll.      Yeah, kind of! I remember you telling me about that day – you looked magical. Did you know I had bellyache from laughing so much?      Did you take them presents like last time? I think I remember you bringing lollipops and kind of wearing a hat backstage.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think they'd do a bit more research before proposing wind turbines on that hillside. I mean, it's not like it's flat plains or anything suitable. The local protest group we chatted to last night, I had to explain half the things again about how coordinates and wind direction matter.      Yes, and if people just read the basic guidelines on the council’s site before applying, they’d see this isn't a feasible site. The planning control committee’s supposed to spot these things, but I heard from someone that they’ve been swayed by big energy firms offering bribes or generous donations to local sports clubs. That’s politics for you, isn’t it?      Bribes or not, the sums are what catch up with the lot of 'em. Those energy companies get massive grants for solar and wind farms, far more than what gets put back into proper R&D for better storage solutions. They're investing in shiny new technology, but the real problem is, what do you do when the sun stops shining or the wind drops—especially in places like the North of England where we get less sun?      Exactly. And the real issue is that we’ve got local protest groups risking it all without a clue of what they’re negotiating. My advice to them last night was, and I'll say it again, gather the facts—wind speed averages, grid capacity, visual impact. And then plan action: petitions, meetings, maybe even hiring a someone who knows development law. But they need to be a bit more organised.      Also, it's not just money and politicians—there’s a psychological side to it as well. People in small villages are afraid of losing control of their surroundings. Wind turbines mean noise, change, a new skyline. That becomes another layer to the ‘politics’—you're not just fighting the developers, you're fighting the emotional ties people have to their land.      You can't fault any of them for trying, I suppose. I mean, I was a teacher. I know how important it is to motivate people and give them the tools to keep going. But sometimes the system feels rigged. I’d be surprised if the appeal committee overturns any of their decisions even if the case is strong. They’ve got more to lose than the protest groups do.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You know, me and mine’ve had her in for a week and she’s still singing at five in the morning like a damn lark. They do this new app where it beeps and tells you what it is, but truth be told, I can still not work out the sparrow from the sparrow! Oh aye, had one when me and the Silly Stones were still together—  never   worked, and the moon was someone at the vet’s with suspicious eyes. Said it was a nosebleed because goin’ on your knees to get the food must have shaken your innards.      Aye—  nosebleeds   can get you at the worst time. I lost me mum to a heart attack during a tea break, and   then   her best friend had throat cancer, and over this bed, we were all sitting like    vultures   —well, not vultures, but kindred spirits of suffering, always with a pot of tea and a stale digestive to hand.

Thank you for that.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You used to see that kind of thing on the telly when we were younger and thought, "Oh, now that's the future!" All the more reason to keep an eye on our own doorsteps, really. I’ve started installing a doorbell camera. I remember once, back in the day when I was still teaching, I told me students time and again, "Education is your key out of the mess." But with t’way things are going now, I'm beginning to think there's another key we're all missing out on—security.      Mate, I often say that, and I know many other teachers do too.
