Just trying to keep a sense of normalcy around the school—shared meals, peer groups, a bit of stability here and there.      You’re doing your bit, then. I was a geography teacher, but talking the talk and walking the walk meant a lot more when you knew your family was struggling. I remember housing issues, sending the kids to the food bank. It made me question the education system quite a lot.      I know it's a difficult balance. I've got two of my own, bless 'em. We try to do as much as we can. Websites for extra English classes, hobby-based learning during the holidays. Not formal exams, but things like coding, art, even growing vegetables in the garden. Keeps their minds active without the stress of tests.      You’re a better parent than I was. I used to sit the telly while your lot was at school.

Right, lads and lasses, I've just popped the chips in the oven—the lasagne’s already warming in the tin, so no running off like last time, eh, Jamie?      Aye, we wouldn’t dream o’ it! Besides, I reckon it was yeh een, Lee, wot took so long fa’ th’ lasagne t’ heat up las’ time.      Cheers, Louise. I’m a kiwi, alright. But I ain’t doin’ no somersaults when me oven colps out agin.      Honestly, you'd think he'd learn, eh? I'm still likin’ the atmosphere here though, Cambridge. You’ve got a proper homely vibe. Unlike my nan’s place back in Kent. Still, no sad disco lights this time.      Mm, we’re still waitin’ on yeh top tips for music in this place. I know Jamie’s been tryin’ to find some decent folk tunes.      Ah yeah, I met a band in Kino—Kino! You know, the arts bar? Proper grief. Kinda like ... Camel in the 70s, but with a little more cheese.      Kino’s alright, I’ve been there once or twice. Though I reckon the best music experience I’ve had in Cambridge was at the Middle Eastern Centre. Had a live set by this ambient group called Spacetime Continuum. Like being inside a comet, honestly.      Ah, now that's more my scene. Still, nothin' beats a bit o’ jazz at Appleby Arms. Steve plays a mean piano round the corner of Pembroke.      Nice! Going back to that then—films. Anyone seen the new superhero flick? I caught a preview for it the other week. Honestly, more tragedy than action. Bit depressing for a Marvel film if you ask me.      I dunno, I thought it was alright. Like  The Dark Knight , but with space weapons and a nuanced villain. At least ‘e wasn’t the owd enemy wearing a green mask again.      Oh go on then, Lee, if you like  The Dark Knight , you’re just in love wiv Gotham's soddin’ bad weather and the one-eyed kid.      Haha, fair one, Louise. Though I think I’ll take a bit of darkness on the big screen o’er one of those fluffy rom-coms that Jamie’s into.      Hey, love stories can be powerful, Jamie. Think  Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind , or  Pamela . Not all ‘emm wih a few laughs.      Aye, Jamie's had his heart broken three times last year and still insists that romantic films are great for inspiration.

So did you lot hear the weather’s supposed to be mad tomorrow.      Seriously. I got up and it was already pouring this morning. Blows my mind how wet it is this week.      No, I mean—get in—my phone forecast was saying it might even snow at some point. That’s Cambridge in   March  , people.      Sounds ambitious. I’m halfway through a side project and I’m already chilled out. Imagine what it’s like for the kids at that camp I heard about. Didn’t it get moved?      Yeah, it did! The one that was supposed to start the weekend after next. My nephew was like  obsessed  with it because they do archery and rock climbing and stuff. His parents had to explain lightning and muddy boots and whatnot.      They’ve got to be tactical when it comes to kids and this weather. I did some work placement at a tech firm near London last year, and even the remote team was complaining. One guy said he’d rather stay over with his parents than try to get out.      What about gyms, though? For obvious reasons, we’ve been using them less—and it’s only been, like, one month. My friend Jen’s been going five times a week, swears it helps mentally.      I know what you mean. If I’m procrastinating on a game asset, I just go out for forty minutes and get back in with a clearer head. It helps more than coffee.      I tried a stretch of morning runs, but then I got  disgusted . You try waking up with the kettle boiling and the coffee machine on mute, and then someone jogs past in leggings and a lycra top and you’re still in pyjamas.      Should’ve dressed the part. Geostrategic move called stealth. Sleep in pyjamas, then strip into something ‘get fit’ ready. Slide into them seamlessly when passing the mirror.      You sound like a gym trainer trying to sell coaching. Anyway speaking of—my boss took the whole team out for a motivational trip around Lake District. Supposed to be away goenvironmental get your life together nonsense.      I like it, though. You genuinely get a boxset vibe sometimes when you’re all alone at home with just noise-cancelling headphones and a laptop. I miss those days, though—geek trips to Paris, Berlin. Anything where you didn’t have to be responsible for something apart from the work you were doing.

Rather skip the Easter eggs and go to the pub, me. This weather’s just cranked up the mood... got me in a proper no-go mood today.      Oh, don’t start again! You swore up and down you wanted to go on a  proper  Easter holiday. Got plans to paint eggs, bake scones, and   whatnot  . Where’s that excitement?      Ah, yeah, well I changed me mind. If I’m going to be stuck in the house anyway, I might as well be drinking. Besides, the kids aren’t even doing it like they’re meant to! Just knocking the eggs off the table and spilling icing sugar everywhere. It’s a nightmare.      Fun is supposed to be a bit of a mess, Gemma. But I get you — it’s raining all day and everyone’s about as cheerful as a wet breakfast roll. Still, I thought you’d like a bit of reprieve with me planting the TV in front of the Premier League final.      Oh, I will enjoy the telly alright. Championship decider—Brummies can’t keep out of it, eh? I only live two hours from Newcastle but I’m watching a Midlands team. Absolutely mad.      Traditional! You get north-south, east-west, all mixed in Cambridge. One min you’re sipping tea with a norf’sk accent, next you’re at a pub quiz with a Bolton man. It’s one big cultural mash-up.      I know, innit? Though the real reason I’m into watching this match is cause I like watching  you  when there’s goals and about five minutes left. You get all fidgety, blinking like you’re trying to see what you’re not seeing. Proper love to tease you.      Oh, shut up. And put the treacle tart in the oven before it melts into the floor.      Oh, I forgot about it! I’ll pop it on, yeah. Not sure how you like that over player of the match, but here goes.      Relax, the match ain't for ages. You got time yet. I’ll get the popcorn goin too. But if Liverpool win or something, you're carrying me into the garden, no arguments.      You're already your own worst enemy. I said I was too tired to paint eggs, not to carry you after a football match like it's a third-level gym workout for you.      Well, I’m not entirely sure if I'm paying for the match, transporting me and making both of us food, so don’t think I haven’t noticed that!

Speaker_1 :   Look at this photo here, Christopher. That’s the one from the London Marathon when he was ten and thought he could run the full thing. Blows me away what kids think they can do these days.   Speaker_2 :   Was he actually like in it? Like seriously running? I thought that was more for adults.   Speaker_3 :   Oh, he didn’t finish, but he got halfway! Of course, he was absolutely knackered by the time someone came and gave him a piggyback for the last stretch. But the pride in his face was worth everything. You should’ve seen it.   Speaker_4 :   Aye, that one’s still framed in our hallway. Funniest photo ever. Ten little legs, red face, Darcy, the dog, licking his head like he was an idiot for breaking a sweat.      We tried to encourage him with a bit of hard earned chocolate later. Only it took him, what, another hour to get that down once he realized it was dark instead of the usual milk.      So that’s your brother? He looks like he’s only ten, but still, the London… That’s the one in England, yeah?      Yes. We got tickets to the cinema later that day for a huge film. I think it was  Harry Potter and the Silly Stones  or something like that at the time, and he fell asleep halfway through. Poor thing—must’ve been a combination of the sugar crash and the running.      Of course he fell asleep. Any child under twelve should  not  be allowed in a stadium about five miles from the start line of a marathon without proper planning. You had to be a bit mad yourself, Patrick.   Speaker_1 :   Oh, I wasn’t planning anything. I thought it was a good idea at the time. He wanted to go. It was something he asked for.      Sounds mad, but cool. I’d like to go to the London Marathon one day. Do people do it just for fun?      Oh you bet. You run with t-shirts and mantras and even go to fancy dress balls beforehand if you've raised enough for charity. You name it. Imagine wearing a green dress with a box of buns on your back all the way to the finish line.      I had a class of kids who had friends running once. I had to take them to the cinema so the parents could go and cheer.

So do you remember how we used to play with those old-fashioned skipping ropes and jumpers, Ma? We’d be out in the garden all afternoons, and I can’t even remember how many times I probably got thrown out for making noise or something like that.      Oh yes, yes I do dear. You and your sister both, and your little cousin Bill. He used to come round a lot. A lot of those children nowadays have too much in the way of electronics, bless their hearts, but it’s nice to hear you’re still thinking back.      Mm, reminds me of the times when even TV was a treat. I used to love cartoons, only shown at certain times like everyone else’s, and I remember you used to knit jumpers for us all, didn’t you Ma?      Oh yes, I did. It used to be a bit of a task when you all grew so suddenly, but everyone has a jumper in there at the back, some oversized and hides, some not so much. I do still knit, you know, I made one for my grand-niece last Christmas, and the grandson had short trousers even.      And do you remember the bookshop in Peterborough, the one by where the little park used to be?      Yes, I do. My mother used to take me there every Saturday. Now I read mostly eBooks, it’s easier on the commute and everything, but I still like the feeling of a real book in my hands sometimes. I often read on the train to meetings.      Oh, and now they have eReaders and whatnot! I remember when your grandmother used to make most of what we ate from scratch. Meatloaf, jelly, all sorts. It was a whole ritual preparing for the week.      I have to be honest, I don’t do a lot of cooking. I always end up ordering pizza or going for kebabs. But the one thing I do know is I love a bit of soup, especially when it's raining like this.      That’s what I always do with lunches, keep the soup on the back of the cooker. My kids adore lentil soup, with bits of potato and carrots. It go's really well with a nice chunk of bread.      Yeah, I remember that. Ma always used to make that on cold days. It was like comfort food before it was a phrase.

Rather fine day today, isn't it?      Aye, it's been like spring in March rather than mid-July, has it not? Not a hint of a cloud in the sky.      That's the lot of us, eh? Sat here in the kitchen, having a bit of egg and cucumber on white. Still reckon it's the best sandwich in the world.      That's because you never had a decent quiche, Ronald. Remember that little place in Harrow where I used to pop in during the week when the bairns were under my care?      Aye, the one with the hippo on the window? Felt like a proper city thing, har! Me and the tonic water! Cost me half my pension, them pastry things and I only took the little sandwich with the paste in it. Cats would have scoffed it in a minute flat.      Oh don't remind me of the cats, not after the last lot. One of them got into the saucepan—vomited out the window like some mad cat Robin Hood.      Har! Did it tell off, then?      Well, I did. Beaten them with the ladle for days. But you can't blame ’em, really. Got a cat once, years ago. Used to sit in the phone box and answer it like it were a job.      A proper receptionist cat. Bet it didn't like the answering machine.      Not at all. Cried real loud at the machine. Like it had lost its customers or something.      That's what I call good service.      Ron, you're impossible. But I like it. Still, it does give one something to do, doesn’t it? Chatting like this.      Aye, well. I used to pass the time counting the traffic lights in Norwich. Not that I ever did much. Saturday morning, Saturday shopping, and the cats watching me like I were mad.      Some people call it eccentric.      Some people call it mad. I call it my day.      Still, I reckon you’d have made a decent gardener. That bloke on the telly, what’s his name, the big man with the green thumb?      Monty Don, is it?      Yeah, him. He wouldn’t half enjoy a chat with you over the geraniums.      Only if the geraniums did the talking. Me? I'd be the one taking notes.      A proper audience, then.      That’s it. Next time you see him on the telly, tell him to write to me.

So did you get the birthday present I sent to Fran? I raided the charity shop in Chester for hours trying to find the perfect thing.      Oh I did! It was the vintage typewriter, right? She was absolutely delighted. Looked like we’d just given her a Hugo Boss award or something! I swear, the smile on her face was   500 years wide  . You should’ve seen her reaction.      Honestly, I’m so delighted you’re into   vintage junk  . Who knew that was the way to Fran’s heart? I tried giving her a car once... like three years ago. Still hasn’t started.      Yeah, Fran and cars have like a toxic relationship. I mean, I get it. She’s tried rally driving, vintage motor shows, classic restorations and I think the only thing that’s ever run was the 1960s Triumph she slept in during a housewarming... for a week.      Honestly, I’m not even mad. I mean, why would I expect her to treat a car like anyone else? She’d rather try and revive it with a hug.      It’s not like that’s the only thing she struggles with. Her rhythm in general. Remember when she tried to do Baptism of Fire bootcamp with me? She ended up trying to bend the kettlebell around like it was   Jimmy Choo luggage  .      Laughing, but I also feel bad sometimes. I mean, she's trying. Her cat is just one oddly therapeutic thing in her life. Also, it   shreds my socks  , but I forgive it.      You know I about blocked her cat after a sock incident? I had the holes inspected by the vet. The cat clearly has a   black belt in feline karate  .      My sister had that problem with her dog. Kept going for socks. The dog was actually banned from several hotels for something extremely similar. One of them tried to stuff a sock into a duvet cover to make a handmade something. The hotel lady looked like she’d seen a ghost.      Some people, no matter where they are, find a way to make the world a little gothic with their pet-vandalism.      Speaking of pets, anyone got anything planned for the holidays? I’m thinking of bonding with some virtual family. It’s been a while since I had a heart-to-heart with those folk.      Oh I’m going to Cornwall with my parents. They promised silence and natural remoteness.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh, the whole mess with that fridge thing? I mean, it’s like... we’re paying rent and all, and you’d think we’d get a bit more attention than a “text me back when she gets back” sort of excuse.      I don’t eenno Harry, I mean we’re both faightfully hard pressed as it is. Times are tough enough with that Aneesa working long hours and this one [pointing at Speaker_4] costing a fortune to keep clothed and fed. I don’t need more stress, I’m telling you.      Honestly, I’m still trying to get my head around the supply teacher job. It’s like that My Name Is Earl bit, you know? Working bursts and then nothing. I’m half obsessed with Darcy and the rest I’m just trying to keep my phone topped up.      I envy you both, I do. I’m marking for hours every week and I’m still not earning what I should as a lecturer. And don’t get me started on that new Waterstones opening near the university—it’s like a whole new world of obsession with Harry Potter. I still mourn the old library, by the way.      You lot read too much. I mean no disrespect, but Mate, I got a real job and I know the difference between a good book and somethin’ that just sits and collects dust. Still, no insult intended.      Fair point. Though personally, I think the books inspired a generation of thinkers, not just fantasy heads. Some of them’d be a fine read if you give 'em a chance.      Oy, I did read the first two once. I bailed after the centaurs had a row with Ron. Not my cup of tea.      You ungrateful lot! J.K. Rowling has made the world a less dull place. Anyway, enough of that. Speaking of the world, did any of you hear about this new group, what’s it called—ISIS? Not to be alarmist, but I’ve seen headlines that make me want to keep the curtains drawn at night.      Oh don’t start with that, Harry! The world is vast goon enough without us fretting over every new buzzword. I’d rather just worry about making that mortgage payment.      Mummy, what’s ISIS?      [chuckling] Oh, that’s rich, Anika. Harry’s already got you talkin’ ‘serious issues’ when you’re just eleven!

Rather skip the new sausages, if I were you. I tried one last week, they’re like... Well, I’ll put it this way—_not_ like your grandmother’s.      Oh, honestly, they’re not that bad! I mean, they’re a bit rubbery, mind you, but we’ve got bigger things to worry about. Like our trip to Nepal next month! I still can’t believe we’re doing this at our age.      Honestly, it’s about time! You’ve got the stamina of someone half your age, Mavis. Besides, I’ve been telling you both for years—stories from abroad are the best stories to tell the grandkids. Just don’t forget to pack your walking boots!      I’m packed already—minus the pastry, of course. I’ve had to go gluten-free again after the wheat allergy flare-up. George is practically taking up second shift in the kitchen trying to make me his own loaf of sourdough, you know.      That’s darling! I remember when we were teachers—ah, I still miss the occasional lunch box with a jelly baby or two. Do you remember, Eleanor, the time we gave out mini ice creams by mistake and then had to call in the school nurse?      How could I forget? We were nearly grounded by the headmaster. But enough of nostalgia—speaking of meals, how’s the new free school meal system working for you?      Well, my son insists they’ve started oddly sour meatballs—George had to pack him a lunch box again. But at least now I don’t have to spend evenings in the school kitchen helping with displays. I’ve had quite the Renaissance lately: watching the Tour of Britain zip past the village!      I saw it too! Right past my orchards. The farmers were out with cameras, trying to get the athletes to smile. And have you heard about Bridget? My niece—she did an Iron Man race last summer. I still can’t get my head around it.      She’s your niece? No wonder you had the energy last year going over there for her graduation. I had a bit of the same when my go-to-place on the loo wall was suddenly replaced by one of those posters of her triathlon stats. Honestly, the box might as well be a recruitment poster!      I must say, I still prefer my saunter down to the Village Shop for a bit of produce.

So did you lot hear about the new weekend project at work? My boss just sprung it on me this morning... got to coordinate some kind of team-building road trip down to York. I've been over this a thousand times in my head already and I swear I'm going to lose it.      Oh no! That sounds like a nightmare if you're not careful. My company had one of those a while back—they planned a “retreat” and all it amounted to was a couple of PowerPoints, bad food, and me grinding my molars for two days.      Honestly, I just dread thinking about it! I mean, I get it—team bonding and all that—but can we not do it properly? Like, actually go somewhere fun? I’m not asking for Burning Man, I’m just saying maybe pick somewhere I don’t want to knock my team off a bridge.      Maybe it doesn’t have to be so bad? My friend at work went to one of these retreats, and it ended up being a mini-art festival in Brighton. They had stand-up, food trucks, some music, and even a raffle with actual prizes. They said it was the most relaxed they’d been in months!      Brighton, yeah? Sounds far better than some corporate estate with rows of folding chairs and lukewarm sandwiches! Honestly, the idea of getting out of Cambridge for a weekend might not be the worst thing in the world. What do they have planned this time?      That’s what I want to know. I mean, what if you’d arranged some adventure or something cool and it got changed at the last minute to ballet-themed icebreakers or whatever?      Haha! That’s a real thing. I had a friend who had to dress like a zebra and role-play as a team superhero in a workshop. It was for the logistics department, no less!      I can’t believe it. I was thinking maybe I could get some of the team on board to help me stick to my budget and not end up being the only one booking two separate lunches to keep the budget from collapsing.      Oh, budget talks around this are like a group therapy session—no one really wants to share, but everyone does eventually end up discussing how much they spend on coffee every week. Honestly, maybe suggest an outdoor team activity or something.

So did you read the letter from the council last week about closing the library?      No, what’s it about?      They’re talking about pulling it down and turning it into… I can’t even read the words—some sort of "community hub." But it’s just a fancy way of saying it’s going to be a car park or retail unit.      That’s ridiculous! That library was my social life when we first moved into Plumstead. All that reading and chess competitions. I practically grew up in there when I was younger.      Exactly! And who are these "community hub" people to decide what Plumstead needs? From what I’ve seen, they seem to only replace things with nothing. Remember when they told everyone the new play area would be multi-use? That turned out to be storage for wheelie bins.      True. You need to start a petition or something—before they make any more moves.      I’ve been working on it over the last few days. I’ve managed to get about twenty signatures already—colleagues, bar staff, even the guy from the chemist. Small ways, but it helps.      Be careful who you’re asking though – Mateo from the café said last night that he heard one of the borough reps telling her staff not to support any petitions that might cause "unwanted complications."      Honestly, this all reminds me of my time in school trying to memorise the order of the planets. You think you had the hang of it, and then the politicians come in and rearrange the planet ballet.      Yeah, like us trying to remember the difference between different borough voting systems. It’s like solving a cryptographic riddle that was written by a bureaucrat.      My brain’s burning out just processing half of this. I tried doing some brain training apps last week hoping it’d help. I think I did worse on the memory tests after waiting till 2 a.m to clear my overworked schedule.      Try not to think of it as "work". We both work far too much as it is. My shift ended at 3 p.m today and I still ended up here after work. Just wanted a loosened schedule for once.      Same here – I’ve been doing double shifts to meet invoice deadlines. Honestly, I live off takeout and naps now, but even then, I’ve been trying to remain focused on this petition.

Rather annoying the lot o’ Jehovah’s Witnesses, aren’t they? I had ’em round again last week, got the door half an inch after I’d just finished my dinner. I was in no mood for “eternal life” or whatever they call it nowadays.      Aye, they’re persistent if nothing else. Me nephew told me one time they turned up at his mum’s place with a wheelchair just to make sure they got in! Proper cheek, if you ask me. Though I suppose they’re just doin’ their thing, like.      Honestly, I don’t hold with any of it. Still, I made them a nice cup o’ tea, only because they looked like they hadn’t had a proper meal in days. Though I told ’em I wasn’t interested and I didn’t want any more literature.      Blimey, you’ve got more patience than I do. I just said I was busy with a crossword and shooed ’em off. Though I suppose, given the state of the world, people like that give you something to talk about.      Oh, I’ve got two words for ye—village characters and the Ministry of Works. You’ve got Marcus on the High Street who insists on painting all the utility boxes national pheasant red, and old Doris still runs that slap-up shop she’s had since her husband died. You know what she charges for a scone these days? Smashing the principles of fair trade, that woman.      That Doris? Oh, she’s a marvel. Some folks still serve up a proper scone with jam and cream. Can’t say I blame her, given the way people about here seem to walk into the coffee shops with broken arms and expect free lattes.      Speaking of places to eat out, have either o’ you lot managed to get a parking space on the A142 near Hunstanton lately? I tried me grandkids’ grandparents for tea last weekend and had to park a mile down the road. I could’ve walked to Lowestoft and back before I saw a single space.      Aye, the council took the fines out o’ my pension for a day last month! I was just cruising goin’ on for a fortnight and there I was, £80 lighter in the pocket. You’d think the ratepayers could afford to pay for a few more car parks, wouldn’t you?      As long as the dentists don’t charge for a consultation either.

Rather annoying I know but it was my choice to get a log burner I know it's inefficient they said like it's the cheapest option.      Blows hot air then it goes out yeah.      We do not have one of those at our house like the two of you it's all electric.      Yeah and that is what people use now as well not logs I mean obviously I had a log burner before but this is a decade ago now.      Yeah it is and we had to buy the logs when the outside company came round and told us how to use the log burner it cost us over a hundred quid for the logs just to test.      My mother still uses wood log fire-place though not log burner.      I had a log burner once and I think it turned out very expensive you had to buy the logs and then we had to have a chimney swept this happened when my H drive in his early days went to Japan.      My H drive was in the Netherlands actually.      Oh yeah, yes well we visited them both times I mean in the land of rising sun and in the Netherlands H drive met my daughter there in-country.      Oh yeah from what you told me Lady – Mate?      Yeah, yeah.      Yeah her flat was quite nice as well and their new place is actually better we were at that weekend, they have a new someone who works in London also.      Oh yeah.      Yeah and the kid got a grant and worked and being able to live in London but he's away now because he works about forty five minutes walk away but he's the area of Shoreditch or something like that.      Shoreditch yeah I know it it's up Market in that area and quite edgy.      Yeah quite trendy actually.      Yeah it is a trendy place.      Yeah I mean when I went there once the market had a handmade fashion type of things but also vintage.      They told me the same thing but also there's a really good café around the corner from him the owners are American go there really on the weekends if you like food.      Yeah I would like that.      Well we went there one time and you could choose your toast.      Yeah we had that those kinds of toast with like toppings.

Rather skip the new house altogether eh?      Aye, it's getting mad up there with all the rates they're charging. I’m more than happy with this old bungalow where we are.      Yes, the taxes are climbing higher than a church spire, if you ask me. I can't understand the government making it harder on folk who are already on their pension.      I swear they think we're all made of money. If I was thirty, pulling in a decent wage, I’d buy the place. But now it's like the blooming moon — just out of reach.      I heard the taxes are different for second homes now. You pay extra just because it's not your main-place to live. It makes no sense, to be honest.      I think it's all nonsense. It used to be a nice place to buy a second property for holidays or to visit family, but now it's criminal what they’re charging. I thought my childminding days had the most paperwork!      Watering the ferns and reading the papers, that's about it for me now.      And the TV! Have you seen what they want for the new ones? Ten grand for a “basic” box – that’s more than I paid for my old one thirty years ago. I miss my old set. All that knob-twiddling for the channels. Now it’s all buttons and touchscreens.      I tried setting mine up last week, and I had to ring a son-in-law in London to help me. He couldn’t even be here in person – did it over the phone! Blimey, I miss flipping channels with the same remote from 1997.      At least he was willing to help. I rang up the lad up in Leeds to do something for me on the Sat Nav, and he said he'd come. A three-hour round trip for ten minutes of fiddling! I said, no, you just tell me what to press. It's as if I'm being asked to go to Moscow with a map drawn on a cocktail napkin.      Still, I suppose these things are useful if you're off cruising the M1 on your own. I've had a go at it, but the thing just goes off into a bog somewhere, blooming machine.      So I asked about recycling bins to help keep costs down, and the council now bundles it with all your taxes.

Right, so the laptop’s still not working, ay? I’ve tried the basics—the reset button, poked the ports, checked the charger. Nothing doing yet. I think it's probably the motherboard, but I don’t fancy £200 for a fix unless it's under warranty.      Yeah, I tried the update last night and it just froze on me. I wanted to send an email with that homework before it’s due tomorrow. Why’s it always have to be last minute?      We can use the family computer for now, love. Or maybe the tablet. You don’t need to panic yet. Mary might still have her email and calendar on the cloud, right?      I guess. I just need to upload the essay, and it's due early in the morning. Is it still in the warranty, Dad?      I think it is—bought it for you two years ago, so it’s 14 months in. Let me check the receipt. I might’ve kept it in the drawer near the—ah, here it is. Rather annoying this new debt collector phoning in, Christopher. I've paid that internet company ages ago, and yet they still keep ringing me up about this phantom bill. I’ve asked for the PPI, and they’re dragging their heels like I’m the one in the wrong.      Oh darling, you’re not the first to say that. I handed over the PPI claim form last year for a travel company I used, but they wrote back saying I never had a policy. I was terribly cross, but it’s one of those things, I suppose. Didn’t even get the full compensation in the end.      Honestly, these companies think they can bait and switch us retirees out of money and get away with it. I had one of those phone calls too—some posh young man from Birmingham pretending to be from Barclays and I nearly gave the card details. It was a farce. Made better sense when I phoned Barclays up directly and they told me I’d been abused.      That’s why I showed everyone the article in the  Express  last week—about how many people, especially older ones, are being conned out of their pensions by unscrupulous PPI companies. Honestly, we’ve got to be careful these days. I remember when lending was more honest. Back in the 80s, you least got a slap on the wrist if you weren’t paying up.      You know what else is getting on my nerves? That new TV series about someone who solves problems for people. They solve everything in a week, but we’re stuck waiting months for something as simple as a debt query. It’s not even a drama, more like bullying, really.      I know! And you can just fast-forward past it on iPlayer. I’ve switched over to old cabaret shows instead. I love it when the women wear hats to the stage, like that Nina Simone clip from Manchester. Oh, and did you hear about the singing they’ve done at St. John’s Church again? I tried to get some seeds for a hanging basket while visiting the Abbey.      Ah, yes, I drove up last Sunday and had the most ridiculous time with the computer in the parking lot. Sat there for ten minutes trying to pay go-only £1 for a 30-minute slot, and it refused my card. Had to park by the supermarket instead, blooming disaster.

Rather a long day, wasn't it? That case dragged on far longer than it needed to.      Aye, it was poor organisation on their part. I've been in this job nearly ten years, and I've seen the same thing happen time and time again—Deputies turn up half an hour late, and then the whole schedule gets bungled.      I've noticed that too. Some would think that this is a place where punctuality is essential. But no, it seems to me that the older the court gets, the more things get bent out of shape. I often wonder how justice even gets  done  half the time.      It's like that in a lot of places these days. My grandson’s school tried to do this climate protest the other week. He says the head teacher gave the kids a lecture about assembling quietly while the cars outside idled. Fumes and all that.      Oh, that’s tragic. I remember as a child being told to keep the lights off to save energy, and now look at it—everything’s spinning backward in some areas. I mean, we’re teaching one thing and living another.      Aye, and the bus system is getting worse too. I had to take the 9:10 from Solihull because the 8:35 was cancelled. It took twice as long as it should’ve to get home, and I’m not the only one in this position.      That’s unfortunately a big part of the transport story now—reliability is a myth. I try and take the train when I can, but it’s not always reliable either. I suppose I’m lucky I live quite close now, near the school. Not much money to spend on anything else, truth be told.      That rings true. My pension’s not cutting it like it used to. I had to cut back on the heating a bit. Doesn't matter how many jackets I have, though, I'm waiting till springtime to get warm!      It’s always the little things, isn't it? I’ve had to scale back on things too—mainly holidays. My parents used to take us away every summer when I was a child. It does make you wonder if kids these days will ever experience that.      You'd think your lot would make more of an effort. But perhaps it's not just about money. Education comes to mind too—my grandchildren both say they don’t have a clear idea of what they want to do.

Right, who’s up for a little chat today? I thought we could have a fun time talking about happy things. You know, what makes you feel happy, and even dream a little about having lots of money. What do you think?      Happy things? Like ice cream?      Yeah! And daddy’s big tractors!      Well, I suppose that counts! But let’s think of a few more ideas. What else makes you feel happy?      When we sing silly songs. “Happy pots, sad pot pies!”      That’s not a  real  rhyme, Evie.      It  is  too a rhyme! You silly melon!      Oh, I like it! “Happy pots, sad pot pies.” Pretty clever. Why don’t you two tell me something better?      I know a rhyme! “The cat ate a hat, the dog looked at that, the cow said wow, the sheep went to town!”      That’s not a  really  good one. I can do better!      Well, competition on! Tell me what makes you smile, Evie. Other than songs and rhymes.      When mummy plays with me, and when we go to the park and swing really high! And when we have chocolate for tea.      When we ride our bikes in the woods and when I get a chocolate bar from my pocket money!      That’s wonderful. So, it’s the little things in life, isn’t it? Family time, fun, sweets...      What about money?      Oh, you mean having a  lot  of money?      Yeah! Like a  million  pounds. My friend’s dad has that much!      Mummy, if I had a million pounds, I’d buy all the toys in the worlds!      I’d get my own helicopter and go zooming around!      That  does  sound fun. Now, if you had  plenty  of money, but still wanted to be happy, what else would you do?      Maybe give some money to the poor? Like in the church collections.      I’d get a big castle with pigs in the garden!      Well, those are all great ideas. It’s important to remember that even if you have a lot of money, the real happiness comes from the things we’ve just talked about—time with the people you love, doing fun things, and even giving to others.      So being rich isn’t the  only  way to be happy?      Not at all! In fact, people sometimes get so caught up on having more money that they forget to have fun. What’s more important to you?

So do you reckon like, if I wanted to be an inventor or something, like, would they let me stay in the lab all night or something? I mean China's got all these inventors, right?      Hmm, not unless you're Elon Musk's long-lost cousin or something. I think the real deal is more about practice than all-nighters. But yeah, China’s making a lot of noise with all their tech stuff. They're like, top of the class now.      Yeah! My dad was saying the other day that in ten years' time, Chinese companies might own like half the inventions around the world. I don't get why the government doesn't help people make patents like that more.      Maybe they do. It’s just more secret-y. I read somewhere that they push schools to make kids think like entrepreneurs. It must be mad there. Like, can you imagine—your GCSEs being about starting a microchip company?      Honestly, sounds like a nightmare. But maybe that’s why they’re so good—because they do it super early. I’d rather start up something in my garage, honestly. If I had a laser cutter, that is.      Lasers? Bro, that’s just suicide waiting to happen. Mate, I got a paper cut and I bled for an hour. Let’s not pretend we're ready for mortal danger at 16.      Okay, fair. But what if I found an invention idea that was solid? Like a real one. I mean, not something flimsy like a smarter shoe or whatever. Something solid. Can you imagine if we could, like, invest in it?      You’d need money, first of all. Not just a wild idea and some corroded nails. Unless you’re one of those uncles who still invests in crypto ‘cos he says it’s the “future.”      Ugh, don’t get me started on my uncle Terry. I tried to explain to him that Bitcoin could fall to zero and he was like, "Well, if it comes back, I’ll gain biggg." He said it extra loud like that for some reason.      Maybe he's got goon shoes on. Anyway, you'd need a real mentor, someone who's in the loop, you know. Someone with contacts or something.      So how do you get someone to take you seriously? Like, am I just supposed to walk into a university with a PowerPoint and say, “Here’s my invention, sir”?

Rather skip the new bar in the hotel and just go back to mine and have her in peace.      But she’s having a lot more fun here, you saw how she was with the waiters.      I know, it's just like when she was little and I took her to that fancy place in Birmingham for her tenth birthday and she kept running up to the waiters with her plate and asking if they wanted more. Let's not even mention the time she thought we had a patio out the back of this place and spent ten minutes looking at the balcony under the dining area like it was Prime Minister's Questions about whether or not there was a back garden to go with it.      She was very persistent. I was trying to convince her it wasn't there, but to no avail.      So, after lunch, what do you think? Shall we go try Ski Hire? Darcy said the last rental was way too restricting when she went before.      Well as long as we don’t take her to a new bar first—she might do the same as when you took her to that nice bar back in the hotel by the go-karts on your own trip here.      I remember that, I had to go behind the box office and lift her out from under the bar. It was like The Great Escape.      And after that she had bellyache from laughing so much.      So, to recap: Darcy is not coming back down unless she's done her "better" bar or done skiing, one or the other, but probably both.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, love? These rackets are practically brand new, and they string like... Well, I don’t know. Like they're made of tissue paper, sure!      Aye, I know what you mean. It's been like that with mine too. I'm thinking now, perhaps we try one of them   cable ties   on the tension wires? I saw something on a forum once—someone used a bit of paracord and tied it   behind the tension strings   to give it that little extra grip.      You mean like... like securing it with some kind of lever?   Like a belt and braces, then?        Exactly. You don't replace the mains or the crosses, just go over the back and use a tight little loop of   some sort of durable material  , maybe   some 2mm elasticated cord, or even a bit of gym rope  ...      And the weight? That's another thing, I've always thought the lighter ones are more reliable—  but not always, is it?        No, not always. I've tried   graphite frames   too—lighter, but the string tension is a nightmare. You have to string them at about 45lbs otherwise, they go slack after one game.      All that just makes it more expensive. I was looking online, proper string sets, they cost   nearly forty quid for a box  . And that's just one badminton player!      So, if you want it to be a decent idea for a   small business  , it has to be   both cost-effective and reliable  .   You can’t just fiddle around with what you've got—you've got to know what works and scale it.   Maybe we could do something like ‘RacketGuard’—market it toward schools first, you know.      You mentioned ‘fleet’ earlier. I tried using it in a sentence today.   “Primary schools usually have a fleet of rackets for indoor games.”        That’s right! And   secondary schools  , believe it or not, often have the same issue—  environmental conditions  , kids are rougher,   misting up in the gym in the winter, leading to tension loss  ...      It’s funny how something as tiny as a string can bring the whole racket down. I was adjusting   Andrew’s strings   earlier on and I   accidentally cut his ear lobe with the clippers.   I nearly cried!      Oh, poor thing! Listen, always take it slow.   Especially with a bad clippers like mine—they’re thirty years old!        Well, I think I’ve fixed his lobe, but his   new stripe on his head is really sharp  .

Rather nice of you two to bring us all in, especially with that promising bit of crumpet in the tin. You've always had a way of brightening up a room with something like that, Philippa. There's pottery again, some sculpture, even some performance art interpretations. We could take you as a group. Let you walk through space and take your time with the pieces that speak to you.      Yes, something around March or April. The weather might even go our way then. If you like, I could go over the exhibition schedule with you, Denis, and maybe we can box off an hour or two your way.

Honestly, I swear some of the girls I work with are like glue sticks—useless and flaky. Won’t take a single hint, asks the same questions  three times a session , and still can’t remember the standard operating procedures. It literally made me want to scream. I said "document the client’s mood and baseline for the day," and she goes "Is that like if they’re happy or sad or if they throw a cup at you?" And the cleaning stuff. “I passed out about tidying up at 6 a.m.” – pass out as in sleep or black out as in faint? I need a translator just to live here.      Honestly, I've reached the point where I just write "neat" next to any sentence and call it a day.      Anyway, enough of my soapbox about nonsense. If you're done preoccupied with your head, do you wanna go out on Saturday? There’s a new little bar near the station with really good vegan options.      I'm down! Procrastinate like it's a sport? Sure. But only if you're buying the chips with everything extra.

Right, so today was the day trip to the farm, and thank goodness it was sunny! I thought it’d be a disaster with all the muddy boots and ducks and chickens! How do you think you two behaved?      I fed the ducks! And picked a strawberry! And I didn’t get stuck in the  mud  like you said I would.      I saw a pig! It went  oink oink oink ! And it was  humongous!       Well done for not crying when the goat nibbled your T-shirt, Tom! You seem like you handled it like a mini explorer, both of you, actually.      I still don’t like melon though. The farmer tried to make me taste one, and Oliver shouted, “Blimey, she screamed like a ghost!”      Wait,  you  screamed? I mean, like... loudly?      It was sour, you didn’t have to try it. You’re not allowed to watch_ratings_3R_evil_creature DVDs unsupervised, either.      Well you  like  popcorn so  you  make the rules!      Listen, if you two don’t stop arguing, no DVDs tonight and no popcorn. Deal?      Deal. But I want to watch the one with the flying  mermaid .      Only if she’s a hero.      Well then, let’s finish the bolognese, and we’ll see what kind of hero you become.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? The cold at Easter. I swear it was warmer in January.      Aye, I’m more used to it in Birmingham, but Cambridge does a fine job of being damp all year round, I reckon.      I’ve just een beginning to learn how to knit. It was either that or sit about doing nothing all day over the Easter break. A friend of mine swore by it as a way to kill time.      Oh, nice! What are you making?      Just a scarf – plain old wool, nothing fancy. Though apparently, I’ve got to learn the “cable knit” for the next bit.      Ah, cabling is clever. I thought I’d maybe make a new one for you at some point – if you don’t mind the questionable colour choices.      Sounds grand. Just don’t make it chartreuse. She took an awkward tumble, but cheers for the laughs.      Exactly. It’s supposed to be about pageantry, but real people tend to look like they’ve been caught between a rock and a hard place sometimes.      It’s all in the charm really, though. The more awkward those moments are, the more real they seem. Just made me think how much poorer celebrities must feel at times – like they’re always being watched.      Totally true. I suppose once you’re always in the public eye, there’s no such thing as a mistake.

Rather do a day out in London, innit? Thought we could catch one of them 3D films... got to keep up with them young ones, eh?      Oh, I’m alright with that. Aright, but we’ve got to get the transport sorted properly, innit? You don’t fancy paying all them extra pounds for taxi – especial with us being fairly spritely, but still not exactly sprinting into the new age of travel.      Oh, I don’t care for that. Them busses in London, though – always running late. And trying to read a map with them oddly written letters on the stops? Half the time I can’t see the bus ‘til it’s nearly gone past me, let alone read the route!      Aye, it can be a minefield. But if we start from the tube, that might be better. Know it’s a bit tricky getting to the museums, but at least the trains are less random than the buses. Still, I reckon them new 3D screens on the tube would show us which one to get on.      3D screens? You sure they’re not meant for the films we were on about earlier?      Now, where's my head? 3D films or goin' on them 3D rails... Either way, it's a sight better than watching telly all day.      True ‘nough. So, shall we get the 3D cinema one first, then head off to the museums for the afternoon?      Perfection, love. We’ll see a film that’ll knock your socks off and then walk about for a couple of hours.

Rather annoying really, but it's not the first time. I mean, you’d think by now everyone would know where to go, but no—half the group still ends up at the wrong venue. I told them again this year, we’re not doing the same as last year.      Aye, and I liked last year’s place, honest. The big old converted factory in Shenzhen? Had that great central heating too. Not that that helps much in January, mind you. It was still bloody freezing once you moved away from the heat. Still, the food was brilliant.      Yeah, but I wanted somewhere more  visible . You know, no need to text people directions for two hours like last time. Just a bit further out, though. The one near the lake, the one I found in a township called Kunshan. Fair bit of a trek, but it’s got a proper Christmas-themed breakfast, and the owners do this whole Anglo-Chinese fusion thing—roast turkey, roasted chestnuts, mulled wine, but also steamed buns and spring rolls. Feels like Christmas, if you ignore the cold.      Aye, as long as there’s food and drink, I’m there. Speaking of, what are we watching after? Last year we tried to watch some festive rom-com, but it got shifted to  The Texas Chainsaw Massacre  because Tom reckoned that “was the real spirit of the season.” Near enough lost an eye, poor bugger.      Oh God, don’t remind me. He thought the guy with the chainsaw had the same surname as his former maths teacher and got confused for like an hour. Anyway, this year I reckons we do a bit of a marathon. Have the proper Christmas movies on— Die Hard ,  Mamma Mia! , maybe dip into a bit of classic stuff like  It’s a Wonderful Life . Burgers and beer, guest speaker and some terrible jokes about it being Christmas in bloody China.      Aye, I’ll be the guest speaker all right. I’ll propose a toast to the spirit of misadventure and bad English subtitles. Not forgetting the snow machine that Tom set up in the garden last year—which started spitting actual gook rather than pond water about halfway through.      Ha! I almost got that fixed. Sue the boxset or something.      So are we planning for the 3rd? I’ve got a lecture on the 2nd, but I’ve wrangled some excuse about overworking and needing to be "interveted."

So did you read the Twitter thread my cousin put up about that restaurant in Margate? Total disaster. Said it was the worst meal she’s had in years. Absolute slap in the face for the price.      Yeah, I saw it! Some places just don't get that reviews make or break a business. I swear, I’ve seen people take   50 quid's   worth of food and then just pan the place to pieces over one under-seasoned starter. It’s like,   ‘Oh you should’ve paid me to come here.’        Honestly, I know how grating that is because it happened to  me  last week. Someone gave my café only two stars on TripAdvisor after I spent  two hours  with them. Said the coffee was ‘mediocre’ and the bread was 'underwhelming'. I said   ‘The bread came straight out of the oven, and you’re calling breakfast  underwhelming ?  ’ Seriously, I was in shock.   Spekaer_1:   Oh, I showed up at the wrong place once. I was walking around Watergate and just got a bit lost in the place. I mean, don’t get me wrong, the food was actually  good , but the layout was so disastrous I left halfway through and then put a one-star review out of frustration. Not with the food, with the design of the kitchen. Like the tap wasn’t near the cutting board and the whole thing was  a nightmare .      Honestly, I get that. I work in a bakery and my boss wants to open a  small restaurant  out the back, but I’m telling her   ‘design is everything’  . No one wants to wait 20 minutes for their plate while eating the same smell the oven just gave out. It’s like cooking in your own living room. Doesn’t work.      Yeah, I’ve thought about designing  my  café like a guesthouse in Margate. Clean, minimal, open to the outside. Let the fresh air flow in. I tried extending the café into the garden last year. It didn’t  exactly  take off but it gave the place a  certain charm . People like the ‘laid-back experience’ even if they’re not eating.      That’s the thing, if you don’t get the vibe right, even the best quality food becomes  disposable . That bloke on Twitter, your cousin, she could’ve said the same thing to the owner and maybe it’d have been sorted, right?      Maybe.

Right, who’s ready for dinner? I’ve made a proper roast – chicken, roast potatoes, carrots, and some green beans. And I’ve got raspberry jelly for afters if we all behave ourselves.      Yucky green beans, I don’t like green beans!      Well, if you eat them all, I’ll get you a big scoop of chocolate ice cream. Deal?      Deal! I like chocolate ice cream bestest in the whole world.      Mummy, can I have some raspberries before dinner, please? The ones from the garden taste super nice today.      That’s lovely to hear, love. You know we grow them ourselves, don’t you? Mummy and I planted the plants last spring, and now they’re giving us treats.      Yeah! I saw a bird in the garden the other day. I think it was trying to peck at the raspberries too. Maybe it wants some?      Some birds do try to grab a few, but that’s why we leave out some bird food in a separate place. I don’t want the birds to think they’re human food.      Oh, speaking of animals, have you been out to feed the gerbils lately?      Yeah, yesterday! I gave them some dried sweetcorn and some apple slices. They like the sweetcorn better.      That’s sweet of you, Oisin. Keep an eye on them though. If they start chomping the apple too much, you’ll need to weigh them again and see if they’re getting too much sugar.      I have a tiger gerbil. My teddy’s the tiger gerbil. I pretend to feed it too.      Oh right! I remember it. You’ve got quite the collection of imaginary gerbils!      I saw a funny bird the other morning by the bin. It was got all dirty trying to dig for something. I think it was looking for the crusts you chuck out after toasting.      That’s the magpie! They're such smart birds. I read once that they can use tools. I bet it was looking for your crumpet crusts!      Crumpets? What’s that?      It’s something Mummy and I used to eat at tea sometimes. Thin, round, and quite delicious with a bit of butter or even jam!      I’ve had buttered crumpets at Aunty Claire’s house! She also makes them with raspberry jam, which tastes kind of like the jelly Mummy made earlier.      I want some of that jelly!      Yeah, yeah, we’ll see if you behave through dinner.

Rather skip the butcher's this week. You know, with how everything's been flying in and out, like... What was I saying? Oh, I’m more than happy to take something up to you both, Mummy. I can pop into Tesco and pick up a few things.      That would be  grand , love. Not many people would think about that now—most of ’em just let things slide when they’re busy doing this and doing that. But you, you always remember. That’s the nice part about you, Liz.      Oh, don’t you fetch everything, dear. I’m  not  a invalid, you know. Still, if you’re popping out that way, a couple of cans of jelly and a loaf of white would do, if you’re not too bothered, love. I’ll be the happiest woman with a cup of tea and a nice bit of breakfast, no doubt about that.      Of course, I’ll do that. No worries, Mummy. And I was thinking, actually, we  might  get into that nice little Italian place in town—Brigids? You remember it? The one with the little flowered window.      Doesn’t look half bad, from what I’ve seen through the buses. But with the prices, I swear it’s more than some of the city centre restaurants.      You know what I say about eating out? Only when they give you a nice bit of meat and a bucket of wine. That’s the way to go, preferably on someone else’s tab.      Any money left at all after the bills come in, you can have about half a plate of chips and you’re the happiest woman alive.      Maybe next weekend then. I can see if Suzy and Steve want to come in? It’d be nice for everyone to get out once in a while. Mummy, I’ll also sort the eyebrow strip for you—I’ve got some left, or I can pop into Boots on the way.      Oh, not again! What with that machine I摔在前年打碎了害臊机, you remember, after I had that row with the bloke in the salon? I still say if you don’t cut mine at the same time as the eyebrows, I look like a gosling that lost its way.      You look fetching to me, Ma.      I’ll sort it all out, don’t you worry. And I’ve been meaning to ask—Mum, how’s Davy getting on?

Right, thanks for making the coffee. You know, I’ve been meaning to ask—the weaning’s going really well, isn’t she starting to like more solids now?      Yeah, she is! I’m honestly amazed. She tried banana and avocado the other day and just munched it up like a pro. I think the formula’s going to start reducing properly soon.      Oh, brilliant. That’s the best news. I remember when you said she was teething; you looked exhausted! Did you manage to get through it?      Eventually! It helped that Nan came over for a couple of nights. Honestly, someone to just sit with me and make me tea and listen to me moan was everything.      Aw, well if you ever need a break, just say. I’d be happy to take her for a few hours.      You’re a star. Mum says I need to start planning social stuff again too—can’t be stuck at home forever!      It’s so true. My sister’s having a little garden party next Sunday. You should come with baby. I’ll get the bouncy chair out again—she’d love it!      That’d be lovely. My friends are talking about planning a trip up to Manchester for the weekend after. One of them works in a creche and offered to babysit if I could go.      Oh, someone to help would be a godsend. You just need time to yourself now and then. Have you had the chance to go to the sign language classes you mentioned?      Yeah, actually I did last week. It was so much fun! The tutor’s a lovely man and he showed us some really useful phrases. I’m trying to teach baby a few too—just “more” and “milk” so far, but she’s already mimicking gestures.      That’s adorable. Do you think you’ll continue once you’re back at work full-time?      Absolutely. I mentioned it to the headteacher too and she said we’re going to be working on some deaf awareness in the school this term. I told her I’d go in and do a short presentation if I’m up to it!      Oh, you’d be brilliant at that. You’ve always had a way with people.      Thanks, it means a lot to hear that. You know, I’ve been meaning to start planning baby’s first birthday—any ideas?      Oh I’ve got a few!

I can’t believe how peaceful it is out here. You can’t get a view like this in London, can you? No way. It’s completely different. Just the sound of birds and the wind is enough to clear your head. Look at that hill over there—do you know what it’s called? I feel like I’ve heard the name before. That’s Raven’s Hill. A few of my students have done small research projects on local topography; apparently, it was a Roman fort once. Small clues in the earthworks and pottery fragments. Nothing too dramatic. A Roman fort near a quiet Norfolk village—what a contrast. I half expected a hippo to emerge from behind that hedgerow. You know how big my imagination can run when I’m surrounded by fields like this. I think the world might be better if everyone spent a bit more time in the countryside, honestly. You don’t notice all the little things in the concrete jungle, you know? Like the way the light filters through the trees, or that smell of damp earth after the rain? Speaking of, should we check out that path going round the back of the village? It looks like it might go through a couple of those old orchards we passed earlier. Definitely. I’d love to see if they still have those ancient apple trees. One of my flatmates used to grow them for cider. If we’re lucky, maybe we’ll find a field of old hawthorns. They’re so symbolic of this part of the country. Some people come all this way just to walk these quiet paths, I bet. Londoners like me are always romanticising places like this—they don’t often get to experience the real thing. It’s not all that difficult to get to, you know. With the train network up here in the East of England, places like this are closer than you’d think. Still, I get it—most people would rather imagine it than actually immerse themselves. You’re getting your lecture voice on. Just like that time in the pub when you explained the entire history of the River Wensum to strangers.  laughs  Okay, but that’s the point of it, isn’t it? To know your surroundings, to feel at home in the space you live in, even if you were born somewhere else.

So did you watch The Batman yet?      Yeah, I did—the one with Robert Pattinson, right?      Yeah, exactly. Mate, I've been telling everyone it's the best version of Batman I’ve seen in years—proper dark, like the Riddler’s on there and it doesn't feel like one of 'those' villains.      Oh I agreed. A lot of DC tends to be too camp or too weird, but this was actually quite grounded. I mean, you still got the bat mobile and the chase scenes, but the story made sense.      Oh,  yes . And Zoe Kravitz as Selina Kyle? That was like a dream sequence, innit? Proper class though.      I didn’t know she was in it, and I think I turned to my sister halfway through and was like, ‘Zoe? What is she doing here?!’ But she was brilliant in it. Blooming mad, but in a good way.      So why did you not mention it before? I text you a million times about it—“Mate I’m obsessed!”.      I did, didn’t I? I said I’d watch it. I been meaning to. Work's been pissing about though—consulting projects, you know it's one thing after another. I promise I don’t ignore you like that.      Nah, nah, been busy—well, what someone said to me this week though was: my friend's job just moved to a new office out in Wandsworth and now they have a real problem with cyclists.      Oh, really? Not in about five years I’ve not heard of such a thing.      It’s wild. She said that her building manager put up a sign saying, “Cyclists to the left, delivery to the right,” and apparently it generates more arguments than it does organisation.      Classic. I think it's impossible to meet everyone’s expectations when it comes to who uses the road and who uses the cycle lanes. London always trying to be all clever and “eco-friendly,” but if the drivers and cyclists just remember that they’re not the only people on the road, go on…      Fair point. But at the same time, I don’t see why cyclists always have to be the ones getting the blame. Cos you see all the lorry drivers just wellying across bike lanes like it's nothing?      Oh, yes. I get over to Cambridge every few months and it's like a warzone—keeping near to the cobbles, people kind of weaving, trying to dodge things.

Rather lovely this place, isn't it? I mean, I've lived in London for years, but it's surprisingly calming out here in the Norfolk countryside.      It really is. I come out here as often as I can, especially when things at work get too hectic. Do you remember the last time we came walking around here with the kids?      Oh yes, a few years back now. They were still so young—barely paying attention to the path and more interesting in picking up every stone and leaf. They’re starting to chase the football around the fields now.      Still, it’s so refreshing to get out and just… walk, think, and not worry about lectures, grants, or emails.      True, and look at the hedgerows—so full of colour this time of year. I was just reading about traditional crops and plant species in Bucks and Norfolk this week. They actually grow a lot of marigolds and lavender for essential oils, didn’t you know?      Really? I didn’t, but it makes sense. These areas aren’t just full of land for cows and pigs. I think the government is starting to recognize the potential in cash crops for local economies. Have you got plans to write about it?      I might, it's interesting to see how the economics of small farms are evolving. Some are leaning into niche markets—organic herbs, decorative flowers for florists, even things like sunflowers and poppies.      That's oddly romantic. You with your marigolds and me with my spreadsheets and regression models. Still, I suppose it’s all part of the same world—trying to figure out what makes the pieces fit.      Exactly. Another thought—you know that new French research project I mentioned? About cross-cultural fertilisation of rural economies in Europe. I’ve been trying to get funding for a case study here in Norfolk to compare it with a few villages in Normandy. I was wondering if you'd be interested in helping out from the economics side.      Hmm, that could be really interesting. I’ve got some students working on comparative rural development models—maybe this could be a group project. Could go hand in hand with your research.      That would be brilliant, and I can teach them a bit of French while we’re at it. The latest version of the fluency app I'm using is absolutely addictive.

So do you want me to bring my car or shall we do mine?      No, you’re sorted, I can drive us both up. I’ve got an extra seat belt in the boot for emergencies. Not quite NASA-grade, but it’ll do.      Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive texts from the estate agent saying if I don’t call them in next two days they’re listing it. Fair enough, this flat isn’t exactly in high demand. It’s got reasonable floorboards and cupboards, but the ceiling doesn’t chase you, so that’s a plus.      Lakelands is still a decent spot to live, don’t knock it. Being minutes from a university definitely helps, even if it left the premises twenty years ago. We had the same problem with the flat in Harpenden — screamed ‘student housing’ for about a decade after the last breakfast clubs moved out.      I’m thinking about the commute, though. If we’re going to move near the Angel of the North, I’d rather not spend four hours a week crawling through the M18 every Sunday. You don’t fancy a quick jaunt to the real north for the weekend?      Only if it doesn’t involve rewatching  The Baptism of St Nicholas  in a Chapel that won’t confirm my baptism unless I promise not to play football barefoot in their car park again. Last time I tried that, the vicar called out someone who looked like my granddad to chase me off.      You’re not still punishing yourself for that, are you?      No, I’m punishing the vicar about how I’m now allergic to turkeys from 2017 to mid-2020. Thanksgiving is brutal. Speaking of which, have you managed to book that tennis match with your brother for Saturday?      Said he’ll be up at 6 a.m. for it ‘cos he had a nightmare about being late for a serve practice. We’re not even going to a pro player acadamee, it’s just us and the local guy who once hit a tennis ball over the road and a cat got caught in a vending machine.      But he’s got a  game plan . Gave me a PowerPoint on spin, serve placement and the psychological benefits of aggressively arguing line calls. He’s like a 1980s conference seminar, just out on a court pretending to care about your life goals.      Yeah, but he at least listens.

Rather annoying the new trial they’ve got on with that Jeremy Kyle show-type thing. Don’t they know people just say what they want on TV and then change their minds? I mean, sure, celebrities are a bit dramatic, but it’s not like the rest of us aren’t either.      Yeah, I liked the old system better, to be honest. At least it had some sort of a ring of truth about it. Not that I watch much telly, mind you. It’s easier pulling weeds in the garden than watching the lot of them squabble.      You don’t like the telly much, Ruth? I used to love watching the real ones—those oldsploits that Myra used to have on late at night. The one where the boy was accused of something and the mothers all yelled and screamed in the back? Good times, if you ask me.      I suppose that was a better time for drama in real life. But you know what really hides drama, Ruth? Watching the geese flying over. They don’t argue about it, just point and fly. I’ve noticed they always take that path over the old railway tracks. Do you know, when I was a girl, watching the geese used to give me the best sense of calm.      I know what you mean, Hayley. Some mornings, I’m out cleaning Mrs. Dobbs’ windows at the crack of dawn, and that’s the first thing you hear. The honking. It’s like a choir of chaos. But then I see the way they fly in that pattern—like a secret language.       Sips her coffee  Geese, eh? My George used to say they were clever birds. He’d watch ’em from his shed and say, “Sheila, those birds know where they're going, even if the sky’s got that hangover kind of look.” He passed 20 years ago now, but the geese still pass over my window every spring. Guess wildlife don’t change with the times like us, eh?      That’s probably the saddest thing about it all—geese keep doing what they do best, and the rest of us just sit here watching the telly or worrying about cleaning up someone else’s mess.       Chuckles  You don’t worry, Hayley. You’ve your own mess to clean up.       Laughs  Well, you’ve all got your roles, haven’t you?

Rather annoying isn't it? I mean I've done six interviews now and none of them even came close.      Six? That seems more than I'd have thought you'd have had!      Yes, the school in Nottingham phoned me yesterday again after I'd sent een cv and they said I was runner up for the Spanish Post.      Oh I'm so sorry love, but that's so strange isn't it? You're so good at interview stuff.      I don't know. The last one I had was at some selective grammar in East London and even they said I did well, but someone else had supply experience in sixth form and they wanted the post filled by September.      Right, well I mean if I was running a school I’d say skills are the most important. But I guess they’ve got to prioritise when it comes to actually getting someone in.      Yeah, you're not wrong there, but still, I had the most detailed teaching plan of anyone that day. I even had the sample book ready and everything.      What did they teach you at uni then, reading minds?      Something like it.      Ha – no seriously though, I'm not surprised, because you were always the best at planning lessons during our time at uni. Remember that lesson on the subjunctive you did with the role plays? Our tutor said it was one of the best they’d seen in a long time.      Yeah, that was a nightmare though. It took me weeks to plan all the scenarios. But it worked out in the end.      And now the parents of this kid I teach cooking for can’t even cook pasta that isn't barely cooked and it is a  primary school .      Oh God, tell me you passed that test with flying colours?     colour was all I had left I swear. I mean when I started making macaroni and cheese and I over-salted it and the kids were eating it like it was ambrosia.     ha, you’re not wrong. Kids eat basically anything as goon as it is. I mean our nephew ate a whole microwave-ready steak once in pieces without even noticing.      And what were we feeding ourselves when we were that tiny? I swear we were raised on pureed fruit and toast soldiers like it was some kind of punishment.      Mm, well I mean maybe the problem is all of us are going for jobs we're kind of already doing remotely, but not in the same way.

I just feel like the future’s completely outta control, y’know? Like, it’s like everyone’s just got to pick a side or something now. I know what you mean! It’s like… when we were at university, it felt like the world was on a slow burn, and now it’s like,  BOOM —everything just explodes onto social media all at once. I think that's one of the things that worries me most. It's not just like, do I have a job? or like, am I gonna get promoted? It's like, can I still believe in anything without it being ruined by a troll post the next morning? Honestly, you're not wrong. I swear, like, one day I’m happy to hear the government’s doing something, and the next day the news is all "Oh, but there’s a better system in Norway and we’re just falling behind everyone." It's like, what do I even do with that? Yeah—and then the whole environment thing too. I mean, do we even get a say in it anymore? I feel like we’re just being told to live like the hobbits from Lord of the Rings… watching everything crumble while we try to grow our gardens. Don't even get me started on that! I mean, I totally get why people don’t recycle as much as they should, but then again, what’s the point, right? Like, someone somewhere in an office plant is making a PowerPoint about a new climate policy, and I’m out here chucking plastic in a red bin. It’s like I’m trying to make a dent in a dam made of about a billion plastic bottles. Exactly! We’re just trying to be good, and the system is like, “Nah, it’s too late for that—have a rebreather mask and good luck.” So what do you think we do then? I mean, do we just give up and start buying electric cars and hope for the best? I don't know. Maybe take it one step at a time? I mean, I’ve started volunteering for this local sustainability group. It’s not the biggest thing in the world, but it helps if you talk to other people who think the same as you, you know? It gives you a bit of control back.

So did you talk to him yet?      Which one? Ash or Jake?      Both, really. You've been so anti-social all weekend, like we’re not even allowed to exist. Not to mention he likes to follow me around like a lost puppy.      Oh my  god , leave Ash alone,   he’s   just confused. Everyone knows who the real problem is here—and his name  starts with J .        Yes!   I mean, Jake texts me like he owns me. If I don’t reply within five minutes, he’s asking if I’m ignoring him. What am I, his servant?      You made that one up, didn’t you? The “servant” bit?      Okay, fine, he doesn’t say it  exactly , but he gives me the vibe. He thinks breakfast, bedtime stories, and me mastering his guitar playlist for the night qualifies as me being his  girlfriend . He didn’t even say the ‘G’ word, and that was two months ago.      Honestly, he might not be the best one for you. Did you tell him you’ve still got a best friend watching him like a hawk?      I’m not a  best friend , I’m a menace, thank you  very much . I saw him texting someone last Wednesday in about five different group chats at the same time.   Us   included.      Who was the fifth one that wasn’t me or you?      Some girl named Holly.   Update:   I looked her up after. Boy, can she throw a party. You would  not  have liked it.      So what? He could’ve just said “no” if he’s dating me. He knows the deal.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? He  told  you he's into you, go out with you for a bit, and now he expects you to be his line of defense when he wants to be the life of the party.      So I’m supposed to be okay with this? I’m tired of pretending to be okay with this, Rachel!      So over this, why not be over  him ? You deserve someone who wants to make plans for  you , not just for them to stroke their ego.      Oh, come on, not  again  with the ego-ist tropes. You’ve used this on every guy you’ve ever liked.

Right, who’s up for seconds? You know what, I think I might just do lasagne tomorrow. I got the ready-made one from the shop today, and I’ve had it three times this week! It is  so  easy.      It is, like, really good. Got cheese all over my face from the first one already.      Teenagers… come on, clean that up before your brother sees you!      If I was as messy as you two, I’d have been grounded before I hit double digits.      You’re just like, ancient, Dad! Not cool.      I am only 43 and yet older than you’ll ever be, young man! Now eat up. Ten more bits on your plate and I’ll feel happy.      Now then, did you two tell your father about the breakfast club trip?      Yeah! We’re going to the Wakefield Mega Sports Centre to watch some hockey. James is in a team there now, and he said it's wicked.      Yeah, he’s way better at hockey than he is at rugby. It took ages for him to pass properly… like, basic circle passes and he’d drop the ball every time.      I remember, and I had to coach him up. Let’s say it was…  entertaining .      Liam! Stop laughing, those are your food groups on your plate. Honestly, you boys are like a comedy routine half the time. Anyway, you had the letters about your science trip to the Peak District next month – did you get those, Sam?      Yeah! I opened it. It says we’re doing this whole outdoor survival stuff. There’s even a bit with climbing. I think I’m gonna be  super  cool.      Maybe you’ll fall off a mountain and come home with just a stick and a minimal understanding of firelighting.      That’s not very supportive, Ben. As long as he goes equipped and prepared, which I assume the school will do.      Speaking of going out, Tom and I were chatting this week – he told me he entered the Great North Run again this year. It’s his fifth one now.      Oh, I saw he posted a Time Trial run near your house a couple of weeks ago. I seriously thought it was a marathon training pace. He’s going to blow us all off!      It’s brilliant, really. He said he’s training with some team from Newcastle. I said if they come down this way next time, they can always stop by for a meal.

Rather annoying isn't it? He finds anything to get grumpy about.
