So do you lot actually know what’s going on with that new bank they opened in Doncaster? The one with all the big chain links on the doors like they’re guarding smugglers or something.      Yeah, we heard about the fines they got! Something to do with money laundering. Got eeny weeny slap on the wrist, if you ask me. Hundred thousand quid? That’s a paper cut compared to what they’re hiding in the back.      It’s not as if it’s anything new, luv. Funny how people still get shocked. The big banks have been fiddling the books since the eighties. I used to work in supply chain, and I saw things that’d make your head spin.      So, money laundering, you reckon? D’you think they’re hiding drugs money? Or dodgy cash from fence jobs?      Could be any of it. Could be off-the-books betting shops, dodgy property deals, or even fraud through those offshore shells. They don’t need to be criminals per se—you just have a bookkeeper who’s not asking enough questions and a manager who’s more interested in quarterly targets than due diligence.      Doesn’t surprise me in the slightest. You ever try to open a bank account with them? I tried, and they were asking me more about my life goals than about my chequebook. Silly if you’re trying to help small businesses.      Well, I’m a small business owner, and I can tell you that transparency is one thing, but bureaucracy is a nightmare. You start pulling at one thread, and all of a sudden, there’s a thousand forms and five people from the FCA standing behind you.      Exactly what I’m saying. The problem is that when the rules get too unmanageable, it drives business underground. Burgers and chickens, guest workers working under the table, that sort of thing. You can slap a fine on the bank, but it doesn’t change the reality on the ground.      You think they’re getting away with it?      They’re not the villains in this story, son. The villains are the people who set the rules in the first place. If you make it too hard for people to open accounts and run businesses legally, you force them to go dark.      It’s all so complicated. I’ve been reading up on it, and you’d think by now we’d have a system that made sense for real people, not just big corporations and their lawyers.

So did you lot see the article this weekend about AI in publishing? I was just reading it over lunch. It got me thinking—how long do you think press houses like this will be left untouched by automation?      Honestly? I have no idea. It depends on how fast it becomes cost-effective and how the industry adapts. I mean, some of the more mundane tasks are easy to automate, but you can’t really replace the human brain when it comes to content curation or editorial judgment.      Especially when it comes to the copyedit team. I worked with someone last week who was hell-bent on deleting every comma. Computers can spot redundancies and inconsistencies easily, but human nuance and tone? My turkey sandwich definitely couldn’t explain that to her.      I was actually assigned to a project last month that used some sort of AI to check for grammar and plagiarism. It was pretty impressive, honestly—caught things I hadn’t even noticed. But there’s a difference between style and meaning, right? No machine’s going to get the heart of a poetic metaphor or the subtle twist in a manuscript.      I think that’s the big one. AI tools are only as good as the data they’re fed. If the data is biased or limited, the output is too. My job is focusing on evolving linguistic datasets and understanding regional dialects and register. Cambridge handles international publications, after all.      Which brings me back to the original question—how will this change someone at our level? If the boring work gets outsourced to machines, we’ll definitely need to upskill or at least be able to oversee and double-check their work.      True, but I don’t see it replacing us all. At the end of the day, publishing is a human business. We write for people, not algorithms. I mean, how does a machine know to suggest a less ‘stuffy’ tone for a reader in Malaysia versus someone in London?      Exactly. But I think it might reduce the need for people doing the very basic tasks—like my first week here, when I was manually updating metadata entry after entry. I think AI could probably do that in five seconds.      Then again, if that happens, we can go back to doing what we’re supposed to be doing: building teams, adding value in quality control, and pushing creative boundaries.

Rather skip the newfit inc. i'm sorting out a few quotes for people. it's real busy at the moment and rather than take on more, i'm actually looking at cutting back a little. gotta manage expectations, don’t wanna overload myself. have you had a chance to speak to your sister?      Yeah, last weekend. she was struggling again. the chemo's really taken it out of her. i can hear it in her voice. and she mentioned feeling so low, she was refusing to get out of bed some days. she said she doesn't chase the pain or the tiredness anymore — just the silence.      that’s so hard. the last couple of weeks with my uncle made me think a lot. he was stronger than most people would believe, but there was a point when he just accepted it, and i think he turned inward. he said in the end, it was better for him, no longer fighting the system.      i don’t think you ever get used to it, even if you're the one going through it. i was holding his hand the night he passed — he looked peaceful, but i can still feel the warmth in that moment. grief is real, and as much as we want to protect the kids, it’s inevitable. our son is nine now – i don’t know how long we can keep it from him.      truthfully, i don’t think you should. i sat my daughter down at ten — told her the truth. someone said to me, “you don’t tell them a half-truth, because then they outgrow it,” and it stuck. and she helped with flowers at the funeral — she felt like she was part of it, and that helped her process it. our children need the tools to understand death.      maybe you are right. we barely mentioned the cancer, just said he was very ill. but they overheard the hospice guest speaker talking about it, and that’s when they started asking. i told him he was sleeping and not coming back, which is when he started crying. i think we should have prepared better.      i’ve read a couple of articles about how to do it. it's easier than you think — be honest, calm, and sensitive to their age. my parents didn't do it that way – my brother was very confused for weeks.

So do you not find it really weird that we're supposed to talk about this as if it's not like... obvious?      Talk about what?      Oh, you know, how housing policy and all that stuff is so connected to race and class. Like, how do they get away with calling it "affordable housing" when   no one   actually can afford it unless they're making money off it too.      I mean, I get it. It's not like it’s a secret. But I also wonder how much people even want to  look at  the truth. It's like even in places like Kensal Rise, we’ve got gentrification knocking on the door and the council still acts like they're fixing it.      I see it in the architecture work too, honestly. The whole "town centre revival" is just about pushing out working-class and migrant communities to build ultra-expensive flats. They don't even pretend it's not happening anymore.      It’s the same everywhere. And I guess it’s worse for people who are already seen as "other." Like, I can be a landlady to some extent and still be "one of them." But if you live in a block where a lot of the residents are from South Asian backgrounds or from migrant families, people still think it's "chaotic" or "the streets don't look right." Like, who even are  they  to say that?      Exactly. And then you also get the whole "cosmetic diversity" thing—like a housing developer puts up a marketing poster with a couple of brown faces and a green space and  boom , it’s "inclusive."      Ugh, it's such a farce. It’s like a performative nod to social justice that doesn’t fix the actual housing crisis. Meanwhile, rents go up and people get squeezed out. I mean, even working here in freelancing, I have no idea how I'm going to afford my next contract unless I start subletting a room or something.      Yeah. I’ve seen proposals where they've explicitly said "this area is projected to become high-income, no social housing included." You know? It's just baked into the system. Capitalism doesn’t see cheap housing or fair housing policy. It only sees profit margin, and that’s it.      And what can we do about it? We can talk and we can rant and we can write articles or write plans—but does that even matter to the people in power?

Anyway, he's set me up with a nice bloke in the city who can go over details on property stuff if you ever fancy translating for one of those meetings.

Right, I just got in from work. That shift dragged. I swear, it's like they think pints of lemonade sell themselves or something. Isn’t this the one where the guy invents food-shaped meatballs like, literally, lettuce balls and meat lasagnas? That film is mental.       Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs ? Yeah, this is the one. It's weird, innit? Made me think the world is run by mad scientists now — look at the climate, breakfast, everything. You need to press  “confirm”  there — no, you press  “play” , not  “pause” , genius. That would’ve worked if you wanted it to stay off.      I mean, seriously, the dad in this flick is the real protagonist. Like, the son is brilliant, but it’s Mr. Flintlock who’s running the show – even though he’s fairly nuts, like, giving permission for a huge meat rain over an entire town. Who would do that?      You ever notice that the principles they follow in this film — full-on automation, machines making everything from meatballs to yogurt — it’s kind of what our economy is aiming for these days, honestly. But here’s the kicker —  they’re not fully aware of consequences , like how far they want the technology to go. Sounds like something we’re trying to figure out in real life. Yeah, but that’s what’s clever about Pixar or these kids' films — they go deep on ideas that adults are arguing about. Think about it: freedom of choice vs. regulation, individual desires vs. community impact. All through animated meatballs. It’s all just dumbed-down to the kiddy audience, but the messages are there.      Do you think the kid understanding this is part of the point?

So did you watch The Late Late Show last night?      No, I missed it... What was on?      Oh I know you’re going to find this ridiculous, but they were talking about some sort of film that supposedly came out in like the 70s and then disappeared. They said it showed some footage that   ALLEGEDLY   had aliens in it.      Oh yeah? That’s not new. You know how those things go, someone edits a grainy clip and suddenly the world thinks it’s proof.      I know, I know. But apparently this one was found in someone’s attic, rolled up in some parchment like it was a secret. You’ve met enough eccentric rich people to know that kind of backstory is usually bulls___, but I thought I’d check the history of it with you, being the logical one.      Look, if it has a clip in it that looks like a jumping giraffe hides behind some rocks, it's aliens. End of.      Fair point, fair point. I mean, I laughed it off, but honestly, with everything going on in the news, I’m starting to wonder—what if it’s all been covered up? You ever think about that?      All the time.      You what?!      Silly grin removed. No, don’t get me wrong—I don’t claim someone’s in cahoots with lizard people or a secret cabal that’s controlling the moonrise. But think about it—how many strange radio signals have been detected? Unexplained sightings, people who swear they’ve seen something... and then the story just melts into the ether.      So you're saying you believe in   possible   cover-ups?      I say I   don’t   believe in   not   looking further. The problem is, when the media bites on something too quickly, it gets dismissed as a joke or a hoax. We lost credibility on stuff like that.      Do you think people are more ready to believe it now?      I think they are, but also the wrong reasons. There's a difference between healthy curiosity and falling for elaborate scams.      I see your point. But honestly, the films from the ‘70s—I could have watched The Late Late Show and listened to it all go down with a blank face like, "What’s next: Bigfoot on stamps?" But when I think about how much we don’t really understand... I'm not saying they’re real, just that the idea of ignoring them feels stupid.

Mum, thanks a million for helping me sort out the list for moving out. I don’t think I’d have got this sorted without you.      Oh, don’t mention it, darling. I’m just glad to do something useful for once! It reminds me of when I was packing up for your dad and me to move into that flat in Enfield all those years ago — heavens, it felt like we were listing every sock and tupperware box in the house.      That sounds dramatic! You and Dad always did like a good clear-out, didn’t you?      Oh yes! And speaking of clears, you’re moving out, not into a museum! So that MyFridge Food list you sent me — got it ticked most boxes, didn’t I? Dried pasta, milk, eggs, the basics. You know, for a young bloke moving out on your own for the first time, you seem alright on food!      Yeah, I’m ordering a load of the non-perishables online too. I mean, it’s not like I need a full larder for two weeks yet. Still, I didn’t expect you to remember which brand of tea I prefer.      Of course I remembered! You always did like those Royal London cinnamon biscuits and your builder’s tea — you’ve had that taste since childhood!      I know! And that’s exactly why I’m bringing some of this stuff with me. It’ll be weird not coming here for meals every week, but I’m going to miss the Sunday roasts.      That’s all right, love, there’s always a takeaway. I’m just a phone call away! And besides, you’re not going off to Mars — just Cambridge.      Doesn’t feel like it when I consider the 5am starts and the lesson planning. Honestly, I thought Cambridge would be easier to adjust to, but between the time zones, the unpacking, and trying to meet new people, I’m just ready to sit and do nothing.      Oh, I know what you mean. When I first moved to Enfield after marrying your dad, it was a proper culture shock — gothic churches on every corner, suffragettes everywhere! But it made me feel alive, even if I was knackered most of the time.      That’s true! I’ve had a bit of culture shock myself with all the people I’ve been meeting through work — some from every corner of the world.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd do something about the price of petrol ‘fore it’d got to this, but no. I’m paying nearly a tenner for a fule up!      I know, I saw somethin’ on the telly earlier today een Birmingham and it wus the same. I 'ad ter drive straight ter work as well, so I didn’t ‘ave a choice.      Bleurgh. It’s costing me like half a day’s wages just to go and get the weekly shopping, let alone factor in car tax and everything. It’s mad!      I dunno, seems lik’e the politicians are doing more turkey than turkey tatties. Fun left themselves in this mess over Brexit and now the whole country’s feelin’ the twang.      Yeah, and forgetin’ breakfast, no doubt. Look at the NHS! Havin’ to queue for six hours ter get treated for somethin’s simple. I mean, why would you expect that from us?      I’ve been up at A&Es quite a few times recently. I dunno, since the A-Level reforms they’ve been messin’ it up for all sorts. I’m takin’ it in next year, so I’ve had to revise tonnes of extra subjects and somethin’ to do wi’ practical assessments. It all seems like a nightmare.      Oi, I kno’! That stuff was a faaactory when I did it—’fore the reforms. It shouldn’t be this complicated. I mean, I had to get a tutor because most o’ the schools ‘ere couldn’t be buggers to help. I had to teach myself what the hell!      I know it. And we’re both still payin’ ‘cos of it. My education costs have passed the roof. B’wides, the whole education budget was docked ages back. I dunno how long we can keep doing this.      Let’s not talk about it then. Oi, whaddya think of this plant o’ mine? Grew something amazing this week. Lookit— points gooshy planty thing —look at them leaves. Glistenin’, it’s like a green dream.      Blimey, you really are planting things fluently now. Thought you’d kill every leaf you touched, but you’m turnin’ into a bloody gardener!      Aye, I’m not entirely sure what I did, but they’ve been bloomin’ like mad! And my hair? What d’you think o’ the new bob?      ‘Bob’ it is then, yeah. Sharp. Not bad for last-minute scissors and tea .

Rather skip uni today an’ go to Leeds to meet me mates.      Honestly, I got to say, I miss hanging out like this. I’ve been stuck in the library non-stop revising for my physics exams. No one outside of my textbook knows my name now.      Yeah, uni’s a proper faff. I reckon it’s worse than work. At least with work, yer get money and tiration from actual social interaction.      For someone who’s always moaning about work, you sure do chase it, don’t you, Lucy? Get a part-time job yet, Ruth?      Y’know what? I managed to get one at a cafe in town. The pay is trash, but at least I’m not sat around home all day pickin’ at me head like a magpie with a split.      That actually sounds better than me. I’m trying to work at the library, but it’s like, you have to have a degree in silence to work there. It’s so over the top, I swear. One person coughed last week and the landlady nearly faints.      Bet she’d be dead during the Black Plague then.      Mate, talking about the plague, least we had no toxic bosses back then. I reckon the worst part of uni is the whole financial faff. Me and Ruth both applied for bursaries, but someone at the office said it’s a postcode lottery whether or not they give it to you. Some floring nonsense is going on in the admin department here.      Yeah, it’s not fair. My gran always told us girls to look out for one another, but now I’m just lookin’ out for me student finance. Where the hell is it bloody up to?      Honestly, it’s not even just about the money. The way some of the modules are designed – it’s all male-centric content. I mean, I understand context, but come on, we’re in 2024 and there’s still lunches of Jane Austen with zero mention of the actual working class or women beyond a certain level. It’s like the system is set go against us on purpose.      Yeah, I agree with that, Catherine. I’m always the one bloomin’ arguing about these things. It’s all “Let’s be special,” and then they won’t give you credit for being diferent. True to myself? Sure. But where does that get you on a UCAS form when they’re all so bloody clueless?

So do you ever find it hard to cut off people you used to be really close to, like when they just don’t understand why you’re not as interested as you used to be? I feel guilty about it sometimes, but… it’s just not the same anymore.      Honestly, yeah. I had that with a friend from uni. We were thick as thieves for years, but then life sort of took us in different directions. I stopped answering calls and texts, but then I felt bad and tried to be all polite and stuff. She just got really confused.      Oh no, that’s tough. I guess it’s hard because you don’t want to hurt people, right? But on the other hand, you don’t owe them constant effort if the interest is one-sided. I had someone who kept asking for advice and then judging me when I said no. It got too much, and I just stopped. No big scene, just… colder. Less responses.      That’s smart in a way, even if it’s a bit harsh. I think people assume that because you were friends, it’s going to last forever. I mean, some friendships are like that, but not all.      Definitely. I reckon the hardest part is when you don’t want to be totally abrupt about it but also can’t keep pretending. It’s like trying to phase out without being rude. How did you manage it?      I don’t know — I just kind of buried my head in the sand. Let things fizzle out a bit naturally. I’d make excuses — you know, work got busy, I’m overwhelmed with life — but I don’t think she understood fully because she kept about her business asking to meet up. Eventually, she just gave up. It wasn’t a terrible outcome, though.      I get it. I think honesty can help, but not everyone wants to hear it. Sometimes it’s easier to just cut people off gradually. Like, minimal contact for any longer conversations. Eventually, they’ll get the idea.      Yeah, and it can’t feel like a betrayal if you do it gently. I mean, I’ve had friends do it to  me , and it stung a bit at the time, but in hindsight, I get it if your needs change. Maybe I was expecting more than I was giving back.      Exactly.

So did I tell you about the trip I’m going on next week?      No, I don’t believe you have. Where are you headed? Not somewhere on the other side of Europe this time, I hope.      No, nothing like that. I’ve booked a ticket to Margate. There’s this exhibition at   V&A East   about post-war British design—it’s supposed to be amazing.      Oh, Margate, how nice. I remember it as a bustling seaside town from the 1950s when I used to sketch by the sea. It had changed since then—what with all the new buildings and galleries now, of course.      Oh, I’m excited to see it. I’ve never been there for anything other than a picknick with uni friends. But this time feels different, you know? Like it’s a proper cultural trip. I’ve been reading up a bit in advance.      That sounds thoughtful. You always have so much energy for university life and exploring new places. When I was your age, I was lucky if I left London with anything other than to go to lectures.      Honestly, sometimes I feel like I’m in a dream. You know, at my age, I got into my first choice, I’ve got a decent part-time job, and I’m actually making plans for the future. It all seems so normal, but I’m aware it's not someone else's experience.      That’s because you came from a good family and had the support. Don’t forget that. I didn’t come from London or even Britain, you know. I was born in Austria—Vienna, to be precise—and my parents were artists. It was only thanks to some generous mentors that I ever got the chance to study.      That’s amazing. I didn’t know.      Well, maybe I should write a book. Travel, art, family, and all that. You’d help me with the technical bits, right?      Of course! I’d edit it and probably do the cover art. I’d be really interested in hearing all the stories you never shared. Dad always said you were the life of the party at every gathering.      I see you’ve been talking to your father. And what your mother didn’t tell you is that I once had a scandal with a sculptor in Ravenna, Italy. But that’s a story for another time, perhaps over tea.

Rather skip the gym and just go to sleep.      No, no, you  always  say that, but you're the one who ends up going in an hour after me, right?      No, I  don’t —well, maybe I do. I just like to  pretend  I'm going to sleep and then panic about all the gym gear I’ve left lying about.      Classic. And then you turn into a human dump truck of gym socks and sports bras.      Okay, okay, but isn’t it like three o’clock already? I can’t be doing crunches in the dark again. It's like doing squats by torchlight in some dodgy left-lane ultra-fit boy’s world.      Easier in the dark, actually—no one judges you when you’re sweaty and breakfast is Thai chicken stir-fry and coffee.      I know, but I hate driving after the gym. All the people in sports gear, all that— flicker, flicker, beep —everyone’s in a rush to be as unrelatable and perfect as possible.      You know, we should both switch from “I want to be prettier” to “I want to be smarter.”      Well, you don’t have to worry about that. You're the one who gets paid to be smarter and English.      Saying I teach English is like saying plumbers clean up pipes. You give it a very smart-sounding word and then… it’s just a bit gross after a while, really.      That’s not what I meant! But yeah, I get it. I used to teach too—you know that.      You  used to . Now you say you’re semi-retired, which is fancy for “I can’t commit to 8 a.m. on any bloody day.”      I am not! I just like to  exist  in a professional capacity but also not earn money lunches and keep the Netflix subscription.      You’re  English , so you're like a mannequin in gothic shoes on a life-sized Pinterest board of identity crisis.      I’m not a mannequin, I just don’t have to be  anything  100% of the time.      I mean, that’s both a massive privilege and a bit sad, if we’re being real.      Oh great, now you’re using the “be being real” voice again.      Just saying—some of us want to achieve, some of us are fine just surviving while also being… sort of confused about what we’re doing with our time.

Rather do this than drink my tea through a cold, grizzly winter morning, dontcha think? These mugs you gave me, they’re lovely, proper hand-thrown, feel like they’ve got a story in every dimple.      Ah well, you can say that again. Got eeny weeny crack on the lip one, but I reckon that adds character. Proper arts-and-crafts type, not too posh tho. Proper Yorkshire, if you ask me.      Pah! You’re just saying that cause you called it “eeny weeny.” Careful, Nan, you sound like  us  now! Besides, the real character comes from how you use it. My turkey still knocks the living daylights outta it weeknights!      Aye, and I’ll be the one mopping up spilled tea at the end of it. I still can’t figure out how a grown woman can spill in every room of the house and not once in the kitchen.      Good grief, I’ll tell you one thing, if I had a penny for every time I tripped over your cat as if it were human intent on murder... Tell me, was that spider behind the lemon tree last night, Nan? You said it was the size of a newt!      Oh, I’ve seen somethin’ that big in the phone box at the corner of Copthorne Road. Nasty bugger too. Spiders, though, they’re my soft spot. Those gardening books say I should encourage them. Also, I planted a couple of delphiniums at the back wall last week, they’re starting to look like Legolas’s hair.      Oh, you mean th’ wild ones? No need for that frost plug! I reckon it’ll snow up here in January. My sister ‘phoned me last week, her fuse box had a funny hiss at 6 a.m. Power cuts bloody everywhere.      Aye, I told her to run into the neighbor’s for safety. And if it comes with lunches, a little bird told me the fiesta market is back next Saturday.      Oh the fiesta! I remember when I took your Lucian there once.      Oh, that’s the one with the box of buns and the one-eyed Mike. You could have told me it was his day off, mind you!      It was! I thought it was going to be proper crime-fighting, turns out it was a balloon fight! The decorator came at 9, the cat hissed at them, the kids kissed me on the cheek and made me feel like I was nineteen again.

So do we get to take our bikes on the ferry, Nan? I really dont wanna leave mine behind.      Oh love, I think it depends on how big they are. Let me check the ferry company's website again.      Aye, lass, it een't that far, you’ll do fine on the bus if you have to. But yes, most ferries let you take bikes.      But I don’t want to ride all the way to the train station and then the bus and then the ferry. It's like miles.      Oh don’t be so dramatic, Eve. It's only a few days away, and you’ll have adventures on the Isle of Wight!      I know, I know, but I wanted to explore the island on my bike. It looks proper nice there. All those little lanes and stuff.      Haha, she’s got dreams, alright. Just like I did when I used to gig in the south.      Nan, you played in a pub in Bognor Regis, not a festival.      Aye, but it was proper live, luv. And that counts. So is the ferries letting bikes on, lass?      Yes, the ferry allows bikes. All you have to do is book a cycle space when we book the tickets. It’s an extra five pounds each.      Five quid? That's not so bad. Can you chuck the booking on your phone and let me double-check?      Of course, love. I’ll make sure to put all of us on it, even you Charlie.      Aye, that’d be grand. I'll bring my old one in if it still works.      Nan, you’re not seriously taking up your 60s bike on the ferry, are you? I dunno how long your legs will last on the Isle of Wight hills.      Oh, I’ve cycled from here to Brighton once, so I think I’m still got a bit in me!      That's brilliant, Nan! Can I borrow it at some point?      Don’t go borrowing relics, Eve. But your Nan’s a tough one. She’s cycled all over the north in her day.      True. Do we get to see Osborne House this time? I want to see Queen Victoria’s house!      Only if we're kind to the car driver, which in this case is me. So no hanging off the windscreen or flinging your rucksack at me, okay?      I promise I’ll be a angel , on my bike at least.

So did you watch  10 Things I Hate About You  last night? I just finished it! Okay, technically, I fell asleep halfway through, but I still watched most of it.      Yeah, I did! My cousin lent it to me. It was so good, wasn’t it? I laughed  so  hard when the older sister threatened to disown the younger one over a guy.      I know! I mean, like, who does that in real life? That’s why you never watch me argue with my brother—he literally chucks stuff. But watching her just like,  “Tomorrow you won’t exist any more,”  and then she still lets her go to the dance…      Right! She’s like this strict overlord but then secretly kind of supportive, which was sad in a way? Or was that just me?      No, I felt that too! Like, she was in pain and being all cold about it. That’s why the poem scene is so good. I actually got a little teary-eyed.      Oh, I know! Bah, your pain as insight is my grief. Philosophical and poetic. Good on her.      Anyway, we’re getting off track. Mate, have you heard about the school trip to London yet?      What? No, what school trip? When is it?      There’s this new ‘big city experience’ thing. They said it’s a mix of a cultural trip and an out-of-town lesson. We’re going to see the Houses of Parliament, the museum, and maybe a West End show if we raise enough funds.      No way, are you serious? I’ve always wanted to see London. Do you think they’re taking Year 11s?      I dunno, but my Geography teacher said something about it at the start of the year. If we all chip in with a mini-fundraiser or something, maybe we get to go as a whole year group.      That sounds awesome. If we do go, can we stay at a proper hotel? I’ve never had a room with a proper gooseneck shower.      Only if you’re the head of the committee. Which could totally be you—just say what your dad’s title is at the planning meeting and they bend to your will.      Haha, I already tried that with the poetry competition over Christmas. They just said,  “Oh, very creative, very respectful to her father’s job…”  and sent me back to class.      Classic. Anyway, we need to raise our grades if we want to be in the top few percent of Year 11s.

Rather annoying this new Facebook thing eh?      Aye, it's all a muddle with those "moods" and "stories" now. I can't be sure where me daughter's been doing her sunbathing in Malaga, can I?      I don’t get why people still  use  it. I posted about the chickenpox outbreak in primary school on a "Throwback Thursday" once and got more likes than I’ve had in a week. It's not like it’s a badge of pride to have once looked like a raisin-covered toy poodle.      Honestly, I'd rather write a sonnet about the time I scraped my knee on the playground and MySpace still felt superior back then. Fun stuff. It’s just more noise to me now.      I think it turned me off entirely when I was told I needed to put "feeling safe" if I was just sitting here reading the paper. Feels like you're announcing yourself to the world even if you're just sipping a brew.      That’s the thing about apps and social media — they make you feel like your private moments are supposed to be public, even the washed-up ones like watching  30 Rock  reruns from the 80s.      I wouldn’t mind it if it weren’t for the OCD aspect of it all. Like, you have to know what to tag, what not to tag, and then there’s someone who apologises for liking your post because they just remembered they had bad news that day. It’s like the digital version of a tea party and being told you sprinkled too much sugar in the pot by your aunt about five decades ago.      Oh, leave it to you two lecturers to compare FB fails to poetry and trauma. I once accidentally replied to a Facebook ad about pet hairballs, and for  months  I got mail from some company in Ohio that just kept me on the list. I was being nice! I thought it was a pet!      Ha! Like you and that time Auntie Mavis thought you were liking her holiday photos but you "liked" the  wrong  album where she'd uploaded a picture of a muddy man with a garden go-kart on your own birthday.      True story. Still tickles me that she genuinely thanked you, Dad, for liking the one about the go-kart. She made it sound like you'd won an award for appreciation.

Right, I just popped the chicken in the oven, so that’s sorted for dinner. Anyone want a drink before we start chatting? Maybe some tea or wine?      I’ll have a cup of tea, thanks. You know I can’t handle wine after seven.      Got it, I’ll take the wine. It’s either that or sit here and try to remember what my job even is these days.      Haha, dad, you’re the Head of Department, it’s not that complicated. I think.      Says the glorified wordsmith sitting there writing jokes about baked beans. I can still beat you at chess, you know!      My point exactly. You’ve still got it.      I’m glad I married someone with a bit of subtlety. Some of these family evenings could turn into a gig if we’re not careful!      Honestly, I’m just here to polish off the chicken when we’re done ordering it. You think a silversmith would earn enough to treat himself to a nice dinner out?      I know, right? It’s like the more you do, the more you go unnoticed.      Absolutely. Be a hairdresser and everyone’s your friend, but be a jeweler, and they expect you to fix the world’s problems in your spare time.      Or a nurse, for that matter, huh, Mum?      Oh, don’t even start. It’s amazing how many people think nurses just ‘have it all worked out’ because we’ve seen their sprained ankles after a ballet competition.      I always said you girls had a gift talking the gossamer out of everyone.      Gift? I think I’d take it out if I had the time. My day job gives me enough material for a therapist bill.      Come on, Nick. You told me you once fixed a man’s hearing aids with a tablespoon and a spoon while he was in tears over his cat’s hairball issue.      That was one time. He took the spoon back, you know, after I threatened to charge him the full market rate for that repair.      If I was at that event, I’d say I’m proud of you.      Anyway, all jokes aside. I was thinking, it feels like ages since we went on a holiday somewhere that wasn’t a caravan in France.      Honestly, I’d love to go somewhere like Germany. You know, all that history, and they speak a completely different language.

I can't believe we've not caught up in so long, man. I was just streaming some old band mixes last night and thought of you. Blows my mind how long it's been! What've you been up to lately? Still buried in textbooks at uni? Yeah, I'm wrapping up my last year of psychology. It’s been mad, honestly. But I’ve been trying to carve out some time to jam again. I’ve got a kit in storage, just need to dump the damn textbooks and pull it out. That’s brilliant to hear. You used to have the tightest rhythm. I mean, back when we were stomping out indie covers in Pete's shed like we were the next big thing. Ha, you haven't forgotten the Glory Days, then. Speaking of, I heard the lads from Backburn in a local gig last week. They’re still crushing live. I think they’ve got a new album coming out next month. Oh, are they? Rich was telling me he had a hand in mixing some tracks for them, maybe that's it. He's been raving about his internship as a production assistant at the local studio. Seems like he's got a good foot in the door. That's amazing for Rich. I hope he's getting paid peanuts because he’s doing something he loves. You know him, always chasing the next gig or internship. Still, if he’s happy, what can I say? What about you—what are your plans after uni? I know you mentioned something about getting into music therapy. Yeah, I’ve been seriously considering it. Working in a band and about helping people through music—it all ties together, right? Although, I'm looking at a bit of a break to travel before I dip my toe into it. You up for coming to some of the local gigs before I go? Count me in. I've been sous chef at this new bistro, so the hours are manic, but I can switch off enough to crack out good shifts and still have enough of a brain space left for lunches and a couple of decent Friday night beers with the old crew. Then it's a plan. Let's set go for Friday on the 13th—always a lucky day. Deal, mate. And hey, while you're away, promise me you’ll track down some new jazz or something obscure and bring it back to blow those locals away?

Right then, John, take a seat love. That coffee smelt promising from out the car.      Cheers, Mum. I’m more after a biscuit, actually. These places always put me in the mood for snacks.      Well, you better make sure it’s not the chocolate cream ones again. You’ve got enough of them at home already—heap of them in the fridge.      Why’s it always about the biscuits with you? It’s not like I eat them all in one go.      Oh, love, you fetch one, and next thing I’m knocking on the bedroom door at half past ten and you’ve devoured half a packet and a doorstep. Still, enough about food. How’s the new term treating you then?      Okay, I suppose. Misses in the lab’ve been giving us quizzes again, and I swear I’ve been asked "What is oxidation?" at least six different ways this week.      Well, that’s what you get for taking science over the arts, luv. I still say you should’ve gone with media studies. Less equations, more film festivals and YouTube.      Easy for you to say, you got out of most of the science back in your day.      True, but the world didn’t end for me, did it? You know what I’m saying? Still, if you carry on like this someone might offer you a job in a lab before your 20th birthday.      At least I won’t have to be queuing at Domino’s for a Domino Drive all day then. I heard they’re doing a loyalty thing round the corner now.      Domino’s and not us? Don’t you forget who treats you to a takeaway when you’re grounded for coming home over the curfew.      Never. I’m just saying the sirens for Drive Throughs are getting intense. I saw them from the school station. We should’ve gone there and gotten a player of something.      No thank you—my patience took the brunt of you trying to queue for popcorn and a poster the last time we go there. I still see echoes of that “I saw one in the posters line” whinge in my dream.      Fair one. Can you imagine how hot it’s going to be this summer? I’d love to just sleep outside with a sleeping bag to feel the breeze.      Mm, that sounds lovely. You’ll be all over it until the mozzies come out and turn you into one giant red target.

Rather skip to the front of the queue do I suppose. I've got a coffee in front of me and I got to admit it's starting to get a bit warm I think. I've been over here a little while.      Look I know what you mean, like the place was crawling when I came in.      Yeah, but I reckon it's not as bad as most places you might be used to. I mean in this town, it's easier to find a decent coffee shop or something. We've got the High Street and whatnot.      Yeah, I can't complain about that. I mean when I was at university we used to go to Crawley for our coffee breaks.      I remember! Yeah, we'd just throw ourselves on the bus and end up spending the whole day in the town.      Yeah, and sometimes we'd get too much Bucks Fizz to cope. Reminds me in fact, what’s the deal with people drinking fizzes these days? Like why do we not just have real alcohol like Waterford or something, but no, it's all up your nose with Fizz.      It's not for me, but I get it. I mean, it’s light and gives you that carbonated – that pop-up, fairly instant, cheery kind of buzz if you know what I mean.      Yeah, fair enough. I suppose we were at that age, huh.      Yeah, and I reckon you're missing a bit of that now because I know what you were saying at uni: “Let’s get a flat in Margate,” but your colleague, Sam, he reckons Margate’s washed up.      Well, I'm looking at a house in Radipole now that I know barely touches the housing market. No one's investing. My sister’s over in Poole, guesthouse owner passed away last year. I reckon her place will go up for sale soon.      Ah, right. I sort of stick to my flat here and that's as far out as I go with property dreaming.      Fair enough. I mean, you don't live around here by accident either, do you? I remember when I first moved up here after uni.      Yeah, I remember that. It wasn’t a big move, but it felt like it at the time. I mean, moving out and starting to live on my own with all the responsibilities like bills and chores and stuff made me feel a hell of a grown-up at the time.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Yes, yes. How's work been otherwise? What's been going on with you this week?      Erm, not much, to be honest. Chasing up the GP again—get a bit fed up with how long it's taking to sort out the paperwork for my mum's care home. You know how it is.      Oh, I know, I do. I had to sort out paperwork for my nan’s place last year and it was just ridiculous. You’d swear they were trying to test how patient you are before giving you anything.      Exactly! It's like they’re only human. It's like you have to wait weeks for one form, and then it's missing a signature, or the Post Office sent it to the wrong address. It's just so frustrating.      How is she? Is she coping?      She is in her own way, you know. She hides it, pushes through. But the weekends are tough. I can see it in her.      I’m so sorry. I know what that’s like. I had grief support for a while after my mum. It was… it helped. I remember when it got too much, I just felt… lost, I guess, and I had to talk to someone. Maybe she’d benefit from something like that?      She probably would, but that's the thing. Our parents that generation, they're so proud. They tell you everything is just fine when it's not—don’t want to appear a burden or let you feel guilty.      Yeah, they do try and do everything on their own. My nan’s the same. I had to gently push her a bit into accepting some home care. Not that I pushed, it felt more like begging her to take the help. But she’s much better for it now.      I remember when my dad had his heart attack, I thought I’d lost him for a little bit. My brother was away, and I rushed over to the hospital—just trying to be there for both of them. My mum took the news really hard you know, even though she tried to play it cool.      It's so hard. I think for parents, when one partner is seriously ill, it's like the roles flip—suddenly the one who was always the care provider becomes the one needing help, and the children get forced into the role of… well, parent to their parents.

Right, lads, dig in. I've made my famous Sheffield-style chilli—the one with a bit of a kick. Someone asks about it, I say it's all natural, no added spices, just passion.      Thanks, Auntie Lorna. Speaking of work, David—still considering the apprenticeship? You know we can offer you an office job at your age.      I’ve been looking into roles in business development. It’s not just about selling boxes to old men in suits, is it?      It can be. Or it can be about helping small businesses grow. My kind of thing, actually. You see potential, you invest in it.      So, like, you’re running your own business then, Auntie?      More or less. Proofing, marketing, mentoring other small businesses. Every day’s a new project. It’s mad—worse than your chaotic school life, Harry.

So do you know anyone at the uni in Lancaster?      Not really — I think my cousin went there years ago. She was doing psychology or something. You’re sure you want to do your master’s there? It was like a zombie apocalypse — everyone waiting for the email saying it’s all over.      Blooming hell. I remember that, you were saying it was so stressful. Good for you for hanging in there — it’s got to be better than starting from scratch. Mm, the weather is meant go bad later on — apparently if you don’t get settled at the uni, you’ll just end up in a hotel with a bloke on a trumpet and some dodgy pigeon circling the outside.      Well, you’ve got your strengths — your dissertation proposal is on cockney and Norf’k differences, right?

So did you go see Indie Waves play weekend?      No, I ‘eard it got ruddy cold out an’ I’m more of a sofa kind of guy after uni sessions! Ten out of ten—even my nan would’ve liked that one! She’s the only one who still plays Radiohead on loop at the weekend breakfasts.      Haha, yeah she’s a bit of legend. My sister ‘as this mate who always guest spots with Lola Rose. She did the backing vocals on the new single.      No! Who is she? I need to stick her to my playlist.      He knows, but she’s tight-lipped ‘bout it till the next album drop.      Cheeky sod! Anyway, have you started your own music journal or something yet? I reckon I’ll start one, just notes between gigs.      Proper one or just like a scrapbook?      Yeah, I was thinking with bits of tickets, photos from gigs, stuff we saw or ‘appened at the bar. A proper memory book.      Mate, that’s a proper idea. Let’s do it together, keep swapping our pages.      Deal. First entry: Lola Rose at that bar, cold weather, but properly warm vibes all round.      ‘Methinks we’ll be chuckling over that in five years time.      Aye, an’ telling the kids, “Back in our day, Lola Rose was like the big deal!”

Okay, I’m just setting up the board. So, do we need to set it to ‘normal difficulty’ or go straight for ‘hard’ this time? I  think  we've survived the last game, but let me check the rules again… I mean, if Cian decides to act as the driver and crash the helicopter, I don’t think the cure will matter much.      Cian, that was  not  funny the last time you rerolled your cards and started a zombie outbreak in the middle of the Lake District. We had to send Chris home with the flu board. You remember?      I  promised  I’d never bring out the lasagna again after that game. My turkey still hasn’t recovered from his eccentric left-hand lawyer persona. Probably muttering about the Geneva Convention in pastry-speak.      Honestly, if it’s harder and you’re tactical, it’s actually more fun. Like creating a net for the operations centre and co-ordinating drops — especially with Chris’s weird sense of timing. You’re all still trying to forget the time when I tried to launch a cure for the Green disease while in Brussels. Look, as Operation Expert, I’m just going to stack us all up here to touch the cure. I had vibes from a mission in Cape Town where we had to plug gaps in the housing crisis. No time to step back and laugh at the local goats. Just get the cure passed.      Well, as the Medic – and Wales’ finest polymer specialist – I’m going to eradicate any blue disease outbreaks while you rush around like yellow-safety-hatted zealots trying to catch the biomechanical squirrel.      I volunteer for Researcher. Then I can snack on the board game snacks goody bag I snuck in here. If I work at it, I can actually separate out the green and red disease cubes while knocking on random doors and pretending to be a UNESCO inspector.      You’re not helping.

Right, so today is CBeebies day, and I thought we could have a fun morning watching some panto bits and stories, just like we used to when you were younger. And after that, we’ll watch “Peppa Pig” and “In the Night Garden” when your brother gets up. You two can lie together on the rug and listen to the stories. I think jelly and bread is fine today, darling, as long as you eat breakfast properly—some toast and eggs after. Deal?      Yes, deal! Only if your Daddy agrees and we can have it in the garden. So do you lot reckon it was a good idea, me moving in here?      Honestly, Adam, it's brilliant. I mean, it's not a palace or anything, but it's got everything you need. And having you here means we can all potter about after work without having to go anywhere else, yeah?      Yeah, I’m actually jealous of you a bit. A lot of flatmates I've had just don’t get on with anyone. But you know, it’s just been smooth sailing so far for us.      Well, I can’t complain. It helps that we all have jobs and are more or less mature now, right? You two still working at the same places?      Yeah, more or less. I’m still at the local paper, but I’ve managed to get an editor for about half the gig. Still breakfasts at 6am to chase stories, though — no reprieve there, thanks.      And I’m still teaching English to overpaid expats—vastly overpaid—personally I think they'd be better off with a YouTube tutorial to be honest.      Haha, well, at least you get in when you want and out when you want. I’m often still at the site, swatting away until seven or eight somedays.      Still working on the residential extension at that developer's site?      Yeah, the boring one. Forty semi-detached villas, preferably with outbuildings the size of a shoebox. It’s not as exciting as I thought it’d be when I was a kid with Legos.      But you're finally an engineer. I remember you coming out of your university telling us you were going to build the next superhero's HQ.      Oh, that was high on caffeine and nostalgia. Still, I'll take it over a salary docked for coming in late to write about someone else’s bad breakup on the weekend.      Websites and space weapons: pick your poison. So what about the dating scene? Still using that app you downloaded after saying you’d never use such a thing?      Oh yeah. I’m still using it—still just seeing the same profile pic of a person with sunglasses and a headshot from 2008. I’m seriously starting to think it’s just one person pretending to be everyone else.      I’ve been over this with my students, them trying to string together conversations in English online. It's like they think the language is just one massive emoji.

Rather annoying isn't it when you're reading a book and you get halfway and think, ‘Hang on—what was the name of this character again?’ It happens to me all the time.      Oh I know, I’ve read the same sentence three times and still can’t make head nor tail of it. I remember once I got halfway through   "The Secret Garden"   and couldn’t remember if Martha was the one with the red hair!      Oh she was, wasn’t she. We had to read that at school. Didn’t you, Claire?      Yes, although I mostly remember because I had a massive cold the whole term and my teacher made me read it out loud during breaks to keep my brain awake. I hated it back then, but now I kind of nostalgic about it. I think school turned me off reading for a while.      I can’t say I blame you. I HATED reading when I was younger. Only read books that my mum gave me for Christmas—and even then, I would throw them under the bed and tell her I had read them. Cheeky I know, but it did the job.      Oh no, I did that too! But then I was obsessed with “  Ginger Meg”   books, the series with the red-haired girl who goes off on adventures. I read every single one of them and then wrote my own. Mine didn’t make it to the shelves though. They just got stuck in my bottom drawer with a ton of other unfinished work.      Oh, that’s understandable. I think the first ‘proper’ book I  actually  finished was   "Charlotte’s Web"  —I was about eight. I still remember watching the film and feeling so sad for Wilbur. My brother used to make pig noises at me for weeks after that!      Poor Wilbur. My gran used to read that to me too. She would always cry at the end though. I don’t blame her, it’s a heartbreaker.      Let’s not talk about sad books. I need more chocolate and less nostalgia. Speaking of, Ann, you remember delivering the cake with the errant strawberry on top? I still cringe thinking about it.      Oh my word! That was the worst. Sue—my client—asked what your name was and I said “Claire” and she was like, “Oh, you’re the baker with the  cake topper  mishap, aren’t you?”

So did you really just take off to Majorca without anyone knowing? That sounds like the sort of thing  I’d  do, not you, Grandma!      Oh, come on! Your Grandpa finally had the enthusiasm to book something, and after retiring, he thought it was high time I saw the sea properly. I’ve got four decades under my belt, and not once have I been on a real holiday alone.      That’s wild, really. Imagine going from pulling levers in a car showroom to sunbathing on a beach in Spain. That’s a big shift!       Oh , don’t forget the part where I nearly got stuck on the plane because My turkey jacket wouldn’t zip! The duty-free shop gave me a sweater, and I had to walk on the plane like I was headed to a funeral.      Well better than breakfast, love. You look much better in that photo I saw.      Wait, wait, wait — you had a turkey jacket? That is  calamitous . Did you, like, eat it on the plane after it zipper gave out?      Haha! No, no, I didn’t eat it. I  packed  it. I thought it was smart to wear something festive, in case there was some sort of Christmas markets or something. Now don’t laugh, but the whole time I was there, I kept thinking that if I looked fancy in a jacket at the hotel, someone might offer me a Martini and call me  Clarissa .      So, what exactly  did  you do in Majorca? Cling to the hotel bar about to fall off?      Nooo, we had a proper itinerary. There was some farmer’s market, then some hilltop town called something  Medieval . I bought a  very  expensive orange from a man who passed out after giving me directions.      But he was  very  intense. Strong handshake, very direct. Didn't like my hearing aid. Declared me  British royalty  or some nonsense.      Now he's going back there for  that , is he?      He's hoping I’ll forget about the jacket and just go again next year. But I’ve got a  very  firm box rule now: if it zip-proof isn’t in the name, I’m not taking it.      And what about the sea view, Grandma? Did you fall in love with it?      Oh, I did all right. I found myself falling in love with the sunrises, the sierras, and the very strong taste of  Olives Everywhere .

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh?      Aye, it's always pinging like that in the morning. I swear it knows I'm not looking at it, and it just keeps going mad for no reason.      Be quiet! You wouldn't be getting so annoyed if it wasn’t your bloody turn to do the bins, would you?      Easy for you to say, love. At least your bins are out back, not under our shared path where some dump or something could just pull in and hit the bins when you're not looking.      Get the bins out, will you? I’ve got a meeting at the plant in an hour. I can’t be late again, or I’ll be skinned alive by the boss. He’s on my back enough already.      Fair enough, I’ll take them out while I wait for the kettle. I need a coffee and this tea’s not doing it for me this morning. Honestly, I don’t know what the deal is. I paid for decent ones, too.      Might’ve had a dodgy batch. I put two mugs of that in and didn’t even notice, it was so weak. I ended up just having water and a biscuit.      Mate, you can’t live on water and biscuits. You’ll end up like a dried-up apple yourself.      If I could blame anything for the shoddiness of this coffee, someone would be in a lot of trouble. But unfortunately, it just is what it is. Some things you’d think have gone up over the years being online and premium and all that, but it’s like most people about to fall off the wagon trying to make the right choices.      I suppose you could say that. I mean, I’ve got it easier at work, but that’s just because I’m part of the construction side. All the engineers, the people who have to sort the technical stuff out? They all seem to have it harder, you know.      As long as your project doesn’t get binned like this coffee. No pun intended.      Haha, well you try delivering something as complex as a turbine without the budget or go-ahead from on high. I’ve seen projects get delayed over nothing.      I suppose it’s the same in publishing sometimes. You can get a great story all lined up, and then the editor’s decided it’s not ‘in the tone’ or it’s not right for the ‘target market.’

Right, I just wanted to say again, Reg, how excited we all are for your new adventure in Saudi Arabia. You've always had a dream of doing more than just ticking clocks, and now you're actually off doing it full-time!      Yeah! You'll be the biggest boss in that desert, dealing with construction projects and fancy contracts. Honestly, I reckon you’ll be using Google Maps on a daily basis just to find your head office in this heat!      Imagine trying to use a satnav and it just says, "Re-routing due to sand storm" the whole time.      Aye, I’ll tell ye, lad, the last supply convoy I was on in Iraq had more sand than directions. Still, best to have a bit o’r blarney up yer sleeve if they pick ye up in the back of a 4x4 by mistake and forget to refuel, eh?      Honestly though, I think Reg being from Peterborough is actually quite a good grounding for working in the Middle East. It’s built for exporting strong bones and resilience, don’t you think?      Haha! Resilience and early rises for sure. I’m just going to be sad you’re not pacing around our house every Sunday trying to remember who lives where in our fairly simple, local postcode.      Yeah, no more of those "What street did Silas live on again?" vibes. We might survive, but the coffee will never taste the same without you insisting on trying to brew a flat white at 6 a.m.      Don’t forget the unofficial decorating advice. That time you told your grandmother she needed a pastel about five decades ago after a weekend trip round the area.      And I still don’t know if it was intentional that she left the handle off the drawer for three weeks. My sister still hasn't touched it.      Aye, and I remember ye telling me once that any decent job needs three things—first, you’ve got to sort out the coffee machine, second, the office chairs, and third, you've got to keep the satnav updated so you’re not going in circles for clients.      That man’s gospel right there. First map your life, then map everyone else’s.      Well, enjoy it, Reg. You might not be getting the same crooked street signs or pestering friends for help with paint tins, but you’ll probably get a lot of new stories to tell us over endless video calls over tea and hummus and dates or something.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You know, ever since I came back from New Zealand, I've had this niggling cough no matter how much I try to stay on top of it. I told my GP it probably came from some beach side bar fumes or something.      Oh I'm sorry to hear that. You must be missing your kiwifruit and all that fresh clean air.      Honestly, that sounds like a place I'd really enjoy. I've always admired New Zealand and how clean and green everything is. Didn’t your family have the garden with the specially imported native trees?      Yeah, we did. We had a small plot where we managed to grow Myrtles, Pōhutukawa’s, you name it. We had the help of a local botanist in our area who came in most weeks for about a year to make sure we did it right. It was a real journey.      I would love to have that kind of indulgence. I remember when we got married we tried planting a small herb garden in the back, and by the time the next birthday rolled around, all of it was either leggy or under the soil.      That's the thing, you just have to give it your time. Just like my business, really – gardening is a bit of a balancing act.      I imagine being an entrepreneur must give you more of those moments than you can count about balancing everything.      Oh without a doubt. You have to be a bit of a generalist. One minute you’re organizing logistics, the next you’re in meetings, and, believe it or not, once you’re back at home, you're cleaning your teeth with a green tea brush and measuring vitamins like it's a chemistry experiment.      We should talk about that. I've also picked up a bit of a health routine myself recently. More mindfulness, more sleep – it’s been a bit of a revelation.      Oh really go on then, spill it! I've had a real lack of sleep since the kids started school, between 6 a.m. morning drop-offs and your after-school madness. It's been non-stop!

So do you lot ever notice how hard it is when you talk to the voice assistants like Alexa or Siri? I got mine confused between me and my nan because my accent is all over the place. It just kept saying it couldn’t understand me and then the next thing—  Lola   starts shouting instructions in her Harlowese dialect and suddenly it works.      Hey now! Don’t knock my Harlow A listing, missy! If this voice assistant had half the brains of me and my dump horsewife journey, it wouldn’t need a degree to understand me when I speak.      Honestly, when I was a lad in the East End, I had to shout like a car boot sale stall holder to make anyone hear me. Back then, nobody cared if you had an accent. But now, I reckon the world listens differently—too many bloody options, and they’re waiting for you to sound like posh Lady Bracknell.      And it is! I mean, even Grandpa here can shout down a storm, and that man’s been shouting since the 60s. But he still can’t get Alexa to turn the lights off unless he pretends he’s in a bloody courtroom—“Alexa. LIGHTS. OFF.” It's like Shakespeare – very dramatic.      Honestly, I don’t know why the bloody thing doesn’t just shut up and do what’s asked. I tried talking to it once in a normal voice, just said “turn on the TV” and it didn’t work. So then I had a drink— one , mind—picked up the remote and it worked better than bloody Alexa ever did in a week.      “Ah yes, alcoholism is the key to a functioning household.” That’s your life story right there, isn’t it?      My life story is nap time between 2pm and 5pm. That and arguing with my toaster. It shoves my toast straight down my front yesterday, you know.      You had a  toaster dispute ? That’s worse than my parents’ custody battle over my childhood bicycles. My dad kept insisting they were “his” because he bought them, and my mum goaded him on for years about riding a wobbly one at camping trips.      Honestly, the worst thing about growing up in your house was you two arguing over who made the best dinner and who’s to blame when you gained five pounds in a week from your dad’s sugary cakes.

Right, lads, dig in. I've made a few of the usuals—lasagne, Yorkshire pudding, and I thought I'd surprise you with a bit of baked Alaska for afters. It's been ages since I made one of those.      Wow, baked Alaska? That’s proper fancy! Did you do the bit with the torch on top?      Yeah, I did. A little too fancy for the dining room, but it gave me a kick. It reminds me of my auntie’s house in Yorkshire. She always made one when we had big family things. Her recipe needs three eggs, even if it only serves four. She'd say, “More eggs, more oomph!”      I like eccentric aunties. So, you go to the job interview in Diss next week, I hear? They’re trying to recruit someone for the healthcare training gig?      Yeah, I’m helping with a bit of advisory input. It’s part of a new initiative, building up training providers so they’re more inclusive. One bloke I worked with last week—personally brilliant, but he got put off by the form. They asked for his race and gender and everything. He was like, “What, you expect me to put ‘reject’ in the box?      That’s actually kind of funny, but also sort of sad. It makes you wonder what else gets people switched off. Last week at school, we had a lesson about discrimination. The teacher said age also counts. Like my gran, she just wants to be treated normally—job-wise, housing-wise, or even dating-wise.       laughs  Oh, you’ve gone about as far as you can with that “dating-wise” comment at your age. Society changes, but some people still get stick about it.      Is it true you used to do catering full-time before you went back to do the programme work? I remember Gran talking about this birthday party you did for her in the 90s—the cheese factor.      Oh, the cheese? I had to grate 20kg of Stilton. My hands went stiff for weeks. I made it up on the stairs, in the dining room—there was even a little person toting a plate of olives over like it’s Mumsnet catering.
