Definitely feels like home, especially over breakfast.      For now. Let's just enjoy this while it lasts.      Agreed. Let’s get some toast sorted, maybe even some clotted cream if we haven’t used the last bit.      Now that's a plan worth sticking with.

Right, I’m putting down "quince" — six letters. That’s got to be solid. We’re in the final round and I’m not letting Jon win again.      Are you sure it’s a real word? No, I mean as in —  is  it a real word or just something you made up to try and throw the game?      It’s a real word. A fruit, if you haven’t encountered it before. Found in jams and chutneys, mostly. My nan used to make quince and apple sauce during the autumn season.      Right, but is it  actually  a word you can use in Scrabble? There was this time at uni Myra cheated by using "eskor" — or however you spell it, the music term — and shouted, "Blimey, the dictionary didn’t check itself for spelling mistakes!" Then the ref kicked her out for an hour.      That’s a bit harsh, isn’t it? She didn’t do it on purpose. Though to be honest, that  was  the third time.      Okay, I’m going to put down "scrabble" itself for two letters. Wait no, that’s not how it works. Oh, stupid me. I’m too tired from preparing for my sociology lecture, and now it’s bleeding into my vocabulary. I blame the lack of tea.      Speaking of tea, you should’ve been here earlier. Our kettle someone — full name,  someone  — left it unplugged again. I had to buy tea hotter than the summer sun from the café down the road. Made me feel like I was in the middle of the Sahara about five minutes after buying a skimmed latte.      Ah yes — what time did you arrive again? I think I arrived at around 2pm, but that was just because I realized halfway that I’d put the wrong date on my sundial.      Unbelievable. Do you even have a phone, Jon?      Not one good enough to stay on. Keeps turning off when trying to upload photos of the Chelsea Flower Show. I took a picture of that irises display the other day and it looked like a dragon set go-to-war on them.      You mean it made the flowers look angry?      That’s one way to put it. Anyway, while I was planning to upload them on my Tumblr, it died. So now I’m just stuck with this artistic contrast of beautiful flowers and a camera screen filled with static silence.

Rather a wet day, isn't it?      Yes, it’s damp in the bones already. I’ll not be going out today, that’s for sure.      Good call. Not a day to be outside in those trousers and wellies you bought last week.      Ha! I was joking about saying I fancied myself as a farmer after a week of shopping online. But tell me, how’s your hip feeling these days? Still as bad as it was?      Not half. The doctor says I might well end up needing another operation, but truth be told, I can barely get up the garden steps, let alone do a day’s work.      That’s not good, love. You need to look after yourself, even if the rest of us are turned to rust.      Oh, we’re all relics now, I expect. You with your videos in the lorry, me with my books and crossword, and not many visitors to shout at.      I do tell you—my computer’s still newer than I am! Sometimes I think it’s still trying to tell me something when I open it.      Well, when it gives up on you, just bring it round, I’ll have a look at it.      Now don’t go making things worse! You broke the toaster already last week!      That was not my doing. It just gave up the ghost one morning, and I had a cup of tea without toast. A fine day if you ask me—saves the waistline.      I daresay. I’ve had a letter in the post this morning, you know.      Oh? Money or more worrying stuff?      Neither, it’s from the local council. They’re doing some work on the road at the end of the lane where the bus stops.      So what? I hope they crack my hearing aid and that’ll be one less thing to worry about.      They're saying the repairs might take a few weeks, so no tarmac and the usual honking goings-on on that road.      Well, at least it’ll give the pair of us a good excuse not to go out.      I was thinking more of how we won’t get any tea deliveries, though. You know how that lassie in the van overcompensates on the milk!      Oh I remember her alright. She once left a note in my bag saying my radio was playing too loud. Me? I could barely hear it myself!

Rather skip the newfit app eh?      Well I was just trying it out this morning... got a bit too enthusiastic with the circuit training bit. I think I saw stars after the last squat!      You'll have to tone things down a bit. We haven’t finished recovering from your Easter cook-along event last weekend you know. I still have cramp in my left eyelid from that nutmeg incident.      I thought it was a very  bold  choice of seasoning. We can't all be professional chefs like me. Although, I might say that now I’ve retired, I’ve even taken to mapping genotypes in my spare time just to keep my brain occupied.      Mapping what now?      Genotypes! I’m part of this online forum, and we’ve been trying to find correlations between genetic markers and taste preferences. Turns out, breakfasts with a high cinnamon content are likely to trigger early alertness in over-60s! No, you didn’t hear that from me!      I think I’d rather stick to reading recipes and avoiding any apps I can’t pronounce. What did you make for dinner tonight?      Roast lamb, rosemary potatoes, and then a humble fruit crumble with – no nutmeg this time I promise – just vanilla and a splash of brandy.      That sounds lovely! You know what I could really do with after the new app workout is a walk somewhere. I heard the new Exeter train station is finally opening next week. It’s taken years to get this far.      Really? That’s good news. I spoke to my cousin in Totnes who’s been lobbying the council for the better part of a decade. She said it’ll solve a lot of traffic issues heading east and will give better access to the local farmers markets. My, time for local transport development seems to be picking up.      Speaking of markets – did you get the Christmas shopping sorted? I tried writing a list the other day but I lost my pen and then I forgot what I was going to write with it.      I’m working on it. I set a budget of around £50 per person and prioritized go-to gifts like soap, candles and handknits – at least I can line-wrap the socks and it’ll be festive themed.      Good plan. I ordered something online for Dave from Northampton – one of those high-powered batteries for his mobility rollator.

So did you watch The Lie last night? That episode where they raided the safe house in Chester?      No, I binned it off after the first ten minutes.      What? Not even with that bit where the bloke picked up the briefcase and then it eeny-meeny-miny-moed 'im?      Yeah, I saw that on my mate’s Twitter before I even started.      Oh, come on, you can't bin it off for that. Didn’t it get better after that?      Maybe. I just thought it was a bit heavy-handed, all that stuff with the politicians and that Myra lookalike.      Yeah, well, the show’s never been afraid to push the boat out. They’re up to their necks in the dodgy corporation plot now, aren’t they?      Exactly. Feels like they’re trying to fit a year’s worth of plot twists in the last few episodes. It’s like one of those Premier League games—always a goals every three minutes and a red card as well.      Tell me about it. I reckon the writer got bored and then just got one of their mates to fill it in with a pen, like, “Here’s a bit of drama.”      Fair enough. You know what I’m still confused about? Why’d they put in all that Shakespeare stuff in the TV show? Like, what does that have to do with a bunch of nutters running around with a red phone?      That’s what I said! I mean, I like Shakespeare as much as the next fella, but blinking Titus Andronicus in a thriller about espionage?      I reckon it’s just for show to make the showers sound smarter.      Probably. Still, I reckon they should’ve done a spin-off called  Hamlet: The Redemption  or something. You know, stick the bloke in a bunker with a ransom note and wait for the twist.      Now that’s a proper idea for a screenplay. Then again, if they started casting actual actors in that bin, maybe it wouldn’t be  The Lie  anymore—maybe just  The Mischaracterisation .      Aye, well. Look, at least it’s better than the conference seminar I went to last week— “Navigating Ambiguity in a Post-Europe World: A Critical Framework.”  I was like, “Is it my sandwich I'm supposed to be ambiguous about?”      You see? Right place, right time. I mean, isn’t that the real issue, though?

Victoria! Oh my god, look at you! You haven't changed a bit. How long’s it been? Like, nearly four years?      I know, I know! It’s so mad to see you. You look amazing, by the way! Still living near Cambridge?      Yeah, I’ve been in Cambourne for over two now. I actually work in Cambridge a few days a week, but I love the village vibe. Still in Oxford?      Oh no! Left Oxford ages ago. I’m now in a flatshare in North Oxford—it’s a bit of a struggle, but it’s affordable. I work at the Pearson office now, marketing for language courses. My job involves a lot of emails and spreadsheets. It’s not super glamourous, but hey, it pays the bills!      Blimey, that’s actually amazing! I envy you—Pearson? I mean, with my job in project coordination, I’m lucky if I finish my day without looking like a mess! I once had to stay late to finish a client proposal, and I literally fell asleep at my desk in full makeup.      Oh no! That sounds exhausting. You must be so used to it by now though, right?      Mate, I got fairly good at working smarter, not harder, after my first year. Now I batch my emails and schedule phone calls. It helps a bit. Still, the job’s never dull. Who have you been dating? Let me guess—someone from work?      [laughs] You don’t know the half of it. There was this guy called Jamie, colleague, and romantic disaster number about five. We broke up about six months ago. Long story, but basically, he expected me to move to Manchester because that was “his deal.”      Ugh, classic. Should’ve known. I ended up breaking up with my last guy for the stupidest reason. I caught him Googling “best places to meet girls under 25.” My self-esteem peaked that night.      Oh, classic London bloke! I’m with you. Now he’s with someone far more exotic, I hear.      Yeah, go you! I mean, if you ever meet someone real soon, I promise not to interrogate you between sips of my oat milk latte. But if it’s someone at Pearson, I might question his sanity.      Fair play. Anyway, enough drama. How’s your family?      Mums the same old—trying to get my younger sisters to study instead of TikTok all day.

Rather annoying isn’t it when you water a plant and then it still looks like it's dying?      Aye, it is. I thought I was being helpful, but my cactus probably thinks I'm trying to drown it now.      Ha ha, don’t worry, I went through the same phase with the fern. I reckon it just wanted to be left alone.      Fair enough. Plants can be funny like that. So what was it like back in Sunderland? Did you manage to take any cuttings before you left?      Not really, truth be told. My mam was nagging me the whole time to ask her about the geranium outside the front doorstep. She thinks it’s got magical powers or something. Says it’s been there for twenty years and survives everything.      Sounds like a proper old-school plant. I envy you that. I’ve been trying to grow herbs in my flat and I’ve already lost the thyme, the basil’s dead, and the mint is just sat there like “well done me, I survived” and it looks proudly average.      You’re human, not a gardener. Try going on Bake Off first before we expect you to bring herbs back from the brink – that’s a whole different skillset.      Fair call. But seriously, I did try watching the BBC Good Food Show the other night. Smacked me around the head with how someone made chicken and sage dumplings. That looked like a chef, not a man with a stove hotter than my flat.      Oh I know – I had a colleague at work make those in about five minutes. She pulled it off like the Renaissance had invented takeout. Honestly, cooking like that makes me want to take up baking and call myself a professional.      Well, for starters, you’d need steady hands and not a cat that views your flour as a napkin. My mate Tom said he used to host dinner parties for his whole family. We’re talkin’ seven of them at the table every week. Do lunches, do dinners – told me the secret’s just “feed them first and talk after” so it’s like the holy grail of family dinners.      That or give them all separate cutlery so they don’t argue over the knives. You know what your lot are like. My sister once made me reshoot a whole family photo because my tea was warmer than hers.

Rather skip the queue and take a seat in the office, Colin. I was just marking essays when you poked your head in. Coffee?      Aye, sure thing, George. Got it in my hand. Thank you, though. Weekend well?      Rather good, thank you. I took the dog for a long walk out at Epping Forest. Bit of a clean day, sun out but not too hot. I got to dig in the garden a bit, pulling out the old herbs and making space for some new stuff. Rosemary, thyme, lavender – you know the drill. What about you?      Oh, fairly routine weekend. I managed to get the turkey feed sorted for the new-place garden. The birds are thriving – I tell you, their legs are thicker than most lads I know! But then most of the time, I spent watching snooker. Bucksy up to frame five with Hargreaves and he’s planting five in a row, you’d think it was a robotics match.      Ah, yes, yes, Championship of it all takes one out of you quite a bit. I watched a little on TV. Tell me, have you been reading the nonsense in the papers about all these young football stars marrying – no, not each other, no – but these very young girls? Some of them no older than twelve, if you can believe it. Makes you wonder about the education of the parents and the people overseeing all that.      Aye, it does. I read a bit about it over the weekend. It shouldn’t be allowed here, but still – where I’m from, there’s talk about about joining the police or the armed forces being the best route out of this for some young lads. At least you know that they’ll get a fair handle on things, decent pay, some respect, and for the hardy ones, steady work.      Well, the armed forces – any entrance there needs some talking through. Strong discipline, waiting till 18. As for the police… Well, academies are always trying to draw in a new generation of people with various backgrounds. Not all of it is a slam-dunk by any stretch, but the goal is noble enough. But let’s get our heads back into marking, eh? Still in the deep end with those essays on Romantic poetry?      Aye, just about. Found a few bright sparks, mind you. And one earnest soul who wrote as if she’s channeling Emily Brontë herself – the girl should be writing her own novels.

Right, so the birthday’s on Sunday. I’ve asked Sarah’s sister to pop in with the cake first thing, and I’ll sort out the dining room so it’s all set by ten. How are you holding up with all the organisation?      Honestly, I’m a bit swamped at the minute. With my placement ending next week, I’ve been working 12-hour days. But I’ve got Aimee coming over later this week to help me finish the decorations. It’s just pulling everything together. We’ve got the balloons, and the bunting from the craft store in Uttoxeter.       claps excitedly  Birthday! Party! Cake!      My little star, yes! There’ll be cake and a teddy bear, just like we promised, Aunty and I bought it the other week. It’s all about the teddy! Wait, does everyone know about the Christening afterwards? Hattie’s at the end of the month.      I did get a text from Sarah, but I haven’t been into town to get my outfit yet. Do we have to wear those posh dresses to both events?      Well, for the birthday, it’s just little ones, but yes, the Christening – we’ll have to be smart, and I know the other mums are choosing a certain set of outfits to coordinate. Sarah sent me a list. There’s a colour scheme — pinks and creams.      Honestly, I’d rather just throw on jeans and a hoodie. But I’m sure the kid deserves a bit of sparkle. Any chance I can help with the Christening plans?      Oh, you’d be gold. I’m still trying to sort out who’s doing what. We’ve got Sarah doing the photos and Suzy handle the car hire for transport to the church.       points at window  Birdie!      Love it when you notice things, love. Birdies are rare about now. Back on your stick. How are you and Ryan handling being away from the baby this week?      Well, I took the weekend off, so I got to see her and help feed the baby early in the morning. I think he misses me. He keeps trying to crawl after my legs in the morning, which is adorable.       throws arms up  Mine! Mine! Mine! Cow!      Yes, yes, I’ll make your cow toadstool sandwich, sweetheart. Just hold tight, Mummy’s making it. You know what, I think we need to plan a bit of time off once all this is over.

Rather skip to a bar in Manchester instead.      That’d be nice. The first floor got too full with tablets.      Not a trouble, we’d have a little rest first. Not quite tired yet, but we’d have a bit of a lie-in in the eeny morn, yeah.      Ay!      Normally you’ve only got so long before the baby decides otherwise, though.      She’s getting better now at settling in the evenings. Funny how quickly they get into a routine.      It really does. Last month I thought she’d never sleep, now she’s quite calm like that.      So, what’s the plan for the weekend? I know you two are off to Milton Keynes tomorrow.      For a few days, yeah. We’ve got a friend up there who’s visiting from New York, and they want to meet us. Maybe even get to see some of the city.      Oh, do tell, are they going to take you up the Empire State building?      It’s on the cards, but we’re watching how the toddler handles it.      Yeah – Baptiste was bawling last time we took her to a huge building. Felt like we were trying to carry a whole library of toys.      Haha, you just have to pack light. Although with a toddler, there are none of them rules left.      I know, I know. Between tea and a nappy, your ballet flat collection is out the door.      Haha! She’s had quite an effect on my house too. My sister came round the other week and nearly fell over a toy superhero in my hallway.      My guest room looks like it was hit by a tornado.      Oh, I know. I tried to make a little tidy station out of the shed, but she manages to drag things out every time.      At least the shed’s big. My parents lost their shed after a storm last year. The weather has been gooners on lately, if you ask me.      I’ve been saying it for weeks – it feels like we went from your wedding in June to winter in October.      That was amazing, though, don’t forget, your garden looked lovely for it, and the reception at the function hall was spot on.      I know, they said the flowers were so bright, they looked like they were trying to outshine the camera flashes. It was such a lovely day.      Mummy, can we go to New York?

So do you want me to go through the whole thing or do you just want me to explain the bits you're confused on?      I think it would help if you just explained where you got this part from. I can see you've got like ten sources cited, but the main one’s that eeny weeny textbook from last term, right?      Yeah, that one’s a bit dense, but it actually lays out the theoretical framework pretty clearly. I built the whole intro around that. The key thing is to link the theory to the case study in chapter five.      Right, but how did you decide which case study to use? I mean, there’s like eight in there.      Honestly, I picked the one on the post-industrial regeneration in Birmingham because I thought it’d be relevant to our area. We’re in Salford, and there’s been a lot of talk about similar projects in the Quayside in recent years. It gave me a bit of local context to work with.      Oh, that’s smart. I just did a generic one on Bristol—probably not as interesting. Was it hard to find secondary sources to back up what the book says?      A little, yeah. I looked up a few journal articles on urban redevelopment through the university library, but they were all pretty academic. I found this one from  Urban Studies  that’s a few years old, but it reinforces the principles from the textbook. You don’t always need the newest reference if it works for the argument.      Yeah, the key is just making the links clear. Did you structure it all as a typical essay or is it more about analysis?      I kept it fairly standard—overview of the theory in the intro, then a breakdown of the case study in the main body. But I tried to do a bit of critical analysis in each paragraph, like pointing out the limitations of the theory or where the case study diverges. That’s what the marker’s really looking for, right?      Probably. I rushed mine and just did a bit of description. No wonder I’m panicking now.      Still, if you’ve got the main idea down, you can go back and map your own references to the structure. Just don’t leave it to the last minute like I did. I was up until two in the morning stitching paragraphs together.

So do you remember your dream last night?      No, not really — just bits... Like, I was standing in a field with ducks or something, and then someone was humming a tune. You know me and dreams — they’re always kind of surreal.      Got it. I had a dream we won the National Lottery. I reckon it was about £250 million. I was in a muddy field in Comberton, picking daisies and checking my bank balance every five seconds. Classic.      Do dream about dogs? Mummy said you can’t have one yet.      That’s her dream, not mine.      No, Sophie’s serious. She’s been talking about rescue dogs for a month now. I think she wants to be responsible for something, you know?      Bucks! Wants to have a big one for bad people.      James says he wants a guard dog, so he can terrify the postman and pretend he’s a police officer. I’m not quite sure whether to be concerned or amused.      Honestly, watching the two of them argue about which dog would “win” — the big one or the fluffy one — was actually kind of adorable. But back to my dream — don’t get me started. I dream I win the lottery and then I’m in a field. Like what?      Maybe because you live in the countryside now? Comberton’s got a lot of fields. Or marshland and beehives, depending on the season.      Or maybe I’m just trying to tell the universe that I miss London. Not really — I like this place. The kids love school, the garden is big, we’ve got privacy. My only problem is the wet socks crisis that’s perpetual here during winter.      Oh, you mentioned that. I thought it was funny — you tried to dry them with a hair dryer and ended up singeing the carpet.      I didn’t  sing the carpet . It just… enhanced the musty smell around the entire living room. That was a gothic room before. Now it’s a haunted one.      I want a dog. I want a big one. And I can feed it and walk it.      We’ve talked about this, Sophie, maybe in a couple of years. First we need to get over this dream phase where you think everything you want immediately can happen. Unless we win the lottery.      Bucks wants one too! Bucks says we need one for bears.      Please no.

I do not know how long I can do this, honestly. My hand was in plaster for  weeks  after that fall in the A&E waiting room last month. I still can’t type properly sometimes.      Yeah, I know, I saw what you were going through. Honestly, if it happens again, you  have  to use the hospital’s form to report it. You can’t just let it slide every time.      I know, I know. I started filling it in last week, and you’ll never believe the queue at the admin desk. I was there for over an hour just to hand it over! And when I finally got to the person, they only asked me "Were you treated at this department?" and didn’t even look at the accident description. I felt like I was talking to a wall.      That’s ridiculous. I was at a different hospital a while back, and they actually gave me a safety awareness booklet for visitors. Thought it was pretty thorough. You could even get a lanyard so people know not to walk too close to you if you’re using crutches or something.      Oh, brilliant. Why don’t they tell us that? I might go in and ask for one. But honestly, when I got hurt last time, the first thing I got was a paper cup of lukewarm water and a form that said “Did you fall due to your own gross negligence?” What is that, a joke?      That’s the problem. They always seem to read it like it’s a fishing expedition. You’d think after all this time they’d get better at being helpful instead of defensive. I had a friend fall because the floor was wet and there was a sign that just said “Danger: Wet Floor” in 8-point font and not a single wipe-down area. She ended up with a broken ankle.      Oh no, that’s not even right. I mean, A&E should be a safe place, especially for people who are already injured or unwell. It’s mad that people still get hurt just waiting to be seen.      And it’s not just the floor—stools, chairs, even hospital trolleys. I had a nurse once who told me that go-karts on hospital campuses are more risk-assessed than waiting room chairs. You’d think they’d invest a little in safety, particularly in A&E where people are stressed and less careful.

Rather annoying isn't it, what’s going on in the Ukraine. I was watching the news before lunch and it got me rather upset to be honest.      Aye, I saw that as well. It's worrying to see such instability so close to home. People like us who’ve lived in the area all our lives, we remember when it was just peace and quiet on the coast. Now it seems like everything is up in the air.      Absolutely. And don’t get me started on the inflation and prices. My monthly pension doesn’t go as far as it used to. I’ve had to cut down on even the essentials.      I know precisely what you mean. It’s forcing me to look at changing my business. I used to run this small surf gear shop down the prom, but these past few years have been difficult. I'm thinking of offering hand-painted boomerangs. Something a bit more unique to draw in tourists.      Now that’s an interesting thought, Ken. You always had a flair for creativity. I remember that time you decided to paint the shop window every week with upcoming events written in quirky fonts. Got quite the attention back in the day!      Oh come on Jack, you're not making me humble now. But seriously – I'm talking to a few people and thinking it might be wise to expand into something new. It's not just about the money for me these days, it's about staying busy, staying proud of what I do.      That's the spirit. I remember when I first retired, I had the same feeling. So I started tutoring at the community college – not for money, but for the joy of passing on knowledge. That’s how I met the wife again, by the way.      That's quite the love story! I've been thinking about sending for my cousin from Perth, Australia. She's worked in guest hospitality there and might be interested in helping out with a weekend initiative – a surf-themed weekend at the shop.      You’re full of ideas, mate. What about your regulars? The ones who've been coming in since the 80s? They’ll want to see you delivering something new.      Oh they go on about it constantly. I’ve had a few ask if I could branch into something different. Frankly, I think a bloke like Tom, your old colleague at the school, would be seriously interested in writing a piece about it for the local paper.

Rather skip the starter and just go for the whole pie, personally. I know it's supposed to be a starter, but I've had them before and they're practically a meal in their own right.      Not bad, not bad. I bet it's been like that for years. Got a bit of a  Happy Valley  vibe to the place, if you ask me—rural, a bit run down but still decent.      Is that a reference to the show or just something you just made up? I don’t get the comparison. It's not glorified farm country... just East London with beige wallpaper.      No, no, I do know the show well. It's definitely got that vibe. You know how they do things there, the way the scenes are shot, the whole sad but comforting sort of place. It's like that.      Maybe a bit more urban than West Yorkshire though. The barmaid was looking at us as if we might cause trouble, for heaven's sake.      Ah, it's the way we're dressed. You still have that scarf from your university days on. It's got more stories in it than a library book.      Be quiet. You still have that – what is it, a tie with a clip that won't clip properly? You looked like an officer who got lost on the way home.      That's a retired air force tie.      And you know what? It still won't clip.      I borrowed it from my dad. Anyway, speaking of university, did you ever finish that project on about how transcribers are the unsung heroes of the office world?      No. I know that was the plan. I even bought a notebook for it. It just stayed in the drawer.      I did. I just handed them a finished one before Christmas. They asked me to present it at a little function. I sort of choked.      That’s a shame. You've always been a little nervous with people. Not that I am not, but you positively freeze around senior management.      Look, I'm not about to risk my job for a presentation. I just tick the box and move on.      Anyway, what do you think about the music here? It's like a jukebox from the 80s that gave up trying to be cool.      At least it doesn’t play modern pop music. The horror of that is enough to make people consider giving up alcohol all together.

Rather skip the new bar in the city centre and come in here. Handles are still full, eh?      Aye, this place pulls in a good crowd on a Friday. Keeps the old haunts full. You wouldn’t have said that ten years ago, though—Dee’s old een saw the place empty more than not.      Aye, times have changed. I’ve been taking a bit of time out this year, picking up the camera again. It’s not like it used to be when we were younger and dragging the camcorder round the hills. You remember that?      Oh aye, you were the one who filmed that row on the train that one Saturday. Still got that somewhere, I’d wager. But now you go proper—full photography, landscapes, the whole nine yards?      For now, it’s a weekend hobby, but I’ve been thinking about doing some courses. The weather’s been perfect for it too—bright, clear skies, those moody clouds that come over the Firth—set the whole scene, laddie.      Aye, as if you’re not already halfway there with the eye you’ve got. I’ve seen your stuff on that site you post on. Looking sharp. Real sharp, I mean, and not because of the equipment. Some of that lot captures the place and the feel better than a holiday snapshot.      That’s kind of what someone said when I showed a few shots of my trip to the Hebrides. Funny thing—never had the urge before, but I started looking at things differently when I was walking along those beaches, you know? I mean, I travel for the photos, but it ended up being the place that did a bit of travelin’ on me.      Aye, that’s the lot, isn’t it? You go to somewhere expecting one thing, and it just shows you something else. Reminded me of my trip to Iceland—storms, glaciers, waiting hours for the light. Feels as if I came back with a different head than the one I went with.      Was it cold?      Bitter, lad. Could go for a smog and a dram after that.      I’ll stick that in my trip folder, then—Scotland’s what your legs and you could handle.      You take it easy, mind. I’ve had friends go off to shoot locations and not come back for weeks. Only food and film were missing when they surfaced.

Right then, love, what’ve you got planned for the week then?      Oh, not too much, really. Just the usual run of things at the school, a parent’s evening on Thursday, and I’m helping a few of the children with their puppet show on Friday. What about you?      Well, I’ve just got this nursery to sort out completely, I’ve been choosing things off this web site that this friend of mine gave me. The woman was in my class years ago and she said it was the best. Didn’t even want to charge me.      Oh, that’s lovely. Is it for the new baby, then? You know, like that My Little Baby Paradise one?      Yeah, more or less – I’m not going too over the top. A bit of a cot, a couple of toys and something to hang up, you know, just to make it seem a bit more like a home, you know?      I think that sounds great. I would’ve gone crazy though – do you remember when I used to shop for the nursery in my pre-home pregnancy days? I had like six different cot colour schemes in my head…      Oh, don’t get me started! – Mate of mine at the gym, she actually had the room done up in the style of the baby’s actual name. Like, for her first child, the room was mexican, and for her second someone called Dakota and everything was outdoorsy.      I can definitely picture that. Though, is it me or do these nurseries look a bit like museum exhibits when people are done? Not that I’m being sarcastic or anything!      I get what you mean. Maybe they do. But that’s why I’m trying to keep things simple – I just don’t think I could manage the whole Enchanted Forest theme like Mandy did. I remember going there one time – it was all fairy lights, giant witches hats, and little plastic owls everywhere.      That  sounds  like a theme park, honestly. So what are the plans for the weekend? You going anywhere, or just trying to get everything packed up by then?      No, I’m staying at home, I just fancy a lazy weekend. I’ve done a big clean already – what about you? Got anything planned?      Not really, I was thinking of watching that new drama that’s on the channel we like, you know, the one where the guy is missing…      You mean  Embarrassing Encounters ?

So did you lot hear about the new bar that opened in town? I was just there with work last week, got to go with some clients after the conference. Blimey, it was packed. The decor was posh as anything, wouldn’t have gone in there on a Tuesday. But it was alright, eeny weeny bar snacks and drinks that cost more than I earn in a week.      Oh, I've seen it, that place off Fen Ditton Road? The one with the neon lights? Sounds a bit out of me league, innit. I can’t afford to go out too often like that. My weekends mostly involve knocking back a couple of tenners at the pub with some mates.      Honestly, I’m just left out of this. I work in manufacturing, and although I’m professional and I make a good wage for my job, it’s still hard to save when breakfast, train tickets, and this month’s takeaway culture hit in hard. When’s the last time you lot saw me ordering a pizza at home? It’s like, I’d rather treat myself to cinema popcorn and hope I can survive on salad for the rest of the week.      Haha, fair play. It’s funny how different we work, innit. I’m running around at events trying to make sure the ice cream and water bottles are in stock, while you, Speaker_2, are out building something with your hands and Speaker_3, you’re the brains behind the machine, keeping the balls in the air. I often tell me dad, "What did I do to deserve this? Sorted out a ten-person tea break and still got no idea if I’m going to be there when it’s about to happen." That’s the life of the events world.      Honestly, you sound like you are doing better than me. I handle big machines, not bits of paperwork and nonsense like that. I like the hard graft, the proper work. The rest? Well, the rest is just something I do to afford my flat and keep the council waiting on me. We all live such different lives. You bloke, Speaker_3, what’s a production controller anyway?      It’s a fancy name for a glorified points person. I schedule everything on the factory floor—when lines are running, when machines are off for servicing, that sort of stuff. Without blokes like me, your builders wouldn’t have all the right nuts and bolts on time and the factory’d come to a grinding halt.

Rather do a nice cup of tea, innit? Bit nippy out this mornin’, so a cup of builder’s or some Earl Grey would do me nicely.      Oh, George, don’t be crass—I’ve already got the kettle on. I’m putting it in a Chinese cup this time, the one with the flowers on. I reckon it sets the tone better than a mug with a cartoon tiger on.      Look, love, I’ve had a cup of builder’s and some toast already. Bit of a morning run in, don’t you know? Still, like to have a second cup. Proper one. I used to brew it in the school staff room and put in one of those milk jugs they had—it left a bit of a film, mind you, but the tea, now that was good.      Oh, do try the proper Darjeeling—this lady up the road brings it from some little place in Devon, you ever taste it? Proper, full-bodied. Richer than the stuff they sold at the corner shop when we were kids—ah, I remember—Brannans in Harrow had that tartan label and only ten pence a time.      Harrow, was it? You’re from there, weren’t you, Doris? I bet it was a long row back then, tea shops and all that.      Bless you, Liam, Doris isn’t comparing supermarkets, she’s talking nostalgia. Honestly.      Nostalgia or not, you still need to weigh your tea properly. Far too many people underdo it now. End up with a weak brew about as exciting as diluted wallpaper paste.      I had to teach a whole class of kids once how to make a decent cup of tea. They’d never boiled water properly. One poor boy put the whole teaspoon in. All I could think was,  Dear me, the future is a strong brew all right.       You mustn’t knock the lads, Doris. They’ve learned since. My grandsons—both in their teens—make tea with the kettle, cup, sugar,  then  wait. I told their mums go out and get them a teakettle with a thermometer.      Ha! You might as well teach ’em Morse code while your at it. But I have to say, I’ve never been one for all that tea with the milk first bellyache. I like it made properly, then swirl in the milk—ain’t that the way?      Technically, it depends where you’re from, dear.

Rather skip the new bar in Norwich. You know what they do. They take an old building they know like...      Yes, they just box it all in, you know, put a little flat-screen TV and call it a 'new' bar!      Yeah, and then the prices? I mean, one pint and you feel like you're paying for a gym membership.      Fair dos. Why not just go to the Green Mug down by the river? Still got atmosphere and cheaper cider.      Or the Red Lion. Had dinner there the other night with my brother. Proper rustic. They serve this weird stew, don’t know what it’s made of, but it’s good!      Ten to one it’s chicken and pig trotters, and I love it.      Honestly, I’d better not. Health and whatever. I’ve been doing CRB checks in my spare time, you know, for that local charity project.      That’s real important—vetting people, especially if they’re working with kids or vulnerable adults.      Did you know they’ve started doing facial recognition on CRB forms now?      No way. How does that even work with the same people still applying every year?      Oh don’t start again like you did about the CCTV in schools!      Honestly, I just don’t get how some people don’t read the details. Like, I had a customer—piece of work, he was—demanding a bottle of spirits at 10 p.m. and started waving around about his ‘rights.’      Sounds typical. You had to be a bit switched-on in customer services. Not that I’d know!      I just found out that my cousin’s son was circumcised last week. They did it without a sedative. I was horrified. He was two weeks old!      That’s rough. I had a mate in London whose family always talk about 'British traditions' but clearly don’t have the same ones as us in Norwich.      Maybe it's because in Norf, we're more rooted in rural traditions. Not much else to do in the countryside, really.      Aye,陕. But I’d have killed for a city life when I was growing up.      It’s funny you mention London. I went over last month for a conference and saw this massive protest near Parliament Square—environmental, I think. Totally peaceful.      You lucky devil. We had one outside the university and it looked like someone had just dropped an entire bee hive in a bag on the grass.

Finally back! How was your holiday?      A bit mixed, honestly. I had a few good days in the Lake District—long walks, fresh air, you know the drill. But then it rained half the time and I ended up in a pub for three days in a row. Got a bit of cabin fever, to be honest.      Oh no! Sounds like a wet British holiday. What about your work? Did you get a chance to unplug?      Most of the time, yeah. They were pretty good about letting me be offline. But my phone did like to remind me of a couple of admin jobs I left pending the day before I left. It was like that one friend who texts "How was your holiday?" on the first day you're gone.      Ugh, not the work email ghost haunting you in the Lake District. How’re things going at your job then? I mean, with everything going on these days?      It's tough to be honest. We’re under more pressure than ever, but I get it—Covid still is casting a shadow. I’m seeing a lot of young people struggling with grief and anxiety, and as much as I want to help, it’s draining in a way I wasn’t expecting at the start of my career. I almost envy you sometimes, having a bit more structure and routine in your work.      Project work can be stressful too! Though I’d say the coffee intake is at least in my favour. I had my own chaos this week—last-minute changes on what was supposed to be a straightforward grant application. It’s like replying to an open-ended question when there’s only a tick box available.      Haha, typical. I had a guy in on Monday—he thought he was answering the world’s biggest existential crisis. Turned out he just needed help coping with his girlfriend ending things. Sometimes it’s the simple human stuff that breaks you open.      Oh, I had a bit of that too. You remember Tom, the guy from our uni group project?      The one who wrote a sonnet about integration tests? Yeah?      He sent me this entire text explaining the metaphor of his go-kart on his life, and I’m just like, “Mate, just talk in normal English.”      Haha, what did you do?      I asked him how he’s been and where those feelings are coming from, gave him a bit of space.

I just heard from Emma’s brother. You know, the one who looks after her—the one who moved up to Nottingham to be with her. He said she had another hospital stay this week.      Oh no, honestly. That’s not good news at all. Her scans haven’t improved at all? I thought she’d been stable for the last few months.      No, they’ve only got worse. The cancer’s spread a bit more. And apparently, she was in a reasonable amount of pain this time. I don’t know how much more her body can take.      It’s heartbreaking. She’s always been so brave and positive, you know? It’s like fate’s just being cruel. I met her at the coffee shop last week, and she was still trying to smile, even when I asked her how she was. It broke my heart a bit.      Me too. She’s still doing her little crossword in the park, the one by the brook near the village. I mean, why wouldn’t she? She’s one of those people who try to cling on to normality in the face of it all.      Exactly. I’ve been thinking—maybe we should call over a little dinner round hers soon. Just the three of us, just to, you know, keep her spirits up. Let her feel she’s not alone.      Absolutely. I don’t see why not. She might not want anything big, but a bit of company can do a lot of good. I’ll talk to her about it this week.      Okay. Now, slipping into another topic… have you seen about the old Smith house for sale on the edge of the village? I had a look at the plans online.      Yes, it is a classic one. The previous owner, Mr. Lewington, moved out last year. Said he was tired of the village life. I remember hearing something about the developers wanting to turn it into two units instead of a single family home.      That’s right. They want to extend into the big garden and do a conversion of the attic. Still, I think it’s a bit of a shame. That gothic-style frontage is one of the few Victorian houses left in the village.      I agree with you there. I’ve always thought it’s a nice building. The garden is also stunning—full of rare herbs and fruit trees.

Rather skip the lot o’ this mess innit. Every time I go upstairs for a break they’re piling shit on my plate at work. I’m more than happy to take a lunch break where I can see the birds chitchatting and the sky, not stuck in this student accommodation hellhole. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive notes on the door   "Please don’t smoke in the lift"   like I don’t know. I know! Why’s it always me then? Because I   am   someone to do it!      Didn’t even want to start with this one specially... like, I’ve had enough of these so-called   "mental health checks"   first thing in the morning. My turkey still hasn’t finished cooking and I got bursts of this ridiculous well-being questionnaire via the app, while I’m halfway through knocking out the morning coffee. It’s like they’ve got no better idea than asking someone if they need therapy while everyone still thinks Game of Thrones isn’t over.      Oh, spare me the Game of Thrones nonsense, love. I mean I do like the odd screen binge, but not when I’m short-changed a week’s shift credit and only real reason I still turn up is cos I reckon the stickers on this job will look good on.cv. Yeah – Mate, I got a sneaking suspicion none of this means anything long-term. I reckon the only way to end up with something’s if I go and shake a few hills in the Balkans, just someone said there aren’t too many boring people out there.      You’d probably still run into some moaners smoking in a hillside cafe – same as here in the city, just with about five more currencies to trip you up. But talking of moany... have you seen this new lack of failsafe coffee machine arrangement we’ve got? Every time I press the espresso button, I get like lukewarm treacle oozing into my mug. Banging it open to the bin is a democratic event all on its own.      I could stick to my good old   Caffè Nero   every now and then but no mate, it’s closed now till next week. That's just  unreal . You're like a man with a pickaxe trying to get your own damn caffeine. If I go one more day without a decent java hit, I might just go box a bouncer at the train station.

So did I! The traffic was absolutely mental. I couldn't get out of herne bay for ages. I got to brighton seafront after about an hour and I was like oh my god where are we even going first? Do we do iced coffee or do we just get like the biggest maffin and then go to the market?!      I reckon iced coffee all round. Though I’ve been caravanning in Dorset so this is a real treat for me. It was quite interesting you know. We had to go to the shops yesterday for supplies when it was still light. You'd think the shop near the caravan park is only 500m away, but no, we had to like climb the turkey hill twice because we kept losing the kids. It was ridiculous! I had to shout their names for about 10 minutes before the eldest came running with a stick and a cat.      Bucksy I've been thinking about this for a while and I was wondering ever since we started shopping, whenever we see a puppy in the window I just feel that like instant urge to buy them a Christmas jumper or a toy or something. You don’t think that’s sad, do you?      No, I reckon it's extra cute. When we got to the market at the end of last year I bought my nephew, who just turned 10, a new set of books and they were all about space exploration and then he told me at Christmas that he’s going to become someone who works in Mars. I was like, oh, really?      That’s something! I have a nephew too, and being a care assistant I’ve had to come up with ways to keep about five little boys entertained for the entire day. English rhyming is the most useful stuff in the world! Like “Where is Billy?” “Billy is out!” “Where has he gone?” “He has gone to play!” “With who?” “With Johnny B. Goode!”      Oh my goodness, I haven't heard that poem in ages! My nan used to tell that to me when I was a young girl trying to find her dog Gracie while we were on holiday in Herne Bay.      Popping in the context of family goings on I remember losing someone very close to me – my brother passed away just before the pandemic and it's always difficult, but the main thing is your family and you carry them with you in the special moments and the roles they had in your life.

So did you watch the news last night about Ireland and that vote they had?      No, what vote was that?      It was about same-sex marriage! They had a vote where people can marry whoever they like, even if they're the same gender.       Oh , so they changed the   Equality Vote  ? I’ve heard of it a bit but I haven’t really kept up. Why’s it so important anyway?      Well, it’s about fairness, like, everyone should be allowed to get married even if they’re a guy to a guy or a girl to a girl. It doesn’t matter who you love.      Hmm, I guess you’re right. I remember when I was at school and I had a friend whose brother was sad because he couldn’t marry the man he was dating. It made me sad too, to be honest.      Exactly! And lots of countries already let people do that, even the UK. Ireland was the first one to vote for it though—can you believe it?      I never thought about it like that. Did it only happen recently?      Yeah, it was only a little while ago. Loads of people – even politicians – got involved. Some still think it shouldn’t be allowed but the majority said “no way,” they want equality.      That’s nice. It’s kind of funny someone said in the news— “if my mum knew I was doing this, I’d never live it down,”  whatever that means.      That  is  a good one. I about fell over laughing. My dad used to say things like that when I was trying to be cool doing skateboard fails. “If your school knew I let you do that, I’d never live it down!”      Ah right, embarrassing parents. They just have no sense of what’s funny any more. Speaking of school, how are you doing in your English class?      Okay, I guess. Except we were recently told a new kid from Ireland was coming, and our teacher said he’s going to bring us birthday cakes! I mean, it's not really my birthday but if you ask  me , I think kids at school are always making excuses to have cake.       I’m  with you on that. I’ve been to enough birthday parties and every single one has cake. You don’t need a reason to eat cake!      I agree. I’m not really into all that big celebration stuff.

Rather annoying this newfit of the lathe isn’t it? My old one was made by Bingham—solid as the day it was born. This one, eh, it feels a bit wobbly, like it was chucked together with a bit o' string and a wish.      Oh dear, William, I’m not one to get technical on you, but I do know a wobble when I see one. If you’re fiddling about with metal bits and whatnot, you should be as steady as a church door.      The newer models do have different tolerances, love. Less heavy-than-it-looks, more clever-tech-and-electrickery. I’ve had a look at a couple for my grandson. Fun to watch him try to make a nut from a bolt, even if he drills the whole the wrong way up.      ‘Course it is, but metal doesn’t mind a bit of a wobble if you ask me. Only thing I hides, Ken, is when the hamster goes clattering off into the microwave. I swear, if I had a penny every time he got in there, I’d be able to afford a real lathe by now.      Oh dear heavens, William, you said it yourself—he’s cheeky as a fairly mint, and smarter than the lot of us. One time he nearly chewed through my phone charging lead trying to get to the cables. Still, the microwave’s never worked properly since he found it. Strictly for emergency toast only now.      Some folks chuck toast at him when he wants to come out, I’ve heard. But he’s a good little rat, about as mischievous as the average toddler. Speaking of which, I had a curry in for lunch—he must’ve caught that smell. I’d better hide the sesame seeds before he starts thinking he found a new toy.      Tut, tut. I’m more worried about the lathe. ‘Course I had a bit of a mishap when I was making a wheel to fit a collet. Let the pressure go a bit heavy and the whole thing snapped over—my spanner flew across the room like a missile. Then Patricia chased it with the broom because she thought it was a burglar.      You’re a menace, William, I’ll give you that. But bless your heart, you do keep things interesting.      You lot live on excitement. I, on the other hand, had a latte and a scone this morning.

Rather annoying the new bank charges, isn't it? Seems like everything wants a fee these days — even if you're just trying to balance your account.      Tell me about it. I tried to pay in cash over the weekend and the branch had closed! You wouldn't believe how much my phone bill went up since I've been relying on the mobile banking app every day.      Aye, I remember when you just popped in and asked a teller for a few quid, and that was it! These days, you practically need a postgrad in IT to keep your finances in check.      I'd rather not talk about money. What did I miss in the news? I caught the tail-end of something about a cat being left high and dry during a flood.      Oh, yes! The poor mite was stuck on a rooftop in Glasgow and had to be rescued by a fire engine. The story’s been doing the rounds — and the best bit? The cat hides behind the rescuer’s leg the whole time!      Ah yes, that's a familiar sight in cat stories — always dramatic flair with no idea what to do. I tell you, when I was headmistress, we had a stray cat in the school who'd hide behind the bursar every morning. He was a regular drama queen.      I’m telling you, if you can’t solve a cryptic crossword in ten minutes, you’re doomed for the day. I found one this morning with a clue like  "mirror-writer's oddly left-handed production" . Just looking at it made my head spin.      That  would  be "live", right? Because mirror-writing is a type of ambidexterity or something?       Wait , lass — that was you! I remember it. You had the same clue. My, you've made the same mistake twice. Aye, cryptic crossword setters have no mercy on the sleep-deprived.      Speaking of sleep... Speaker_1, did you tell her yet?      Tell me what?      Well, I took the liberty of looking up house prices in our area and... we might owe more on the mortgage than the property is worth.      What? Again? I was hoping that was a typo the last time!      Don't be too daunted, dear. Houses and marriages take time to bloom — just like gardens. You don’t start off with a rose garden.      Thanks, that's comforting. You know my mum would be gloating right now.

Right, I just wanted to bring up something I’ve noticed. I know they love their time with Minecraft and Ninjago, but they’re not really reading as much as they used to.      But Mummy, I built the Temple of Glow!      That’s brilliant, Lily! But I was thinking—maybe we could mix things up a bit? Like read a book together before building?      I got a dragon in my world. It breathes fire!      That’s cool! Can it eat the Temple of Glow?      No! It’s my friend!      That’s great, George. My point is, I wonder if there are ways to make reading just as exciting as building or exploring in your games?      But books are boring, aren’t they?      Not always! There are books about dragons in Ninjago, you know. There’s even some adventure stories where the characters build and explore like you do in Minecraft.      Can I read one too? I like words about bricks.      That’s only because you read the cheat code books, George!      Oh, come on—isn't that sneaky and exciting?      Yeah!      Well, maybe if we could turn that sneaky excitement into a love for reading, that would help. What if we picked a book about a Minecraft adventure or a Ninjago quest and had a little reading hour before you start your games?      So, like, a mission about finding Legos or a map to a hidden fortress?      Exactly! Maybe even write your own story about it and draw the pictures. George could help you with the map, like he made the treacherous forest in his world last week.      Could I build the castle from the story?      If you read the whole story, then yes. Let’s make it a challenge with a reward. That way you earn the right to build.      So no cheating like before?      No cheating unless you read the whole thing properly. Deal?      Deal. But the box of books better be near your bed.      Only if you promise to read first and then build.      I like that plan.      Mm, okay. I’ll read... so I can beat George's castle.      Beautiful. Now, who’s going to get the first book? It’s an offer you can’t mine away!   Speaker_2 &    Not without a story!      Exactly. Let’s head to the bookshelf. Choose wisely, Ninjagos. Your next mission awaits.      Do we get a mission logbook?      Only if you read the whole first story by tonight.

Right, thanks for having me over, love. That coffee smells lovely – you got it from that new place in Lichfield, didn't you? It's better than the one by the train station, isn't it?      Yeah, I do! The one near the library, yeah? I'm obsessed now, honestly. It’s got this really nice almond milk they use – better than most I’ve tried. So, how’s your side of things? Still keeping busy with the grandkids?      Oh yes, I practically live at the chase when I'm not here. You'd think at my age, I'd slow down, but no, someone's always needing something. You know, like that Myla, my youngest one – she's got this week-long rally over in London and I had to go and pick her up in the rain? Half my coat is soaked by now and she's out there, tracking mud into the place.      Oh no! I'm sorry, Nan – sounds like the drama’s back home too. Good job you don’t live in Manchester, otherwise you’d know mud and rain all too well.       Laughing  It’s not funny, love, but I suppose it's better than silence in the house. So, how was your trip down here, Lily? Did you actually take the train on time for once?      Ugh, don't even get me started! It was delayed for twenty minutes at Stafford, someone said there was a problem with the overhead line or something. I thought I’d definitely miss out on getting here on time. But I worked the radio through most of it, had to get a good start at home about an hour earlier. Just glad I’m here now.      And I just flew in! Going to that place you told me about, the car boot sale in Burntwood, right? Turns out it’s not even open on weekends anymore. Busted my plans to buy something retro for the flat, but I ended up in some little café instead and had the best scones I’ve ever had in my life. Yellow cake with lunches and a little chocolate drizzle – insane!       Giggling  Sounds like you found your new thing goin on on your own mission again.      You’re just in the holiday mode now. But you’re welcome to come with me one day. It could be something to do for a rainy day – oneesan out the hours with something interesting?

So did you lot watch that new series on Netflix last night? The one with the spies and all that. I got so confused half the time.      Yeah, I binged it over the weekend. It’s wild, honestly, like half the people in it are in a secret society or something. I couldn't sleep after the third episode, kept overthinking it.      I’ve only watched the first one, but from what I saw, it reminded me of one of those old Cold War shows we watched in the history classroom. Didn’t Mr Peters use to play clips of that old military documentary every year around exam time?      Oh, yeah! You know what’s funny? I still get called "Mr. Spy" by one of the teachers, because I dressed as a commando for World Book Day. Honestly, I had no idea it would’ve stuck for so long.      Fair. I did a cowboy, and they still call me "The Sheriff" in the sixth form. Also, the way Mr Peters talks about the Watergate scandal, you’d think he’d been involved or something. Honestly, half the time he might as well be teaching  his  life story.      Honestly, I think he tries too hard to look cool. Remember when he said he was gonna take us to a café after the mock exams and then forgot? We waited for like 20 minutes and then he just said, “Oh, sorry, someone must’ve booked us in. Carry on revising, chaps.”      Classic! But yeah, speaking of café… here’s my question: does  anyone  know how to make a decent sandwich anymore? I went to the shop near the college this morning and bought a "sparkle chicken" one. It was like barely a layer of bread, a toothpick to hold it, and for £6.      Mate, that’s just them trying to upsell you. I asked for a bacon and egg, and the shop assistant started listing all the fancy cheeses and dressings. I said, “No, just… basic.” And he was like, “Basic is so over, you want a  tasty experience .”      That sounds exactly like my cousin. He got into catering college and now thinks he’s some kind of food connoisseur. Insists on calling a cheese sandwich a “artisanal dairy protein construct.”      Haha, honestly, I’m not even gonna question it. I just want something that doesn’t fall apart halfway through.

So did you watch  17 Again  last night? I was ages trying to get it through IMDb.      Yeah, I did! Blimey, it was decent, innit? I laughed so hard when he ended up in the same classroom as his old teacher.      Yeah, yeah, the one who was   so   onto him when he was 17.      That one! I mean, Miss Ward? In real life, who’d wanna do that?      Didn’t even want to watch it at first, but like, half of it was  us . I kept seeing our form tutor, Mrs Robson, in like everyone.      Oh my gosh, you’re  so  right! And the way they showed how sad the school food is? Blimey, that’s our school dinners almost breakfast, no doubt about it.      Oh don’t remind me. I had that lasagne last Thursday and it was like, why do we still have powdered meat?      I know, I know! Honestly, the only edible thing is the salad. And  please , we’ve got like three slices of cucumber.      Ugh, remember that one time with Miss Haines and the physics lab?      Oh don’t start me off. Silly cow thought the bunsen burners were on and tried to pour someone a full beaker of water over his head to “show how bad evaporation was.”      And Sam nearly lost an eye through that! I mean  literally , there was a nearly about five-second gap while he was trying not to touch the glass because it was so hot.      I was trying not to laugh but it didn’t work. I was just,  hup , hiding behind my textbook like I wasn’t even there.      And then Miss Haines had to go and write about it in our English reading lesson. She was like  proud of herself . And the worst thing is, when the lad from 10A asked if  it was true , and Miss Haines was like “Privacy issues,” like it was a horror story and not a physics experiment gone wrong.      Honestly, I think all of our teachers were once 17 and forgot. Our English teacher always says “You can’t write a perfect essay when you’re not used to real grammar, you know,” but last week he said “comprise” wrong in front of the whole class.

So do you lot reckon we’ve got a chance of anyone going to Transylvania this summer? ‘Cause if it’s just me, I’m probably not doing it. Back in Australia, we’d rather blink and try to fling the dust out than pay gold for the touch-up.      Touch-up? That’s another thing I don’t get. Look at the outback, mate. If you panic and whine about the wrong path, you’re stuck for a century. So yeah, we just say 'no worries go'.      Fair enough. Just don’t expect us to not pirate your tinnies anymore. That bloke at the bar your told me about sounds like the worst.      Oh, he’s alright, just always belly-laughing like a hyena when he says “baron of bikkies” when ordering the macarons. I mean, they’re just fancy biscuits.      I don’t know.

Rather skip the exam results till later. You've done very well. I know it's been a string of... What was it, mid-teens now? Rather annoying isn't it, this weather. I was looking forward to getting the garden in order before the first frost, and now it's just pouring down like November. I can't even tell if the gooseberries are ready yet.      Yeah, it's been wild all week. I tried playing Chinese chess with my dad on the tablet the other day and he kept getting distracted by the rain on the window. A lot of shouting and piece-moving!      I watched a programme about animal communication the other night. They said some animals can tell the season by the frequency of rainfall. Though I suppose we're more likely to just grumble about it, eh?      You sound like one of those documentaries I’ve seen on the telly. Remember when you told me you were working on a unit about animal communication in school?      Yeah, and it got linked to British birds mostly. I've been thinking about how animals in South Korea might communicate differently. I remember one doc said the way they whistle helps them find shelter quickly in heavy rain—something I could do, maybe, instead of standing around grumpily in the garden.      It’s funny how much we’ve got on our plates at once. I was up all night stressing about booking a new dental appointment and sorting out my morning routine. It's not like university was this bad—then again, did you ever have to schedule a shower between tuition fees deadlines?      You've got to be kidding me. I had my own chaos with work meetings and doing the breakfast rush for the residents at the shelter. I swear one of them once challenged me to Chinese chess mid-meal because he reckons it's good for the mind!      I had a student ask what links Winston Churchill to New Zealand the other week. I nearly choked. At first, I thought he was joking. Turns out there’s a memorial in one of the parks dedicated to Churchill, complete with a kiwi sculpture nearby. He thought it was funny, I think.      You’d better not end up being asked about Scottish independence next. I had a son-in-law leave the house last year because he said it was a "tiring tiff." Still, I suppose go at it if you want, as long as it doesn’t end in deportation like in the news last week.

Rather skip the new season of  The Crown , I prefer to talk politics anyway. Felt like a first-world problem to be honest with you. I’m more interested in how pension reforms are treating people back home. I keep wondering how we’re going to make it last until 80 now.      Yeah,  The Crown  is okay, but honestly, it feels so far removed from most people’s lives these days. Like, yeah, this show is top-notch, but how many people in my classes actually watch it? Most are more into  Lupin  or  Bridgerton . I like to mix it up, honestly—movie nights, binge sessions. It’s only another form of escapism anyway.      I get it. I’ve tried to watch bits of it, but I can’t pick and choose in the middle of a series anymore. Used to be able to do it when I was younger, but now I’d rather just drive in silence and not miss anything. I remember that, you didn’t have a laptop in the car when we were in Crete.      Yeah, we had maps written in pen, landlines as mobiles, and only real news came from the TV. These days, I can work from a roadside café in Tarnow and mark essays on my iPad. Sometimes, I think it’s easier being a teacher now despite all the admin. Back when you did your first TEFL course, we were using cassette recorders and sticky-backed plastic. Now, it’s all apps and AI read-backs. Pretty wild.      I’d never have thought in my 20s I’d end up  semi-retired  because most people about my age are still paying off student loans from 20 years ago. I didn’t go into debt, but it wasn’t because I was clever—just unambitious in that way. But I realized early that burnout was no good. I did my BTEC, worked a year or two, got my TEFL qualification, tried Germany, Italy, and Bulgaria. We both know how that ended up for me.      Yeah, I think it takes a different mindset now. I mean, you don’t even get interest-free student loans the way we did. Most of my students who are 18 or so now think about college like it’s a cost-to-benefit analysis, not an investment.      So how have things gone for you? You seem quite settled now.

So, I heard you got an offer for Human Sciences at Oxford. That's massive, mate. Well done! What made you go for that over, like, Physics or Maths? I've been thinking about a joint honours… physics or chemistry or… I dunno.      Cheers! Yeah, it was a bit of a toss-up for me too. I love the idea of mixing Biology with a bit of social stuff too. I mean, this human sciences thing is like a science degree with some psychology or sociology. Know what I mean? It felt like the best of both worlds.      Yeah, I guess. I’m still dead set on doing maths at uni, only if I can push my grades. I know it’s tough, but my brother’s doing it and he says it’s right up my street, all logic and problem-solving. But I'm thinking of combining it with something else if I get the chance—maybe computer science?      Oh yeah, comp sci and maths are a good combo. If you're good at the pure stuff, you’ll pick that up quick. Might get you into some of those cool AI development jobs or even a startup. Could be a way off, but still.      Exactly! But before all that, got to survive A levels – and rugby season, obviously. How’s your team doing this term?      It’s alright, we’ve got a new coach who’s cracked on with training. Lost a few games at the start, but we’re starting to gel. You? Still second row?      Yeah, and I’ve been trying to add a bit of weight – lifting more, eating more protein stuff. I’ve been cooking up steak and eggs every morning to bulk up. My mum hates it. "More protein and less drama!" she says.      Ha! Maybe she just prefers her standard toast and marmalade. But if it helps, stick with it. You'll need it if you're aiming to play university ball.      Definitely. I'd crack my head off over that. Even though I know it’s going to cost a fortune to do uni. Not if I play well, though—heard a few places are giving scholarships for sports now.      Yeah, that's a thing now. But while we're not there yet, I say we go with this round on me. Pass the lager over—let’s get lost in the day dreaming for a bit.

Rather skip to the front of the queue, isn’t it? A tax cut for the top ten percent and yet we’re supposed to grin and bear it because the Chancellor said it’ll somehow trickle down. I’ve been doing ledgers for nearly forty years, and I’ve never seen one yet that balances lie.      Dad, I’m just trying to understand where the money actually goes. Everyone says the government’s in the red, but how does that happen if we’re paying so much tax?      Well, you start by paying payroll tax when you start your first job. Then you pay income tax, VAT when you buy your bloody cuppa. Then there’s the national insurance, which is supposed to go on your pension, but I’ve met enough retired folks who’d rather laugh than talk about the state theirs is in.      But why can’t they just spend more wisely? Like better schools, or more funding for the NHS?      Oh aye, you ever looked at a budget, lass? Easy to shout for more money, but that’s not how it works, is it? The government borrows, spends short-term, leaves it to the next lot to clear up. Tell me, if I spend more than I earn, will I be rich next year?      No, I suppose not. It just feels like we’re the ones picking up the pieces.      Aye, and that’s the rub. The policies are written out of London in one-year election cycles. All they care about is the next headline. Look at what’s happening with housing—buy-to-let profits being poured into offshore accounts while house prices in Birmingham soar because of supply and demand. But what about the rest of us trying to afford a flat?      So what do you think is the fix? Do we need a new tax system entirely?      Maybe. Maybe it’s high time they did something radical and taxed the sort of blokes who land their jets at Birmingham Airport and call it ‘economic activity.’ Until then, the rest of us are stuck with bloated budgets and grand plans with no plan at all behind them.      That sounds exhausting. But I guess this is why you started your own books goin’ on your own about savings and investments.      Precisely. If you don’t know where your money goes, what your tax is funding, or why the bills go up every year, someone else is making those decisions for you.

I can't believe the amount of meetings I've had this week. I swear, if I spend one more hour in a Zoom conference, I'm going to start whispering my own notes by accident. Aye, we do our fair share of those at school too. ECDeputies, SLT, and now with the new Ofsted protocol, it's like someone just turned all the meetings on a loop. A lot of it’s the same every time, to be honest. Honestly, do they not think we’ve got better things to do than just repeat the same things over and over like parrots in a school playground? I mean, it's the same supply list, the same training video everyone has seen a hundred times. I swear to God, one day I might ask the camera back what the point is. Oh, I know exactly what you mean. We had this breakfast club volunteer from last year who happened to still be in the building at GCSE moderation and looked completely lost, thinking the meeting was a social event. Good for a laugh, though. Poor woman looked like a lost pup in a staff room full of wolves with clipboards. Haha, that sounds bloody hysterical. I can just see it—her sipping her cup of tea, trying to figure out whether she was still on shift or not. Oh don’t laugh too long. Silly as that was, we’ve had our fair share of mishaps too. Last week one of the girls from the choir was in the staff meetings oddly because she helped out with the tech. She thought the intercom was being mute and tried to speak through it in a whisper because she thought about forty people were listening to the entire story of her last holiday. I had to stop myself from laughing and not corrode that child's trust in the building. Jeez, that must’ve been awkward. But you passed it off with that old-school headteacher mentality of nodding and giving the silent treatment until it passes, I bet. You always did stick to the good side of that middle professional ladder. Ha! I’ve tried to do things the "traditional way," you know, even though I’m nearly 60 now and go out of my way to be more patient with everyone. But I swear, some of the things that come out of the box now—like these new touchscreens we've installed—it's like I’ve to speak to them like they're my grandchildren just to get them to do anything coherent.

Rather skip the newfit and go through the request, right? I've had her in for a week and it's still not sorted out.      Yeah, I've been over that with Katherin. Well, from what I can remember, it was mostly red, fairly cheap, and none of the bottles have labels. Probably a somethin’ that got opened and never finished. I’ve told my younger cousins if the glasshouse's set, they might come too.      go ahead then, but let me warn you, if you're planning on drinking that old wine, I can guarantee we’ll need a rubbish clearance plan the next day. I can't believe the conference’s in Brighton this year — anyone fancy a day trip after it’s over? We could grab a bite, maybe even do the i360? That sounds lovely, I’d love that.
