There was a wall chart? I thought I left that behind… You did. But they painted their own. Got it framed after the tragedy of the pie incident. Still on the classroom wall. Oh, I am so proud. You know, honestly, the best part of being a TEFL teacher is getting to see the weird and wonderful ways people interpret your ideas. Defo. But serious now — are you applying for the early bird go-to event on pond life in educational settings or am I just preoccupied because my head of department asked me to submit a themed poetry unit involving dahlias? Pond life? I might’ve seen that listed under “Bureaucracy vs Creativity.”

Rather skip the gym and just go for a long walk in Rzeszow instead, don’t you think? It’s so much friendlier. I’m more of a wander kind of person anyway.      Yeah, I hear you. I’ve been going to the gym a few times a week, but honestly, I don’t think I can   handle   the dusty machines in that gym on a rainy day. Prefer to save my muscles for this and the odd yoga video instead. It   feels   more organic.      Oh, I love yoga but I’ve never really stuck with it. I tried it once with a friend, and it felt like I was only doing it to make her happy.      Ha! Yeah, I used to do it to look like I had a life, and I think it turned into something real. I was about 19 then. I still remember the instructor’s name—Nitasha or something like that. People’s names stick in my head, you know?      That’s funny, I was just thinking about you and reading. I’ve noticed you always have a book with you. Did you read Nitasha’s book too?      No, not quite. I read “Meditations” – that one by Marcus Aurelius, and I’ve just started on something by Yuval Noah Harari. You?      I’m reading a book that isn't even out in Poland. It’s one of those   e-books   that I bought just for the purpose of pretending I’m still doing something productive.      What’s it called?      “The Narrow Road to the Deep North” – the   biography  , not the travel one. I think it’s about her life before   marrying   David Malouf.      Oh, I like that one.      I have no idea where it is going. I think it might have disappointed me a little. You ever had a reading choice you didn’t like that much but kept at it because you were invested?      All the time. My volunteering experience taught me something around this idea of commitment.      You mean your work at the volunteer centres?      Yeah, that. It taught me a lot about showing up, even when it’s tough.      Oh, I think I would start off earnestly and then fall off to Facebook on the way home. Sounds like I need to be more like you.      You know, I often wonder about where I started, and it always feels so far away now.

So do you know much about telomeres, Ann? They’re the ends of our chromosomes that shorten as we age, and some researchers think slowing that process could extend lifespan.      I’ve heard the term before, but I’m not sure how it works. You mean the longer they stay intact, the longer we live?      Exactly. There’s this enzyme called telomerase—it kind of rebuilds telomeres. Some studies show if you can boost it, you might age slower or even reverse some age-related damage. Isn’t that fascinating?      Sounds like science fiction. But I guess it does make sense. I remember learning about the pyramids when Rob was younger and how they lasted so long. You’d think humans could last that long too, if their bodies figured it out.      The pyramids? Now that you mention it, there’s something about their construction, too—maybe the materials used were more stable for the environment at the time. Geologically speaking, the Earth was more stable back then, less tectonic activity near where they were built.      Oh, I never thought of that. What about the Vikings, though? They were such amazing explorers. I read somewhere they reached North America centuries before Columbus. You ever think about how long they must have lived to make such journeys?      Probably not much longer than we do now. Life expectancy’s not that different in some ancient societies. What’s interesting is how modern medicine and improvements in living conditions have pushed it way up. It’s amazing we’re living into our eighties and nineties now in places like Ireland and the UK.      But there’s a cost, isn’t there? Pollution, global warming, all the comets we worry about… I suppose you could say life is longer, but not necessarily better. The energy we consume, the resources we waste—it’s like we’re living faster than the planet can keep up.      Oh, I agree. Renewable energy is key, but it’s a balance. I’m all for offshore wind and solar, but it’s not just about technology. It’s about how we use it. Now, speaking of using things wisely—when are we actually going to plan the weekend trip away? Kayaking on Lough Derg sounds like a real adventure.      I’m up for it—just need the baby to nap a bit longer. But I have to admit, I’m a bit scared about falling in.

Mummy, can I take the baby chair to the café with me later? I promised my friends we’d go after the big test at school.      That’s sweet of you, darling, but we only just got it. What if it gets spilled on or something?      Aye, I don’t think it’d look right if yer brought a baby chair into a café with yer A-level pals. Not the best look, lass.      But it’s not just any baby chair, it’s this new one with the fruit tree print. You know, like, apricots and strawberries—proper trendy! Besides, the baby’s only got her veggies in there. My friends are gonna be jealous!      Well, I’m not saying yes or no, let’s just make sure the little one doesn’t mind, alright? And you better not get it stained—your uncle just gave us that voucher for the baby store.      Oh, the voucher’s a good shout. Good money, that. I was over at the hardware shop last week and saw some proper fancy sunglasses on sale. Got one for you, luv, and one for me.      For heaven’s sake, Martin. Sunglasses at the till of a hardware store? How cheery does one expect to be while choosing grits and pipes?      If the sun’s out, I’m in, luv. Proper sight for sore eyes. Although I might not read the small print if them glasses are on.      Daddy, can I borrow your sunglasses next time I go to the beach? Ours at school are blocked from seeing any social media until September.      Not a chance. Use your own. Oh, and you might need some extra cash if we’re going to the café, Lucy. I was processing some guest mail last night and saw the referendum results have been on the TV again. If things change, the café’s prices might too. You might need your own budget from now on.      He’s right. Town’s not what it used to be, love. I saw Tom down by the chicken coop last week—said he’s thinking of getting a few more hens. Said there’s demand at the market. Thought about it myself, actually. Might go with fruit trees next, what with all them vouchers.      You and your plants, Martin. Last week it was roses, this week it’s fruit trees. What’ll it be next, palm trees and a pool?

Rather skip the newfit and go to the gym tomorrow, do you?      Yeah... got to pick some stuff up after work today, and I fancy a gym session after.      Not quite as fun as baking mince pies on a weekday morning, was it? I saw the smoke alarm go off while I was on the staircase.      Oh my god! A Christmas tradition starting already?      Oh, don’t start, Ant. That was just me being messy, not set on fire. Although, the dog looked at me as if I’d burned the house down.      What breed are they again?      Just a bit of Cocker Spaniel and a bit of nobody knows what – I called him Bosch, he used to be a rescue. But he’s coming for Christmas, and you better believe breakfast is now a shared agreement.      Oh, he’s coming over too! That’s going to be mad. I mean, he’s lovely, but I’ve got three friends coming round for drinks on Christmas Eve and I’m short on space.      You can’t fancy someone’s lap like that for the whole evening, can’t all the way. How’s the Mate doing with that planning?      Oh, he’s a bit of a planner, as you know. He was meant to go back to Germany for the first week of December, someone at work gave him a birthday gift: a trip to Berlin to look at some memorial stuff with friends.      Oh, Berlin’s got a lot of  memorials , let me put it like that. Not a bad trip, but it can be very heavy. Not for a holiday, really.      I know, but he said it was to do with rebeling for the first time in a while after work stress. Still, I’m trying to get it sorted – probably go with my sister to some farm near you for the weekend.      Oh that’ll be nice. Her space always smells of rosemary and static from the wool sweaters. And no, you don’t get around with candles like that, it’s a go-to room on fire thing if you ask me.      I’ll remember that when I go in with matches this year. Anyway, about the tree. She gets distracted so easily these days—don't know what she was thinking.      At least we’ve got the TV working, sort of. I caught a re-rer of the Big Brother one goin' on. Talk about nonsense. If I was at that age, I’d go mad living with a group of strangers, bickerin’ and all.      Oh, I never see the point of that programme. I never had the stomach for it.

Rather skip the new Disney one eh?      Aye, it's all real flashy and all, but I've had enough of the same old reboots. I've been over that type of thing since uni. We used to have film nights and queue for the big premieres — now it's all just carbon copies of the same formula.      Aye, I heard most a the cast is from the original one tho. Proper confused me, like, watching someone else as a character you already know! My nan was like "Who's that? Is that the daughter or the stepdaughter?!" It's enough to make  me  throw me hands up and grab a drink!      My turkey curry's done, you want some left over on this bottle? I made it for the week. Roast and all in the oven? Or we could actually watch the film and forget it?      Curry sounds good. Film can wait. Though my brother’s been bleating on about how he wishes he’d seen it in the cinema. Worked late again though — he’s got a book fair in Leeds next month I think.      Oh, I love that time of year — parties, fancy dinners, the works. I remember when I got offered that job at the marketing firm in London. I was still living with my mam and dad back then, and she was like, “You can have tea on the table and still be at your 8pm drinks in Knightsbridge!” Spent my first paycheck on a proper suit and shoes just for that night. Gone out in them the following week and skidded on a hill in Margate —  cringe .      Aye, I know what you mean! My first big event job was for a charity ceilidh in York. I thought I’d be dancing the night up, but I was just running up and down the stairs handing out lanyards and chasing after sods who’d lost the timings. Still, got my feet under the table for once.      We should really do a night out ourselves. With a real dinner and a proper plan. No Netflix and digestive biscuits like last time. My sister’s coming up for a visit in a fortnight; we can go out to one of them Thai restaurants near the uni.      That’s a good idea. I’ll box this up properly when I leave. Cos you know I’m not made of china — and if I’m out, I’m out proper!

Rather do I! The lot o’ ’em up in Scotland talkin’ ’bout hopin’ off... What next, eh? The Yorke shall declare independence!  laughs       But… why would Scotland want independence? Is it because they don't like England?       sipping tea  Not 'cos o’ me, I tell ya that! I reckon it's all politics and policy, luv. Some folks think they’d be better off runnin’ it themselves. More control o’ the cash, the oil in the North Sea an’ all. Get the lot o’ it, rather than handin’ it over to Whitehall.      My uncle says it’d be a big disaster. No money, no food, loads o’ problems.      Aye, he’s not entirely wrong about that. ‘Course it doesn’t come for free, this independence. They’d have to sort out their own taxes, their own laws, even their own army. And don’t tell me, we’d still be stuck with the same problems down here, too—sorted by someone else.      Do you think they’ll vote to go independent?      Well, from what I’ve heard, the referendum’s been planned fairly long, and I reckon they'll vote. Some say aye, others say nay. Seems like a big generational divide, don’t it? Younger folks might want someone else in charge, while the older crowd tend to like the way things are.      But what if the vote goes the other way? If they say  no ?      Then Scotland stays a part of the UK, just as it is now. And if they say  yes —well, then it's time for kings and queens, laws and borders, to ‘ave a proper rethink. Either way, it’s a big deal. A union o’ centuries, aye, and it might very well come to an end.      So you  don’t  think they should go independent?      Well luv, I’ve no voice in Scotland, and I’ve no say in the vote. But goin’ on what I know, I’d rather keep things as they are. I’ve no wish to see this family—a big one, with plenty o’ rows and arguments—break apart over it all. We’ve enough to worry about down here, never mind all that bonfire o’ talk in the North.      Is it true they'd keep the queen if they did leave?      That's one o’ the interesting bits, luv. They could keep the queen, or they could do it ‘alfways, and have their own monarch—though I doubt they'd find a better one than ‘Er Majesty.

Blimey, listen to this bloke's utter, do yer? He's got such a posh accent, it's like he's sippin' tea off a gold plate or somethin'.      Aw, don’t be takin’ the mick! He’s probably just een Liverpool and got used to soundin’ important 'cos he’s on telly all the time. I reckon he sounds like a toffee-nosed prat sometimes, honestly.      Honestly, someone should do a whole show just about people mockin’ people for their accents. Like, not just Jeremy Kyle but all of them! I mean, I love listenin’ to people talk, especially when yer get that lil’ bit of elision goin’ on. It makes things more interesting.      Yeah, and I think it’s funny how people take themselves too seriously when they’re talkin’ on programmes like this. I mean, like, I could walk in and say, “Well then, fanks for askin’,” and they’d probably chuck me out.      Honestly, some of them accents up here in Yorkshire make your head spin. I were at uni in Wakefield last semester and this one lad would say, “I’m gennin’ t’go – cheek it owt” and I was, like, “Blimey, I didn’t quite catch that.” But it’s all part what makes us who we are.      Aye, but it’s also suspicious when people try to change they accent to fit in. Like, you know the type—tryin' to sound posh so they can get more money in a job or something.      I reckon Jeremy Kyle's accent is deliberate, too. Not just a Liverpool bloke gone posh. I bet he practiced that luvverly lilt to sound reputable.      Definitely. And if you notice, when people get all worked up on the show, any attempts at sounding posh go straight out the window. Like, “I’m not gonna put up with this!” or “That’s ruddy cheek if I’ve ever heard one!” It’s the best.      I love it when people on the show accidentally go back to their normal way o’ talkin’. Just shows they’re human, y’know? You don’t go from bloke on the street to Jeremy Kyle’s guest all in one go.      Oh, and those challenges he sets people—like, “Shall we see if ‘this’ is true or not?”—is that supposed to keep the audience entertained or make the guest nervous? Honestly, it's both, but always annoying.

Rather skip the half-time chat eh? You know what, I think they've got more squabbles on the pitches than in the commentary box. Bloody poor show this lot!      Aw come on Lucy, don’t start grinning at half-time! You know they’re saving it for when it really matters. This is just the warm-up, mate.      Easy for you to say, love, but I knitted this top for ya last week and I watched   every   match to keep motivated! Not to see us losing like this.      You knitted me a top? Still haven’t tracked that down, have I? I found the mug with "Midlands Muppet" on it, but you still owe me that jumper.      You're a dunce and I’ll be the one deciding if you get it warmer sooner or later! Wait, if we actually start playing this half, maybe I’ll be generous and hand it over tonight.      Deal. Now, what’s the news on that Olympics? I swear, if someone wins gold in swimming, they might as well legislate it as their job title for the rest of their lives.      You'd think it was a birthright. Though at least Baptiste won't be sneaking in fake swimmers this time. No babies, no Bronze baby names to contend with this year. Still, I reckon we need a list for the next one in Paris.      Just don’t name a kid "Team" or "Golda" like the last lot did. What’s next? “Olympia” or “Sprintley”? Sounds like about five mispronunciations waiting to happen.      Honestly, if I ever have kids, it’ll be “Granny Janie” or nothing. You’re the one, Luke, who says "football" like you passed grammar school with honours.      You know, I once had a professor from Sunderland who couldn’t say “cough” without looking like he was being choked out by it. And here we are, the English language war continues!      That’s a bit harsh. I’ll have you know I still say “milk” like it’s a real liquid, not some abstract concept, unlike that lot.      Aye, well, you speak nice, I fluently quote obscure academic papers while watching poxy football matches, so we all have our bits to be proud of, eh?      You're welcome. S’all my coaching. Pass me the butter, would you? I need both hands free to knit my next masterpiece, and by that, I mean the sweater I swore I’d finish you before midnight.

Right, so the kids watched  The Bee Movie  again last night, and now they think they know  everything  about bees, including how to rule a kingdom of them! Eamon was telling Ama that bees have queens and that we should totally have bee royalty as well. Which is why he was asking again if bee kings wear crowns like the Queen does.      I said that Ama is the bee  queen , and I’m the bee  king . We have a throne made of cereal boxes and a sceptre from a spaghetti stick. It’s the most serious political revolution I’ve ever been a part of.      What’s a revolution?      My word, you are living in a palace of cereal and imagination, Eamon. But I’m not lying, he was sad to find out he can’t just run for president of his school yet. I tried to explain that you have to be at least 18 and not currently be five.      I told him that he  could  start early—voting for puddings and being Prime Spaghetti of the After-School Sandwich Club.      It’s wild how quickly kids go from thinking they live in a republic where  they  are in charge to realising that they have to wait their turn and actually learn to spell before they are eligible to vote. It’s enough to make you want to burn down the electoral college.      Can you just get into castles for free though? Like my friend’s Daddy took them to Buckingham Palace once and paid like 50p. I want to be rich so I can live in a palace and never have to go about paying for secrets or crowns or bannisters or whatever they have up there.      Eamon, it is a  royal  palace, not  royal  fruits. Unless you happen to know a pineapple that’s been knighted. I think you mentioned that before.      I want to be a princess who gives out free vitamins and goes to the Olympics to see the diving with lunches and a new swimming pool! They have such big boards there, you must get silent around them.      That’s because it’s pond life if you don’t get it right, Eamon. Missy got that from a TV show with big bouncy men and one man who’s older than the Queen.      I think that was  Strictly Come Dancing . It’s a programme about dancing in shiny outfits over very loud lights.

Rather skip the queue, isn't it? That tip in Thirsk was a world of difference compared to this one, I’ll tell you. Remember when we used to clear out the attic every spring, Muriel?      Oh, heavens, yes. Used to be a proper drama when eeny weeny William wanted to keep every one of those little toy horses. Almost threw them all on a bonfire once before I remembered they were in a box marked “sentimental,” bless.      We’ve got to clear my room when I’m older, but Dad says he won’t fetch the bin bags again if I leave my football boots littered about the hallway, only another time.      Just wait till you’re older and left to your own devices! I had half my bedroom floor taken up by magazines I bought off the kerbside thinking I’d be a fashion icon. Ended up with a load of ants!      Aye, and I remember the time we sold a few bits at an auction in Masham. That old oak sideboard nearly fetched three hundred, and we sold it to some woman dabbling in interior design.      It’s funny how today’s throwaway items are tomorrow’s treasures. I sold a few old books last week at a second-hand book sale near Keswick and actually made quite a few quid. Though I’m telling you, my laptop still won’t work after I dropped it trying to catch the cat—this is what someone said when I tried to get a refund from customer service: “What did you do? Send it to the moon??”      Still, at least it wasn’t in the tip like most people about now. Steve—Speaker_4—how many e-readers do you have? I’ve seen your lass Sarah with that newest one and I have to say, for my £5 binoculars over here, it’s mighty shiny.      I have no idea. I just told him he needed to buy a new one when his screen sparked at me!      Sparks from a screen, good grief. In my day, a fire was the only thing you had to worry about when you set a house alight by mistake! Still, I suppose go on then, Steve, if you’re going to go rambling about laptops and warranty, let’s hear it.      Aye, well, you see, the retailer’s warranty expires in a few weeks, and the official one’s gone with the company.

Rather skip the Museum o’ Liverpool today innit? Seems like everything’s closed for renovations again.      No way! We’ve saved up for months just to cover the parking ticket, and now we can’t even get in? That’s f       riotous.      I know right! I mean, I told you we should’ve driven to the Ullet Road Car Park. That’s only £6 for the day. Why’d we park on.Grid?      Oh, bollocks! I thought the museum would be open when I booked the trip. You'd think the website would update it! Anyway, what’s the plan now?      Well, if the Museum’s closed, we could still chill here and watch that Tenr I queued for the whole week for, or we could go get the presents for the wedding in Birkenhead.      Bucks of shops closed early on Fridays though — in’t it? I remember the Queenie’s shopping centre shutting at 2 so I’d say we need to be there by one or we won’t get anything.      Fank ye for the reminder. I only applied for that Masters interview in Manchester on Friday. I’m trotting in first thing. You’re coming too – Mate’s been bugging me to take her along for moral support.      Mate? Is this the one who was meant to be our bridesmaid? And yes, I’m going.      Yeah, Emma. She’s just moved up here. Anyway, you’ll need to weigh in on the interview prep. They’re asking all sorts — future plans, how I’d integrate about teaching in Scotland. I don’t fackin’ know why I have to be a language teacher there!      Because you handle the unteachable lot in the Mersey. That lot need someone calm and steady — like you.      You say that now. What if I end up teaching witches and stuff? You know I told you about my kid in class that sprite of a Websites mentioned space aliens with lunches of mushrooms and chips?      That's not a child, that’s a parallel universe.      I know! I told our head teacher – give me kids who line up, read, and don’t randomly box punches in the corridor.      Well, I’ll manage the kina while you're off pretending to be a student again. True to say, we should start thinking over where we’s gonna be at Christmas. I’m not fancying up the flat for the fifth time.

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode with the Queen and Margaret was wild, innit? I got so confused half the time—like, how are they all related again?      Honestly, I can’t even keep up. I binged the whole series two years ago and I still couldn’t tell you who the hell was who. I reckon it’s not easy being royal, but you’ve got to act like you know what you’re doing, right?      Yeah, and imagine having to watch your whole family cause drama in a TV show. Proper messed up. I like the jokes on TikTok about it though. That one where the Queen’s like, “Right, let’s all go on holiday to Balmoral and forget this week ever happened” was the vibe I needed, honestly.      Oh I seen that one, classic. But forget The Crown, have you been on TikTok lately? They’ve taken over YouTube and Instagram, you ever looked at what’s trending? Some of the dance challenges are wild.      I tell you what, some of those dances would be way easier with alcohol. I’ve tried one and ended up on my arse in my hallway watching it back, like,  “mate, what is happening?”       Haha, that’s the vibe. Anyway, enough of dance madness—what’s your weekend plan? Still going to that Italian place with your mates? The one in Humber Bridge?      Yeah, the pizza there’s oddly sourdough-y for something called “authentic.” I swear the dough tastes like it’s been baked by someone’s grandma who stole the recipe off a 1970s man in the street. Anyway, I’m cooking lasagne for my sister on Sunday. She barely left the house this week, so I’m doing the sisterly thing.      Aww, you’re the best. I wish I had a sister—I miss my cousins so much. I’m just waiting till I get a flat to myself and then I’ll probably adopt a dog to fill the hole of a family.      Yeah, but you remember when you got that cat mask and told me you got goth vibes on your life? You looked like a walking Halloween decoration.      I was  channeling . Anyway, I might get some body art myself at some point. I’ve been obsessed with this artist on Instagram—total unicorn tears and all that. But I need to start saving up, obviously.

So did you get the Pikachu card I wanted to trade for? I’ve been dying to upgrade my deck.      Oh love, I completely forgot about it. I was going to message you on Skype later. Do we still know the kid in Ballydehob?      Pikachu!  Points at the plate  Pikachu   IN THERE!        Aww, look at you! That’s from your dinner, Oisin. Come on, open up like a good lad and eat it properly.      He still thinks food looks like Pokémon. It’s like his whole world is yellow.      That’s not far off, is it? Just look at you! You talk like you’ve been marinated in Pokémon cards yourself.      Hey, I’m just trying to stay up to date. I’ve been learning guitar chords while I’m online anyway. Maybe I can make a Pokémon rapping song.      You’d be the next big thing, I reckon. Just don’t forget to wear your skinny jeans when you start the world tour.      Ehh, they’re called “skinny,” not “discomfort.” But I will, if I get signed.       Squirms in chair       What is it love? Do you need changing again?       Shakes head  No, just sleepy.      Yeah, he’s had a long day. You guys went to the shops earlier, right? I thought you might’ve got some ice cream for him.      I did! I got chocolate and the green one — the one with mint and stuff. Maybe that’ll cheer you up, Oisin.       Mumbles something incoherent  Po…po…      Pokey? Is that the Ramen shop? Oh, love, we haven’t gone for Ramen in forever. We should arrange it as soon as we can.      Yeah, and maybe you can pick up some extra Takis for me. I’m low again and Rioglyph’s waiting for go-kart map updates.      Go-kart? Is that the new game you're always on? You’re getting better at your dodges, by the way. I saw you on the screen last night while making tea.      Oh right? I didn’t hear you. I was just trying to learn the new moves. I think I figured out how to get past the ring of Dynamax Pokémon, but my Pikachu keeps flinching.      Maybe it’s just shy, like before a fight. You should’ve dressed it in sparkly clothes. That always does the trick.      I’ll keep that in mind. Maybe I’ll dress it in something from your old fashions, too.

Rather skip this, but it's been in that cupboard for ages. I was just wondering if you remember that... oh dear, what was it called? It had all those wooden bits, you know, with gears and wheels...      Oh,  Bako ! Of course, how could I forget? That was  our  building set. I used to sit on the floor in the morning with a clean cloth on my trousers and just piece things together all day.      It wasn’t just a toy! It was practically like an engineering course for children. Did you know I made a little windmill once? My dad nearly fainted when I explained how the gears worked, only to find out I made up the science a bit.      Oh, you always were the imaginative one! And I was the one who just made fences and little houses. It drove you mad, didn’t it?      It did! I kept saying I wanted to build a  train  or a  launch pad . You always built the boring bits. But I still have a photo of it somewhere, all lined up on the mantelpiece in full glory.      And the other one... the gardening gear. The little mini tools, trowel, rake, wheelbarrow — remember?      How could I forget? We used to “plant gardens” in the sandpit out the back. You even made up names for everything! The flowers, the soil, the ‘big rock which is also suspiciously a stone’.      [Laughs] Oh yes, the “Majestic Stone of Sensibility” — still a good name, in my opinion. We spent about half the summer pretending to be landscape architects.      [Laughs] I suppose we did! Going through that lot now makes me feel like it’s  meant to be spring , but outside it’s still raining constantly. All that mucking about with imaginary plants, and the real gardening season is being ruined by the grey.      I know! We had such good summers then. You always say it was always raining with us growing up, but clearly we must have had  some  nice weather, since we had so many outdoor toys.      Yeah, but it was more our  imaginations  that made it sunny in the head, I think. Anyway, I’m not sure what your feelings are about these — should I chuck it all? Or should we keep some bits for the grandkids?      Oh yes, for the grandkids, absolutely. They wouldn’t believe that existed now! You can’t buy wooden toys like that any more.

Rather annoying isn’t it, the amount of swarms of mosquitoes we get this time of year?      Honestly, it’s like they run a whole operation from this area. It’s not just buzzing in your ear, it’s the whole park being a feeding ground.      Right? Every time we come out with the baby, I end up slapping myself like I'm a mannequin in a test lab. What's worse is she squirms when I try to swat them away.      You're the lecturer who can analyse the effects of climate change on ecosystems but can't even make it ten minutes in a park without turning into a blood bank.      Ha, ha, very funny! I’m telling you, there must be some sort of DDT they pick and choose not to use round here. It's like they’ve got gig tickets for breakfast, lunch and dinner.      Which isn’t the topic, but by the way, you didn’t tell me about that gig you went to last weekend—was it the one by the river?      Yeah, the one with the indie band and the tent that kept flapping in the breeze—it wasn't exactly a rhythm and blues night. But it was lovely – very atmospheric. You should’ve come.      I wish I could’ve. I did end up stuck in traffic on the A12 for almost an hour, and by the time someone decided to move, I gave up trying to get a seat and just came home.      Oh no, I can imagine being wedged between a lorry and a minivan, trying to balance on the clutch while eating a half-chewed sandwich.      Exactly what it was! I know that highway like the back of my hand after sending so many students to and from lectures over the years. But that was something else.      Traffic’s getting worse every time I travel to university. I tried cutting through some little villages today just to avoid it, and then I ended up doing a roundabout trying to find the right exit.      Was it that road near the cemetery?      Yeah, go there again on your own if you want a broken wheel. I swear, one more pothole and my steering wheel was going to say goodbye.      Well maybe I’ll manage the conference seminar roles after next week so you can take the scenic route without worrying about lateness.

So did you get an interview today?      Not yet, just had a call with a recruitment agent. She said she’d email the next steps by Friday, but I've been waiting for a week now.      That’s frustrating—get on them. Maybe it was automated again and they didn't actually mean to say by Friday. Give her a quick call.      Maybe. I just don’t want to sound too anxious. They hate that in interviews, right?      Nonsense. I’d rather be proactive than sit around twiddling my thumbs. Get the details sorted. Still, at least you're applying, which is more than I can do some days.      You’ve been busy though. The golf this morning? I heard you had a tournament on the outskirts of town.      Yeah, it was a bit of a nightmare breakfast, honestly—four alarm clocks just to make sure I didn’t oversleep, thanks to your dog snoring on the bed. But the course was nice, sunny, and I made one birdie, which is something I can be proud of.      That counts for a lot. You’ve still got momentum going, so keep it up. I saw a post on social media about a new open-day at Royal Liverpool next month. Maybe that's something to aim for?      Yeah, I’ve been saving up for it. Might need a shout if I want to get out of this Rutland routine. But seriously, why don’t you come down to Manchester with me? Take a break and have a laugh?      That sounds good, but I’ve got my parents coming over for Halloween. They want the "full scary-house experience," which I think means they just want to see me cook without burning anything.      You could wear my toga and chain up the dog. That’d be spooky enough.      Classic. I don’t mind a laugh, but I did get a call from them about the ghosts in the hallway. As if that’s something I can fix…      Ghosts and bad Wi-Fi must be their top concerns. Still, remember when you got caught by your dad reading my old lyrics in the bin?       I still don’t know how you managed to write that without rhyme. Who lives in the "moonbat house" anyway?       It was poetic license, my friend. And now I’m doing push-ups at 7 a.m. for a living, so give me a break!

Right, lads and lass, let's get this going. I was just in the garden stringing up some lights for the ceilidh this weekend. D'ye need a hand after ye've finished yer dinners?      That Ceilidh is going to be mad, Dad. I'm thinking of bringing my mates Liam and Ned. They haven't been over to Cork yet.      Oh, but would that be too much of a hassle, Martin? It was quite a day getting Daniel to settle before the singing started earlier. Didn’t even want to sit with us.      Mama! Mama! Maisie sing! Maisie sing!      Ah now that’s our little songbird, alright. She left bursts of C’s lyin’ around the room earlier. Knew her ABCs before she screamed for Jammy Dodgers again.      I still can’t believe Daniel starts singing songs like “The Auld Triangle” before he ever gets his ABCs sorted. Grandpa told him that story once and now it’s stuck.      Well, I’m not the one who plays the bodhrán to go with it. If he wants to sing, he can sing, but I’m not drumming like I’m in a session – no chance of that!      Now, now, woman. Lighten up. We did have ceilidhs in the old days and we were all shakin’ those bodhráns at full volume. Let the boy have a bit of fun.      Yeah, come on Mom. It's not like the baby is going to sleep anyway with your ballet sessions going on most nights about how you never worked a day in your life.      Oh hush you, Keith! Like you were any better when you were Daniel’s age! Maybe I never worked, but I brought up four kids, held down a home, and cooked dinners while you were off trying to get a pass in biology.      Alright, alright. Let’s stick to talkin’ over dinner. Keith, what’s with all the lunches you keep bringing to school? They're all the same. Chicken curry and a sandwich. You're like a man with a routine goin’ on.      Well, I think it’s just better than the school dinners. Honestly, the last one looked like gray lumpy mash and I could have sworn I saw a hair in there one day.      Just like your school canteen back in Bristol, Keith?      Yeah, that was the problem! The lasagna at Bristol School was a myth. It looked like soggy cardboard kissed by baked cheese.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, me going to bed in my pants and everything. I swear, I've woken up half the bloody time and I can't be sure if I'm dreaming or not because I'm still in my boxers. It's like living in a pant-loop.      Oh don't start that again. I reckon it's not your pants making the dreams—it’s the house. This damp old cottage! I swear, every stick that creaks, every mouse that scuttles, it's got to be the setting of your nightmares.      Mummy, what are they  arguing  about? Are the walls haunted?      My love, they’re not arguing. Your dad’s just making things dramatic, as usual. And Oliver, don’t say haunted in the dark—it’s not healthy for the imagination.      Well I’m just saying, if I had taken off my pants properly, maybe the ghosts wouldn’t have found me looking so vulnerable.       Ghosts?  Come off it! You’d rather sleep in your pants than admit your dreams are all made up and entirely your own imagination.      Daddy, why don’t you just wear clothes to bed like me?      Because I value my comfort, thank you. And I reckon it’s not that bad—now that’s a grown-up detail sorted out!      Comfort? Let me tell you about the cold: my feet are already socked up because I  actually  like waking up with a bit of feeling in my toes. Not like  some  people, who would rather have flannel dreams than actual feeling.      Oh come on, I had a dream last night where I was selling plug sockets in the middle of a field. You’re the one who  works  with budgets and guestimates—I should know about imaginary things.      Plug sockets in a  field ? That’s you for you. Always making sense while you sleep. Anyway, moving on. I mentioned to you the other day about the idea of extending the conservatory?      Oh yes, with the big window overlooking the garden? I was thinking about that too. Imagine knocking through to make a snug—maybe even a separate room for the kids.      Exactly. It’s not just about space, it’s about  flow . We live out here for peace, but even peace needs a bit more room for life, wouldn’t you say?      I’m all for it—just one condition: they install a full bathroom next to the new room.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it?      Aye, it's been a pleasant shift from the usual mid-July downpours. I’ve actually been meaning to pop out for a bit of sun with the missus this weekend. We’re thinking of redecorating the spare room.      Oh, you’re doing a room now? I’ve been trying to resist the urge to rip out the wallpaper in my study for years, but then again, I was brought up in Cairo. We didn’t do interior design like this!      You know what? That’s one of the things I envy about you—your global perspective. When I was working on my thesis in the 90s, I wished I’d heard a bit more about how everyday life in other countries informed academic thought. I think it adds such a depth you don’t get often.      I agree. I mean, here in the UK, we often get too insular in our thinking, even in academia. Speaking of which, I heard your funding application for the environmental policy project—passed, I hope?      Passed as in read and left to gather dust? I might as well have submitted it during Wimbledon finals!      No, come on. I got a sneaky peek at it myself—excellent work. You’ve got scope for funding, but you might want to make it more relevant to current policy. Pop up the coffee machine someone?      That’s unfortunately a machine that’s been left on Auto Pilot since 1998. I think the last person who tried to fix it got grounded by the water company in about five different ways.      Ha! We had an engineering lecture a few years back that joked it would cost more than the national housing budget to fix the university’s plumbing system. Should we put the kettle on instead?      Aye, by all means. While it’s boiling, did I tell you about our trip to Italy last year? We were in Torino for a conference, and I got to take a tour of the Hadron Collider collaboration site? Wasn’t far from CERN after all.      No go on! I remember reading about that project—massive investment, even bigger expectations. Did they see anything significant?      Nothing concrete, but you could feel the excitement in the air. Like we were in some mad futurist film. You know, I’ve been telling my students for over thirty years now—big ideas tend to come from the fringes, not the centres.

Right, who’s ready to sort through the Lego? It’s taken over the bedroom, and I’m starting to feel like I’ll never find the vacuum again.      It’s where we left it, Mummy. You said not to tidy it up until you sorted it all out.      Yes, I meant the box, not   the entire room  ! Look, come on—it’s Friday, and if we tidy this mess, I’ll take both of you to the cinema on Saturday. We can see that Harry Potter movie everyone’s talking about.      But Mummy, the new Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles show is on tomorrow. Raphael’s still my favourite.      Oh, I know! Raphael is brilliant. But you boys can watch the show after the movie. We pick and choose, right?      What about the old bricks with the weird shapes—like the ones that look like mini Hagrid in Harry Potter?      Ah, those are the ‘Harry Potter excluded’ bricks that escaped the purge when we got rid of some of the sets. I think we might have a few from the original early-2000s releases. They’re not part of any specific set, but we can make our own wizard stuff with them.      Can I build a castle for the film?      Of course! You can make the castle and then bring your Pikachu Legos for the movie. Let’s just get this sorted first. You know Auntie just did some massive renovations at Granny’s house, and now   she wants to borrow our ‘castle-building’ talents for future visits  .      Why’s Granny’s house so bouncy now? It makes everything slide.      That’s because they put in new floors and things. It was a bit wonky before, like the Simpson’s house. Remember how you thought it was funny that the floor could move like it was holding its breath?      Yeah, but when I ran, I slipped and had to catch myself on Auntie’s leg. She said I was a little greased pickle.      Then Granny told her that the pickle was pickled in chocolate on Easter.      That   was   quite the chocolate weekend. Who remembers how many eggs we ate?      I remember I lost 3 and hid one in my hoodie. It melted by Sunday.      Oh no, not again! Last year we had a jelly-coated slab near the sofa. I think it’s part of the furniture now.      Mummy, can we get a new colour of chocolate eggs this year?

: Right, you've got to be kidding me — six weeks and I had to buy my own cereal. I got the big packet of Coco Pops because I thought I'd be trendy or something. Now there's none left. Not a single flake. Did you eat it?     : I'm not that hungry for cereal anymore, thanks to your theory that it's not actually food unless it has "granola" in the name. But fine, I might've had a couple of handfuls when you were at sister's house and I got hungry at midnight. Eat your own.     : You're a menace! And speaking of midnight snacks, I watched the Euros on my own for the final. My turkey still managed to cry more than me. I miss you during dramatic bits.     : Oh no! The Euros? I didn’t get to watch much — shifts at the weekend are, um…  not fun . But I did get in on the final’s social media vibes enough to know you didn’t win. Also, I warned you,  calm down over sports . Remember when we used to listen to the commentary in the bar with your ex from Manchester and he only cheered louder when someone got a red card?     : Oh god yes. Tony. Tony who?     : Tony who had the self-esteem of a dandelion and picked fights with waiters for changing his order. Bless him.     : Honestly, I miss him in an ironic way. But not my real ex — the one I left. That was hotter than the summer I got sunburned and still poured myself Margaritas  outside  as punishment because I thought I was being artsy.     : And then you had to document it on your blog. Going “ raw with barely a filter ” does  not  mean the neighbours should see that. I still wake up screaming every time I think about that.     : You're such a drama queen. I tried being raw for your benefit once. We ended up in tears over Aldi’s chocolate brownie mix.     : At least the chocolate brownie mix was edible.  unlike  your attempt at a “raw” lasagna that was more pond life than pasta.     : Okay, but let’s talk about food. Who’s cooking this week? I can’t do Shawarma at 10 am on a Monday and I won’t go down to the café again because of the guy who keeps asking if I “work in fashion.”     : Ugh, my cousin’s coming for Sunday dinner, so I kind of have to be romantic and serve something that doesn’t look like dried glue.

Right then, John, take a seat love. Your grans and I had a right job cleaning up after you last weekend. Someone had a  lot  more chocolate than they needed, didn’t they?      Not me! That was Sarah, my cousin. She’s the one who finished half the tin and went  bouncing  out the door like a mad thing.      Aye, Aye, but I know that  someone  here gave me a right job washing flannel mouths, and it wasn’t the cousin. You always insist on gobbling the lot and then not saying a word.      Oh, let the boy live a bit, Nancy. He’s in sixth form now, a proper young man! Besides, left’s a bit of fun, ain’t it?      I’ll be the judge of that if he turns up for his mock exam with breakfast still in his teeth.      I’m not a kid, you know! I’ve got my options sorted for A-levels. I’m doing Maths, Physics, and Computer Science, like you said, Miss—er I mean, Mum.       That’s  my boy. Good on you. Proper future in any of those, especially if you want to build rocket ships or figure out how to make cheques work on the computer instead of the post.      Aye, but if he wants a career, I say he’d better start washing up. I’m getting too old to be mopping up custard creams at ten o’clock on a Sunday night!      Hey now, I still do the  plates  when there’s a bumpy on the kettle. Just not the ones with jelly still clinging to the bottom.      Stop it, both of you! I’m trying to watch  Blue Peter . They’re making a rocket out of card and it’s  proper  scientific. Can I have some sweets before it finishes?      Only if you finish them before your homework. No sliding off to the sofa and pretending to study. I know when you do that, I’ve marked your face in various classrooms since you were five.      Now, now, don’t be goin’ on at him like that. He’s still got your looks, even if he’s got your husband’s stubbornness.      Aye, and I’d take  that  any day over someone who’d go on about exam halls and triangles in triangles!      You were never good at Geometry, Grumpy.      Oh I’ll have you know, son, I had a triangle once, and it was  love , not angles.

Right, so today we watched  Peter Pan , and grater’s been asking her questions about it ever since... What do you think she thought about Peter and Captain Hook?      I think she thought Peter was really cool and Captain Hook was kind of funny but also like the baddie. I saw her drawing a picture of Peter with the crocodile and ticking clock later on!      Aww, but I think Tinker Bell got top marks for being the most sparkly! Grater clapped when she was doing the dance at the start when she flies around with Peter.      Oh, I thought that was a really clever part of the film, how they managed to bring the magic to life with Tinker Bell. She’s one of the more complicated characters – like, she flies, she helps Peter but then she gets a bit cross with Peter later on.      Yeah, I noticed that. Grater asked me if Tinker Bell was ever not nice, and I didn’t have a great answer. I had to tell her that sometimes even friends can have a fall out, and that doesn’t mean they don’t like each other still.      That’s probably something she can understand, especially if she feels like her best friend forgot about her at playtime or something!      True. I remember when her friend Ruby forgot to pick her up at nursery one time, and grater stormed off for like half an hour. So yeah, I think she got the idea.      I wonder if they made a movie specifically about Tinker Bell. I’ve heard there were some Disney ones – she looked at her iPad and did a little spin while she talked about “fairy potions and magic flowers” so maybe she liked those.      Oh, the  Legend of Never  series? Yeah, there’s a few of them. They’re aimed at older kids, though. I could see the appeal – a fairy being all adventurous and talking to animals and stuff. You ever take her to the cinema for a movie that’s more of a family-friendly one?      Not really yet, but I want to take her to something around Christmas time. I’ve heard the Great Ormond Street Hospital Charity has a few screenings of  Peter Pan  and shows off how the films helped raise money for the hospital.      Oh yeah! I remember reading about that a few years back. They had a special 3D version of  Peter Pan  a while ago, and over half the profits from the film went directly to the hospital.

Rather annoying driving up from Exeter to the airport when you do everything the slowest, it’s not like I got to go far at all. I’m more used to driving from Taunton where we used to live before. Not quite as convenient, but at least you picked up some scenic bits of the M5 along the way, yeah?      I reckon it depends on your rhythm of the day. I only manage to sleep properly if I go to bed after 10, so getting up at 5.30 to be here makes me feel like a zombie, but the kids seem fine. I suppose they’re still in school mode—up with the lark and all that.      It’s a good job they’ve adjusted. Moving from Wellington to this house in Exmouth was a big enough change, and now I think the whole family’s finally making it stick. My sister’s still back in Taunton, working at the primary school there. She says she finds the commute from there to Bridgwater to be near the same time as this one, but nothing like as interesting.      Taunton’s got its own frustrations, I’ll give you credit for that. But since I retired, I’ve been spending more time remembering what it was like commuting. I used to knock about down near Bridgwater, and I never really thought about the hours unless I was stuck in traffic.      I suppose it’s one of those things you only notice when you’ve someone counting the hours for you. I often read about the rush hour blues when I’m marking—pooring the kids out early in the morning and being back at home late in the evening. But there’s a kind of rhythm to it now.      And speaking of rhythm—how’s the house-warming going? Have we got the dates fixed? I know a few people mentioned coming up from Taunton for the weekend, and your sister passed on a few names.      It’s pencilled in for the last Saturday of December. Might be mad getting people together while everyone’s either over at home or doing last-minute festive shopping, but we’ve got the place decorated now, and the kettle’s always on.      That’s the spirit! I go back to my parents’ place in Dorset for Christmas proper, but I’m sure the kids will be more than happy with a house-warming feast and some virtual facetime with the grandparents.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd have decent cups of tea in a place like this... What was it, some charity bazaar today, wasn’t it? I've been over by the hospice building all morning, helping spread the tinsel round the track.      Right, yeah, I was down by the nursery grounds earlier, helping sort out the chairs for the working party. A lot of toing and froing about budgies and women being equal. It all gets a bit samey after a while, don’t you reckon?      Equal? Oh, I agree with it, course—women deserve a square deal. But I’d rather have a decent hot water bottle and a Swedish massage after all this! Me and my late husband always used to joke about men in spa centres getting all the pampering.      Massages? Blimey, I haven’t had one since my wife passed a decade back. She used to be the one to sort us out after a working shift—and I mean working, not this lot—running the Accommodation, all that paperwork and such.      Oh, do you live around here then, by the track?      Nup, out of West Midlands. Birmingham, actually. Wife was born near here, in Small Heath, before the whole family moved over somethin’ like 40 years ago. Bit of a coincidence, eh?      Well, in Somerset we tend to say everything is just a bit of a coincidence. Funny thing—time. Also, have you heard about the ME event next year? I was told it’s a big one. I do hope they’re finally going to show a bit more of what women can do.      Yeah, that was mentioned at the working party. Me, I say if the lot of ‘em put their minds to it, they can do anything. Though I have me doubts the event planner told us ‘specially about women being involved in them organisation committees. Seemed all the talk was about words and terms being ‘political’ now.      Oh, the terminology! It’s like you have to get a whole other language these days. That artist in me still wants to make a point with paint—not with policy. But I digress.      You’re bloomin’ right. Pass me that cup of tea, will you? I’ve had enough of words and chairs for one day. Tell me, do you know when they’re going to fetch proper tools for the track work?

I just booked the flights, Mummy. You're going to hate me when you hear the cost, but I... got us seats with some extra legroom because your back's been acting up. Oh, Lucy, don't start with the flights. You know I wouldn't dream of complaining if it's all booked. But I’ll say one thing—I   did   mean it when I said not to go overboard with the economy premium or whatever they call it these days. Still, if you were firm about the legroom and you didn’t end up booking us first class again, then I'm happy. I didn’t! Honestly, I checked and double-checked the prices, and legroom for an extra ten quid a side was reasonable! Besides, you’re going to be more comfortable on the five-hour flight. We pick up the hire car the same day—Donna promised to look after the boys for breakfast, so we won’t even need to eat out for the morning at least. That’s thoughtful of Donna. And the car? What did you go for—something sensible or one of those tiny, impossible-to-find-a-parking-space-with ones? I got a medium SUV. You said in your last email how it rains half the time in the mountains and most of the places we're visiting are off the main roads, so I thought something with a bit of ground clearance would be better. Plus, it was on promotion. Hmm, promotions are rarely what someone means when they say “I’ve not spent too much.” But let’s not dwell on it. Did you at least confirm the hotel in Chamonix? That’s where I was most worried about because most places about five-star are fully booked this time of the year. Booked a four-star and not too far from the gondola station. The reviews said the breakfast was especially recommended, so that helps. I’ve got us Friday to Monday, with a couple of open days so you can decide if you want to do a bit of skiing or just relax with a book by the fire. I  did  include one night in Nice as a 'split holiday' because you said the Mediterranean feels too fast-paced when you’re in the highlands. Oh, go on then! That wasn’t necessary. But I  know  you’ll enjoy it.

: You lot watch The Football League on the telly, do you?     : Aye, I caught some of it this week. Not as much as I’d like, gotta be honest. Work keeps me pinned down sometimes, but when I get a minute, I’m glued to it. That Lincoln City game last weekend—wild one, eh?     : Oh aye, I saw it. Fair dos that keeper saved three penalties. You’d think they’d get easy goals in those situations, but nah, he was on fire.     : That’s the beaut of it. You can never tell. I love the unpredictability, you know? On the island [Barbados], I didn’t get to watch much, but back home, I was obsessed with the Windies cricket and the Premier League. Even now, if I’m at a barboin back there, someone always pops up with a match on a little screen.     : Nah, you didn’t have the Football League down there?     : Nah, not really. I mean, the occasional highlight if we were lucky. But you’re in Lincoln, right? Tell me you went to watch the team proper.     : Aye, twice last season, actually. My cousin works at the stadium and gave me the cheapest tickets she could find. It was something else. The crowd was loud, the energy was mad, and the food was all chips with everything. Honestly, I’d die for a good curry pie like that at home with you.     : Hey, you know what—I’ve had your curry pies! You lot have about five variations of it back in the UK, right?     : We do! My sister’s boyfriend runs a takeaway up the road. He does a chicken one, a shepherd’s pie mash-up, and even a vegan one now. Parents were  not  happy about it at first.     : Ah, right. You Brits stick to tradition hard, but I get it. Even in Barbados with lunches and cricket nights, you hear the same sayings. My grandad used to say, “Football or cricket, it’s still goin’ on!”     : Aye, I like that. It’s like you always find a bloke on the street who knows more about the game than the players!     : Definitely. And I’ll tell you this, I’ve had games in the office over this. Work lot, them sporting types—they’ll go on and on about one match for weeks. Totally love it. You want to catch a game? I can pop in for a bite to eat, we could make it happen.

Rather annoying this newfit Skype eh?      Aye, it's all ‘press and hold’ and ‘swipe’ and I’m more used to just picking up the phone. Still, it is nice being able to see you lot, especially as you’re all scatterbrained across the country now.      Same with me, really. I tried getting the kids to help with a globes project once, but they were more interested in social media than geography. Mind you, it’s not as if I blame them these days. Everything's digital now.      You'd think the world would get smaller with all this technology, wouldn’t you? Still, I can't fault the video bit. It was nice to catch you lot up last week on the Yorkshire holiday, didn’t I tell you I stayed in one of them youth hostels? Blimey, they’ve really spruced it up, no doubt about that!      Oh, did they? I remember when we used to go to them as kids—and I mean,  proper  walking distances between one and the next—my knees’d still be up near my ears with all the hills!      That’ll still be the case, watching how the kids trot off on their bikes these days. Though at my school we did a fairly radical project last term, linking up with a secondary in Manchester. We had them visiting as part of their history program, all ‘living history’ and whatnot—well, what someone at the education summit called it.      Aye, I do remember what you were saying at the family get-together. Anyhow, Margie here had a bit of a wobble with about the underground system—poor thing tripped over the stairs at Charing Cross and said her leg was not happy after that.      Oh, don’t mention that. My ankle’s been playing up since. I had to skip the gardening club for a week, which was a slap in the face as I had this new rose bed I was waiting to sort out.      I know what you mean—though I've recently taken up sitting by the pond in the school gardens with the kids for reflection time after lunch. Paves the way for a bit of calm before the day kicks in again.      You’re all in separate houses, between us. Me with bloomin’ bad leg and all. But still—it’s good to be together on this screen, having our tea hours just like we always did, even if we can’t see the china over this lot’s broadband!

Rather skip the new Thea eh?      Aye, her new album’s been panning out alright on Insta, but I’m more of a “still gives me the goosebumps” person with the old stuff. No disrespect, innit.      Same. Got eeny weeny passive rabit runner with the '95 album. My mam actually put me on a playlist that only had stuff from before the millennium! I got to be honest, I started listening, and it sounds a bit… dated, if I’m being fair. But, don’t get me wrong, I like to keep it real!  laughs       Oh, don’t do that! Being posh and all. You’ve still got to pay your taxes like the rest of us, right? D’you know, I think it’s just nostalgic for most of us. Back in the day, when you couldn’t press 'replay' with a flick of your finger, you had to replay the tape, or even wind it back by hand!      Oh yeah, do tell, luv! I still got the VHS of me watching a video to her early hits when I was like, seven or something… watching it now, I’m like, “Blimey, what a cheeky face!” I’m not proud, but I  was  me.  laughs       You always were a cheeky one! And I’m not saying she’s perfect, someone said in one of the comments that she changed her voice, and I was like, “Well, yes, she got older.” You can’t be Thea at 22 your whole career! You’ve got about five decades left to sing the same bop! She’s had time to evolve!      Yeah, that’s fair! I mean, if she was still in that skin-tight outfit for every gig like she was in the '95 tour, I reckon her fans might say something. But I think it’s cool, really. I mean, I sort of stick out my ears as long as she’s doing what she wants.      Aye! That’s the thing with folk like her, innit? You respect their journey, their sound, go where it goes. If you like it, great – if not, well, it’s out there. And we can boxset bop through what we like.  laughs       So, what’s in the mix for your next project?      Just been working on restructuring some client timelines. We had them fitting like 10 productions into one week, so I had to do some kind of production-based magic, like, casting runes and all.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, the whole phone lot. My number was working fine until they said they’d got to port it over to the new lot. Blows me how something like a phone contract ends up costin’ £20 more a month than what it used to.      That is so typical of telecom providers, isn’t it? They always seem to find a way to charge you extra once you’re halfway through your contract. I got letters last week from three different providers, all offering better rates—of course, after my contract's up.      Honestly, I wouldn’t even know where to begin comparing them. I've got the same plan I've had for years now and Myra keeps saying I’m being stubborn, like I’m not just scared I’m going to accidentally end up on a plan I don’t understand. Half the phone is in German, and the other half doesn’t work half the time.      Oh don’t I know it. I thought I was ordering a spare button battery and the pack had three or four different ones and it looked the same on every page. Chefs I don’t need no lessons in that.      Have you tried going into the shop? You can get a little workshop-style session if you book ahead. I signed up for one last year, and they walked me through all the cheapest options and even showed me how to message phone companies without getting lost in the maze of menus.      Well, I’m more suspicious than confused. Used to work in a court, I know what flim-flam some companies can pull. It’s not just the phone prices, it’s the bills, the statements, everything. My blood pressure's gone up the last week trying to sort out my broadband and whatnot.      Aye, it is a faff. I had Myra’s nephew out the other week guestein’ over here, and his mobile shows me a picture of his dog any bloody time it rings. I tried to do the same with mine, but the photo didn’t like the background of the wallpaper and it ended with me texting a picture of the cat with half its head.      That’s funny. Mine started doing the same go with photos I didn’t even intend to put up. Phones have made my life better, no doubt, but I think they might have made me more anxious about losing things.

Right, so we've got this list we're making of our five favourite things for the flat blog. We already got the food, but no luck on the music or animals! Any ideas?      Well, for animals I’m definitely a dog person. C’mon, who doesn’t want a dog that nudges you with its nose for snacks at midnight?      Oh aye, I love dogs but I’d side with cats, honestly. Cats are low maintenance and don’t bark at the pizza delivery. My aunt’s cat doesn’t chase the vacuum or anything. She just looks at you like, “Tomorrow,  after  I sleep for 20 hours.”      My nan still has a dog—a collie left by a previous tenant. I’m terrified I’m gonna trip and push it into the hedge. But I suppose if I was forced to pick, I’d go with horses. My uncle keeps a few, and I used to help out during holidays.      I’d say hamster. Small, cute, and I could hide it under the bed if we get in trouble for not cleaning up. Or a goldfish. Goldfish only live two years, so there’s a built-in expiry date.      Okay okay, but what about food? I’m not saying I’ve tried  all  foods, but I’m quite confident that pizza is the pinnacle of human achievement. There’s no situation that can't be fixed by a pepperoni slice and a fizzy drink.      I’d definitely put out a bake-off between Indian spices and chocolate. Chai tea is essential—I don’t care what anyone says, it’s about the warmth and the sugar kick you get from it. And don’t get me started on what you can do with chocolate. Bread dip? Yes. Banana dip?  Yes . Hairball de-dipper? Maybe not.      I’m withŜ 1 on pizza, but any pizza with pineapple is a crime. Pineapple belongs in deserts or on the beach, not  on a crisp cheesy base . Except maybe with a bit of coconut chips and digestive biscuits—wait, is that even a  thing ?      Yeah yeah go on then, but let’s not forget  proper  food! You ever had that fish and chip shop food with the box big enough to live in your legs? The greasy, golden, crunch-on-the-side-of-the-fry kind? That’s real food, not this healthy kale nonsense we see in ‘gram posts.

So did you finish that art essay yet? I’ve been staring at mine for hours and it’s not like it’s getting any easier.      Not properly, no. I think I’ll leave it for a bit and go do some gaming to clear my head. Want to join me?      Nah, I don’t think I can look at a screen for any longer. My brain’s already fried. I just want to walk around this room, maybe draw something instead. It’s easier pulling ideas from a blank page than from the one I’ve got in front of me.      Fair enough. I get that. I’ve been stuck with the same dumb debate about Expressionism vs. Modernism the whole time. Honestly, I’m wondering what’s the point of art anymore. Why would you paint a house if it’s not realistic? Like, surely you’d just take a photo.      Because then you’re just creating something someone else could make in a split second. Painting gives you space to feel something. Like when I look at those abstract ones, I don’t know what the artist was thinking, but I can guess. You don’t think about whether it's a tree or a person, you just feel something—it kind of makes you question everything, right?      Mate, I don’t know, I think it just makes me question why the artist didn’t make it  clearer . Maybe I was meant to feel something, but I just end up feeling confused.      Maybe that's the point though? It's not always about a clear message. Art is more about how it makes you feel being exposed to it. Like when your grandmother watches Hello! and cries about people who don’t even matter to her. It just hits something in her.      Yeah, I guess that’s true. But it still doesn’t help my essay. My tutor’s like 'You need to connect your personal opinions to historical context' and I’m like, I'm a student, not an art historian.      Just talk about what the art makes you  feel , as cheesy as that sounds. And maybe throw a couple of whistles at the hierarchy of art over time—like, why Expressionism came out of the mess of the gothic or something.      That might work. You’re a better art person than I’ll ever be, I’ll say that.

: Right, so I’ve got this recipe I found online for spicy lentil curry—the photo looks awesome. Think we’ve got everything?     : Hmm, I’ll check the cupboards. Oh well, maybe we can improvise or do without.     : Or I can pop out later. You know I like to cook with it, makes everything taste like a restaurant.     : Yeah, well… you know I’m not too fussed. I just tried to save money on takeaway this month, with all the bills I’ve been getting for work. It’s a bit tight.     : Oh no, really? What’s been coming through?     : Oh, the usual—travelling for meetings, hiring temps, printing stuff for the team, and now some weird fee from the building management for the landline. Rather than share a speaker’s consent form, I suggest we do everything we can to simplify it. The first thing we need to do is ensure the session has more than one focus. I think it depends on how much of a formal approach we take with the seminar. If we go all out, we can stretch it into a panel or introduce it as a case study. I also wonder what the best way to get the most engaging data from the audience is without it being overly clinical—what works best with postgraduate students, don’t you think?      Ooh, I like the case study idea. Ten minutes or so from the audience, with some push and pull in the structure? But then you’d need to vet the questions first. I see no issue if we use a continuous dialogue format for the discussion itself. It would also allow for interaction, which is important for a seminar like this. I reckon we can even rope in the audience if we book some of them as backup!      Here’s the thing—outhouse, let’s say we launch something on cross-cultural communication. We can then branch into how it shapes communication methodologies in international business settings. I’ve read some recent literature on this, and the jury is out on whether to model it through cognitive or affective frameworks. The universities in our network, they all want this aligned with the business studies criteria. Just trying to keep a balance here.      Affective, is it? So you’re looking at things like emotional intelligence in cross-cultural contexts, or is it more about how individuals internalise cultural cues?      We could explore both. I’ve seen some good reports from the University ofReading that take it as a hybrid approach. The title of our seminar could be something like  'Cultural Intelligence in Global Business: Bridging the Gap'.  It’s not too broad, and it gives scope for introducing case studies or real-world scenarios. As for the structure… I propose 15 minutes of input from each of us, with a 10-minute buffer in between for reflection and audience input.      Yeah, go on then. But let’s make sure there’s a clear action plan at the end—ike, some tools or templates the attendees can use when managing international teams.

So do you get how we’ve gotta do this economics project on poverty? Our teacher said it’s not just about stats and numbers, she wants us to think more about  why  people live in poverty and what systems make it worse.      Honestly, I wouldn’t have guessed it was that deep. I thought we’d just do some research and write a report about places where people don’t have a lot of money. But “systems” that make it worse? What does that even mean?      Well, like, I read this article the other day about how the cost of rent in Slough is going up even more. People can’t afford to live anywhere near here anymore, especially if they work minimum wage jobs. It’s not just about being poor; it’s about how the world is set up to make it hard for people to escape poverty.      Yeah, and it’s linked to, like, consumerism too. Like, how much money people waste on unnecessary stuff and then there’s not enough to help those who need it. My auntie told me about this project in her village—there’s a shop that takes donated food and puts it out for people for free. It’s run by volunteers. She said it’s saving people.      That’s so cool. My nan used to say the same thing. She worked for the council for years and knew all the hidden places that helped families through hard times. Like, if you were struggling with bills, she said there was someone at the library who could help you apply for grants or something.      That’s something we could mention in the project. Maybe even look at what’s going  locally . I bet most people about our age don’t even know about these places. And it makes you think—do we even notice the people living in poverty around us?      Honestly? I don’t think we do. I mean, look at how high up the trees are on the estates around here. I used to think they were just there for decoration, but I found out they help block out the noise from the motorway. That’s not luxurious, but it’s a way the government tried to make things better for people who live near big roads.      Maybe the project can go even further. Like, if we talk about poverty, we should also look at how schools are affecting it.
