Right, so the DVD’s playing. You sorting the popcorn or am I?      Go on, you’ll forget about it and I’ll have to smuggle it in after you’ve watched three minutes of the title scene with no sound.      Fair point. Right, I'm on it. What we watching today then?   V for Vendetta  ? Bit of a dark pick. A change from your usual  Paddington 2  marathon, innit?      Aye, was me flatmate's old copy. She said it's a classic. Get the full Wile E. Coyote tragic revolutionary vibes with a dash of Hugo Weaving charm. You like that type of film?      I like Hugo Weaving, yeah. I wrote a story about a masked anarchist in Leicester once. Halfway through I was like, “Nah, I’m no V,” and just switched it to a jazz musician running a bootleg record shop. Kept the masks in though. People love a masked protagonist.      Fair, you get the grit without the speechifying. I remember you read a bit to me back in uni. That one with the busker and the Tory MP. Hit me in the gut. You ever publish it?      Nah, I had to pull it after my nan read it and demanded to know “why all the coppers are evil ‘like they’re not fed properly’.” Told someone at the pub my plotline was a conspiracy to defund the West Midlands police.      Aye, and you thought being a writer was safe?  You’re a threat to national security about to make Steve Coogan look reliable .      [Laughs] Fair one. At least you know that I know rho I’m taking. Unlike  him —you lot, ‘ coding ’ your guest speaker last month called it. Banging on about phonemes and intonation. ‘This is the future of literacy, mate,' he said. My brain just said “nope.”      Aye, I keep meaning to ask—was it the same bloke who told us that the word ‘village’ started with an ‘f’? I still see an  f  every time I say it.      That was the one bloke who claimed the ‘th’ sound in ‘think’ was illegal to his conference in Bournemouth. As long as he never had to stand in a classroom trying to teach that ‘bath’ is spelled ‘baath’ I’m not entirely sure what I did for a living.      Listen, I take it serious. I had a class in Toxteth last week saying they pronounce ‘ask-INNER-gy’ as ‘ask-Energy’—loads of variety, babe.

Rather skip the newfit and go to the request, right?      Yeah, like I got the email from work about it this week, and I just kind of panicked a bit.      Why panic? Look, you’ve got a job now, haven’t you? Hasn’t been a year yet?      Yeah, it’s only been nine months. I taught year one this year, so this is my second school.      Second school? What’s wrong with the first one? Didn’t you get on with them?      No, they were lovely. I just wanted a new challenge, and this school is in a bit of a deprived area, so I thought it’d be a good opportunity. I’m working with their inclusion team too, which I think is good for my teaching career in the long run.      Well if you’re happy, that’s all that matters. And I hear the head there is supposed to be brilliant.      Yeah, that’s what I heard too, and the PD they offered was really solid. Anyway, what about you? You’re not doing anything on Easter, are you?      Well I was just thinking about that. My friend Jen is throwing a fairly large Easter bake sale because her daughter’s getting christened and her husband’s gone and got them all involved in some sort of ‘wedding fund’ nonsense, and the family just wanted to help. So I’m making a cake to sell.      Oh nice, are you going to do the chocolate and fruit tea cake again like last year?      Yeah, I think so. Although I’m toying with the idea of doing something a bit different this time. Maybe some kind of lemon and thyme sponge.      That sounds good. I baked something for it last year too — a Victoria sponge with raspberry jam. Sold it in a minute, everyone said it was the best they’d ever tasted.      Like always. You’ve clearly taken after me in the baking department. I wonder what your kids would do if you passed that talent on.      Maybe their kids can go to your christening cake if you ever have one. Although personally, I think it’s all a bit unnecessary. Who needs a $9 cake to ‘bless’ their baby?      You’re not wrong. But I suppose it makes for a nice excuse to dress up and have a little gathering. Jen promised me a slice of that lemon and thyme one in return for helping her today.

Rather skip to the front of the queue, isn’t it? A few people just jumping in when it comes to got to pick up tablets from the dining room yet?      I mean, it is rather amusing how we do this, but it does make for a great conversation topic, don’t een? So,  not  the one you want handed over if you're not in the mood for a chat. A lot of people just walk in from anywhere, really. Oh, and what was it like teaching Spanish again this year?      Fun, but exhausting. You know how teenagers like to talk more than they listen—especially when I’m trying to correct their pronunciations. It’s like My turkey, my sunset, my jelly—it’s all one note. And I’m constantly saying, “No, pick and say it again.”      Ah, I remember those days when I was trying to teach literature in London. Hitting a brick wall more times than ever. You have to wonder how some of the parents even thought their kids would enjoy that—v ery different from, say, Spanish or French.      You’ve still got it. Haha. Tell me about life in Birmingham. How are the kids?      Oh, Mateo is at college now, and, let me tell you, he gets his independence from me—don’t worry. Silly little rascal still leaves his socks on the floor and never remembers to call at the weekends. But the dogs: they’re a nightmare, honestly. One of them—Barney—continues to think the garden is a hill he must climb all day. I’ve given up trying to understand how his brain works.      You had a dog when I met you, didn’t you? I remember you told me you adopted it after a terrible experience with the last one. Burgled the whole garden, nearly bit the postman.      Ohhh, don’t remind me. I tried to calm him down with a spoon and ended up with a blister. He’s doing a lot better now with lunches and a new blanket from my daughter. She’s studying beauty, you remember, the one with the course in aromatherapy? Actually, I started trying her mixes at home—lavender and chamomile line in the bath, it's like a box of tissues on a rainy day. Reallly nice.      That does sound amazing. I’ve never had the patience for that sort of thing.

So do you lot actually know what you're meant to be doing for the Seder tonight, or does Halina just turn up with a giant box and make us all do it blindfolded again?      Oh don’t start, Jamie. You know Halina wouldn’t dream of missing the Seder—especially since she brought those beautiful homemade matzah balls and chicken soup.      I’ve only done it once or twice in my life, honestly. But it’s so meaningful, pulling out that story and retelling the Exodus. You get deeper into it, the more you do it. I like to read a bit more each year—stories, commentaries.      Yeah, like that one you told me about Marco, who found the hidden afikoman and then made the whole table argue over whose kid was the sneak? Pretty funny.      Oh wait, better not breakfast, Marco—your agreement to pay everyone for a week in Paris goes out the window the second you hides the afikoman again. We’re still waiting for that.      Come on, we need more than just the story. You don’t just walk into this and say, “Oh by the way, this is Passover—and it’s also a little like Italian cooking.”      Well, fairly, there’s actually a lot of overlap. Some of my family in Italy used to mix Passover with their own traditions—roasted lamb with zucchini, and this sweet-ish cake made with dates. Strictly not allowed now, obviously, but it was so good.      I thought in Italy you were still allowed some stuff like that as long as it wasn’t leavened technically. My aunt once swore up and down she lit Shabbat candles and they flickered into Passover bread. Don’t know if I believed it, but the bread was legit.      Maybe you should guest-edit my next cookbook, Kat. I’m trying to get it off the ground—Jewish food with a twist, you know. Like, “How to make good brisket that doesn’t take a week,” or “Kosher meets New York fusion.”      You think you can make a passable latke without the burning? go for it. But let Halina or I sample it first.      Actually, Jamie, I think you might have something there. Passover recipes are often all or nothing—either 300 years old or completely inaccessible to the modern kitchen.      Exactly. Look, imagine this: a food series called  Passover and the City .

Rather skip the new series of Doctor Who.      You think it's that bad.      Oh it is honestly more than I can take I've seen one episode and it is.      That bad.      Erm it's not een beginning to.      So what are you watching then.      I've been watching these true crime documents on BBC this one about a Miss Scandal and she was some sort of local celebrity and she gets murdered by her like slimy architect when he's supposed to be doing her extensions.      Oh.      What's slimy about him.      Just his vibes I met his twin brother once he tried to sell me wallpaper.      Oh no I think he turned me down for an assembling job at a Catsfield.      Oh I hated that place.      Wasn't the manager a total arse.      Yeah he was like directly from like Watergate or something you know.      I mean if we're talking about true crime and grief I started reading this book by a best friend of mine she's got this book out called "Merry Old Lady – tales of terror with a teacup".      Oh that sounds fabulous.      Silly name what's it about.      It's this someone who solves crimes using her knitting group because everyone in the village counts them out because they're all just like very old.      But she's got like all the gossip in the village because she runs about five knit and natter type groups.      Oh I've seen a Netflix special about that.      I mean it is a classic British crime trope the older woman solving things like the Mystery of the Flower Show or whatever.      Are there any examples where any of those books have been turned into accurate adaptations.      Not really.      No they're always trying to do like a Grisham spin with like murder and courtroom drama but you can't.      The points of the goings on on the life are like ant queens.      Yeah it’s all just like genuinely.      Heartwarming.      Yeah I think they’re writing like roles where women are seen as earnest and just like genuinely hearing gossip and stuff and not putting two and two together until like chapter 15 when they go I think I should probably like call the local bobby.      Yeah it's probably not like serial killer true crime documentaries and the kind of stuff.      That we're used to.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You've got me with mine sorted out, but I've been pottin’ about with this Nokia since the 80s! Mind, it does what it's supposed to—aint' no bells or whistles, mind you. Just rings when it’s supposed to and takes a photo if I'm desperate.      I know! It's so weird you’ve never had a smartphone before, considering what you do for a job. I thought all English lecturers were au fait with all the techy stuff. Didn’t your students get the giggles when you asked what a meme was?      That was a cold one, that was. Just 'cause I’m foreign and got a bit of a accent, they figured I was Darcy from Pride and Prejudice turned IT inspector. But I’m German, not giggle-worthy! Besides, I teach the literature, not the culture of TikTok and Instagram, thanks ever so!      Fair enuff. But now you’ve got this shiny new thing here, don’t you? Saw you faffing with it in your hotel room last week and thought, "There goes someone having their universe flipped upside down."      You’re not far off! I got this fairly new, and mind you, it’s not one of them flashy ones. Just enough to check emails, use a map, and—most importantly—keep me from getting lost again.      Now, I need to set up the Wi-Fi. How do I get here through this lot of buttons and menus?      Here, I'll show you. Tap the little cog icon at the bottom. Then "Settings," and then—"Wi-Fi." See? Then you'll see a list of all the available networks, like that Pikko Mikko guest network we passed earlier.      Ah right, I was stuck on "Home." I tried Germany’s Wi-Fi once, but all the security questions gave me the hump. Websites asking if I've recently been a victim of identity fraud or if I lived with someone who knew Gorbachev. Pah!      You've had a real ramble in Salzkotten, haven't you? But yeah, Nordic countries keep it straightforward. Just type in the code, and you're in. Oh, and mind you turn Bluetooth off, otherwise every table in this pub might start playing your ringtone over their Spotify.      Now that I can live without! I was once at a conference in Bremen, and one chap had his phone set to "Disco Inferno."

Right, so today is the day we start sorting out your birthday party, sweetie. What colour do you want the decorations to be?      Maybe green! Green for the forest where the red pandas live!      Oh, that sounds lovely. You like red pandas more than your Malamooche, huh?      Well, Malamooche is nice, but red pandas are amazing. They’re like cats and bears but cooler. And my cat, Miso, is just a regular cat. She meows and jumps on the iPad, but she’s okay.      Miso does  not  like me using the laptop, I’ve told her a million times that it’s not a toy!       Mewww .      I think Miso is just trying to protect us by checking our screens! Wait, does everyone know about the Malamooche? Mom, you should see the Malamooche videos on TikTok. They’re so funny!      I’ve seen one, yes—person is dancing with this really big dog in a Malamooche costume. I think it was called “German Malamooche,” but it looked quite West Country from where I’m from.      I’m getting you one for your birthday, Mom. One that you dance with! You could be the Silly Malamooche Queen.      Now you just want to put me in a costume in front of your friends. That’s oddly cruel, but also flattered.      It’ll be epic. Can we invite Tommy and Aisha? And invite Fin about the birthday?      Fin! She’s your best friend. Of course. Maybe your friends can bring their toys too. I was thinking of doing a superhero-themed craft table and a ‘guess the animal’ game with photos of red pandas, Malamooche, and your cat.      Oh, I can write them on little cards! Like a quiz! And we can vote on who picked the cutest panda.      That sounds brilliant. What about snacks? You like sugar, so maybe cake and some fruit juice?      I want panda-shaped cookies or something!      Panda-shaped? I might have to improvise with a cookie cutter or get your dad to make them at the bakery. Speaking of, how’s the schedule looking? We’ve got gymnastics next week and your dad is going on that ‘weekend in the wild’ camping trip near Cardiff. So I think we need to have the party this Saturday, after your lesson, maybe?      Saturday is good. I could wear my superhero shirt and my gymnastics shoes before the party, just in case we do acrobatic panda games later!

So do you lot actually do anything for Christmas, or is it just a bit of telly and presents like... proper presents?      It's not  that  bad, but where we are in London, half the people I know have like... weird traditions. One of my cousins brought in a piñata once, and we were all expecting some proper Christmas cheer, and it was like a birthday party with tinsel.      Oh, now that's a new one to me! When I was teaching, we used to have carol services in the church hall with mulled wine specially bought from the Co-op. Nothing too fancy, but it felt important to keep it going.      My family still travels to Bath for Christmas though. Nothing like this piñata madness – we do the same thing each year: turkey, the lot. Same dishes, same dress code. Probably better for breakfast, honestly.      Honestly, I reckon if we tried piñatas in Barrow, Grandad would have a fit. He once refused to open a present because it came out of a black box and he thought it might be Bah Humbug.      It’s funny how different places go about it. Back in the Philippines, it was all about “pamamanhikan” – visiting family from one house to another for weeks before Christmas. And the food – donuts, turkey, and whole pig roasting. There was no stopping that pig, let me tell you.      Oh my God, that sounds chaotic – and oddly wonderful. We never had any of that. It was always “stay here, be quiet, no slipping over in the hall because your Nana’s watching.”      But it worked, didn’t it? I mean, you and Dad kept it going all that time. Doesn’t it feel kind of strange to do the same thing over and over?      I think nostalgia does that to you. You start to believe something was better back then, even if it wasn’t. I remember your Gran used to sing “White Christmas” in the bath every year – with a kazoo.      Kazoo, really? That’s brilliant.      I mean, it's not really my time, but I miss not having real snow for Christmas. We had fake snow that came out of a box last year – it smelt like damp socks. It was like Christmas for goblins.      And now, don’t even get me started on accents and how people sound over the holidays. I swear, every year I’m convinced I’ve been invited to a Christmas party in a completely different country.

Rather skip the new series till we catch up with the old one.      The first one got a bit dire at the end, I think. I prefer the prequels.      Not sure I'll have time anyway—had a bit of a backlog to get through on transcriptions. Work's been a nightmare lately.      Is that not the job you’ve always had? At least the one from home.      It is, but it’s just been grinding. I keep thinking about switching to teaching, but the coursework is exhausting. I barely have time to even curl my hair these days.      That’s what I like about My Kindles. You can dip in and out. I tried the new Hill novel—full of suspense. But I thought I'd try the little local cozy mystery everyone was talking about. Made better sense when I was baking scones and boiling water for tea in the background.      You can’t tell me you didn’t want to deductive your way through Watergate with her, though.      I never did quite make that leap. But I did find a new fancy bookshop in Isleworth. They have signed copies and little chairs where you can test out the books.      I need to get out more. I’m buried in work and fried chicken takeaway for the foreseeable future.      What, no roast dinners this week?      God no, I had to clean up after a dinner with my sister—she forgot to switch the gravy from being poured into the turkey to the veg. Massive mess. Took me about an hour to walk away without verbal feedback.      Honestly, cooking is chaos and fails. I prefer to let friends cook and handle it all up for me to do something less ‘culinary.’      I did cook once. Invited friends over. It turned into a culinary critique.      You must practice your detective skills to navigate that.      Except trying to catch up with the detectives on screen is hard enough when you work full-time and have no idea where your socks are.      I think life is more of a mystery than any of those shows.      True—especially when you're trying to figure out where you left your invoice file or lost your cat.      On that note—should we meet up more? For catch-ups where we don’t have to be perfect?      Absolutely. I propose a theme—Food and Failure. With wine, obviously.      Done.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp week after week. You'd think by now it would make up its mind! Erm, I saw a forecast this morning—says it might clear up over the weekend?      Aye, that’s all we get, isn’t it? A 'might'. Makes me think of all them evenings stuck in with nothing to do but watch telly and listen to the rain. Oh, and stewing in my own mind. Not me, mind, I like a good chase when it's dry, but not too many chances to go walking these days.      That's the way of it. On the other hand, you know, I’ve actually found the weather’s pushed me to do some proper work I’ve been meaning to get round to. A bit of administrative cleaning up in the office, and properly sorting out some old invoices and such.      That's ever so posh, Alan. Me, I’m stuck looking after the grandchildren again. Goodness, those girls—vibrant, full of beans, and very clever too, I grant you, but as to keeping still and behaving for more than ten minutes—absolute fantasy!      Oh, children. You want to bottle the cheek they have at five! I still remember when they were small, Bert. You’d set out for a walk and within ten feet of the front gate they were already arguing about which one of 'em wanted to hold which hand!      And they never run out of stories. Some made up, some half-imagined, and a lot I still don't make head nor tail of! Not that I mind—they’re lovely children. I just do wish the parents had a bit more time to be around and not leave it all to me and the outings to the park.      That’s the burden of being the guest parent, Bert. On the bright side, you'll become a legend in the family. I mean, I’ve met too many little ones who don't know their grandparent’s name but can say “Mr. Alan” in one breath and “hurry with the biscuits” in the next.      Aye, well, as go the biscuits, so goes peace and quiet. Any chance of a plate of scones and jam between us before the telly catches on? I can always do with a nice hot cuppa.      That’d suit me just fine.

Okay, so the recording of the last twenty minutes of Horace’s reading was just uploaded, right? We should be able to hear his vowel reductions now clearly enough for the phonetic breakdown.      Yeah, I just gave it a quick listen. Sounds like he’s really leaning into the RP stylisation—especially when he gets to the end of the poem. There’s that /æ/ in “plants” that sounds a bit flat, like /ɑː/, which is interesting. I thought we might dump that for the North American accent, but maybe it doesn’t matter when he’s reading slow and deliberately.      I mostly just made sure the background noise was cut out, and that we can hear the complete last five lines. Oh, and there was a bit of a moth fluttering around the microphone—probably from the office plant I brought in. I tried to swat it while the mic was off, I swear.      Haha, I saw you at the end of the session! That poor moth didn’t have a chance. But seriously, the recording is solid. I do think, though, we should listen again for prosody in the rhythmic patterns. I flickered through the transcript and the caesura placement is kind of... off rhythm in parts. Want to compare?      Yeah, let me pull up the transcript. Oh, and the IPA symbols are in place, right? I sent them over to the team in Reading for verification. Should be back by this afternoon.      Just a quick note—between the moth incident and the slight out-of-time delivery at lines 38–40, I suggest we include a brief editorial commentary in the project notes about how even trained readers sometimes falter. It humanises the data and gives our editors a chance to explain the adjustments we made.      Good point, Sarah. It’s tricky, ‘cos we don’t want it to look like we did too much editing, but we do need to keep the sample as authentic as possible.      I’ll add a section to the metadata. Just say "minor temporal deviations observed in the final segment; no phonological inaccuracies recorded". That should cover it without sounding like a disclaimer.      Oh, go on then—I’ll share a picture of the moth on our team Slack. Thought it was a dragonfly at first.      God, Louise. The latest party invoice came in too, by the way. We’re expecting those 23 team members, right?

So did you get your maths results back yet? I’ve been dreading it all week.      Yeah I did yesterday. I got a 6. Not bad, I think. I was honestly expecting a 5 to be honest.      That’s actually really good. I got a 4, and I’m still sore about it. I studied  so  much over the weekend.      Honestly, so did I, and I still messed up the last question. What did you get on the algebra section?      It was okay… until the one with the three variables. I couldn’t even start it. All I could think was, “Why is this like that? Why can’t they just give you straightforward numbers?”      I felt the same, honestly! I spent five minutes just staring at it. It was like they were testing our sanity, not our maths skills.      Haha, yeah. And then you had to remember to convert the units at the end of that graph question. I forgot that—again.      Same here. I even checked it two or three times, and still didn’t spot it. Honestly, I’ve got a headache just thinking about it.      I’m so glad it’s over with. I can barely think about anything else these days. English was easier, don’t you think?      Yeah, the essay question was okay, and the poem was actually not too bad. Although I still can’t decide whether the author was being literal or ironic with the ‘storm at dawn’ metaphor.      That’s what I put in mine! I wrote a whole paragraph about how the storm represented her internal conflict. But my teacher always tells me I overthink things.      Well, I’d rather overthink it than miss the point completely, like last year when I thought that play was about friendship when it was actually all about betrayal. I got told off for that.      I know what you mean. We just need good grades so that we can get into the sixth form next year, right?      Yeah, let’s hope so. I’m applying for the humanities course, and I reckon I need a 6 in maths and a 7 in English at least. What about you?      Same here—humanities. I’m still hoping to do psychology as well, but I think we’ve got to wait for the final GCSE grades first.      Oh, don’t worry—you’ll be fine! It’s not the end of the world if we don’t hit the exact grades.

Rather skip the starter, actually. I'm just not very hungry. I had a late lunch with some colleagues... got home and thought I'd be starving, but no. Just a main, thank you.      Not sure I'll have the starter either. I wouldn't say I was full when I left the office, but I’m just twitchy about overdoing it. I’ve been trying to eat clean this week, you know, before the weekend goes to pot. Oh, and what was it, someone mentioned a new gluten-free option? I wonder what that’s like.      Oh, the gluten-free pasta? I tried it last week and it's the worst, honestly. You can taste like you're eating a doorstep. Still, best to have it than not be able to eat at all, if you're sensitive and all. Aunty Sharon had an allergic reaction to a starter once – almost breakfast, no less. Looked like she’d been taken in by a lion’s paw!      Goddess, I can’t even imagine. I would’ve thought by now restaurants would be keener on labelling properly. I work in admin, so health and safety is high on the list, but still... there was this meeting last year, and someone sneezed into a cup of tea – no joke – and the HSE nearly came swanning in to investigate. One raised eyebrow nearly had the boss rolling his eyes at me all night.      And let’s not even talk about work in general. I’m a project co-ordinator, so meetings are a fact of life. Just yesterday, some meeting in the café next door got split between three rooms when one colleague spoke louder than most people do on a regular walk to the bin. Eventually ended up having to reconvene at a table where they had to raise their voices to barely be heard over the hum of the espresso machine. My ears are still ringing!      Aye, funny that. I remember when the biscuits used to land on my head once in a meet-up I had waiting for a friend who was late. Not like that again in a while! Work-wise, I’m a sales advisor – been in the same spot for over fifteen years. Changes a bit with the seasons, the customers come and go, but I usually see about the same number of people at this time of the month, no surprises really.

Victoria, thanks so much for helping me out with the place earlier. I know it's been a busy week with all the kids coming and going after school.      Don't mention it! It's always a bit of a circus in your house, Lorna, but I know how much it means to you to have everything spick-and-span when your sister comes over. Teenagers are not known for their tidiness, are they?      No, you’re right there. Both of mine seem to live in the living room and under the dining table, but the worst is my son,Daniel. I swear he does it deliberately. His bedroom looks like the inside of a paint factory some days. But what’s even worse is that he got detention last week for not doing his homework.      Oh no! That’s the third time this term, isn’t it? How’s he coping with all the GCSE stuff? He still alright?      Honestly, I'm not sure. He’s got so much on his plate, and he’s trying to do part-time work on the weekends too—some supermarket in Rushden. Between that, school, and his mates, he doesn’t have time to breathe. I tried talking to his teacher, but she said he needs to find balance or else he might not be able to stay in his chosen subjects.      That’s tough. You know what it’s like with education now. It’s all about what someone’s going to end up doing. God knows I wasn’t one for books, but I’m floring the floors now.      I know, but I worry about him. He doesn’t talk much at home. I think he’s just trying to be rebellious. Not much I can do about that. Anyway, I shouldn’t be worrying you. You sound like you’re doing better, after that operation.      I am, thank you. Still a bit sore, but the surgeon said I was very lucky. It wasn’t as bad as first feared. The cancer was caught early, thanks to a routine scan. Do you know how many people just ignore the symptoms?      I’m so glad it was nothing too bad. That go-to-the-doc routine is something I need to get into. I’ve been meaning to go for that mammogram.      You should, Lorna. It’s not much fun, but it’s better than putting it off and regretting it later.

So did you not find it better living in a bigger place like Sheffield or was it just the usual malarkey with the landlord?      No I think it's probably better where we are but it's probably £20 more a week than what you're spending. But it was just that I'm working at Newton Park and the wage was ridiculous. I reckon it's not as bad as most places though. A lot worse than Northampton in this economy.      Yeah, I know it's just me grinding through the service and whatnot. But, I mean, at least I get the three breaks a shift and it's not like I've got to clean toilets or anything. It's like that Myton Court bar where I waitress. Fun atmosphere. It's just more of the usual lads in for Friday night and I think the world is ending. But I was at uni and working full time when I was younger so I've been doing it a bit longer than you.      Yeah, I think I've only been working for like six months and I was doing it voluntarily, but it's gone full time now I think.      Did you say voluntary? What, like charity shop or something?      No, more like national trust – doing estate maintenance with the horticulturists and stuff like that. Yeah, but it was just to clock up the hours for the work placement and now they've offered me a job. Like, someone said full time. I'm not trying to live a posh life but it's not what I had in mind either.      I mean, horticulture is not a bad thing. I did a bit of horticulture when I was 17 at the college. I mean, it’s not like we’re injecting it with nano-robots or anything.      You’re getting your info from documentaries? Like  Curb Your Enthusiasm ? Because that’s a little different from credible research.       laughs  Okay, but like, the points still stand. Look, I get it if you don’t wanna try it, Clara, but I’m curious. I might be a vegan extremist one week and eating a steak the next. It’s all over the place.      And you know what makes me sick? The contrast between factory farms and ‘eco-conscious’ places like ours. We talk about sustainability and yet so many of us still support meat consumption.

Rather skip the new pasta sauce again, love. Thought you said you’d bin it last week.      I did! Or I’m more than  likely  I did. That’s the problem with us… we can’t even bin things without being frightened it might come in handy.      Honestly, I’m with you, Gran. Why would you keep something that stinks a bit and is half full? If I open a bottle of wine and don’t finish it in one go, it’s straight in the bin the next day. Didn’t even want to waste it.      That’s you. Youth and waste go hand in hand, I’d say. On the other hand…      Oh don’t start on that. I know the look you’re giving me, Frank. I’ll be the one crying if you chuck out my grandmother’s jam jar collection when I’m old.      Well in fairness, they’s not ever getting in the way, are they? Sorted out a room once, full of that junk of yours and looked like a museum. I mean, the washing machine’s next to a 1940s teapot. Tell me that’s not domestic archaeology.      So is the cat – Mateo – got a hanger in the food store room again today. One of her walks of life, obviously. Seems like she was spotting the best spot for a nap.      Let me guess, also suspiciously near my knitting?      You’d think she’d at least pretend to notice I give her money. Can’t even make it near the Prime Club treats I do for her.      You still watching that show “Dinner with the Stars,” Jackie?      I have it recorded, yes. The chef with the ‘very European’ accent always makes me laugh. Said he cut his hand at 6 a.m. and mentioned ‘suffering with intense agony.’ I mean bless him, but who talks like that at  breakfast ?      I keep meaning to show you the wedding video from my cousin’s big day in Spain. You’d like it, Gran. She goosed her priest halfway through the vows.      Again? Thought she’d learned her lesson with the duck in the hen house at your brother’s wedding.      That was impressive, mind.      You missed the best bit: the priest tried to over-act the whole silence bit and said “from the desert of sin” to her and she said “well I can tell you, it’s not casting a shadow.”

Rather annoying isn't it? I mean butterfly forks — what do they look like? Tiny little delicate forks like... like for picking at a salad of flowers?      I've seen them! They’re shaped like butterflies with the tines like the wings—sorta creepy. But why make a fork like that? Who  uses  them?      Probably for fancy meals… like on a plane? A lot of airlines have weird cutlery. They gave me a fork once that looked like a little scorpion. It was ridiculous. You couldn't chase it halfway across the plate with your meat.      Ha! I can imagine. All the same, I still can't get over how many My turkey came out with one of those butterfly numbers. It looked ridiculous! I had to switch to the normal one. Made the whole thing look like a fancy dinner party for a clown.      Maybe they’re just trying to be fancy... but in the wrong way. Like the time we went to that restaurant in London and the waiter brought a  spoon that spiraled . It looked amazing—until we tried to eat the soup. It was like a whirlwind and nothing went in.      Oh yeah—what was that? The  spiral spoon ? I remember – it was one of those “upmarket” places with  excessive  cutlery. It took us 20 minutes to get the soup out and then the waiter made a big show of just chucking in an ordinary one. Pretended like it wasn’t noticed.      Ugh, and it's not just cutlery—Russia is so bizarre when it comes to how they eat. I mean, I was once in Moscow and the waiter lit my spoon on fire. It was part of this failsafe “modern cuisine” thing. I nearly set my mouth on fire trying to drink a soup that was baked like toast!      Wait,  your  cutlery was on fire? Why would he do that?      I don't know! Something about  flambéing dining accessories . It was weird, expensive and honestly, I’ve never had an omelette set on fire after that.      Yeah, go to Moscow on your own if you want weird cutlery and fire. But in the spirit of weird food stuff—what about the two minutes silence?      That’s not food-related!      Well, last year I had to eat dinner during two minutes silence. Very awkward—trying to swallow food and not make a noise. Ended up choking on lasagna.

Right, so the kids mentioned they really enjoyed Adventure Island in Cornwall. I was just wondering if they’d like to plan a short trip down there after the school holidays?      Oh yes! I loved it there. The slides and the arcade and the rides! The motorbike race was so fast!      I like the trampolines best. And the café had chocolate muffins. Did we have those when we stayed before, Mummy?      Yes, you did. We had to check the menu for the gluten-free stuff again though, didn’t we? You’re getting better at remembering what you can’t eat.      I know now that cornflakes are okay but turkey twizzlers are not. Fun fact!      And the hotel had sea views, didn’t it? Do you remember the green lighthouse, Finley? It looked like a giant pickle!      Yeah! I thought it was a gingerbread house too! Mummy, can we take the laptop? I want to draw some more trolls for the V&A exhibition.      Of course you can, love. I’ve still got a few more exams to mark, but if I work for an hour or so in the evening, I can finish them – then we can all focus on the trip planning.      Can we go on a Wednesday? Term finishes the next day and we could go back on a Thursday. Like our Cornwall holiday was.      Yes, sounds like a plan. I remember we had a lovely B&B just outside the resort. It had real sea air, and the owners even had a horse, Sam. He was about five foot tall and liked the chocolate biccies.      And he tried to steal my sister’s water bottle. I think he was jealous of the superhero label on it.      I’d tell him my name was Muffin and he told me the seagulls liked my lunch best.      That little madcap. We should maybe book a hotel that’s also dog-friendly if they start bringing lunches to Adventure Island again!      Mummy, you remember when the lift broke and we had the hotel room with the bad plumbing on the Cornwall trip?      Oh yes! That was the day I had to improvise with a bucket and a plant pot after the V&A exhibition postcards made me late!      And you made the best cup of tea from a kettle on the balcony, Mummy. The best!      Now that I can live without, honestly. But it was an adventure.

So did you get the History coursework done yet? I’ve been stuck on that for like, two weeks. I got to the part where I’m supposed to compare the battle strategies of both sides and then my brain just flatlines.      No, I’m still on the introduction. Honestly it’s all just ancient wanking to me. I didn’t know we were doing this as an essay, I thought we were gonna act it out in battlefields and everything.      Mate, you said you were gonna help me with the timeline. Didn’t even get the email I sent you.      Yeah I’m so sorry, man. My laptop’s still broken. It won’t charge past 5% and I’m skint to get a new battery. I’m using my phone for everything, which is sad but it’s 2024 for crikey.      Bucksy? I mean, you did get in trouble at GCSE for leaving your desktop in the rain didn’t you. Should have seen it, full on bloated Waterboy moment.      Mate, I tripped, okay! It was a water fountain. Bad luck. Bad design. Real bow to modern engineering.      So is that why your Mateha is bailing you out with her old laptop?      Yeah, she did say I can have it if I clean out her garage at the weekend, which fair play, someone’s gotta do it. But seriously, why do we have to write 1500 words about the Battle of Agincourt? It’s not even a fun battle!      I don’t know, man. Our teacher’s the History litmus test. Half our class skipped his lesson last week and now they’re doing extra reports and stuff.      My sister told me he hates being challenged. Like if you even question him once, he dials the whole school on you. She said he once gave someone a detention for waiting till 3pm to ask “So what time do lessons finish?”      Classic. At least we’ve got the party next week, you remember? You’re not gonna back out on me again because of that binocular comment, are you?      No bro, I’m in. It’s the boxset house, right? Passes the test. I just gotta get hold of a new bra for my sister otherwise she won’t feed me for a week.      Sounds serious. Right, and don’t forget we’re gonna have my cousin over to.

Rather skip the new road ain't I heard it’s a nightmare. Took me an hour to get up p’durn the other day just to check the roadworks and I ended up on the A19 for three miles before I realized I’d gone the wrong way.      I’ve heard it’s a bit of a mess. I was going to cycle out that way on the weekend to get a bit of fresh air, but now I’m thinking maybe I’ll stick to the bike path by the river. It’s a bit longer, but at least I don’t have to dodge delivery vans.      That sounds safer. I’ve been riding my bike to work a few days a week and it’s the best, honestly. Less stress, though I do miss the radio in the car – I’m not a fan of my head in the clouds while I’m making sure I don’t fall off the road.      Fair. I’ve taken to listening to cricket commentary on the train when I can, to be honest. There was that Ashes Test last week—did you see it, or are you more of a rugby nut?      I did catch the highlights, love the way they play here—it’s got that extra rhythm in it. Mind you, most of my cycle ride is with the wind in my face because the other lane is broken. I reckon the council thought that would be a good use of the budget: paving a road that isn't even the main route.      Sounds like my kind of chaotic planning. I had a client out in Newcastle the other week and spent three hours looking for their office because the Google Maps update thought it moved. Took a wrong turn at a roundabout the size of the Titanic and found myself on an industrial estate with no signal and not a coffee shop in sight.      That rings a bell. Had that happen on the way to a meeting in Harlow last year. I was trying to get it sorted on my mobile, and the thing fell into a puddle. Spent the next 20 minutes with a sprite of water out the screen trying to find directions.      Some people would call that a proper adventure. I’d call it a reason to invest in go-karts on your own street. Not everyone’s got one, though—if you're looking for a bike path with a bit of speed, I might know some shortcuts you could take.

Okay, I just called the usual Chinese place we go to, and they said they’re shut for the next couple of days. Some kind of staff shortage or something. I can’t believe it. It’s a Wednesday for heaven’s sake!      Ugh, well that’s a bummer. I was kind of  hoping  they’d be open just to prove that I actually remember what General Tso’s chicken tastes like. Not that that helps us right now…      Honestly, you two. We can just go to the new place that opened in town the other week. You know, the one near the library?  Lotus Garden . Have you tried it yet?      My friend Amber did. She sent me a photo of her hot pot – it had like five kinds of meat and pickles and noodles. Pretty much a banquet for one, and the wait time was almost breakfast hours. I’m thinking this could be a thing for us if we need to be non-drunks on a Friday night.      Hot pot? You mean one of those big round things on a table that takes three minutes to heat up and as much time to grief over?      Yes, exactly! You order it and then it just… hovers there – steaming slowly while you wonder, like, does the chicken confirm it’s done, or do we just go by smell? Silly question, obviously no one ever asks that.      Well, I’m also suspicious they might not have the plum sauce. I had a  disastrous  experience at a Chinese place in Chelmsford last year where I requested it, and they brought me about five different sauces and a map of China to figure out which one was “the one.”      Don’t you mean the time you accidentally ordered  spicy prawns with a side of regret  and ended up wearing your face upside down for the rest of the evening?      Oh come on, that was you! You were convinced your tandoori fish was  pasta .      Okay,  fine , but I do have a point. Some of these places are a bit too experimental. I just want the classic go-to stuff on the menu, you know? Roast pork, sweet and sour, dumplings that don’t smell like burnt batteries.      Look, I’m with you, but let’s just take it easy. We_ratings are never going to agree on anything more thrilling than pineapple or ‘dumping’ the food at the end.

Rather annoying the new folk in across the road to be honest. They’re always playing music late ‘n all... got the kids wakin’ up on Sunday mornings thinkin’ it's midweek. Livin’ in Liverpool, you'd think they'd know respect for a good siesta after a night in. een?      Aw, I   ain't   heard much about them yet, but I’ve noticed a few things—like that woman who takes the dog for a ramble every mornin’ at seven. It’s like the dog's never run when it's still dark. You'd think she’d let it sleep! Not that I complain much, mind. I'm only up at eight myself like that.      Ha! Yeah, but you nurses are always on the go, innit? Always used to being dragged out of bed early. I, on the other hand, been a uni lecturer for long enough to think everyone should be allowed in till at least ten. Only time I'm not, is when I have to do that bloody early-bird seminar— funding academia, challenging norms, etc. , blithering twaddle.      I tell ya, it's like they think they're paid to circle the globe in PowerPoint. Mind you, I remember my first nurse training, I thought I was gonna die just standin’ in the corridor somethin’ awful listenin’ to a lecturer drone on ‘bout metabolic pathways. Still, better than hospital food.      Ah, now there's a topic—NHS. You out there still pluggin’ away in the wards? Still not been considered a  professional  as they call it in about five different policy papers I’ve had to read lately?      To be fair, some of it’s better now. I mean, it’s  still  underfunded,  still  understaffed, but you learn to roll with it. I remember a few years back when I was on night shift, I ended up helping a little lad with a tummy bug for  four hours  as the system was waitin’ for a specialist to “hitch up.” Some lad, no parents in, and I was nearly dead. But the lad was grateful. That’s the best thing about nursing—most of the time, people just want to say “thank you.”      Aye, well, you see that in academia too, to a degree. The students, they start off all cocky like, but once you teach them about poetry ‘n proper grammar, they start to learn respect.

Rather annoying this new eligibility cap they've set for welfare, innit?      Oh aye, I've heard about it on the telly. Not a few folk round here are proper upset, rightly so. When I was young, we lived off half a bob and a loaf. Got eeny harm outta the state then. Not like these days.      It's funny how things change, but not necessarily for the better. Still, easier said now when we've got reasonable pensions. Know what I mean?      Aye, well I won’t disagree with you there. Still, I reckon some jobs go begging round the docks, only these young ones won’t touch 'em. Always waiting for something flashy to pay themselves.      I've spoken with some of my students in the area – a fair few of 'em are unemployed but not registered. They're scared of the system, some say the police are cracking down more on immigration and it's causing panic, even among those who've got the papers.      Nonsense, if you're working properly, the police don’t legislate your way. Course, I dunno, since the war there's always been a bit of extra tension in the streets. You ever seen them – Mate, I got a chap down the shops, proper friendly bloke, gets his tea and saveloy every week and never asks a single question.      There are positives outta all this. Though I’m not trying to paint a rosy picture. I do think some community-based initiatives could help. Whether folk accept the help is another story – pride’s a funny thing in these parts.      Oh you bet, talking of which, I had a laugh a week ago. My sister was telling me that her neighbour’s lass managed to run away to the mainland, ‘cos she says "Liverpool's no place for proper food!" Can you believe that?      Haha, very relatable, I suppose. Though I hope she found good food as well as a better quality of life.      Aye, lass took the kettle and toaster too, so I reckon she made a proper start. No hard goin' on that front if you ask me. And that lad, just in, I see the council’s talking ‘bout knocking down the old community hall. Now that’d be a proper shame if they did.      I think there’s a vote coming up on it. Know where you can get the proposal?

So did you lot see the latest Corpus update request? Seems like we’re getting more queries about ‘normal’ than ever. I swear half the corpus is now just people saying “is this normal?” over and over.      No, I didn’t! But honestly, can’t blame ’em. Everything feels abnormal these days. Or maybe it’s just that we’ve all got more self-awareness. You’ve got to wonder if “normal” is just a word we use when we don’t know what else to say.      Funny you mention it, I was just reading some recent transcripts from the British National Corpus, and “normal” is popping up like everywhere, especially around mental health and like social anxiety. Even kids are using it. “Do I act normal?” “They didn’t seem normal,” etc. It used to be more vague, now it feels like it’s a badge of diligence almost.      That’s interesting... I wonder if it’s related to the discourse around mental health becoming more mainstream. People are using words to define themselves or reassure others. I mean, if someone says, “I’m feeling pretty normal today,” it might as well be code for “I’m fine, leave me alone.”      Oh, I got that from my sister – 18, fairly typical, and she swears by her new “normality check.” It’s this whole thing where before she goes to school, she checks every part of her routine: “If someone sees me in this outfit, they won’t think I’m abnormal.” I mean, poor kid’s got a spreadsheet now.      Okay, but seriously, when did “normal” become a performance? I mean, I use it all the time, but it’s usually in a grammatical sense. Like, “She was speaking in a normal tone of voice,” not in that, I dunno, emotional, like, identity-check kind of way.      You know, I was thinking about it the other day. Maybe it’s regional too. Growing up in Buckinghamshire, people were always being asked, “Are you with your family?” and “Are you settled?” But the Northeasters I knew used “normal” with a bit more sarcasm. “Can’t really get normal life if you’re working ten hours at the warehouse, love.”      Yeah, I can see that. In Lincoln, you could sum up a whole conversation with a single “she’s okay, quite normal really” and that was it. Like, it was a euphemism for “doesn’t stand out” or maybe even “doesn’t make waves.”

Rather annoying isn't it? I mean I used to watch that programme ages ago.      What was it called? The Italian one with the cars?      Yes!  Top Gear . Not quite as funny as before, mind you. The new presenters just don’t have the spark.      I agree. I watched the first series on Channel 5 with that bloke from Slough, what was his name, Tim or Chris? It was comedy gold.      Chris Evans and Jeremy Clarkson. Oh, the days. Anyway, reminds me of when I lived in Italy. I used to go to motor shows in Bologna. You know, like that one you told me about in Barcelona?      Yes, the one I volunteered at. But I was sad in the head and didn’t know anyone, so I eventually gave it up.      Well, you did get to speak a bit of Spanish out of it, right?      A little. I still can’t pronounce the "ñ" properly. Try saying "cañon" in a sentence. It’s like trying to say "cannon" with a stone in your mouth.      That’s so funny. My Italian is alright, but I can still say "buffo" instead of "buono" by mistake and end up sounding like a joker.      It’s all in the rhythm though, isn’t it? Learning a language is like learning to dance oddly. I remember being in a classroom at some teachery thing in Chichester once, trying to speak French in a group, and I about wet myself laughing. Everyone was so serious except me.      I’ve been there! Going to that TEFL course in Brighton, trying to sound French in front of 20 over-qualified Aus construction workers.      And I remember you telling me about your time teaching in Ghana. Was it really as chaotic as you said?      More. You think of a classroom with 30 kids and think “hmm, quite hard.” Try 40 and a board that’s three feet high on the wall because nobody's taller than 4 ft 6.      Sounds like a circus, but genuinely fascinating. That must have been when the internet went down for weeks at the school?      Yes, exactly. No emails, no Facebook, just a lot of talk and poetry. Honestly, I miss it at times. It taught me how to go without the constant buzz of the internet.      Makes you appreciate it more, doesn't it? I mean I can't go two days without checking an email.

Right then, John, lass, anything to add before we talk about this Sunday's garden work? We’ve got the big fence to fix after the wind last week properly knocked a few planks over.      Not sure I’m allowed to add anything! But, can I ask if we can get a new fence  not  the boring grey one again? Could it be maybe green? Or blue? Like something that actually looks nice?      Now hold on a tick, William, there ain't no room for colour in the Ferriby style. Black, or the garden planks hold no weight. We like it united. Proper garden. Proper fence. No fanciful notions!      My dear, if I had my way, the whole house would be painted pink and the garden would be filled with pickles. But fences are for dividing people, dear, not delighting them! Still, if he wants a bit of blue, let him have it. A spot of blue won’t kill anyone, will it?      Good one, Nancy. Alright William, we can see if we can find some blue planks in the builders’ market. But don’t get too excited, it still might be grey if they ain't got any stock. Be realistic.      Mate, I got a deal with you, it's  blue  or the pickles come in.      You know what I said about pickles? Give me one pickle in this house and I'm off!      Now, John, we can’t be shouting about pickles at our age. What would the grandkids say?      They’d say it’s about time! My geography teacher does everything in the garden, she had this compost heap and a bee box and everything. She said she used to grow everything on it. No plastic fertilisers. My, I’d like that.      Ah, William, that’s droll. I’d like something fresh as well, but I’ve got enough on my hands getting your granddad to clear up  his  mess of old newspapers in the shed. That place is more of a time capsule than a working building.      Don’t talk about the newspapers! That goon bin on your life if you start going through mine. Gave me line in the paper that I don’t go boxsetting about.      So, have you ever found anything cool in there, granddad?’      Cool? I found a forgotten sandwich that went over thirty years. Mouldy! It had a note attached:  “John, if you touch this, I will haunt you.”

Rather skip the new museum and go through the old part of town. I know it's supposed to be a bit off the beaten track, but the photos you took of that courtyard with the calligraphy on the wall are still haunting me.      Ah yes, that courtyard—it’s like a hidden postcard from another century. I remember one of the locals saying that it used to be the courtyard of a Ming-era merchant house. Some of the tiles were cracked, and there were kids playing on the stone steps like it was just another afternoon.      Exactly, that’s what made it feel... frozen. I mean, who  wouldn’t  want to live in a place where time decided to stop? My friend Morwenna messaged me the other day saying you should put together a proper photo essay of your travels this year. She’s the one who started that little website about expats in East Asia.      God, she did? I’ll message her later. She always says we should document the mundane things—the qiaofu8 details, the way shopkeepers greet each other before opening, that kind of thing. I never thought about it as much as she and the other writers do.      Well, you’ve been doing it anyway. Every photo you take somehow ends up with a story, and sometimes it’s just about the way the light hit the wall or how the smell of jasmine tea was stronger in one shop than another. That’s what makes it different.      Maybe. I just like seeing places before they’re rediscovered—by the developers, at least. You know the central square? That used to be a ballet school in the sixties, and the old man who owns the baozi stall said he used to dance there as a child. Now it’s concrete and neon and a bit of plastic.      That’s why I love being here with you. You notice all the things I’d just walk past. Last time, you insisted we go to that village an hour from here because someone told you about a temple that had yellow roofs instead of red. Yellow’s the special colour for the emperor, right?      Precisely. And it was like a secret—just one gothic room with faded dragons, and no one else was around for miles. It was almost too perfect.      You know what your problem is?

Okay, I swear I haven't slept in weeks. Why do we always stay out 'til 3 on a school night?      It's not  that  late, Luce! You’re just a sun worshipper now. Look at you—get a life. Or a nightcap.      Ugh, I was up   sewing   at 1 am trying to fix that dress Aimee gave me before the prom. I’m not going out looking like a sad potato.      Wait, the one with the sequins? The one that made your head look like a disco ball?      Shut up! I look fab, and you know it. My turkey still hasn’t stopped laughing at me.      I didn’t know you had a  turkey  in the first place. Living with your dog, a cat, a gerbil, and a bird? I mean, no wonder you need friends to stay sane.      They’re not   all   mine. My aunt keeps dropping her birds off and forgets to take them back. Lucy, the one I named, says a rude word every time I tell her "prom.''      Okay, that bird is a legend. Tell her I said hi – and maybe tell her I’m not still on the no-alcohol thing. I’m 18! I can be a responsible drunk now.      She’d just say “  Stick someone in the bin.  ” And not even in a fun way.      Ugh, don’t remind me. I still feel bad about DJ – the idiot who thought it was a great idea to climb onto Steve’s back while he was spinning in the hall. I had to document it on my phone.   Literally the best night of the year.        My highlight was that bloke at the guest speaker event. Said he was into  philosophy , then asked where the ‘get it on’ bit was. I mean, I sort of get it—      Let me guess—then you went 'Oh mate, it's Friday night, do you wanna go out?' and poof, gone by midnight.      Look at you being funny about it. If I go out alone, I just end up making a boy cry. Who lives in the UK and what?      That’s flukey, Lu. You’re cute, you’ve got the dress fixed, your life’s sorted. Wait—did you overdo the coconut oil again?      What? No! Coconut oil is conditioning, Clar. I looked like a hippo last week because I used Vaseline instead. I've learned.      Good. Because no one wants to see your face resembling a coconut cake.

So did you manage to sort out the weekend plans with Nana then?      Oh aye, I’ll be popping over on Saturday morning. I’ve asked Eilis to bring a little cake with her. You know how the old fella likes a bit of baked goods with his tea.      That’s very sweet of her. I reckon she dotes on him a bit too much, if you ask me.      Well, she was his first grandchild. We’ve all got our role to play, don’t we?      Right, I’ve sorted who’s bringing what. I’ll handle the fruit, and Eilis and I will set up the board games later. The kids are starting to get into  Monopoly  now—minus the screaming, which I think is the real challenge.      Speaking of games, I’ve been trying to get back into  FIFA  lately. Blooming touchline is enough to drive you mad, I say. But the lads keep telling me I need to learn when to get off the pitch.      Aha! That’s what grief is for, love. You’ve got to know when to pass the ball and when to just sit it out.      I know, I know, but when you’ve had a lifetime of telling people to “get their heads up,” what do you expect when you’re the one who should’ve done that at full tilt.      I wish your FIFA skills had translated into your planning ability, by the way. You left the central heating on for three days when we went away last weekend. I about froze!      Oh come on, it was an oversight. I’ve been trying not to worry about that too much. I have more important things on my mind. Like,  how  I’m going to survive Friday night poker again.      Oh, you? That’s it. You don’t play for money—you play for your pride. And good grief, that pride of yours nearly broke the table with your last  bluff !      You should remember,  technically , you left the room early because you were afraid I was going to win. And I was.      Alright, alright. Sue me. I’m retired from the oil business and you think I have the fluency to handle this? I blame the high tea and the biscuits.      Oh yes, and overcooked scones at that!      Speaking of scones, we do need to plan the weekend potluck properly, right? Someone should take charge.

Rather annoying this new laptop’s brakes. You know, the touchpad sticks a bit, and it takes like ages to boot up sometimes. Just went to update the software and it froze again.      Honestly, I feel for you, I had one of those models. Mine would make this awful buzzing noise if I spilled any water on it—and trust me, if you use it in bed like most people do, water is inevitable.      Oh, don’t even get me started on laptops. My sister’s one was so temperamental when she was teaching, she had to use a different one every three months! Still, at least you don’t have to worry about bin strikes keeping you stressed about where to dump the plastic anymore.      Well, I never messed around with technology much in my day, and I’m not starting now. Living with Edith’s cat and working full days when I was younger was more than enough tech for me!      Speaking of water, have you guys tried those alkaline water bottles? I saw one in the shop and it looked super fancy. Another thing you know that gives you barely a week of peace: packing for Brighton to walk around, and then falling asleep with the TV on while trying to fix your contacts. Wasn’t that you once, after saying goodbye and stopping at the postbox to go back and get your glasses? It’s like losing glasses became your brand!      Honestly, I’ve had that happen when I leave after saying goodbye. It’s like I get to the door and something in my brain says “Wait—did I turn off the kettle?

Rather skip the new Thea eh?      Aye, her team lost real bad. I got the text from Karen saying it was like 6-0 up by half time. That's rough for them. It's not like it's the end of the world. Though I have to say, your Simon did do alright in the last test, didn’t he? Real good on the reading. I get the birds go in one direction and it's like trying to follow a conversation in a crowded bar. Imagine trying to explain that to the boxset bingers. Ten out of ten – I’m in. But I’m bringing in the snacks. You lot never remember the popcorn.      Only if you don’t bring sweets again... I’m still unpacking the lego from last time, remember?!      That was you, that was you – and tell me again how inappropriate it was for the movie we were watching?!      It wasn’t inappropriate, it was iconic!      Well, from what I hear, the new bar’s got a fairly large screen and decent speakers for screenings and stuff. Events co-ordinating vibes? I’ve seen your emails – are they telling you to "personalise the unpersonaliseable"?      Poetic, Geo. Poetic. But honestly, I’m dreading the client meeting on Tuesday. They want the event to be something “outside the box” but stick to their budget as tight as a belt. It’s like trying to draw circles with square hands!      That sounds exhausting. I’m a bit jealous of you, actually. At least you get to make life look like a conference. Me? I’m stuck line-managing spreadsheets between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. with no time to breathe.      Yeah, I'm down with the simplicity. Waking up to dig a hole in the morning, fill it up again at night – no expectations. Suits my kind of life.      Honestly, both of you always crack me up. You're either embracing chaos or minimalist simplicity – I’m stuck in the middle trying to make PowerPoint look like a work of art.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd have decent coffee and cake in Gordon Square, and yet here I am with this coconut scone that tastes like I’ve bit into a biscuit that's been left in the rain. Panda watching is a bit pretentious—isn't it? I mean, it's just a huge cat that naps on bamboo and somehow gets thousands of phone calls a minute through WeChat. I’m guessing they're not the cuddly type. You know I did a survey on travel patterns in rural China the other week. Turns out, most of them don’t even like pandas. Said they were too slow and looked like unmade-up pandas to do something, like for tourists.      Said what? They just want them to do something—bite something, climb a wall, I dunno. One woman said she’d stick to visiting Tibet as long as they served tea with more salt than the lunches we have on the Isle of Wight.      Ah, come on, the Isle of Wight can go easy on the pond life if you take the ferry properly. But I digress. I’m trying to teach English in a secondary school in Birmingham at the moment. The latest joke from the kids?

Right, I just wanted to double-check the address again before we get there. I don’t want to get lost in the middle of nowhere again. Remember last time? Hazelnut, no sugar— exactly like your desk at work .      You do remember that I  moved  from the team so I could be out and about, right?

Rather annoying isn’t it? I’ve had this cough for weeks. I thought it’d clear up when I stopped working the conference, but no luck. I swear it was one of those ones that fails to survive that first transition from bowl to pond.      That’s  very  vivid. Enexpected. Should’ve called a friend. I’d have believed you.      If you don’t rest you’ll be passing out at conferences. Last thing you want is to propose a keynote speech to a room of conference delegates and then whack out like a tomato.      Then again, if I pass out I can go viral on the conference app if it's filmed.      Finally, a plan to go from "speaker" to "internet legend."      Honestly, seriously, take it easy,   Speaker_1  . So did I! The way he spoke to me in front of the interns was just cringe. Honestly, I don’t care how long you’ve been at the firm, there’s no need to embarrass people like that. Oh God, that’s going to be like a drama fest.

Right, so today we're going to talk about good and evil. But first, let’s start with a question. What do you think makes someone evil?      I know! It’s when they’re mean. Like the witch in the Gingerbread Man! She was really mean!      Yeah! But the Gingerbread Man was annoying first. So maybe he was bad… not good?      That’s a really good point, Charlie. In a lot of stories, there's a journey—characters might start doing the "wrong" thing, but then they learn. Sometimes what we think is bad is just part of the story. Now, in the real world, can people change from being "evil" to being "good"?      Maybe. My mummy was naughty once, but now she's nice. She even listens to my rules in the house!      But what if someone never says sorry? They just keep being bad?      That’s a tricky one. Let's think about the stories we know. In "The Three Little Pigs," the wolf is clearly bad—he wants to hurt the pigs. But do you think he only did that because he was hungry? Maybe he wasn't evil, just in the wrong.      But he was on fire! That’s not kind!      That’s true. But did you know that the first version of the story didn’t even have the wolf? It was just someone who came knocking. As the story evolved, people made the wolf more evil to match their fears.      So evil can come from what people  think , not just from what people do?      Exactly! And that’s the thing about legends and folk tales. They change depending on the person telling them. For example, the British have the legend of the Headless Horseman, but over time, people added more horror elements to make it scarier.      Like a ghost on a horse trying to catch witches?      Something like that! And then there's Robin Hood. Even though he steals, people think of him as good—because he steals from the rich and gives to the poor. So evil or good sometimes depends on who you ask!      So does that mean Santa is good, even if he goes into your house at night while you’re asleep?      Santa doesn’t take toys! He brings presents!      Point taken. But it’s still interesting how people use stories to teach about right and wrong. Now—here’s a challenge for you both.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      A bit.      We had got to go to this school trip this week, and I can't say I found it particularly interesting.      Yes, the film trip?      Yeah, coordinates again een? I thought that was more the teacher's job.      It was not very fun.      Not particularly. The kids got to be in a film, though, which was something. We had to film them pretending to be superheroes outside the school. Rather glorified playtime, if you ask me.      That sounds more like fun than school!      My opinion, definitely.
