And go easy, okay? You’ve your legs for you to run after them for years to come, and I won’t have you growing up with bad knees because of your dad chasing you down the corridor over a stolen chocolate bar at the age of 7.      Can I have a doughnut too?      You're allowed one, but only one.

Rather skip the starter and just go for the main, old chap. I had that crème brûlée last time and nearly lost a tooth. Sugar like grit on my tongue.      You’re lucky they don’t do dessert first in this place! But yes, the crème brûlée—well,  someone’s  got an iron jaw. Haven’t seen you in weeks, Mark. You’ve been huddled up in that school too much again, have you?      Oh, just keeping the rascals in check. Year six can be a glorified car park these days. Far more chatter about  Instagram  than  The Great Gatsby . But you? Still trading like a madman on those boots?      More like persuading the punters their Danskos are still worth £20 after a decade of stamping about the M25. I tell you, if I knew half of what I know in Brighton at the age you retired, I’d have bottled the wind for a few bob. Good money, though. Feels better than when I lugged crates of beer around the pubs in my twenties.      And how's the wife? Still on about watching municipal waste stickers?      Constantly. Has this new zealous phase about the Green Party. She’s trying to get the council to install apple pie recycling bins next. Silly old cow. Last week, I catch her writing letters to politicians at someone else’s dinner party— letters , not emails. It’s like we’re in the 18th century.      Still, at least she’s got her stride. You know I about blocked myself doing the local health walk round the marina. Twenty minutes in and I could’ve sworn my hip cap was loose.      Health walks? You’re the last person I’d put on treacle waters. Though I heard about this chap up at the chemist. Older bloke, nice pair of shoes, tried to sell him waiting till 9 a.m. for his dose of pilates. Websites mentioned it: pilates for  men  over 60!      Pilates for men? Mark my words, the next go-round is going to see us stretching our brows into eyebrows. But I digress. Business-wise, between us—how’re things looking on the fiscal front?      Ticking along. Thought about retiring after next year, truth be told. But as long as I can talk about the ‘80s, nobody will notice if I’m a little...  keeping it vague  on the books.      And always a man for the moment.

So did you watch The Late Late Show last night?      No, I missed it... What was on it?      I think it was Survivor. It’s a programme I follow. Not quite my usual topic but it’s interesting to see how people act under pressure. Hasn’t got a lot to do with research, but I reckon it builds character.      Aye, but would you ever go on a reality show yourself?      God, no! Not unless I got paid triple the salary of my job. Still, watching it... like, it’s kind of like a social experiment, innit? You get people thinking they know someone and then the boot comes out. It’s brutal!      I see what you mean, but I’d probably say in the first round. I’m not one to fake nice to people for breakfast, no matter if I’m on television! Haha.      Fair enough, I can see that. You always have been more honest than most.      Yeah well, I’ve had too many PhDs under my belt to start pretending to like people for a prize.      Haha. Speaking of, how’s your research going at the moment?      Let’s just say I’ve been buried under data files and not enough sleep. I started analysing the trends in donor sentiment after the 2016 election.      Oh God, don’t mention Trump. I had a housemate in Newcastle who used to play his speeches on loop at tea time. I thought I was going mad!      I know! He used to do it just to wind people up. Anyway, what about your research projects? Any new developments?      Yeah, I’m just finishing up on a big development for education policy in the Nordics. The focus is on peer evaluation systems in schools. It’s all about how teachers are supported, rather than just getting told what to do from the top.      That sounds proper nuanced. I mean, I’ve had enough teachers in my day who could do with a bit more support!      Yeah, exactly. I think our education systems are at a crossroads. If we don’t invest properly in the people delivering the learning, what chance do we have with the kids?      Fair point.      You alright with your third?      Aye, and them large bitter I order last time? The waitress said they’re out of them completely.      Oh right, so you're stuck with lager and pasties?      Yeah.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think they'd do something about the internet in primary schools by now...      Oh, I'm not sure they need to. I saw a bunch of Year 5 kids making killer whale puppets the other day — one of them even put on an orca vocalisation video and mimed a whole 'attack on the tuna boat'. Classic Blue Peter with a twist.      Wait, I don’t remember speaker_3 being mentioned in the speaker list. Let me continue the conversation between the couple.   Speaker_2 :   Classic Blue Peter with a twist. I swear, kids these days are out of this world. On the other hand, our university kids seem to have forgotten how to write a full sentence between their tweets and their TikTok captions!      Oh, don’t get me started. I had a student submit an essay written almost entirely in emojis. "The whale 🐋 was very 😵‍💫, ate the 🐟 and then 🌊!" I had to give them extra credit for creativity — or was it incompetence? I can never decide anymore.      Hah! Tell me about it. I had one last week who thought a markdown-generated suicide note was a good example of literary angst. I almost squatted in the room trying not to laugh.      You and your dark sense of humour. Squatting — isn't that what people do in disused phone boxes in East London trying to live for free?      Only if the Wi-Fi's still working. Hey, speaking of squatting — remember when we spent that weekend at Norfolk about five years back and ended up locked out of the guesthouse? You had to climb over the fence and squat in the garden to plug in the kettle while I tried calling the landlady on a ‘cosy’ antique phone that didn’t work?      I remember it well. You got all philosophical about how it was a ‘back-to-the-land experiment’ while I was halfway through a full-blown anxiety attack trying not to burn a pot of tea!      You looked like a Victorian portrait with that teapot balanced on the wall. Anyway, I think it was your parents who told you about the "Blue Peter" whaling badges, weren’t they? You know, the ones your dad used to collect — puffin-shaped badges with conservation warnings and killer whale illustrations?      Oh God, yes. He still has them in this glass case upstairs.

Rather skip the queue and take a seat in here, old thing’s promising.      Oh, got to admire that one.      I know, I know. It’s a little hush hush.      You frightened me, sounded like it was in good working order.      It was, till I got onto the motorway last week, sounded like a cow in a flatulent tummy too.      The old heap, pulling like it’s got gold in the bonnet and dragging me along like it don't want to stop.      Still, at least it works, worse things could happen, right?      My turkey shop closed down years ago. Terry left it in the lorry, gone now.      Easier in the world now.      What about you then, breakfast, no doubt.      Haha, hard earned, I would say.      Still working the old man down, I reckon.      My dad ran a café in Birmingham for thirty years, never a day off as far as I remember.      Good on him, always wanted to work.      I remember when my Mate Reg held out a deal, still, it was a long time back.      You know what they say about Reg, eh?      Nup.      That fellow also ran a bookie in Norwich, just down the road a bit.      So, you worked in a shop as a young lass?      I did, at Harrow, all gold bangles and the like, but mind you, it was mostly customers wanting to know that the plug hole wasn’t dry.      Jokes, jokes for the day.      I did manage hostels at uni, a right laugh that was.      With all them boys waiting on tables.      Right ho, being academically trained comes with lunches and a little bit of fun.      You set the rules.      I did, set go's on the pond life if you like, got so tired of kids slipping on the greasy floor.      Time to lay off your hobby of lecturing at the university.      Yeah, I'm onto writing articles now, not as fun to say the least.      Only food and them pictures missing I suppose.      Nailed it, the only kind of thing you miss, always take 'em backs out from under the mattress when I fancy looking.      Oh no, not again.      Not those, the good ones with Irwin. Was he a fine fellow.      Still, should of been a farmer then, quite a fitter minder.      The worst part is seeing friends go like it don’t matter.      Women in the nursing home not a one of them daft.

Morning James! How's the first week going so far? Settling into lecturing yet?      Good morning! Yeah, surprisingly okay, actually. I mean, I didn’t expect to enjoy it this much. The students are… I don’t know, fresh. It’s a bit of a change from my old job in recruitment, that’s for sure.      Oh? I didn’t know you were in recruitment before this! I assumed you were always into academia. How did that work?      Yeah, most people are surprised when I tell them. I spent about five years headhunting for mostly tech and finance roles in Australia. It was fast-paced, competitive, and honestly, the kind of job where you either love it or hate it. I did, to be honest—loved the push and the challenge. But after a while, I was burnt out and figured it was time for a shift. Academia just felt like a better long-term fit for me.      That’s pretty impressive. I mean, not many people can pivot like that and do it successfully. You must have a good understanding of people and what makes them tick to work in recruitment. That must help as a lecturer, too—especially with grading things like academic literacy. How do you assess that effectively?      That brings up a really interesting challenge, actually. I’ve been trying to design assessments for the first-year students that go beyond just content knowledge and really assess their ability to articulate ideas academically. It’s not just about whether they can write a full sentence or not—more about the clarity of thought, the structure of an argument, and using evidence effectively.      I completely agree. I’ve been trying to do the same in my secondary classes. Academic literacy is absolutely essential for students to progress. But you’re right—it’s not just about grammar or vocabulary. My challenge is that the students come from such varied educational backgrounds, especially here in the UK with the mix of home and international pupils. I often find myself revising how I assess to make sure I’m not unfairly disadvantaging anyone.      Oh, that’s a big one! I had a student from Norway who wrote stellar essays in terms of ideas and insight, but the grammar was so clumsy it almost threw me off. I had to give it extra time to make sure I was grading the content, not the language.

So do you newbies often get lost in here? Seems like a maze.      Oh yeah, I nearly ended up in the poetry section the other day! Erm, I'm Liv.      Liv! That's a lovely name! I'm Martha.      And I'm Priya. Erm, nice to meet you! So what course are you on?      Ah, I'm a first year, um, studying Art Foundation. Erm, it's a bit different to retail.      That's brilliant, Liv! Retail... like, is it even a proper job? I studied sociology.      Honestly, it’s not what you'd call "academic," but it pays the bills. Ten hours, six days... yeah, I'm glad I’ve got school to look forward to most of the time.      Martha—relaxation therapy student. Yeah, I spend my days being hugged by five oversized teddies, and I get paid to do it. It's surreal, I know.      Wait, you get hugged by actual teddies?      It’s not that weird, Liv. It’s about comfort, boundaries, and healing from emotional trauma. It's actually really important work.      Oh, I see. I thought it was some kind of hippy thing with Silly String and pot plants.      There are people out there who think it is—my grandma still says she wants to "go to a therapist who gives you a good back rub."      Er, no—I mean, some people are into it, I suppose. Not quite what I'm doing.      I'm from… a mix of places. My family moved to Manchester when I was small. I was born in India. My parents say that made me "a guest in the UK," so I better make friends fast.      Oh Priya, you don't need to make friends—you’re already one. We just needed to meet you properly.      Yeah, I think we're all just here trying not to get caught napping in the library. This place catches you out.      True!
